"Everyone will go home with a smile on their face, and for at least the next three or four months, no one will be questioning the German national team," Klopp told German public broadcaster ARD, referencing that Germany will not play again until the end of March 2027.
"Instead, they'll be thinking: 'This could really turn into something. We have wonderful footballers, great characters," Klopp said, and added: "The lads are even surprising themselves."
The former Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund coach took the job in July after Julian Nagelsmann paid the price for another German early World Cup exit, this time to Paraguay in the last 32. Klopp always preached patience, particularly after his first two matches yielded a fortunate 1-1 draw with the Netherlands and a 1-0 home loss to Greece.
Klopp hallmarks starting to emerge
It paid off on Monday as Germany performed with the hallmarks of Klopp's great club sides — fierce pressing, intensity, pace and a measure of joy. Perhaps it is in Florian Wirtz that Klopp's impact is more notable.
The 23-year-old has struggled to make a significant impact at Liverpool since moving to the Premier League from Bayer Leverkusen at the beginning of last season. But he has four goals in his last four games for Germany and is demonstrating the ability that earned him a €125 million ($137.5 million) move to England.
"I only knew him from television. I was shocked when I saw him on the pitch for the first time. An extraordinary footballer," Klopp said after the Netherlands match.
"We've also found the right position for Flo. It helps that he's so vocal. He's the first pressing player, he can press two players without getting tired."
That quality was evident in Wirtz's first goal on Monday, when he won back possession on the edge of the Dutch box before combining some dazzling footwork with a brilliant, curled finish.
Scherhant, Gruda and Wirtz make their cases
But Wirtz wasn't the only attacking bright spot for Germany. Rookie wingers Derry Scherhant and Brajan Gruda both scored and were a huge threat throughout. Klopp gave debuts to both earlier this year as he sought to spread opportunities. The pair have offered Germany a pace they often lacked under Naglesmann and his predecessor Hansi Flick.
"They can both play, my goodness," said Klopp.
Scherhant, who opened the scoring with another stunning strike, spent many days of his boyhood on the terraces of the Olympiastadion in Berlin, where Monday's game was played. Unlike many pros, he bounced about Berlin's lower league clubs as a youth before Hertha Berlin signed him up. He then moved to Freiburg in 2025 and is rapidly emerging as a player who can implement Klopp's style and reflect the coach's attitude.
"A few years ago, people told me I wouldn't make it as a pro. Then I became a pro. And even then, some people still said it wasn't enough—that the Regionalliga (Germany's fourth tier) was the best I could hope for,” Scherhant said.
"It's just unbelievable that I get to stand here now with the satisfaction of having proven those people wrong."
Proving people wrong is also a major part of Klopp's remit. After failing to get beyond the quarterfinal of a major tournament since 2016, the German public's interest in and enthusiasm for its men's national team had waned. Klopp's mission he said, was to "to prove to Germany and the world that we can play soccer."
Germany need to change perceptions
While that was achieved on Monday, the loss (and subsequent 0-0 draw) against Greece in the Nations League game were evidence that it won't all be plain sailing. Indeed, Germany have had plenty of false dawns of late, as captain Joshua Kimmich alluded to.
"We've been through a tough time," he said. "A clear victory doesn't make all that go away," he added before saying that the task was to "turn potential into quality and a team that's all about 'what ifs' into a team that's all about 'reality.' That's the art of it."
Klopp too, for all his hype, was keen not to get too far ahead of himself.
"We want to gradually solidify it. We're not done yet. We still have a few areas to work on. But I'm looking forward to our future — it's crazy what's still to come," he said.
In Nations League terms, that will be a matchup with world champions Spain, or Portugal or Belgium before qualifying for Euro 2028 begins. For now though, Klopp and his players can enjoy some time with those smiles on their faces.

noticias.titulo: Could the Airbus' €3 billion loan row reignite a US-EU trade dispute?
noticias.resumen: The US says a record €3 billion financing package for Airbus may conflict with a transatlantic aircraft-subsidy truce. EU officials insist the funding complies with market-based rules.
noticias.texto:
Could the Airbus' €3 billion loan row reignite a US-EU trade dispute?
November 17, 2026
A fresh row over a record-breaking EU loan to European aerospace company Airbus could reopen a long-standing rift with Washington and threaten an existing EU-US trade truce.
The European Investment Bank (EIB), the lending arm of the EU, agreed in June to loan Airbus up to €3 billion ($3.4 billion) but US President Donald Trump's top trade advisor recently suggested the loan breached a 2021 EU-US agreement on state support.
"I had sincerely hoped that trade-distorting European subsidies to Airbus were a thing of the past," US Trade Representative Jamieson Grier said in late October. "For decades, France, Germany and Spain have aggressively supported Airbus, their national champion aircraft manufacturer, to gain an unfair advantage over US aerospace workers and business."
He also suggested there was a lack of transparency around the terms of the loan. The EU insists the loan does not amount to subsidies, that it is in close contact with the Office of the US Trade Representative and "will provide all necessary information," a spokesperson told DW.
An Airbus spokesperson told DW the company is "actively engaging with the relevant authorities and are happy to share more information about the loan with governments."
A thorn in the side of EU-US trade relations
Airbus and the US company Boeing, the world's two largest plane manufacturers, were previously involved in a 17-year corporate trade dispute.
The World Trade Organization (WTO) ruled that both the EU and US provided the companies with state subsidies, resulting in years of tariffs, tit-for-tat retaliation and claims of victory by both sides.
A deal to end tariffs with strict provisions on state support was finally agreed in 2021 and strengthened in 2025, but the latest row threatens to reopen the dispute and could potentially threaten the wider EU-US tariff deal agreed last year, experts say.
The previous Airbus-Boeing dispute was one of the longest-running corporate disputes in history and led to billions of dollars' worth of tariffs leveled by both sides.
"Trade experts tend to hate to talk about it because there are so many ups and downs to the story, it took so long to get resolved and it always tends to creep back up again," Inu Manak, a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics who specializes in international trade law and policy, told DW.
She says because the issue is such a "persistent thorn in the side," it has the potential to spiral, but for now the US is only signaling displeasure before things escalate. "They want to talk about this, and that conversation will need to happen before anything goes further," she said.
Does the €3 billion Airbus loan amount to state support?
At the heart of the current dispute is whether the €3 billion loan from the EIB, the largest corporate loan ever authorized by the bank, amounts to illegal state support.
"The EIB loan to Airbus is a standard loan on market terms," a European Commission spokesperson told DW. "It carries interest, it must be repaid in full, and it is the type of financing the EIB provides every year to companies across many sectors."
A spokesperson for the bank told DW the €3 billion loan is "a standard EIB corporate loan, implemented under the bank's established procedures and on market-based terms." It says it considers the financing to be "fully consistent with the market-terms principle" of the 2021 deal.
A spokesperson for Airbus told DW the loan is "a standard corporate financing facility, similar to commercially available loans we've signed in the past."
Fredrik Erixon, founding director of the European Center for International Political Economy, says the lines are still blurred when it comes to what counts as a subsidy and what is just a loan and that only a comprehensive World Trade Organization investigation could establish the full facts.
Another potential issue is how the €3 billion will be used, including the share earmarked for research and development and how much funding will support defense-related activities versus commercial aircraft development.
Inu Manak says it is impossible at this point to determine if the loan amounts to the provision of illegal subsidies or not, and that it depends on the very specific terms of the credit provided and whether or not it could be proved to be damaging to Boeing's business.
"If it's a market-based loan, if it's not providing below-market rates that would provide an unfair advantage, then it should be fine," she said. "That remains to be seen."
In Erixon's view, the situation is further complicated by the fact that the aerospace sector is "a highly murky business" due to the amount of defense contracts companies like Boeing and Airbus hold with governments and the high costs associated with that in terms of research and development.
"The problem is we've ended up in a world where there's only two large aircraft manufacturers," he told DW. "And it is a business with high upfront costs when you're going to develop different things."
He points out that while Boeing may have a legitimate grievance over this loan, Airbus and the EU can point to Boeing's own deals with the US government.
"Boeing does R&D contracts for military purposes, which end up producing technology and support for the civil aircraft program for Boeing," said Erixon. "That's also what the World Trade Organization found previously."
It was Boeing that originally asked the US trade representative back in July to intervene over the loan, linking it to Airbus' plan to develop a new single-aisle aircraft program, which could spark a new era of intense competition between the two giants. Neither the US trade representative nor Boeing responded to a DW request for comment.
Why the Airbus-Boeing subsidy dispute keeps resurfacing
Inu Manak thinks the next obvious step for the US would be to launch a Section 301 investigation, which is an official inquiry to determine if the loan "violates an international trade agreement or is unjustified, unreasonable or discriminatory, and that burdens or restricts US commerce."
She thinks the Trump administration has no interest in engaging with the WTO and believes it has the potential to threaten the broader EU-US trade agreement.
"I don't think there's a lot that can stop the US trade representative from taking action if they decide they want to do it," Manak said. "They may think there may be something else to extract from the European Union."
Fredrik Erixon agrees that "it's going to be a point of leverage that the Americans can use against Europe," adding that the dynamics underpinning the aerospace sector — that both Boeing and Airbus need greater government investment due to ramped-up military spending — is the fundamental underlying problem.
"We are getting into a state aid race, which basically means these companies just need more and more and more money," he said. "That in itself is an escalatory development."

noticias.titulo: Germany news: Plans for Rwanda migrant hub come under fire
noticias.resumen: Human rights groups have slammed plans by Germany and four other EU states to send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda. In other news, business start-ups in Germany are on track to reach the highest level since 2015.
noticias.texto:
Germany news: Plans for Rwanda migrant hub come under fire
Published November 17, 2026last updated November 18, 2026
What you need to know
- German human rights group Pro Asyl has said plans by Germany and four other EU states to send rejected migrants to Rwanda will be a "shipwreck"
- A UN agency also expressed concern over the plan
- Germany expects to see the highest number of new businesses opening in 2026 in more than a decade
- A massive leak of internal documents from Deutsche Bank has exposed misconduct and incompetence at the lender, media say
Here is a roundup of the top news stories from and about Germany on Tuesday, November 17, 2026:
That's a wrap
We'll be back with the latest headlines out of Germany tomorrow, thank you for staying with us. Tschüss!
Germany's Pistorius defends Ukraine after bridge strike
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius backed Ukraine in the aftermath of the Crimea bridge strike.
Pistorius said criticism of Ukraine's deep strikes in Russia was misplaced.
In particular, Pistorius responded to US Defense Under Secretary Elbridge Colby, who said Ukraine's "deep strikes" against Russia "have not been effective in driving an end to the war."
The German defense minister said "criticizing strikes like that in Russia to destroy strategic military and military-used targets" was "quite a stupid thing."
"Instead of criticizing that, we should rather criticize and talk about the terroristic strikes every night and every day on... energy, water, and heating infrastructure in Ukraine. This is kind of terrorism," Pistorius said.
He added that attacks inside Russia against non-civilian targets and sites used by the military are legal and legitimate targets.
Biden shares Merkel's bewilderment over Trump in new autobiography
Former US President Joe Biden's new autobiography "Promise Me, America" hit bookshelves on Tuesday, and it features anecdotes about several global leaders, including former German Chancellor Angela Merkel.
In the book, Biden dished on conversations that he and Merkel had about his predecessor and later successor, Donald Trump.
Citing conversations from early 2021, Biden wrote, "Angela was candid about her frustrations with my predecessor, who refused to shake her hand, and who seemed 'emotional' in their meetings, driven by mood swings rather than facts."
"She also wondered," wrote Biden, "why he was 'fascinated' by Vladimir Putin and other politicians 'with autocratic and dictatorial traits.' That was a mystery I could not unravel."
Merkel and Trump were often at odds over issues tied to NATO, trade, climate policy and Germany's dependence on Russian energy but one of the most infamous meetings between two came in the Oval Office in March 2017, when Trump awkwardly refused to shake hands with the German leader during a press availability despite photographers loudly encouraging him to do so.
Merkel reflected on the moment in her own 2024 memoir "Freedom" saying that after initially approaching Trump as someone "completely normal" she quickly sensed that he viewed their public meetings as a kind of "you or me" competition.
UN rights chief voices concerns over Rwanda deportation plans
The UN's high commissioner for human rights, Volker Türk, has joined the chorus of those voicing doubts about a plan by five EU countries, including Germany, to send rejected asylum seekers to a deportation hub in Rwanda.
Türk said he had not yet seen the draft proposal but that his office was "concerned about the human rights risks raised by the proposed transfer of people from five European Union countries to Rwanda, where they have no genuine connection and which has its own set of human rights challenges."
Instead, he called for a "comprehensive approach to migration governance anchored in human rights."
The Germany-based refugee advocacy group Pro Asyl said on Tuesday that the plans would end in a "shipwreck" (see entry below).
German universities draw in largest number of foreign students in EU
New figures from the EU statistics agency show that just over one quarter of all students from abroad in various EU member states were enrolled in tertiary education in Germany.
Of a total of roughly 1.65 million foreign students in 2024, around 1.1 million of them were from outside the EU and the rest were moving within the EU, 438,260 were in Germany.
France was next in line by sheer numbers with almost 285,000 foreign students, and the much less populous Netherlands was third with over 176,000. Germany, France and the Netherlands combined accounted for more than half the bloc-wide total.
The Netherlands, unlike France and Germany, was also one of the countries with the highest proportion of foreign students in tertiary education. Even excluding doctoral-level students, around 18% of students in the Netherlands hailed from abroad.
Only Luxembourg, at 51.5%, Malta (35.6%), Cyprus (21.6%) and Austria (20.8%) had a higher share among full EU members, though Switzerland's ratio also stood at roughly 20%.
Greece (2.6%), Croatia (3.5%) and Spain (4.6'%) had some of the lowest percentages of foreign students, with the EU average at 8.7%.
Lufthansa and VC pilots' union negotiations end without breakthrough
Mediation between German flagship carrier Lufthansa and the Vereinigung Cockpit (VC) pilots' trade union ended on Tuesday without a clear breakthrough.
The airline is trying to cut costs while the union is trying to optimize pay and conditions for members in a dispute dating back to September 2025 that led to several disruptions earlier in the year.
VC said that it favored a package resulting from the mediation, which it said Lufthansa had rejected. VC said it was giving the airline until November 23 to reconsider its position.
"The ball is now in the employer's court," VC said in a call with media. It did not specify what action it would take after the deadline but did say it considered its commitment not to strike during the arbitration process to be satisfied.
Lufthansa, meanwhile, said it had submitted a proposal to VC for up to 1,000 new cockpit hires by 2033, up to 150 additional captain promotions each year, a one-off payment for 2027 and 2028 followed by salary increases from 2029 onwards.
VC said it would be willing to make further concessions on pay and conditions if Lufthansa would respond with job guarantees.
The airline also said arbitrators had indicated a willingness to continue negotiations if the latest round proved fruitless — though it wasn't clear whether that also applied to each side of the labor dispute.
Berlin bans association accused of supporting Hezbollah
The government of the city-state of Berlin has banned an association accused of supporting the Lebanese group Hezbollah, which has been deemed a terrorist organization and outlawed in Germany since 2020.
Police in Berlin searched a total of 28 properties on Tuesday, including premises belonging to the affected groups and the homes of select members.
The ban affects El-Irschad e.V. in the Neukölln district and three subsidiary groups: Al-Qaem e.V., Al-Thaqalyn e.V., and Qalam Bildungszentrum UG.
The city's senator, or Cabinet minister, for interior affairs, Iris Spranger of the Social Democrats, said the group was "directed against the notions of understanding between peoples," and that its "purpose and activities" contravened criminal laws in Berlin.
The ban prohibits the public display or distribution of the organizations' symbols and logos. Their websites have been shut down and their assets seized.
Spranger said the group had given Hezbollah a platform to spread propaganda among Neukölln's Shiite community, using youth activities and a mosque to do so.
Rwanda migrant deportation hub scheme condemned by rights groups
A number of human rights groups have spoken out after Germany, along with Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands, announced plans to set up a hub for rejected migrants in Rwanda.
The deportation center would be the first such facility outside the European Union.
The Germany-based refugee advocacy group Pro Asyl said on Tuesday that the plans would end in a "shipwreck."
Pro Asyl managing director Karl Kopp said that even rejected asylum seekers had rights.
"Rwanda is not a model democracy. Opposition figures there are arrested and sometimes tortured," he said.
"If those affected need help, we will stand at their side with legal support."
In a statement issued after the announcement of the plans, 45 NGOs from 15 countries also condemned the move.
"These plans allow people without a right to stay in the EU to be sent to countries with which they have no connection at all," the statement said.
"These policies shift people, and responsibility for their safety and rights, out of public sight and beyond scrutiny," it said.
Criticism from within the coalition
The junior partner in Germany's coalition, the center-left Social Democrats, has also maintained its criticism of the plans, which are heavily supported by Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), the sister party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU).
"Dobrindt's plans are short-sighted with regard to foreign policy and harm Germany's credibility," SPD foreign policy spokesman Adid Ahmetovic told the Reuters news agency.
"Rwanda violates the sovereignty of its neighbors and supports the M23 rebels in eastern [Democratic Republic of] Congo," he said.
"Such a regime must not receive any political concessions just because it is to take in refugees from Germany," he said, adding: "Human rights are not bargaining chips for deportation deals."
Rwanda deportation hub planned for 2027
The announcement of the plans comes after an EU reform of its migration policy this year granted broader detention powers and allowed for the creation of return hubs.
According to Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker, the aim is for the first center to be set up in Rwanda next year.
Diplomatic sources say the Rwanda hub will be initially run as a pilot with some 100 people, 20 from each of the five nations.
German government at odds over Rwanda plan
The plan to establish the deportation center in Rwanda has drawn criticism not only from a wide range of human rights groups but also from the junior partner in Germany's ruling coalition, the Social Democrats (SPD), as this video details.
Germany funding $300 million more US arms supplies for Ukraine — Pistorius
Germany will be purchasing $300 million (€273 million) of US arms supplies to give to Ukraine as it fights against the Russian invasion, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius announced on Tuesday.
He said that Berlin was making a fifth contribution to the PURL (Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List) mechanism coordinated by the US and NATO, under which European countries finance the purchase of US weapons for Ukraine.
Most of the new funds will go to buy guided missiles for Patriot air defense systems, Pistorius said in remarks made on the sidelines of a meeting with his EU counterparts in Brussels.
He said Berlin was also planning to provide Kyiv with IRIS-T air defense systems, as previously announced, as well as new radars to improve air surveillance, ammunition for F-16 fighter jets, and drones.
He also said that Germany was preparing to make IRIS-T missiles compatible with NASAMS air defense systems being supplied to Ukraine by Norway.
Pistorius stressed that supporting Ukraine, although an act of solidarity, was "not a charity event," as Russian aggression posed an associated threat to Western Europe.
He is to host a meeting alongside his British counterpart Wes Streeting later on Tuesday that aims to drum up further military support for Kyiv.
Wadephul wants closer ties with Azerbaijan, Armenia to counter Russia
Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has said he would like Germany to expand its relations with the former Soviet republics of Azerbaijan and Armenia as a counterweight to an ongoing bid by Russia to maintain its influence in the region.
"In the South Caucasus too, we are seeing Russia try to retain its influence at the expense of the people and their future," Wadephul on Tuesday before setting off on his first visit to the two countries as foreign minister.
He said Russian President Vladimir Putin was opposed to countries deciding their own destiny under a European order of sovereign states, making it important for the two Caucasian nations to retain their self-determination over their futures.
Wadephul also highlighted the South Caucasus's role as an interface between Europe and Asia, which he said meant the region had great potential for trade, energy partnerships and new transport links.
German foreign minister in the Caucasus
Germany's top diplomat is first to visit the Azerbaijani capital, Baku, where he is set to meet the country's authoritarian head of state, Ilham Aliyev, and Foreign Minister Ceyhun Bayramov.
He is scheduled to travel on to Armenia on Wednesday.
In August 2025, the two countries signed a joint declaration on a US-brokered peace treaty ending a decadeslong conflict over the Nagorno-Karabakh region.
This came after Azerbaijan captured the region in 2023 in a short but heavy offensive, with most of the region's population — more than 100,000 ethnic Armenians — forced to flee.
Deutsche Bank shares plummet after reports on incriminating documents leak
Shares in Deutsche Bank took a nosedive on Tuesday after media across the world published reports with information gleaned from millions of leaked documents that expose dubious past business practices at the lender.
The documents, which were shared by unidentified whistleblowers, throw light on the banking giant's activities over the past 20 years, which include dealings with Russian oligarchs and the late convicted US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
The name Donald Trump also appears in the documents from the time before he became US president.
The leaked documents, which include emails, have cast doubt on the success of chief executive Christian Sewing's efforts to turn around the institution after a series of scandals.
Among other things, they indicate that Sewing himself was involved in a working group that sought to expand the bank's Russian operations shortly before Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, despite warnings about regulatory and money-laundering risks.
The investigation, called "Inside Deutsche Bank", was conducted by over 200 journalists from a media consortium that included The Financial Times, Der Spiegel, Le Monde, the New York Times, the German public broadcaster ZDF and the Austrian daily Der Standard.
Deutsche Bank has not disputed the authenticity of the data, though it refers to the documents as "purported internal documents."
It also said that many of the incidents referred to in them belonged to a distant past and that it is now "a different bank."
European Commission doubles growth forecast for Germany
The European Commission has almost doubled its forecast for economic growth in Germany, raising it from a prediction in spring of 0.6% to 1.3% now.
The commission said stable domestic consumer demand and a rebound in exports justified the more optimistic figure.
The higher forecast comes despite the high inflation rate caused by the war in Iran.
Number of start-ups set to reach highest level since 2015
Some 286,000 new businesses are expected to be founded in 2026, a rise of 3.4% compared with last year and the highest level of start-ups since 2015, according to the National Association of German Cooperative Banks (BVR).
The BVR said the boom in start-ups could be partly attributed to the fact that developments in artificial intelligence (AI) and a difficult situation on the labor market were making self-employment more profitable.
However, the association warned that the increase was fragile, as it was largely driven by government support and exports rather that the private investment needed for more sustained growth.
In July, the German government adopted a start-up strategy that aimed to cut bureaucracy and provide support for future technologies, thus creating favorable conditions for young entrepreneurs.
The BVR also cautioned that the number of people in the 30-40 age group — those most likely to start a business — was falling, meaning that the surge will probably not last.
The association also said that even though there was a rise in AI-related start-ups in 2026, Europe needed to do more for AI development to keep up with the US and China.
Welcome to our coverage
DW's newsroom on the Rhine in Bonn wishes all readers a guten Tag!
Plans announced by Germany and four EU partner states to deport rejected asylum seekers to a hub in Rwanda have provoked a wave of criticism from human rights groups.
Migration hard-liner Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, one of the main advocates of the plan, has, however, given assurances that it will be executed "in line with human rights" and "in accordance with European and German law."
Meanwhile, more new businesses are expected to open in Germany this year than has been the case since 2015, a rise partly driven by the growing presence of artificial intelligence.
And internal documents leaked by whistleblowers from Deutsche Bank, a lender that has had more than its fair share of scandals in the past, have exposed more cases of malpractice and misconduct in recent years, media say.
Read on here for more on these and other German stories!

noticias.titulo: Anthropic IPO raises record $81.3 billion on strong AI demand
noticias.resumen: The five-year-old artificial intelligence powerhouse priced its initial public offering at $83 a share, shrugging off growing concern about a possible AI bubble and volatility in tech stocks.
noticias.texto:
Anthropic IPO raises record $81.3 billion on strong AI demand
The artificial intelligence company Anthropic said on Wednesday it sold more than 956 million shares at a price of $83 a piece in a record-breaking initial public offering that makes it one of the most valuable companies in the world.
The five-year-old AI powerhouse raised around $79.4 billion through the offering, exceeding the $75 billion IPO haul of Elon Musk's SpaceX earlier this year. Anthropic said in a statement that "certain stockholders" also sold more than 23 million shares as part of the IPO, bringing the total haul to more than $81.3 billion.
Anthropic's shares will start trading publicly on Thursday on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT.
The listing was oversubscribed, despite coming at a time of growing concern about a possible AI bubble and volatility in tech stocks.
The number of shares sold and the price exceeded Anthropic's original expectations. The listing prospectus targeted a sale of 825 million shares at $70 to $78 per share.
Anthropic is a financial supporter of NPR.

noticias.titulo: After Nepal's epic flood, they're restoring their community ... and their lives
noticias.resumen: As the emergency response to the flood ends, aid workers turn to the hard work of rebuilding communities that lost everything. Many of those workers lost everything, too.
noticias.texto:
After Nepal's epic flood, they're restoring their community ... and their lives
"I thought I wouldn't survive," says Januka Dhital.
Just minutes before that terrible thought, Dhital was busy preparing snacks. She ran a catering service out of her house in Uttargaya, Nepal, and was getting ready for an event later that day. Her work was interrupted by a man on a scooter, warning of a flood. She stepped outside to look.
"When I turned around, I saw darkness, dust and what looked like the entire hillside coming down," she says.
She grabbed her young son and hopped onto the back of the man's scooter. They raced to higher ground, eventually reaching safety. But she didn't know if her husband and daughter were safe, since they were at work and school when the waters came.
"It felt unbelievable"
After hours of waiting and searching, they were all reunited. Her husband was naked, covered in blood and badly injured, she says, but alive.
"It felt unbelievable that our family had survived," says Dhital. But the wall of water and mud that descended from the mountains had obliterated their home, along with thousands of others. "We have lost everything. We have nothing now."
Dhital and her family are among the 100,000-some people whose lives have been upended by the devastating floods sparked by glacial melt, a phenomenon made worse by climate change. At least 1,500 have died, and more than 5,000 are still missing. Thousands are still living in temporary shelters or tents.
The flood damaged or destroyed seven health facilities, 23 schools, 10,000 toilets and 64 water systems, according to the United Nations. And there are early signs that malnutrition is spiking as winter approaches.
"The magnitude of devastation is unimaginable," says Shyam Pathak, a chief of health at UNICEF. The din of helicopters circling the wreckage looking for survivors has faded, he says. International attention and aid has fallen too, sources on the ground say, as the response turns to the arduous, but intimate work of helping these communities stitch their lives back together.
This disaster is somewhat unique, Pathak says, in that many of those doing the work are trying to rebuild their own lives at the same time. Dhital is one of them.
"I felt like I was losing my mind"
In the immediate aftermath of the flood, Dhital and her family moved into a holding center, one of a couple dozen that housed the displaced. They stayed there for about a month before moving into a relative's house. Those days were not easy.
"For almost a month, I felt like I was losing my mind," she says. "More than money, I am in great need of work."
She found that work through Helen Keller Intl, a nonprofit that's helping the response. After a short training program that included mental health support, she began helping her community rebuild. There's a lot to do.
"I go out into the community, we work with postpartum mothers, pregnant women and children under five," says Dhital. "This is the only thing keeping me going right now."
One of her jobs is screening for malnutrition among survivors.
Preliminary data suggest a notable increase. In Naukunda Gaunpalika, for instance, moderate acute malnutrition — a condition that can slow growth, weaken the immune system and become life threatening without treatment — appears to have gone up from 0.8% in June of this year to 8.7% in October, says Pooja Pandey Rana, who directs Hellen Keller's work in Nepal. These are likely conservative estimates too, she says.
"It's a big jump," says Pandey Rana, and likely driven by fallout from the flood.
In addition to losing homes, many families lost the gardens or local farms they relied on for nutritious food. "As a result, they have to depend on dried and packaged foods, such as instant noodles and biscuits," says Dhital. Poor sanitation and lack of clean drinking water is an issue too, she says. And many have lost their livelihoods, so they don't have money to pay for food.
Workers like Dhital are handing out supplies and cash to families in need. In some regions, that's a challenge.
Many of the communities along the flood's path were connected by bridges. More than 100 of them are now destroyed, according to the U.N. And for many living higher up the slopes, mountain roads were a lifeline that have now been severed.
"There still are places, especially in the upper north part of the impacted areas, which have been cut off by the flood," says Ayush Joshi, who works for the non-profit Save the Children in Nepal. "There is still a challenge to deliver food and life saving support to these areas."
"Our hearts cannot bear to see the destruction"
Pushmaya Tamang is a community aid worker trying to reach those areas. Often, she must cross the makeshift bridges hastily constructed to make up for the damage.
"The bridge shakes, making it difficult for elderly people to cross," she says. "It becomes dangerous when people try to cross the bridge from both directions at the same time. It almost overturns, making it extremely frightening."
Such damaged infrastructure is a start reminder of what's been lost, she says. Tamang is from a village in Nuwakot that's essentially gone after the floods.
"Our hearts cannot bear to see the destruction," she says. "The village that was once full of colorful lights and life has now become gloomy and dark."
Tamang's heart is heavy with grief over the loss of her younger sister, too. Many of the families she helps in her work with Helen Keller are also grieving unimaginable loss, she says.
"When we visit other affected families, we do not even know what to say or how to talk to them," she says. "We do not have the words to comfort or console them."
Many survivors need significant mental health support, says Pathak of UNICEF, which is teaming up with other aid organizations to mobilize health workers who can provide counseling. Like Dhital and Tamang, many of them are trying to help rebuild their communities while dealing with their own trauma.
"A hallmark of this response is that the health workers, despite being the victim themselves, are back to the work," says Pathak. "This has helped a lot."
"Everything has been wiped out"
Winter poses distinct challenges for survivors.
Colder temperatures are threatening those who still live in temporary shelters or flimsy tents. "Winter in these areas is very harsh," says Joshi. "Exposure to cold, overcrowded living, poor ventilation in the tent, damp bedding and inadequate clothing can also increase health risk."
Responders are winterizing tents and getting families into safer shelters, says Joshi, in addition to providing food and medical care.
In the longer term, there's the question of rebuilding what was leveled.
"We still haven't really seen [plans] on where to rebuild, how many homes are needed, how do we fix the water systems, how do you rebuild the schools?" says Pandey Rana of Helen Keller. "Like everything has been wiped out."
Preliminary estimates put the cost of rebuilding at roughly $5 billion, a steep figure for the small nation. The U.N. Climate Fund, aimed at helping countries harmed by climate change, approved $20 million for recovery. Domestic and international donors have contributed over $100 million in additional funds, but it's still far short of what's needed.
For now, aid organizations are focused on the immediate needs of survivors. Tamang says the daily work helps keep her going amid so much loss.
"What else can I do," she says. "Life goes on, and we have to accept what nature has brought upon us."

noticias.titulo: Alleged Russian agent arrested for spying on Silicon Valley tech firm
noticias.resumen: The company was not named in the indictment but was described as a large, publicly traded technology and defence firm with offices across the US, including in Palo Alto, California.
noticias.texto:
The company was not named in the indictment but was described as a large, publicly traded technology and defence firm with offices across the US, including in Palo Alto, California.
A Russian national has been arrested in California on suspicion of spying on employees of a Silicon Valley technology and defence company that provided support to Ukraine, US officials said on Wednesday.
Igor D'iu faces charges of conspiring to act as an agent of a foreign government, operating as a foreign agent without notifying US authorities, stalking and fraud.
"Igor D'iu was allegedly recruited, directed, and funded by the Russian government to stalk employees of a major US technology company," Roman Rozhavsky, assistant director of the FBI's Counterintelligence and Espionage Division, said in a statement.
Rozhavsky said D'iu used "physical surveillance, electronic tracking devices, and fraudulent identities to gather intelligence."
US Attorney Craig Missakian said the company was targeted because of its "assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia."
"We will not tolerate any efforts -- by foreign governments or otherwise -- to turn Silicon Valley into a base for foreign intelligence operations," Missakian said.
What does the indictment say?
According to the indictment, D'iu travelled from Turkey to Mexico in June 2026 before being smuggled into the United States, where he allegedly communicated with his Russia-based co-conspirators via Telegram.
They allegedly instructed him to gather information on company employees and visit a coffee shop near its Palo Alto office to "photograph their laptop screens while they worked."
FBI agents found $18,000 (€15,500) in cash, a fake US passport under the name "Hugo Landry Johns" and two Russian passports during an October raid on D'iu's home in East Palo Alto, according to the Justice Department.
If convicted, D'iu faces up to 10 years in prison for acting as an agent of a foreign government without notifying the US attorney general, five years for conspiracy, five years for stalking and one year for fraud.
He is scheduled to appear in federal court on 24 November.

noticias.titulo: Bukele confirms airstrike on Haitian gang leader Jeff's luxury mansion
noticias.resumen: The Salvadoran president welcomes the destruction of the home of Jeff Larose, one of Haiti's main crime leaders. It is not clear whether Jeff was in the building during the bombing.
noticias.texto:
The Salvadoran president welcomes the destruction of the home of Jeff Larose, one of Haiti's main crime leaders. It is not clear whether Jeff was in the building during the bombing.
The president of El Salvador, Nayib Bukele, confirmed on Wednesday that his forces had attacked and destroyed the luxurious mansion of one of the main leaders of Haiti's criminal gangs, known as "Jeff" Larose. For now, it is not clear whether the leader was killed in the strike or whether he was even in the house when it was bombed.
Bukele posted a video on the social network X showing images of Jeff posing in front of his mansion, followed by Salvadoran helicopters that approach the building and open fire. The footage shows several columns of smoke rising above the property.
"My gift to the Haitian people on the anniversary of the Battle of Vertières," the president wrote, referring to the 1803 battle that helped secure Haiti's independence from France and make it the world's first black republic.
Thousands of Haitians took to the streets of Port-au-Prince for the second day in a row to celebrate the operation and chant the Salvadoran president's name. "Jeff is a criminal and I hope he is dead. We asked for help and Bukele answered us," said Mario Jean-Pierre, a 45-year-old vendor.
Jeff Larose, also known as Jeff Canaan, Jeff Gwo Lwa or Taliban, leads a gang that has controlled the community of Canaan, north of Port-au-Prince, for years. According to Haiti expert Diego Da Rin of the International Crisis Group, speaking to AP, it is one of the country's most structured criminal organisations and one with the greatest territorial control.
The strike comes after Salvadoran forces also attacked the residence of Wilson Joseph, leader of the 400 Mawozo gang, on 8 November. The two leaders were allies and are considered two of the main criminal bosses in the capital.
Salvadoran deployment endangers civilians
Bukele deployed about 2,500 troops to Haiti last month, after four Salvadoran soldiers were attacked on 18 October in gang-controlled territory and went missing.
The use of helicopters and explosive drones has made it possible to step up operations against criminal organisations, but it has also increased the risk to the civilian population.
Experts warn that one of the main challenges remains keeping control of the territories that have been retaken and preventing the gangs from taking reprisals against residents.

noticias.titulo: Data watchdog probes massive Deutsche Bank leak of 15M files
noticias.resumen: A German state data regulator has opened an investigation on Wednesday into Deutsche Bank following a massive data leak. The authority is investigating possible data protection violations.
noticias.texto:
A German state data regulator has opened an investigation on Wednesday into Deutsche Bank following a massive data leak. The authority is investigating possible data protection violations.
Following the massive data breach that leaked over 15 million internal records, the office of the commissioner for data protection in Hesse has said on Wednesday that it has launched a probe into Deutsche Bank.
Alexander Rossnagel, the data protection commissioner, said he will check whether the bank had appropriate data protection measures and if the leak was reported in a timely fashion.
"I am investigating whether Deutsche Bank promptly notified the affected individuals," Rossnagel said.
Whistleblowers leaked internal documents to a group of international media, revealing that the bank had reportedly ignored repeated internal warnings about money laundering, corruption or sanctions violations.
Among the bank's clients are Russian oligarchs, US President Donald Trump and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
Deutsche Bank CEO admits errors
"When you look at the events today, you naturally question whether something could have been done differently," CEO of Deutsche Bank, Christian Sewing, told German newspaper Handelsblatt.
"Looking back, you can always say that at a certain point in time you might have been able to prioritise differently," Sewing told Handelsblatt.
When asked whether he took internal warnings seriously, Sewing refuted: "During the customer review, I asked whether a private customer needs the same complex process as a large company with 300 subsidiaries," Handelsblatt reports.
"That doesn't mean I wanted to put risks aside."
A blow to Deutsche Bank's reputation
Although Deutsche Bank said the matters "date back many years" and that it had reinforced its controls, the leak has dealt consequential damage to the bank's reputation, sending its share down.
The bank claims it proactively informed the appropriate authorities about the leak and that testing found no account information, login credentials or payment data were accessed.
While the probe won't investigate the documents, it will assess the technical and organisational measures put in place to judge if they were appropriate.

noticias.titulo: US Defence Secretary announces military cooperation in surprise Caracas visit
noticias.resumen: The US Defence Secretary met Delcy Rodríguez in Caracas ahead of a planned visit to Colombia, where he is due to discuss bilateral security cooperation.
noticias.texto:
The US Defence Secretary met Delcy Rodríguez in Caracas ahead of a planned visit to Colombia, where he is due to discuss bilateral security cooperation.
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth announced a military cooperation agreement with Venezuela on Wednesday, state TV reported, during an unexpected visit to Caracas.
Hegseth was received by Venezuela's interim leader, Delcy Rodríguez, in the capital ahead of a planned visit to Colombia later Wednesday.
"We see this as a renewal of our defence partnership and an opportunity for our two great armed forces to work together," Hegseth said, according to footage broadcast by VTV, Venezuela's state television channel.
The trip, which had not been publicly announced by the Pentagon, marks another step in the rapprochement between Washington and Caracas following the capture in January of Nicolás Maduro.
What does the agreement include?
The cooperation agreement announced by Hegseth and Rodríguez provides for the resumption of technical and military cooperation between Washington and Caracas, which had been suspended for years amid deteriorating diplomatic relations between the two countries.
According to the Venezuelan leader, one of the main objectives is to strengthen the training of Venezuelan armed forces personnel through joint training and cooperation programmes. Rodríguez said the initiative would help improve the military's preparedness to respond to shared threats.
The agreement also aims to improve the operational equipment available to Venezuelan forces and provide access to new technologies. So far, neither government has provided details on the timeline for implementing the agreement, the resources to be allocated or the specific mechanisms through which cooperation will take place.
Washington and Caracas strengthen ties
Rodríguez took power after Maduro was captured, although her continued leadership of the country remains shrouded in uncertainty. Her interim mandate expired in July and there is still no announced date for the next presidential election.
The rapprochement between Washington and Caracas has also been marked by agreements over Venezuelan oil and by the United States' strategy against drug trafficking in the Caribbean and the Pacific, which has caused the deaths of at least 240 people since September 2025 in attacks on vessels suspected of carrying drugs.
Hegseth's visit is part of efforts by Donald Trump's administration to expand its influence in Venezuela. The defence secretary is the third member of Trump's cabinet to travel to the country this year, following trips by the interior and energy secretaries, focused on Venezuela's oil and mineral resources.

noticias.titulo: EPP moves to suspend Serbia’s former ruling party
noticias.resumen: SNS will have 12 months to deliver on the EPP's demands, or face expulsion.
noticias.texto: The center-right European People’s Party leadership decided Wednesday to suspend the Serbian Progressive Party, the political home of former Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić. The move comes after the Serbian party, also known as SNS, lost the October 2026 general elections , ousting Vučić, its de facto leader and the country’s president for nine years. The decision, seen by POLITICO, will need ratification by the EPP’s Political Assembly on Dec. 7-8. After that, the SNS, which has associate member status because Serbia is not an EU country, will have one year to deliver the reforms demanded by the political family. If it does not meet the demands by then, it risks expulsion from the group, as reported earlier in POLITICO’s European Parliament Insider WhatsApp channel . The reforms include ending political alignment and ties with Russian President Vladimir Putin and his United Russia party, aligning with EU sanctions against Moscow, distancing SNS from the Chinese government and renewing its commitment to EU integration. The EPP also wants SNS to halt its “glorification” of deceased convicted war criminal Ratko Mladić. The report describes the state-assisted funeral for Mladić as a “game changer” for many within the EPP that helped trigger the suspension decision. SNS has also been asked to work more closely with civil society organizations, commit to strengthening media freedom, and ensure a peaceful transition of power to the Student List party, which won the parliamentary election at the end of October. Since September 2025, the EPP has been conducting a “scrutiny process” into whether SNS still respects the political family’s fundamental values following democratic and rule-of-law backsliding and a crackdown on protesters. The Serbian party’s leadership must report monthly to the EPP, which also plans to send an observation mission to Belgrade in spring 2027. SNS did not respond to a request for comment by the time of publication.

noticias.titulo: Grand Theft Auto VI is here. The EU has 6 reasons to pay attention.
noticias.resumen: The long-awaited new installment of the GTA series is a global entertainment phenomenon. But it also has a policy plotline.
noticias.texto: BRUSSELS — Gamers of the world will be taking the day off Thursday to play Grand Theft Auto VI, billed as the most anticipated digital entertainment launch in history. The EU’s buttoned-down staffers may be too busy to notice. Yet even a diligent Brussels bureaucrat has reason to buckle up for the latest installment of the Grand Theft Auto series, which comes 13 years after the previous version of the controversial video game that challenges players to go on crime rampages around U.S. cities to the tune of an eclectic soundtrack. According to Sensor Tower data , GTA VI is already the biggest entertainment launch ever, with 17 million copies sold for a total of $1.6 billion (€1.46 billion) before it’s even released. The game lands in a vastly different world than the one the previous version entered in 2013, one where EU regulators are trying to protect kids from harmful online content and handle the onslaught of AI. Here are six reasons an EU policy maven should pay attention to all the fun and games: 1. It’s a European game, sort of The Grand Theft Auto series was originally made by two Scottish programmers, David Jones and Mike Dailly, at a Dundee game studio called DMA Design. The rights to the series were later sold to an American company, Take-Two Interactive, in the late 1990s, although its subsidiary Rockstar Games still has large offices in Edinburgh. Meanwhile, the EU’s right to claim a Scottish success story as its own lapsed with the 2020 EU-UK withdrawal agreement. A young man plays Grand Theft Auto IV on the game’s day of release on April 29, 2008 in London. | Cate Gillon/Getty Images European leaders worried about the bloc’s declining competitiveness are turning to a number of policy solutions to encourage innovation, from new funding mechanisms to changes in public procurement rules. 2. EU rules may be on gamers’ side Prior to the game’s release, gamers were concerned that GTA VI’s online version would include the same micro-transactions and in-game currency that fans say are making games “ dull and repetitive .” The game being released today won’t have these features, although a later online version might. The European Commission is proposing new rules to curb the use of these features by kids, or at least make them more transparent, because Brussels says they encourage spending. The gaming industry says these proposed rules under the Digital Fairness Act will be catastrophic for EU businesses. 3. Kids aren’t supposed to play GTA GTA VI is rated 18+ under the PEGI system, which stands for Pan-European Game Information rating mechanism. That means it’s not recommended for minors to play at all. The rating is a self-regulatory tool created 20 years ago today and still in place. It is based on whether the games include things like profanity, drugs, violence and sex — all hallmarks of the GTA franchise. Games rated 12 and up are reviewed by the U.K. Games Rating Authority, whose reviewers actually play the game before assigning a rating. 4. But Brussels can’t stop them Some EU countries and the U.K. do require buyers to show identification when purchasing a physical copy of the game. Online stores like PlayStation’s also carry out age checks to make sure that 13-year-olds don’t get access to age-inappropriate content. But nothing stops a parent or an older sibling from giving that game to a younger person. PEGI’s Director-General Dirk Bosmans said that “at the heart of PEGI is helping parents making informed choices.” If a parent wants to give their teenager access to GTA VI, the PEGI system lets them do so knowing that it contains violence, drugs and sex. “We are more concerned about parents saying, ‘here’s some money, buy whatever you like’,” Bosmans said. 5. It may be the last big game not made by AI The CEO of Take-Two Interactive, Strauss Zelnick, has said that generative artificial intelligence has “zero part” in what the firm has built for GTA VI. The gaming industry is increasingly using generative artificial intelligence to create new titles. The latest State of the Game Industry report found that 40% of game developers use genAI in game creation, including in work on some of the biggest titles. These include the shooter Call of Duty and critics’ favorites like France’s Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 . The industry has also seen thousands of layoffs, with one-third of U.S. video game industry workers saying they have been let go in the past two years. 6. It’s a safety-first world As the industry has moved into the mainstream with blockbuster releases like GTA VI, the European Commission has firmly set its sights on creating the first industry-specific rules for the gaming industry through the DFA and broader rules on protecting minors under the Kids Act. In the video game section of Fnac, a child tests a Nintendo Switch demo unit displaying Mario Kart 8 Deluxe on a large screen, amidst the accessories and consoles on display in the store in Paris on August 1, 2026. | Riccardo Milani/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images The idea that violent video games contribute to violence in real life was largely debunked in the early 2010s, around the time the previous GTA installment was released, Bosmans says. But the debate around content has moved from what is “harmful” to what is “inappropriate,” he says. Scientific research informs the PEGI system, but the regime also reflects societal norms around “appropriateness,” he explained: one f-word can land a whole game in the 16+ category. As regulators introduce more measures to protect kids online, Bosmans said, “it feels like we’re now in a stage where we may have forgotten some of the history,” and the difference between what is harmful, what is banned, and what is inappropriate.

noticias.titulo: UK sanctions on Israel leave EU unmoved, despite ‘man-made catastrophe’ in Gaza
noticias.resumen: In a voice from Gaza, Ahmed Abu Jami, a 28-year-old doctor, who lives in Khan Younis, told EUobserver via WhatsApp: "Things are bad, really, Gaza is descending into hell."
noticias.texto:
New UK sanctions against Israel have spotlighted the EU’s inaction on the “man-made catastrophe” in Gaza and raging aggression in the West Bank.
The UK blacklisted eight Israeli construction firms, which built homes for West Bank settlers, on Tuesday (17 November), as well as the Tzav 9 activist group, which blocked humanitarian aid to Gaza.
“My message on E1 is clear: do not bid [for contracts], do not build,” said British foreign secretary Ed Miliband, referring to the new ‘E1’ settlement, which is designed to cut the West Bank in half and kill the prospect of a two-state solution.
Israel is currently being led by a caretaker government, amid post-election coalition talks.
But Miliband noted that “more settlements have been approved under the four years of this Israeli government [of prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu] than in the previous 20 years.”
Floods in Gaza, after Israel destroyed its EU-funded water-management infrastructure, have left 4,000 people homeless, while 1.4 million people were living in tents in wintry weather, but Israel was blocking deliveries of tarpaulins and timber, Miliband added.
EU foreign minsters are also clear-eyed about what Israel is doing in Gaza and the West Bank.

noticias.titulo: EU asylum agency floats idea of foreign ‘processing centres’ to handle asylum claims
noticias.resumen: Innovative solutions is a catch all phrase that describes return hubs in Rwanda and Italy's controversial deal with Albania. Now it also applies to "process centres" for asylum seeker hopefuls.
noticias.texto:
Late last year, the EU tweaked laws allowing member states to have a person’s claim for asylum heard somewhere abroad.
Now, discussions are taking place to create a so-called “processing centre” in a foreign country, where the asylum seekers who initially landed in Europe would have their case for protection heard.
Nina Gregori, who heads the Malta-based European Union Agency for Asylum (EUAA), floated the idea in a passing remark about possible innovative solutions on migration control at the International Centre for Migration Policy Development (ICMPD) conference in Vienna on Tuesday (17 November).
‘Innovative solutions’ is a catch-all phrase that has also applied to return hubs in Rwanda and Italy’s controversial deal with Albania.
Asked to further elaborate, she told EUobserver that the idea is already backed by European law, citing the so-called “safe-third country concept”.
The concept essentially shifts EU member states’ responsibility for processing asylum claims to foreign states, even if the asylum seeker has never set foot in the country. The concept itself is not new.

noticias.titulo: France dethrones Sweden as EU gender equality leader — but overall progress is slowing
noticias.resumen: Europe still has a significant gender gap. It's in employment, in who takes care of children, in places of power. It's stronger in places like Cyprus and Bulgaria, while Spain and Denmark prioritised its gender politics. But full gender equality is still a distant goal, as Europe still lags behind pre-pandemic levels of parity.
noticias.texto: France is leading the way on gender equality in the EU, according to a study published on Tuesday (17 November), with more female representation at decision-making levels becoming the main push for gender equality. The European institute for gender equality ( EIGE ) publishes an annual index measuring how close the EU is to equality between men and women. This year’s report shows a small improvement, though noting European societies are yet to recover from a post-pandemic slump in progress. The agency says this is “a sign that the momentum built over the past decade is losing strength”. The proportion of women in positions of power has grown faster than in any other sector, with increased representation in economic and social decision-making positions across several member states. Even so, it is still the lowest-scoring area of the index. While still remaining severely underrepresented in leadership positions, particularly compared to the Nordic countries, France and Spain have encouraged more policy action on gender equality. Read more EU reduces funds for women’s rights groups, in wider budget bonfire of good causes However, some of the Nordic nations have started to fall back. Sweden, whose 13-year record in leading the gender equality struggle was overtaken this year by France, is “kind of stagnating,” EIGE’s statistics officer, Davide Barbieri, told EUobserver. “We are going in a good direction, but we can do even better, and we need to do that together, member states as well, its regions, civil societies, companies, employers,” said EU commission executive vice-president for social rights, Roxana Mînzatu, at Tuesday’s launch event for the index in Brussels. “How we make sure that gender equality contributes and fuels growth, it’s always three levels that we need to act upon: it’s skills and education, it’s the quality of jobs, and it’s the availability of care” This article continues, but the full version is available only to EUobserver.com subscribers. noticias.titulo: EU freezes €62.5m of Slovakia’s recovery funds over plans linked to ousted environment minister
noticias.resumen: Internal government warnings, downgraded wind plans and controversial zoning tweaks by ousted environment minister Taraba’s team now emerge at the heart of the Commission’s decision, exposing how months of behind-the-scenes manoeuvring may have sabotaged Slovakia’s own green transition money.
noticias.texto: The European Commission has suspended €62.5m from Slovakia’s eighth recovery-plan payment over inadequacies in the zoning of national parks and preparation of a wind energy zone. The sum concerns the Recovery and Resilience Facility , part of the EU’s plan to emerge stronger from the Covid-19 pandemic by issuing funds for the green transition and country-specific investments. After the commission’s decision on Monday (16 November), the Slovak government now has two months to prepare its position and send the missing documentation to Brussels. The commission confirmed it only partially approved the eighth recovery-plan payment worth €735m, adding that Slovakia had not fulfilled two commitments concerning national park zoning and preparation of a wind farm zone. In its plans, Slovakia had not classified all threatened forests under the highest level of protection available. And the country also failed to show that the area chosen for a wind energy acceleration zone was suitable for building wind farms with a capacity of at least 300 megawatts. As a result, €62.5m is expected to be withheld. “Should the Commission, following Slovakia’s observations, confirm its assessment that the milestones in question have not been satisfactorily fulfilled, it will proportionally reduce the amount corresponding to this milestone and target, out of the total €548m under this payment request,” read an EU press release . Read more MEPs warn against EU rush to restarting funds for Hungary while corruption and plurality concerns remain Ex-environment minister to blame? Both problematic milestones are linked to steps taken by the former Slovak environment minister Tomáš Taraba. Taraba was removed from office in September 2026 after falling out with the right-wing Slovak National Party who had appointed him in 2023. Slovak prime minister Robert Fico has taken over his office for the time being. The office of the deputy prime minister, temporarily headed by education minister Tomáš Drucker (belonging to the left-wing Voice party), blames the previous cabinet for forest and wind energy zoning plan problems. noticias.titulo: EU Commission again rebukes Temu over failure to stop illegal product sales, exposing Chinese giant to another hefty fine
noticias.resumen: Temu failed to take sufficient action to stop illegal or unsafe products being put on sale, the EU Commission has found preliminarily. It comes as part of a probe into the company's compliance with the Digital Services Act. The Chinese shopping website has disputed the latest findings.
noticias.texto: Temu failed to take sufficient action to stop illegal or unsafe products being put on sale, the EU Commission concluded on Tuesday (17 November), as part of a lengthy probe to assess its compliance with EU law launched in 2024. The commission found that the online marketplace had “ineffective controls” in place to ensure that products sold on its platform met EU safety requirements. It also says this amounts to a breach of the Digital Services Act , the EU’s rulebook for online platforms, which has been in force since August 2023. The commission’s latest findings of insufficient mitigation against the sale of illegal items follow a decision in May that Temu’s risk assessments were inadequate, leading Temu to pay a €200m fine . The Chinese online shopping retailer has been investigated over the alleged listing of illegal products, as well as addictive design, recommendation algorithms and data-sharing. Temu has more than 120 million users in the EU, according to commission officials. “We’re happy to see the Commission has taken consumer organisations complaints and evidence seriously regarding how Temu’s fails to meet its obligations. Consumers should be able to shop safely on these very large online marketplaces,” said Agustín Reyna, director general of consumer protection body BEUC .
