noticias.texto:
Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia.
The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover. The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who said they had been moved without the necessary permissions.
The department of forestry, fisheries and the environment confirmed the trees had been destined for Georgia but did not name the buyer.
The case echoes an episode in Kenya four years ago, when eight baobabs were uprooted to be exported to Shekvetili Dendrological Park, owned by Bidzina Ivanishvili, an influential Georgian billionaire and the country’s former prime minister. Ivanishvili has filled the park with ancient, giant trees from Georgia, transporting them by boat along the Black Sea.
The export of the Kenyan baobabs was initially blocked after an outcry by environmentalists, who condemned their export as biopiracy, but later allowed to go ahead.
Otherwise, such exports are very rare, say experts. David Newton, programme office director for east and southern Africa for Traffic, an NGO that monitors the trade in wild animals and plants, said: “It is very unusual to see baobabs being used as ornamental plants … mainly because they are exceptionally difficult to dig out of the ground and transport, and then to successfully re-establish.”
Sarah Venter, founder of the Baobab Foundation, who has led efforts to replant the South African trees, said she believes they have a good chance of surviving if they are replanted quickly. The winter months of May to October, when the trees lose their leaves and are dormant, is a good time to move them.
“As soon as spring starts [in November], the trees use their water to flush their new leaves, and that’s when we need to get them into the ground as soon as possible,” she said.
The rescue mission has faced delays because of the challenges associated with moving such large trees, which are transported on special trucks capable of carrying abnormal loads. The five baobabs weigh between 19 and 29 tonnes, have a diameter of up to 4.5 metres (15ft) and a height of up to 12.5 metres.
Baobabs, known as the tree of life, are protected under South African law, which means a permit is required to cut or disturb them.
“A baobab isn’t just part of an ecosystem, it is an ecosystem in itself,” said Wambui Ippolito, a landscape designer, lecturer and horticulturist from Kenya. “These trees are biodiversity anchors.”
Animals ranging from bats and bush babies, to grey-headed parrots and the southern ground hornbill shelter in its cavities, while elephants, monkeys and warthogs feast on its fruit.
The trees have huge cultural importance, added Ippolito. “It has always been a sacred tree in Africa. It doesn’t matter where you go: Senegal, Mali, Ghana – wherever you go, if there is a community around a baobab tree, that tree is sacred,” she said. “Somebody’s great-great-great-great-great-grandparents sat under that tree, and it is part of human history in that area.”
Baobabs have shallow roots, which means they do not need to be planted very deeply, and these regrow fairly quickly, said Venter. Once replanted, the trees will be stabilised with cables and protected by electric fences to prevent damage from elephants.
The trees are thought to be between 200 and 300 years old. “Baobabs easily reach 1,000 years old, so they’ve got a few hundred years ahead of them if they survive,” said Venter.
A criminal case has been opened against the owner of a landscaping company allegedly responsible for the illegal harvesting and transportation of the trees.
Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

noticias.titulo: One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN
noticias.resumen: Almost half of women in west and central Africa cannot withhold consent, with girls worst affected, UNFPA finds One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report. In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund ( UNFPA ) published on Thursday. Co
noticias.texto:
One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report.
In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) published on Thursday.
Younger women and girls aged 15 to 19 had even less power to say no, compared with older women aged 45 to 49, according to analysis in the report of eight countries with comparable data (Angola, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kazakhstan, Malawi, Mali, Nigeria, Tajikistan and Zambia). The findings align with research showing adolescent girls endure very high rates of intimate partner violence.
“These are really sad figures,” said Jean-Paul Murunga, a lawyer with the global human rights organisation Equality Now. “Especially given that the continent of Africa as a whole has adopted the Maputo protocol, which sets [binding legal standards for] equality between women and men. We still have a lot of work to do to ensure women and girls benefit from these commitments.”
The Maputo protocol, a landmark treaty adopted by the African Union in 2003, guarantees women’s rights and obliges states to protect women from violence. It affirms that marriage must be based on full consent and guarantees women’s right to health.
“The underlying principle is unambiguous: sexual intercourse without free and voluntary consent constitutes sexual violence, including within marriage,” said Murunga. “Marriage does not create perpetual or implied consent. A woman retains the right to decide whether, when and how she engages in sexual activity”.
He said that as a first step rape laws across the continent needed to change. According to Murunga’s 2024 report, rape within marriage is not criminalised in some African countries. Seven countries expressly exempt husbands from prosecution for marital rape, including Côte d’Ivoire, Ethiopia and South Sudan. Some countries, such as Tanzania and Eritrea, only criminalise marital rape when the couple do not live together.
In countries where child marriage is permitted and marital rape is not criminalised, children are left unprotected. A legal loophole is created for what, outside marriage, would be classed as rape, and young wives have few options when it comes to protecting themselves from sexual violence and exploitation. In Gabon, for example, when a man has married a child he abducted, he can only be prosecuted after the marriage is annulled.
Underpinning these laws is the mistaken belief that marital rape does not exist as a concept because, by marrying, wives are assumed to have permanently consented to sex with their husbands. In many areas, religion plays a key role in affirming these beliefs.
Alimatu Dimonekene, founder of A Girl At A Time, an organisation supporting adolescent girls in Sierra Leone, said a conversation around consent in marriage had yet to begin in Africa. “We’ve not even started the conversation [around marital rape],” she said. “Women will never call it rape; they make excuses for it or even blame themselves.”
She added: “In west Africa, sex is seen as an obligation in marriage. You must do whatever your husband demands.
“Once he has paid your bride price [a traditional marriage custom in which the bride’s family are paid money, livestock or goods by the groom], he owns you and you cannot reject his demands. Whatever he wants, he gets, including in terms of intimacy, finances and raising the children.”

noticias.titulo: Datacentres to create 70% more carbon emissions by 2030, IEA report warns
noticias.resumen: Global energy watchdog forecasts huge rise as US and China turn to fossil fuels to power AI growth agendas The world’s datacentres will create 70% more carbon emissions within the next four years as the US and China turn to fossil fuels to power their AI growth agendas, according to the world’s energy watchdog. The International Energy Agency (IEA) warned that datacentres will consume twice as much electricity by 2030 compared with today, with the global expansion of artificial intelligence accounting for three-quarters of this growth. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
The world’s datacentres will create 70% more carbon emissions within the next four years as the US and China turn to fossil fuels to power their AI growth agendas, according to the world’s energy watchdog.
The International Energy Agency (IEA) warned that datacentres will consume twice as much electricity by 2030 compared with today, with the global expansion of artificial intelligence accounting for three-quarters of this growth.
The Paris-based agency found that the breakneck pace of the industry’s growth means that within four years AI datacentres will consume an extra 350 terrawatt-hours of electricity every year, or more than the annual electricity consumption of Great Britain.
Its influential annual report warned that the world’s energy future was less certain after the impact of the Middle East war, which it has described as the greatest energy market disruption in history.
“I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before,” said the IEA’s executive director Fatih Birol.
Instead, it will be reshaped by the policy decisions governments make after the crisis to meet the increasing demand for energy to power a growing global population, the rising need for air-conditioning and a booming AI economy, the IEA said.
Datacentre developers have emerged as the world’s biggest corporate buyers of renewable energy to help fuel their servers which have a connection to local power grids. Despite this, the report showed that the appetite for fossil fuels is expected to grow even faster, particularly in the US and China.
By the end of the decade, around half of the electricity needed to power China’s AI datacentres will come from coal power plants, according to the IEA. The rest will come from renewable energy, with smaller amounts from nuclear reactors and very little from gas plants.
In contrast, the US is expected to rely on gas to provide about 60% of the electricity for its datacentres by 2030. There were plans for about 180GW of new gas-fired power plants linked to US datacentres in August this year, the agency said. That is almost as much new gas capacity as the total now installed across the European Union.
As a result of the growth in fossil fuel generation for datacentres, emissions associated with this sector were on track to rise by 70% by 2030, the IEA said.
The appetite for gas power among US datacentre developers is more than 16 times higher than in Canada, where the IEA identified plans for 11GW of gas generation to power their servers. In the rest of the world, AI developers have put forward plans for new gas plants with a combined capacity of just 4GW, the agency said.
This is because renewable energy is expected to play a greater role in supplying datacentres outside the US and China. In the EU, the IEA expects datacentres to rely on renewables for about 70% of their electricity by 2030 – followed by nuclear power, gas generation, and a very small amount of coal power.
The agency based its forecasts for the notoriously opaque industry on data showing the annual global shipment of AI servers, which have climbed eighteen-fold since 2020. It also used space-based imagery to track the buildout of 93 large “AI factories” around the world.
Its analysis suggests that the world’s datacentre capacity has climbed tenfold in the last 24 months to 17GW. By the time the AI factories were completed, their combined capacity was likely to be about 50GW, the IEA said.
The world’s existing stock of datacentres, including those with AI-optimised servers, now stands at 120GW, with 80% of this capacity in China, the US and the EU. A further 120GW will be built by the end of the decade under the IEA scenario often considered its central base case, of which three-quarters will be AI datacentres.

noticias.titulo: Mark Speakman resigns and says Liberals face ‘existential threat’ as NSW exodus continues
noticias.resumen: Former NSW opposition leader warns party against becoming ‘Labor lite’ or ‘One Nation lite’ in late-night speech Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Former New South Wales opposition leader, Mark Speakman, will not contest his seat at the March state election, the latest in a mass exodus of MPs under the Liberal leader who replaced him, Kellie Sloane. In a late-night speech on Thursday, the final sitting day of NSW’s legislative assembly ahead of the vote, Speakman said he would not contest his south Sydney seat of Cronulla, which he has held since 2011. Continue readi
noticias.texto:
Former New South Wales opposition leader, Mark Speakman, will not contest his seat at the March state election, the latest in a mass exodus of MPs under the Liberal leader who replaced him, Kellie Sloane.
In a late-night speech on Thursday, the final sitting day of NSW’s legislative assembly ahead of the vote, Speakman said he would not contest his south Sydney seat of Cronulla, which he has held since 2011.
He is the eighth out of 24 current Liberal MPs to announce they will not re-contest their seat in March, following Jordan Lane, Mark Coure, Tanya Davies, Ray Williams, James Griffin, Mark Taylor and Alister Henskens.
The announcement comes almost a year to the day after Speakman resigned from the leadership of the opposition in a spill in favour of Sloane, who was elected unopposed.
In that time the Coalition has gone from commanding 28% of the primary vote in New South Wales to 23%, Sydney Morning Herald Resolve polling suggests.
Labor has gone from 37% to 30%, while One Nation, which Resolve did not start polling separately until March, is currently at 26%.
Last week, Sloane said her party would not form government with One Nation, but she did not rule out a confidence and supply arrangement. The Australian Financial Review has reported many of her MPs privately expect the Liberals to go into a coalition with One Nation.
In his speech in the dying minutes of the parliamentary term, Speakman, a member of the party’s moderate faction, warned the Liberals against becoming “Labor lite” or “One Nation lite”, saying they should stick to the values of “Menzian Liberalism”.
Referencing Pauline Hanson’s notion of “monoculture”, Speakman said Australia was “the most successful multicultural society on the planet” and was “so much better for it”.
“You know, we hear certain people say we want a monoculture, and that people who don’t support that monoculture somehow are enemies of Australia, hate Australia,” he said.
“I love Australia for its multiculturalism. Diversity is our strength. It is our strength, and we should build on that.”
Speakman, a barrister, served as minister for the environment between 2015 and 2017, and was attorney general between 2017 and the Perrottet government’s defeat in the 2023 election.
He was chosen as Liberal and opposition leader following Perrottet’s resignation, a position he held until November last year.
On Thursday, he said being opposition leader “is often said to be the toughest job in politics” and while it had “ultimately unravelled” for him, he had mostly led an opposition “which was competitive with, or even ahead of, the government in the polls”.
He said his record as attorney general included legislating for NSW to be the first Australian jurisdiction to criminalise coercive control, introducing affirmative consent tests in criminal sexual assault trials and reforming criminal and civil child sexual abuse cases.
Speakman’s resignation, ending speculation which bubbled up again when he spoke during question time on Thursday, is the latest blow for Sloane, who he said in his leaving speech had the “attributes to be a great premier”.
Earlier on Thursday, the NSW premier, Chris Minns, announced former Liberal councillor and parliamentary staffer Tanya Raffoul would contest the Liberal-held seat of Epping as a Labor candidate.

noticias.titulo: Guardian Australia takes home two Walkley awards for excellence in journalism
noticias.resumen: Stories revealing Pauline Hanson’s US trip with Gina Rinehart and the systematic betrayal of Kardell Lomas before her death recognised Guardian Australia journalists have won two Walkley awards, one for a story about the systemic betrayal of a woman who was killed by her partner, and another for an exclusive story that revealed Pauline Hanson had travelled to the US with mining billionaire Gina Rinehart. Investigative reporter Sarah Martin won the award for print/text news report for her exclusive story that revealed the One Nation leader and her chief of staff, James Ashby, travelled with Rin
noticias.texto:
Guardian Australia journalists have won two Walkley awards, one for a story about the systemic betrayal of a woman who was killed by her partner, and another for an exclusive story that revealed Pauline Hanson had travelled to the US with mining billionaire Gina Rinehart.
Investigative reporter Sarah Martin won the award for print/text news report for her exclusive story that revealed the One Nation leader and her chief of staff, James Ashby, travelled with Rinehart on the mining magnate’s Gulfstream 700 on 27 October last year.
The pair stayed at Rinehart’s Palm Beach mansion, close to US president Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago resort.
After Guardian Australia published details of Hanson’s flight, her office lodged an amendment to the registrar of senators’ interests declaring the sponsored travel.
Queensland correspondent Ben Smee and the Guardian team won the award for coverage of Indigenous affairs for the story of the betrayal of Kardell Lomas, who repeatedly sought help – from domestic violence support services and the police – to escape the violent and dangerous man who killed her.
Lomas had 24 interactions with various agencies – and she repeatedly disclosed fears for her safety, death threats, serious violence and other abuse.
Smee and Martin were finalists in two other categories, Martin for ‘Inside One Nation’ and Smee for his feature “‘Starting to frighten me’: the final weeks of Hannah Clarke’s life”.
Business editor Jonathan Barrett was also a finalist, in the print/text feature writing category, for his story “‘A child goes to bed and doesn’t wake up’: the families left in shock after the sudden death of their healthy children”.
The 2026 Walkley print/text award for feature writing under 4,000 words was awarded to the Australian Financial Review’s Sam Buckingham-Jones for the story “Maccas in a Rolls: inside Kyle Sandilands’ pivot to $100 tradie plans”.
For feature writing over 4,000 words, the Age and The Sydney Morning Herald’s Melissa Fyfe and Carla Hildebrandt took home the award for their story “Virginia: the Final Chapter”.
The scoop of the year was awarded to the ABC team behind “Bondi: what ASIO knew”, which included Sean Rubinsztein-Dunlop, Olivia Caisley, and Michael Workman.
Tony Wright, an associate editor and special writer for The Age and The Sydney Morning Herald, took home the award for outstanding contribution to journalism.

noticias.titulo: Tammy Shipley was supposed to be monitored in prison. Instead she died after drinking 20L of water
noticias.resumen: If the Aboriginal woman had been checked at regular intervals as required, her ‘excess consumption of water’ would have been prevented, inquest finds • Warning: This article contains images of and references to Indigenous Australians who have died Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast The death of an Aboriginal woman who collapsed after drinking at least 20 litres of water in a New South Wales prison cell was preventable and the result of systemic failures, a coroner has found. Tammy Michelle Shipley, 47, died at Silverwater women’s correctional centre on 20 December 202
noticias.texto:
The death of an Aboriginal woman who collapsed after drinking at least 20 litres of water in a New South Wales prison cell was preventable and the result of systemic failures, a coroner has found.
Tammy Michelle Shipley, 47, died at Silverwater women’s correctional centre on 20 December 2022.
State coroner Teresa O’Sullivan ruled on Thursday that her death was caused by low blood sodium levels resulting from excessive water consumption and complications of schizoaffective disorder.
“I’m confident in finding that Tammy’s death was preventable,” O’Sullivan said.
The mother of five had been taken into custody on remand 11 days earlier, after being charged with shoplifting offences, but didn’t disclose her mental health issues to police. Police also didn’t double-check her answers about her health, despite the fact she had attended a police station two weeks earlier and told them she heard her neighbour talking in her head.
O’Sullivan found there had been a missed opportunity to recognise the mental health issues that were present, and to potentially divert Shipley away from the criminal justice system.
When she appeared in a local court over the shoplifting charges the next day, the magistrate was not told she had been refused bail on other charges, so made orders they thought would secure her release.
“There was a clear systems failure,” O’Sullivan found.
Shipley should have been continually monitored – both physically and electronically – after twice attempting self-harm in custody.
It was a serious failure that this had not been done, O’Sullivan said.
“If observations had been carried out at the intervals required, it was likely that Tammy’s excess consumption of water would have been … prevented,” she said.
She deemed it unsatisfactory that Shipley had not been seen by a psychiatrist or mental health nurse at any point during the 11 days before her death.
She added that Shipley should have received medical care from the time she started vomiting, after 10am on the day of her death. Instead, she said, Shipley experienced seizures shortly before noon and was seen lying face down on the floor of her cell around an hour later.
A period of 23 minutes lapsed between when she was first seen lying on the ground and the commencement of resuscitation attempts, which the coroner found was unacceptable.
One corrective services officer had hastily closed the door to her cell after smelling faeces in the room earlier in the day.
“It was completely inappropriate that Tammy, who was known to be suffering a mental health condition, was left in that condition in her cell,” O’Sullivan said.
O’Sullivan made 10 recommendations to NSW police, Corrective Services NSW and Justice Health, including a review of the “austere and depressing” unit in which Shipley was held, which was intended to be a therapeutic space but left the coroner gravely concerned.
She also recommended regular monitoring of footage inside the jail and improved maintenance and cross-checking of records related to mental health conditions.
The coroner acknowledged the jail had already made changes after Shipley’s death.
Outside the court, Shipley’s mother, Vicki, said she hoped the findings would force the system to assess how people are treated.
“I honestly thought that at this stage of our country’s development, we have moved past how convicts were treated,” she said.
“The system – every system – eventually caused trauma to my daughter, until eventually it killed her.”
Vickey Shipley urged the NSW government to quickly implement the recommendations.
“If they’re not made, there will be some other family standing here doing exactly the same thing that I am,” she said.
“All too often we hear the cry: ‘There’s not enough money.’
“How much is a life worth?”

noticias.titulo: Mother whose twin baby died was determined to have home birth despite advice of experts, NSW inquest hears
noticias.resumen: Inquest into deaths of four babies in northern NSW between 2022 and 2024 told mother refused to give birth in hospital after hearing others’ traumatic stories Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Baby B’s mother was so determined to have a home birth she ignored the advice of experts – including her own midwife, an inquest has heard. The inquest heard she was pregnant with twins, which she described as a “wonderful shock”, and didn’t want a hospital birth because she had heard of others’ traumatic experiences. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Baby B’s mother was so determined to have a home birth she ignored the advice of experts – including her own midwife, an inquest has heard.
The inquest heard she was pregnant with twins, which she described as a “wonderful shock”, and didn’t want a hospital birth because she had heard of others’ traumatic experiences.
The New South Wales coroner’s court in Lismore heard on Thursday that the local medical community in the Hunter Valley swung in to action, warning the mother – who cannot be named for legal reasons – that a home birth was risky while also preparing in case something went wrong.
Baby B died of a bacterial infection, while the other baby got sick but survived.
Baby B’s death is part of an ongoing inquest into the deaths of four babies – Baby R, Baby D, Baby DH and Baby B – who were born in free births or home births in NSW’s northern rivers region between 2022 and 2024.
The first three babies died after a free birth – where no medical professionals are present. By contrast, four midwives were part of the birthing plan for Baby B. The main midwife continued to support the woman.
“The alternative was that she would birth at home with no support whatsoever,” the midwife – whose name is suppressed – told the court.
The court heard that expert opinion found that the midwives’ treatment was “reasonable and appropriate”, which was a clear distinction from the other three births being examined at the inquest.
“It will also be clear from the expert evidence that a home birth was still considered by the experts to be not suitable in the circumstances,” the court heard.
Expert witness, Prof Hannah Dahlen, said that was because it was a twin pregnancy, that it had continued beyond 41 weeks, that there had been no specialist review, that the family were far away from the hospital, and that “there was a possible need for urgent operative birth and the need to provide simultaneous skilled care and resuscitation for two babies”.
But the mother declined multiple checks, and her distrust of the medical system was only reinforced as the pregnancy progressed.
She had scans at 12 weeks and at 22 weeks, but chose not to have hospital antenatal care, or to consult with an obstetrician. A local doctor followed up, but she told them she was doing well.
Her midwife recommended monthly ultrasounds, and induction at 36 to 37 weeks. She declined. The midwife told the court she warned the mother about the risks at every visit.
In evidence read to the court, the mother said she had always planned to have a home birth after hearing traumatic birth stories from other people.
“I did a lot of research and found the midwives, so … I felt comfortable to still home birth the twins,” she said.
She said she was “quite selective” finding midwives with home birth experience and had researched the experience online and in books.
The court heard “a lot of staff” at the local hospital were concerned about the plan, and the ambulance service was worried enough to organise a second paediatric resuscitation kit. There was collaboration and communication between the midwife, obstetricians from the local hospital, and a local GP.
In court, the midwife said the mother wouldn’t have hesitated to seek help if it was needed, and that she thought she could convince the mother to go to hospital, or at least somewhere closer to it.
But then ambulance officers – and later, police – turned up at the home to do a welfare check, making the mother angry, upset, and more determined not to enter the health system.
“She felt quite violated because they came to her home,” the midwife told the court. “They were coercing her to attend the hospital.”
The mother went into labour at home, and the first twin was born successfully. Baby B “gave an initial gasp”, “appeared stunned” and needed help to breathe spontaneously.
Everything seemed to be fine, the court heard. The mother said the next night she could hear the baby breathing, and did not notice any changes. But in the early hours of the morning, Baby B was no longer breathing. When emergency services arrived, they noted that Baby B was “pale, unresponsive and not breathing, with no pulse, although she was still warm to touch”.
Hospital records show continued they continued to work for 45 mins to save her once she arrived there, but she was flatlining. Her blood sugar and temperature were low, and she died.
By that stage, the boy twin was limp and grey. He likely had the same infection but it was less severe, and he survived.
The midwife said she surrendered her registration after the death, both because of its effect on her and because of the way the health system treated her.
She said she wasn’t told when Baby B died. When someone from the hospital rang to ask about the surviving twin, she assumed they were asking about Baby B and asked whether she was being transferred to a bigger hospital.
“Oh, she’ll be going to the coroner,” the midwife was told.
The inquest continues.

noticias.titulo: ‘Remarkable luck’: wreck of first Australian-built warship discovered exactly 128 years after sinking
noticias.resumen: HMCS Spitfire was commissioned by colonial government to protect against Russian warships during the Crimean war The wreck of Australia’s first locally built warship has been discovered 128 years after sinking off the coast of far north Queensland. Marine archaeologists found the remains of Ex HMCS Spitfire on 21 August, the anniversary of its sinking in 1898. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
The wreck of Australia’s first locally built warship has been discovered 128 years after sinking off the coast of far north Queensland.
Marine archaeologists found the remains of Ex HMCS Spitfire on 21 August, the anniversary of its sinking in 1898.
Celeste Jordan, the principal heritage officer at Queensland’s Department of the Environment, Tourism, Science and Innovation, said it was “remarkable luck”. Rediscovering lost shipwrecks would “help ensure the stories of our past are preserved, celebrated and protected for future generations”, she said.
The 19-metre wooden gunboat, designed and built in Sydney in 1855, was commissioned by the Australian colonial government to protect against Russian warships based at Vladivostok during the Crimean war and amid concern about the French military presence in New Caledonia. It was designed to carry a 32-pounder cannon, although evidence suggests the armament may never have been fitted.
The clipper later served Queensland as a pilot vessel, before it was sold for £300 into private hands as a sea cucumber fishing vessel.
A 1981 article in the Naval Historical Review described the boat as “a sturdy little vessel”. Constructed from ironbark and blackwood, and sheathed in copper, it was designed and built by the Sydney shipbuilder John Cuthbert, and launched by his wife Susan Cuthbert from Darling Harbour in 1855.
On 21 August 1898, Spitfire developed a leak and foundered on a voyage off the coast of Queensland’s Cape York peninsula, according to the Australian National Maritime Museum. Its crew were rescued by the Japanese steamship Omi Maru.
A crew from the Australian National Maritime Museum, the Queensland government and the Royal Australian Navy found the wreck while aboard HMAS Diamantina, a minehunter vessel. The month-long expedition searched an area based on archival records, with sonar picking up the Spitfire as an acoustic anomaly.
The chief of navy, Vice Admiral Matthew Buckley, said the Spitfire occupied a unique place in Australia’s naval history. “For sailors today, this vessel represents the beginning of a story that continues in the Royal Australian Navy.”
The wreck is protected under the Underwater Cultural Heritage Act, and is one of more than 8,000 shipwrecks, sunken aircraft and other heritage sites in Australian waters.

noticias.titulo: Tusk appears to mock Trump’s Putin comment as Ukraine’s allies meet in Berlin – Europe live
noticias.resumen: After US president called Putin a friend, Poland’s PM said: ‘God, protect us from such friends’ For what it’s worth, the China-US-Russia ‘peace declaration’ issued after their meeting, and published by Chinese state media , includes absolutely no mention of Ukraine or Europe whatsoever. There is only one, rather generic, line that could be seen as close to these issues: “The three heads of state exchanged in-depth views on the current international situation and pledged to maintain strategic stability and international security.” Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
'God, protect us from such friends,' Poland's Tusk says after Trump's 'he's my friend' comments to Putin
Poland’s prime minister Donald Tusk – one of Europe’s five negotiators – does not seem to be impressed by what he saw in Shenzhen.
“God, protect us from such friends,” he said on X in an apparent reference to Trump’s enthusiastic greeting with Putin.
Poland’s foreign minister Radosław Sikorski was similarly alarmed, telling reporters:
“Indeed, it is difficult to judge, by their fruits we shall know them, but the optics of this hugging Putin, calling him a friend, causes us some concern.
Because the question arises – who is he more of a friend with, Putin or our president? And what will he possibly do if push comes to shove, which friend will he choose?”
Air defence, energy, financial support and diplomacy among Ukraine's priorities for talks in Berlin, Zelenskyy says
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy has now arrived in Berlin for today’s meeting of the Coalition of the Willing.
“More than 40 partners will be represented, including the team of the American President. Ukraine’s priorities are strengthening our air defence, energy and financial support, the diplomatic track, and the next steps toward ending the war and guaranteeing security,” he said.
Zelenskyy added Ukraine was “doing everything to ensure Europe’s full participation in the negotiation process and to make these meetings productive.”
“Bilateral meetings with European partners are also planned, and, of course, with chancellor Friedrich Merz. There will also be a format involving the American side and European national security advisers.”
The European Commission’s foreign affairs spokesperson Christian Wigand responded in very general terms to the trilateral meeting in China.
Speaking at the European Commission’s midday briefing, he said:
“We will continue following reports coming out of the discussions; we’ve also seen the statement that was published just a few minutes ago, so I would at this stage not go into any details here.”
Asked about Trump’s “he’s my friend” comment on Putin, the Commission’ chief spokesperson Paula Pinho said “in general, we do not comment on friendships.”
Wigand added:
“Russia, under Vladimir Putin’s command, is continuing its relentless attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure in Ukraine, and we would support all efforts, of course, to end this.”
France’s foreign minister Jean-Noël Barrot had little time for Trump’s summit with Xi and Putin, telling French media that he did not expect anything important to come out of that meeting.
“These three leaders fundamentally disagree on everything, so they cannot agree on anything,” Barrot told French broadcaster RTL, quoted by AP.
“And as for this photograph that has generated so much discussion, it isn’t quite a photograph of the world’s three greatest powers, because the world’s three greatest powers are the United States, of course, China and the European Union.”
“These three countries are meeting because they have something in common: They all border the Pacific,” Barrot said. He added: “These three leaders agree on nothing, so, in a sense, nothing is going to come out of this meeting.”
For what it’s worth, the China-US-Russia ‘peace declaration’ issued after their meeting,and published by Chinese state media, includes absolutely no mention of Ukraine or Europe whatsoever.
There is only one, rather generic, line that could be seen as close to these issues:
“The three heads of state exchanged in-depth views on the current international situation and pledged to maintain strategic stability and international security.”
(Side eye at Putin.)
The document also includes a commitment to promote UN reform, increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products, as well as the leaders’ criticism of the international criminal court and declaration of intent to work on reducing nuclear risks and preventing proliferation.
EU ministers are also getting some questions about tomorrow’s EU-UK summit, 10 years on from Britain’s vote to leave the bloc.
Ireland’s EU minister Thomas Byrne said the main areas to be discussed on Friday “will have very significant benefits” for all parties, with the sanitary and phytosanitary agreement set to resolve “one of the biggest problems out of Brexit.”
But he was cautious talking about future relationship with the EU, saying that while he had “no doubt that the EU and Britain will want to go further on that path, we have seen how complex even dealing with the issues for tomorrow is and how long it takes.”
Sweden’s Jessica Rosencrantz stressed it is “up to the citizens of the UK to decide how close you want to work with the EU.”
But, again, asked if Britain could rejoin the bloc and keep its historical opt-outs and rebates, she dismissed it as “a highly speculative question.”
“Let’s remember how the discussion was at the time of Brexit. In that light, I think it is amazing that we now can have a big summit together, with discussions on how we can come closer together when it comes to trade and mobility,” she said.
Poland’s EU minister Ignacy Niemczycki said Warsaw’s approach “has always been very pragmatic,” as he stressed that te EU after Brexit is “weaker.”
“I would like us, wherever possible, to work out such mechanisms so it works for both of us. … This is a country that thinks similarly to us in Europe on many issues and there is no reason for us to treat each other like enemies. We are friends and let’s find the right formula for that.
In a rather cheeky comment, he added:
“I would encourage everyone to think seriously about the benefits of being in the EU, … and I think the people of the UK see it [too], now that they are outside the union.”
Meanwhile, foreign ministers arriving for the EU foreign affairs council meeting in Brussels are heroically trying to avoid saying anything remotely interesting or controversial in response to reporters’ questions on Trump’s meetings with Xi and Putin.
Clearly, they would prefer to leave the talking to their bosses who are expected in Berlin later today.
And so, Spanish EU minister Fernando Sampedro merely said that Spain and the EU remained “strongly committed” to supporting Ukraine.
Asked specifically about his views on Trump’s comments on “his friend” Putin, he only sheepishly smiled and once again repeated his previous lines.
Sweden’s EU minister Jessica Rosencrantz said that “we don’t really know the details of this meeting, neither the agenda nor the specific issues" the leaders were planning to discuss.
“But the general principle is there should be no talks about European security without Europe;there should be no talks about Ukraine without Ukraine. That is our general attitude when it comes to issues about European security or Ukrainian security,” she said.
(For what it’s worth, her boss, Sweden’s foreign minister Maria Malmer Stenergard, was a bit more outspoken when she said early this morning that it was “worrying if we have great powers who think they should decide how the world should be governed.”)
Ireland’s EU minister Thomas Byrne struck a similar note to his Swedish counterpart, saying “nothing will be decided about Europe without Europe.”
“The only way peace can work is if Russia decides to stop its invasion.”
Meanwhile, Poland’s Europe minister Ignacy Niemczycki dismissed any comparisons between the Shenzhen meeting to the Yalta conference in 1945, saying “Europe is still very strong,” and so “the situations is very different than historically.”
“Even if some decisions were to be made, their implementation would simply be impossible without Europe’s participation,” he said.
Danish parliament votes to ratify Greenland security deal with US
Meanwhile, Denmark’s parliament unanimously ratified a security agreement with US president Donald Trump covering Greenland, hoping to end a standoff over the Arctic island’s future that has rattled transatlantic relations, Reuters reported.
The US, Denmark and Greenland signed the agreement in September to resolve tensions after Trump repeatedly threatened to take control of the mineral-rich island, a self-governing Danish territory that is home to 57,000 people.
The deal was backed by 109 Danish lawmakers and none voted against, the parliamentary tally showed.
Crimea bridge has been attacked again, says Russian-installed governor
Meanwhile, a key bridge connecting annexed Crimea to Russia has been attacked again last night, a Russian-appointed regional governor has said, two days after Ukrainian strikes caused serious damage to it.
“Following a new attack on the Crimean Bridge, traffic has been temporarily halted. All relevant services are on site and at work. An assessment of the damage is under way,” Sergei Aksyonov, the Kremlin-appointed governor of the Russian-occupied Crimea, wrote on Telegram.
The Russian transport ministry said on Thursday that no one was wounded in the attack and that train services across it had been halted.
Wednesday’s attack is third this week on the highly symbolic bridge that links Russia with Crimea, which it seized from Ukraine in 2014. A 227-metre section of the road spanning the Kerch strait was destroyed this week, but the rail corridor appears to be operable despite sustaining some damage.
'We are going to be discussing the war between Russia and Ukraine,' Trump says
On Ukraine, Trump says at the beginning of the trilateral meeting:
“We are going to be discussing the war between Russia and Ukraine, and we already have. President Putin and I have had a long discussion today for quite a while. That’s what pretty much what the discussion was about.
And I think things are happening.
I think that he and – I hope - the other side would like to see an end to that war.”
God knows what that’s supposed to mean in practice.
'Together we are making history,' Trump declares as trilateral with Putin, Xi gets under way
The trilateral meeting is now getting under way, with Trump declaring “together we are making history” with the three leaders facing “a special responsibility to maintain open, respectful and productive dialogue on issues impacting not just our people, but the entire planet.”
Our coverage of the Apec summit is here, but I will pick up any lines on Ukraine:
'God, protect us from such friends,' Poland's Tusk says after Trump's 'he's my friend' comments to Putin
Poland’s prime minister Donald Tusk – one of Europe’s five negotiators – does not seem to be impressed by what he saw in Shenzhen.
“God, protect us from such friends,” he said on X in an apparent reference to Trump’s enthusiastic greeting with Putin.
Poland’s foreign minister Radosław Sikorski was similarly alarmed, telling reporters:
“Indeed, it is difficult to judge, by their fruits we shall know them, but the optics of this hugging Putin, calling him a friend, causes us some concern.
Because the question arises – who is he more of a friend with, Putin or our president? And what will he possibly do if push comes to shove, which friend will he choose?”
Morning opening: Ukraine's allies meet in Berlin, anxious to hear about Trump's meeting with Putin, Xi
Jakub Krupa
Several European leaders from the Coalition of the Willing are meeting in Berlin today, just hours after US president Donald Trump, Russia president Vladimir Putin and China president Xi Jinping are due to meet in Shenhzen.
The trilateral meeting is due to get under way any moment now, though the tone of Trump’s earlier talks with Putin will already be worrying for Europeans.
“Who is he? He’s my friend!” said Trump, absolutely beaming, as soon as he saw Putin.
These images will send a shiver down the spine of Europe’s top leaders as they prepare to leave for Berlin to attend the “coalition of the willing”’s latest coordination meeting.
Europe’s newly appointed negotiating team of Andy Burnham, Emmanuel Macron, Giorgia Meloni, Friedrich Merz and Donald Tusk plus the EU’s Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa will be joined by several other leaders for a meeting with US peace envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, where they are expected to get a read out from the meeting in China.
Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Nato’s secretary general Mark Rutte are expected to attend, as are several other key European leaders, including Finland’s Alexander Stubb, Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen, Sweden’s Ulf Kristersson, Norway’s Jonas Gahr Støre, and Ireland’s Micheál Martin (and many others).
I will bring you all the latest from Berlin and reactions to Trump’s trilateral meeting.
It’s Thursday, 19 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

noticias.titulo: Myanmar committed acts of genocide against Rohingya minority, world’s top court rules
noticias.resumen: Judgment ends seven-year legal battle and is seen as critical test for dealing with most serious of all state crimes Myanmar committed acts of genocide against its Rohingya minority during “clearance operations” nearly a decade ago, the world’s highest court has ruled. The judgment from the international court of justice (ICJ) – which has never previously found a state responsible for genocide – ends a seven-year legal battle and is seen as a critical global test for dealing with the most serious of all state crimes. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Myanmar committed acts of genocide against its Rohingya minority during “clearance operations” nearly a decade ago, the world’s highest court has ruled.
The judgment from the international court of justice (ICJ) – which has never previously found a state responsible for genocide – ends a seven-year legal battle and is seen as a critical global test for dealing with the most serious of all state crimes.
“The court is fully convinced that Myanmar committed acts falling under … the genocide convention with an intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population in Myanmar,” the ICJ president, Yuji Iwasawa, said during a reading of the judgment.
A 2016-17 campaign by Myanmar’s military forced more than 700,000 mostly Muslim Rohingya to flee across the border into Bangladesh, with refugees arriving with stories of mass killings of adults and children, gang-rapes and burned-down villages.
Governments have been anxiously awaiting the decision, handed down in The Hague, the Netherlands, where the UN-run court is based, in part because the ruling will set a precedent for genocide claims, notably a high-profile case against Israel.
Genocide, defined after the Nazi Holocaust by a 1948 UN convention, is harder to prove than war crimes because it requires evidence of specific “intent” to destroy a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.
Myanmar’s case was raised by the Gambia, a Muslim-majority state, on behalf of Myanmar survivors. It rested on claims of genocidal statements and “patterns of conduct” that showed attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state, including gunning down people as they fled and blocking their return.
In January, the ICJ held closed-door sessions to hear from survivors who travelled from camps in Bangladesh. More than 1 million Rohingya still live there in the world’s largest refugee settlement, and fewer than 600,000 are estimated to remain in Buddhist-majority Myanmar.
Refugees who fled to Bangladesh told the Guardian in 2017 of a massacre in the village of Tula Toli, where survivors described systematic shooting of civilians, mass graves and the drowning of children in a river. That village, which satellite footage later showed had been burned down, was one of several analysed by rights investigators and built a case for genocide.
During hearings, the Gambian justice minister, Dawda Jallow, told the court the case was not “about esoteric issues of international law”.
“It is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings,” said Jallow. “The Rohingya of Myanmar. They have been targeted for destruction.”
Legal experts see Thursday’s judgment as a key test for sexual violence in genocide assessments, as the convention says the crime can include acts with the intent to “prevent births”. Investigators have said gang-rapes and accounts of soldiers mutilating women’s genitals were carried out intentionally and systematically to stop reproduction.
Myanmar denied carrying out a genocide and claims its actions targeted a Rohingya militant group that conducted guerrilla-style attacks. Its military responded with massive “clearance operations”.
The country’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-2017 attacks, has a pending arrest warrant from the international criminal court (ICC), which prosecutes individuals and not states like the ICJ, on allegations of crimes against humanity.
The former general overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely discredited.
While the ICJ does not have the power to enforce rulings, its decisions are considered binding, carry diplomatic weight and can shape international action, including sanctions.
Israel and its chief ally, the US, have been closely following the Myanmar case as the decision provides the strongest hint of how judges might assess the Gaza case, brought by South Africa. UN independent investigations, as well as genocide scholars, have already said Israel committed acts of genocide in Gaza.
A judgment finding Myanmar had breached the convention has been predicted to lead to the US imposing sanctions on ICJ judges, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay.
Washington had considered the Rohingya crisis to be a genocide, based on a decision by the Biden administration. However, the Trump administration has been on the offensive against international rights bodies, including imposing sanctions on the ICC.
Two other ICJ cases dealing with atrocities in the 1990s Balkans wars fell short of finding states directly responsible for genocide, although Serbia was found legally responsible for failing to prevent or punish genocide committed by Bosnian Serb troops at the Srebrenica massacre.
Other UN tribunals have established genocide in only a handful of cases since the Holocaust, including Cambodia’s Khmer Rouge rule in the 1970s and the 1994 mass killings in Rwanda.

noticias.titulo: Violent protests and killings in Bangladesh ahead of exiled Sheikh Hasina’s planned return
noticias.resumen: Awami League party called for ⁠nationwide protest on Thursday after the government rejected Hasina’s request for passport Parts of Bangladesh were shut down Thursday as protests by supporters of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina sparked clashes, bomb blasts and arson attacks, with the ancestral home ⁠of former leader Muhammad Yunus set ablaze in the violence. Hasina’s Awami League party had called for a ​week-long programme of protests and rallies to mobilise support ‌for Hasina’s planned return in December , culminating in a ‌nationwide lockdown on Thursday. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Parts of Bangladesh were shut down Thursday as protests by supporters of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina sparked clashes, bomb blasts and arson attacks, with the ancestral home of former leader Muhammad Yunus set ablaze in the violence.
Hasina’s Awami League party had called for a week-long programme of protests and rallies to mobilise support for Hasina’s planned return in December, culminating in a nationwide lockdown on Thursday.
Hasina, who has lived in exile in neighbouring India since she fled Dhaka following violent protests demanding her resignation in August 2024, has requested a new passport and identity card to facilitate her return. Her supporters are protesting against the government’s rejection of that request.
To deter violence, 97 platoons of the Bangladesh Border Guard fanned out across seven districts, including Gopalganj and Faridpur, considered to have many Hasina supporters, a spokesperson said.
Police said former interim leader Yunus’ ancestral home in Chattogram, about 300km (186 miles) south-east of Dhaka, was set on fire late on Wednesday.
It is likely that flammable substances were thrown into an unused ground-floor room, police told Reuters, adding that Yunus’ paternal family members, who live on the upper floors, are safe.
Reuters could not immediately reach the Yunus Centre thinktank that speaks on his behalf to seek comment. Yunus and his government, which led Bangladesh after Hasina’s ouster, have faced hostility from her supporters.
During the last 10 days of protests, police have reported dozens of crude bomb blasts and incidents of vehicles being set afire in at least 28 districts, injuring several police officials and members of the public, media have said.
Late on Tuesday, an activist of the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist party (BNP) was allegedly killed by unidentified people during a protest near Hasina’s home district of Gopalganj, police said.
On the same night, a crude bomb exploded outside the Dhaka residence of cultural affairs minister Nitai Roy Chowdhury, and the house of a BNP lawmaker and shops belonging to BNP supporters in Gopalganj were set on fire, police added.
On Wednesday morning, a bus company helper was burnt to death in the southern district of Pirojpur after two buses were set on fire, authorities said.
Tuesday marks a year since Hasina was sentenced to death by a local court that found her guilty of ordering a deadly crackdown on a student-led uprising against her in 2024. She has lived in exile in neighbouring India since fleeing Dhaka.
On Thursday, authorities detained former education minister Nurul Islam Nahid, who faces charges over several killings during the 2024 protests, from his house in Dhaka, police told Reuters.
At least 37 branches and offices of Grameen Bank, set up by Yunus, have been targeted in arson attacks or attempted fires since 10 November, with 14 more attacked since midnight on Tuesday, the bank said.
On Tuesday, the home minister Salahuddin Ahmed accused Awami League leaders abroad of inciting supporters to destabilise Bangladesh and torch property, adding that those involved in violence would be identified and prosecuted.
Awami League leaders, most of them in hiding, could not be reached for comment.

noticias.titulo: Badenoch says using amputee athletes to justify cutting disability benefits was ‘message of hope’ – UK politics live
noticias.resumen: PM has asked Badenoch to withdraw her suggestion that benefits should be cut because ‘double amputees run marathons’ These are from my colleague Peter Walker , who was at the Tory event where James Cleverly was named as the party’s candidate for London mayor. Peter posted this before the result was announced. Khan (who may or may not stand a 4th time) has thus far faced a dilettante who decided to campaign on a racist platform (Zack Goldsmith) and two oddballs in Shaun Bailey and then Susan Hall. Not even he can be lucky yet again Interesting that [the Conservatives] did not say how many votes
noticias.texto:
Badenoch says using amputee athletes to justify cutting disability benefits was ‘message of hope’
Good morning. At PMQs yesterday Andy Burnham said that Kemi Badenoch should withdraw the “double amputees run marathons” comment that she used to justify the Tory plan to cut sickness and disability benefits by £14bn. It was “crass and insensitive”, he said.
This morning Badenoch defended what she was saying claimed that, in fact, she was delivering a “message of hope”.
In an interview on the Today programme, asked if she accepted that her remark was insensitive, Badenoch said she didn’t. She went on:
I will speak the truth and I will say what I believe is common sense. And what I know is that, if people can work, then we should encourage them to work.
And what I’m saying is actually a message of hope, that if people even with significant, problems can work, then those who have ADHD and mild anxiety should go to work.
When the presenter, Nick Robinson, put it to her that it was unreasonable to use an exceptional case as a guide to what most disabled people should be doing, Badenoch did not agree. “We do use extreme examples to illustrate things,” she said.
Robinson tried again, saying she was taking “one extreme case [to] imply that anybody on disability benefits should just get on with it”. Badenoch accused him of “faux outrage” and “tone policing”. She added:
People are free to disagree, but they know where I’m coming from.
I will post more from the interview shortly.
Today the news will be dominated by two summits. This afternoon Burnham is in Berlin for a meeting of the pro-Ukraine coalition of the willing. We have coverage of this on our Europe live blog.
And in China, Vladimir Putin, who invaded Ukraine, Xi Jinping, his leading ally, and Donald Trump, who is seen by many as a closet Putin ally, are meeting now. You can read about that here.
We will have comments open in about an hour. That is because I will be doing a Q&A this afternoon, probably from about 3pm, and I will try to answer as many questions as possible. Do post them below the line.
Here is the agenda for the day.
9.30am: Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state and Cabinet Office minister, takes questions in the Commons.
10am: The Conservative party announces the results of the first round of voting in the election of its candidate for London mayor for 2028. James Cleverly, the former home secretary and former foreign secretary, is expected to get more than 50% of the vote, meaning a second round of voting should not be necessary.
11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.
Noon: Heather Hallett, the Covid inquiry chair, publishes her report on the test, trace and isolate system.
Around 12.15pm (UK time):Andy Burnham arrives in Berlin for a meeting of the pro-Ukraine coalition of the willing. He is expected to speak to the media later in the afternoon after the plenary has finished.
1pm: Chris Bryant, the Northern Ireland secretary, attends a meeting of the British-Irish Intergovernmental Conference in Dublin.
Labour has issued this statement about James Cleverly being selected as the Tory candidate for London mayor. It is from Bridget Phillipson, the Labour chair.
James Cleverly has a record of failure and now wants to inflict his disastrous CV on London.
He backed a no deal Brexit and Liz Truss’s disastrous mini-budget, voted for cuts to policing and youth services, and opposed action to clean up London’s air.
Londoners should never forgive and never forget the damage the Conservatives did to our capital. They deserve a better future, not a return to the same old Tory failure.
UK must decide whether it wants to be or not to be in EU, says Rosencrantz at EU summit
Jakub Krupa
Jakub Krupa writes the Guardian’s Europe live blog.
Over in Brussels, EU ministers are arriving for foreign affairs talks, with questions already popping up about tomorrow’s EU-UK summit, 10 years on from Britain’s vote to leave the bloc.
Ireland’s EU minister Thomas Byrne said the main areas to be discussed on Friday “will have very significant benefits” for all parties, with the sanitary and phytosanitary agreement set to resolve “one of the biggest problems out of Brexit”.
But he was cautious talking about the future relationship with the EU, saying that while he had “no doubt that the EU and Britain will want to go further on that path, we have seen how complex even dealing with the issues for tomorrow is and how long it takes.”
Sweden’s Jessica Rosencrantz stressed it is “up to the citizens of the UK to decide how close you want to work with the EU”.
But, again, asked if Britain could rejoin the bloc and keep its historical opt-outs and rebates, she dismissed it as “a highly speculative question”. She added:
Let’s remember how the discussion was at the time of Brexit. In that light, I think it is amazing that we now can have a big summit together, with discussions on how we can come closer together when it comes to trade and mobility.
Poland’s EU minister Ignacy Niemczycki said Warsaw’s approach “has always been very pragmatic,” as he stressed that the EU after Brexit is “weaker.” He said:
I would like us, wherever possible, to work out such mechanisms so it works for both of us. … This is a country that thinks similarly to us in Europe on many issues and there is no reason for us to treat each other like enemies. We are friends and let’s find the right formula for that.
In a cheeky comment, he added:
I would encourage everyone to think seriously about the benefits of being in the EU, … and I think the people of the UK see it [too], now that they are outside the union.
Cleverly accuses Burnham of being 'anti-London', after being named as Tory candidate for mayor
These are from my colleague Peter Walker, who was at the Tory event where James Cleverly was named as the party’s candidate for London mayor.
Peter posted this before the result was announced.
Khan (who may or may not stand a 4th time) has thus far faced a dilettante who decided to campaign on a racist platform (Zack Goldsmith) and two oddballs in Shaun Bailey and then Susan Hall. Not even he can be lucky yet again
And he posted these later.
Interesting that [the Conservatives] did not say how many votes were cast, just the percentage - which perhaps indicates it was not a huge number
Cleverly’s speech is mainly an attack on Labour and Khan, which is likely to be a theme for his campaign: “Burnham can’t stand London and Khan stand up to Burnham.” Also a pitch about building houses and cutting crime, and boosting transport.
Cleverly says he would “end Khan’s war on motorists”, which is a sign he might lean into the anti-cycling and walking rhetoric which the London Tories have a habit of espousing. Expect talk about LTNs and 20mph zones.
In the media Q&A Cleverly is pinned down on whether he backs the Tory party line on wanting to leave the ECHR and opposes net zero. He confirms he does (as he has to). Such things will be ready ammunition for Labour.
Cleverly says of Andy Burnham, “His residual behaviour is to be anti-London”. This will very much be a theme of his campaign, it seems. Not sure how resonant a “poor London!” message will be even in London
Tories choose James Cleverly as their candidate for London mayor in 2028
James Cleverly has been selected as the Conservative party’s candidate for the next London mayoral election.
The former foreign secretary and former home secretary won 86% of the votes in the ballot, beating Westminster councillor Festus Akinbusoye and former parliamentary candidate Sara Gezdari. A fourth candidate, communications professional Alex Challoner, was eliminated before the shortlist was drawn up for the ballot.
The next election for London mayor will take place in 2028.
Cleverly said he was “all in” for the race and would not be seeking reselection as an MP. He represents Braintree in Essex.
After the result was announced, Cleverly said the current mayor, Labour’s Sadiq Khan, was letting London down. He said:
People are leaving London, or not choosing to come here in the first place, businesses, job creators, families leaving London, and by the time of the election in 2028, Khan will have been mayor for 12 years, and those two things are related.
The problems London faces are the symptoms. Khan is the cause.
When I ask Londoners, do you feel safe walking home at night? The answer is no.
It’s shameful, it’s a failure, and it’s not just crime.
We have had the worst period of housebuilding since the second world war and only the highest-earning Londoners can afford the cheapest houses in London.
Congratulating Cleverly, Kemi Badenochsaid London was in decline and Labour was to blame.
This afternoon I will be answering questions from readers. Please post your questions below the line (comments are open today), and I will be answering from about 3pm until 5pm, or a bit later.
This is the latest in a regular Conversations series where Guardian journalists answer questions from readers. I last did one in April.
Please feel free to ask about anything related to British politics. I will try to answer as many as I can, but in particular I will focus on a) the ones that seem most interesting and b) the ones where I think I might have something sensible to say.
Tulip Siddiq says she is considering legal action against former Bangladesh leader
The former minister Tulip Siddiq has said she is considering taking legal action against the former interim leader of Bangladesh over corruption allegations made by his administration led her to resign from the UK government last year, Alexandra Topping reports.
In her Today programme interview, Kemi Badenoch said that she was “worried” by the idea of the government intervening to get the Russell Brand prison message video removed from YouTube. (See 10.04am.) She said that, while Brand had been convicted, his wife (who posted the video) was a separate person.
Badenoch said:
My personal opinion is that Russell Brand has been convicted. He is guilty under the law. The rule of law applies to everyone in this country.
His wife is a separate person. She can make the protestations that she likes. I’m very concerned if people in prison are able to use other conduits to be able to send messages. I think that that is unorthodox.
But YouTube is a private platform. I think that immediately demanding the private platforms take things down without looking at exactly whether a law has been broken is not where I would start from.
If we want to make legislation for that, then we can look at that. But I’m quite worried about government intervening.
During his interview round this morning, Matthew Pennycook said the Ministry of Justice is in “dialogue” with Google as it tries to get the tech firm to take down the Russell Brand video. (See 10.04pm.)
A spokesperson for the Ministry of Justice said:
It is only right that the government asks for content that is distressing for victims to be taken down and we strongly believe YouTube should remove this content.
Removal ultimately depends on the platform’s own terms.
Meta disabled Brand’s Instagram and Facebook accounts after his conviction, the Press Association reports.
A Google spokesperson said:
We’re aware of the new content and our teams are investigating. We suspended Russell Brand’s channel from the YouTube Partner Programme in September 2023. The channel has not been able to monetise on YouTube since then.
Minister admits government cannot force Google to remove Russell Brand prison video from YouTube
The government has no power to make Google take down a YouTube video with a message from Russell Brand from prison claiming he is innocent of his crimes, a minister has admitted.
As Nadeem Badshah reports, the government has asked Google to take down the video.
Google has reportedly denied the request because it determined its rules had not been broken, the Press Association reports.
Asked about this in an interview on BBC Breakfast this morning, Matthew Pennycook, the housing minister, said:
We don’t have any power to mandate a removal of content. That is up to Google. It’s based on their terms and conditions.
But as I’ve been very clear, we’ve made a request in this instance because we feel very strongly that victims shouldn’t have to see this content.
We hope they do so because they have taken action on their platform before. They banned, for example in 2023, Russell Brand for making money off the platform because his off-platform behaviour was seen to cause harm.
BAE to slash 1,000 jobs across head office and air business to streamline orders
BAE Systems has announced plans to cut more than 1,000 jobs from its workforce, triggering calls for ministers to place extra orders with Britain’s biggest defence contractor, Lauren Almeida and Jasper Jolly report.
Badenoch says it's 'disturbing' that Xi, Trump and Putin look like they're 'trying to carve up world between them'
Alexandra Topping
Alexandra Topping is a Guardian political correspondent.
Kemi Badenoch was in a straight-talking mode on the media round this morning, calling the historic meeting between Trump, Xi and Putin “disturbing”, saying it looked like they were trying to “carve” up the world” between them.
Speaking on the Today programme, the leader of the opposition said the meeting was “absolutely not reassuring”.
She said:
There are three world leaders who look like they’re trying to carve up the world between them, a tri-polar world where Xi gets Asia, America gets the western hemisphere and Russia gets Europe, and that is very concerning, especially seeing Donald Trump call President Putin his friend.
Russia is not America’s friend, it certainly hasn’t been during my lifetime. But also at a time when we’re all worried about where the Ukraine war is going, the message that is sending to President Zelensky and of course the other summit that is taking place … is very concerning indeed.
And what I want to know is where we fit in in all of this. I don’t want to be in a polarised world run by Russia. I’ll do everything I can to make sure that doesn’t happen.
Badenoch went further than the prime minister, who was asked about the meeting by Ed Davey at prime minister’s questions yesterday. The Liberal Democrat leader said “the security implications of Trump, Putin and Xi cosying up” should highlight the need for a fresh deal with the European Union.
Burnham replied that he would be in Berlin for a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing to support Ukraine in China, but stopped short of expressing concern about the meeting of the three world leaders.
He said:
The thing that we need to do is continue to stand squarely by Ukraine and that is what this government will do.
And on this issue, I do pay tribute to all sides of the house because that is what we’ve managed to do in the years since the conflict began and that is the right thing to do … Let that clear message go out as that meeting takes place in [China] – this country is squarely with Ukraine.
Badenoch says using amputee athletes to justify cutting disability benefits was ‘message of hope’
Good morning. At PMQs yesterday Andy Burnham said that Kemi Badenoch should withdraw the “double amputees run marathons” comment that she used to justify the Tory plan to cut sickness and disability benefits by £14bn. It was “crass and insensitive”, he said.
This morning Badenoch defended what she was saying claimed that, in fact, she was delivering a “message of hope”.
In an interview on the Today programme, asked if she accepted that her remark was insensitive, Badenoch said she didn’t. She went on:
I will speak the truth and I will say what I believe is common sense. And what I know is that, if people can work, then we should encourage them to work.
And what I’m saying is actually a message of hope, that if people even with significant, problems can work, then those who have ADHD and mild anxiety should go to work.
When the presenter, Nick Robinson, put it to her that it was unreasonable to use an exceptional case as a guide to what most disabled people should be doing, Badenoch did not agree. “We do use extreme examples to illustrate things,” she said.
Robinson tried again, saying she was taking “one extreme case [to] imply that anybody on disability benefits should just get on with it”. Badenoch accused him of “faux outrage” and “tone policing”. She added:
People are free to disagree, but they know where I’m coming from.
I will post more from the interview shortly.
Today the news will be dominated by two summits. This afternoon Burnham is in Berlin for a meeting of the pro-Ukraine coalition of the willing. We have coverage of this on our Europe live blog.
And in China, Vladimir Putin, who invaded Ukraine, Xi Jinping, his leading ally, and Donald Trump, who is seen by many as a closet Putin ally, are meeting now. You can read about that here.
We will have comments open in about an hour. That is because I will be doing a Q&A this afternoon, probably from about 3pm, and I will try to answer as many questions as possible. Do post them below the line.
Here is the agenda for the day.
9.30am: Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state and Cabinet Office minister, takes questions in the Commons.
10am: The Conservative party announces the results of the first round of voting in the election of its candidate for London mayor for 2028. James Cleverly, the former home secretary and former foreign secretary, is expected to get more than 50% of the vote, meaning a second round of voting should not be necessary.
11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.
Noon: Heather Hallett, the Covid inquiry chair, publishes her report on the test, trace and isolate system.
Around 12.15pm (UK time):Andy Burnham arrives in Berlin for a meeting of the pro-Ukraine coalition of the willing. He is expected to speak to the media later in the afternoon after the plenary has finished.
1pm: Chris Bryant, the Northern Ireland secretary, attends a meeting of the British-Irish Intergovernmental Conference in Dublin.
