noticias.titulo: Trump, Xi and Putin meet as global alliances hang in the balance
noticias.resumen: President Trump, Xi and Putin have met in Shenzhen for a historic trilateral meeting, with Ukraine, Iran and nuclear disarmament on the agenda.
noticias.texto:
Trump, Xi and Putin meet as global alliances hang in the balance
SHENZHEN, China and MOSCOW, Russia — President Trump joined Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin for a trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China on Thursday – capping two days of talks characterized by high-minded tributes to the role of great powers in maintaining peace, even as the men who led them had a role in starting some of the most intractable conflicts around the globe.
"History tells us when great powers are at peace, the world is secure," said Xi in opening remarks before cameras. "When great powers clash, the world is in chaos."
Putin noted their nations could make a "significant contribution to strengthening security and stability in the world."
"In that sense and I think in lots of other ways, we are making history," said Trump, who called it a "special responsibility" for the three countries to work together.
Yet, they offered few solutions toward peace, with the leaders offering divergent agendas going in:
Trump wanted to talk about reducing nuclear weapons and his mission to keep Iran from obtaining them; Putin was looking to push for an end to the war in Ukraine on terms favorable to Moscow; Xi was signaling he hoped to avoid wading too deep into either topic — preferring to showcase China's growing global clout with more general statements promoting peace and economic stability.
There were also topics to avoid: Trump refused to engage with journalists' questions over China's alleged role in an espionage plot to steal high end Nvidia chips.
In the end, the summit's key deliverable was arguably the image itself: the president of the United States gathering with authoritarian leaders from China and Russia for the first time in American history.
Summit speed dating
Despite being billed as a summit of "groundbreaking significance" by the Chinese hosts, sit-down talks between Trump, Xi, and Putin were relatively brief — with some of that time taken up by interpreters delivering simultaneous translation.
Trump's meeting with Putin lasted 42 minutes. His talks with Xi went about an hour. The trilateral group session went on for an hour and a half.
Still, it was enough time for familiar Trump bonhomie to emerge.
"Who's he? He's my friend," said a smiling Trump upon seeing Putin ahead of their bilateral meeting.
"We've known each other for a long time," added Trump after he and the Russian leader warmly shook hands. "And I think a lot of wonderful things can come of this. Or at least start."
Similarly, Trump told Xi "as long as you and I are in charge of things, we're never going to have a problem."
Both statements were tacit admissions the clock is ticking on Trump's remaining two years in office — with change coming even sooner to Washington when Democrats take control of Congress come January.
Getting there
The China gathering was first proposed by Putin during an October phone call with Trump — an offer to meet together with President Xi when China hosted the Asian Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) conference in China that November.
For Putin in particular, the meeting was always going to be a coup: the latest sign that — with Trump and Xi's help — he has effectively chipped away at Western attempts to isolate him politically over his invasion of Ukraine.
Back in Moscow, state media showed footage of the three leaders huddled together seemingly on loop — proof that Russia had regained what the Kremlin sees as its rightful place among global superpowers.
Ignored by Kremlin-friendly media were hints at more subtle power dynamics at play.
Xi greeted Trump on the tarmac personally — returning a gesture Trump had given the Chinese leader during his recent visit in Washington — while Putin received a more scaled down delegation upon arrival to Shenzhen.
Similarly, Trump was offered the top spot next to Xi during the APEC group photo and sat next to Xi during the APEC dinner reception — with Putin positioned at a separate table.
Was it a slight to Putin? A calculated attempt to flatter Trump? A reflection of Russia's vastly weaker economy? Whatever the answer, Xi wasn't ignoring his Russian guest entirely.
The two gathered privately for two hours on Wednesday — a sit-down China-Russia watchers estimated to be their 50th meeting all told.
Xi and Putin also echoed each other in their public speeches— both touching on familiar themes of the dawn of a new "multipolar world" and criticizing the use of sanctions as a sign of Western influence on the wane.
A new Yalta?
From the outset, critics of the summit voiced concern that Trump, Xi, and Putin would seek to carve the world into each country's perceived sphere of influence.
In Russia, the event was billed as a potential "new Yalta" — a reference to a moment in 1945 when the leaders of the U.S., Soviet Union, and United Kingdom hastily agreed to a post-World War II order for Europe.
Instead, the Shenzhen summit reflected the far more fragmented priorities of its participants.
Trump made no secret he hoped to include China in arms control talks — what Trump calls "denuclearization" — at a moment when key landmark nuclear treaties between Russia and the U.S. have all expired.
The catch: his Chinese hosts had little interest in the issue.
Beijing has repeatedly rebuffed U.S. attempts to include it in negotiations with Russia — noting that its arsenal remains far below those of Cold War-era rivals Moscow and Washington.
Differences also extended to the war in Ukraine, where Putin had hoped to press for U.S. and Chinese support for a settlement tilted in Moscow's favor — including a redrawn security map for Europe that would amount to a rollback of NATO from Eastern Europe.
Xi has insisted Europe have a seat at the table in any negotiated settlement. Trump has largely relied on his trusted envoys — real estate developer Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner — to hash out the complexities of any peace deal.
Following Trump's meeting with Putin, a Kremlin aide would only say that Ukraine had been the focus of the discussions — adding the Kremlin leader had left "in an excellent mood."
It was hard to see why.
Just hours earlier, Ukraine carried out a missile strike on the lone bridge linking mainland Russia to the annexed Crimean peninsula for the third time this week — effectively disabling the structure for months to come.
The bridge is widely considered the Russian leader's pet project — a symbol of Russia's claim to territory illegally seized from Ukraine in 2014 rendered in steel.
Additional research by Jasmine Ling.

noticias.titulo: UK inflation hits 12-month high on surging motor fuel costs
noticias.resumen: Britain's inflation rate edged up in October to the highest level in 12 months, official data showed on Wednesday, as the Middle East conflict drove up motor fuel costs.
noticias.texto:
Britain's inflation rate edged up in October to the highest level in 12 months, official data showed on Wednesday, as the Middle East conflict drove up motor fuel costs.
The Consumer Prices Index increased to 3.6% from 3.5% in the year to September, the Office for National Statistics said.
The October reading matched analysts' consensus forecast.
"Inflation rose slightly in October, with fuel prices once again a major contributor to the increase in the annual rate," ONS chief economist Grant Fitzner said in a statement.
"Annual costs of both raw materials and goods leaving factories continue to climb, driven by higher crude oil and petrol prices, respectively," he added.
The average diesel price at UK pumps reached a record high in October, surpassing the level seen in the wake of Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
"The conflict in the Middle East and Russia's illegal invasion of Ukraine have pushed up costs around the world," the Labour government's chief secretary to the Treasury, Emma Reynolds, said in response to the inflation reading.
In a bid to combat rising inflation, the Bank of England raised its benchmark interest rate this month for the first time in more than three years.
Alongside the increase, the central bank warned that inflation risked climbing to 6.2% in the third quarter of next year, in a worst case scenario of oil prices soaring far beyond $100 a barrel because of the Middle East conflict.
The BoE's central forecast is for UK inflation to peak at 4.9 in the second quarter of next year.
The bank's Monetary Policy Committee tightened borrowing costs by a quarter point to 4.0% in early November, catching up with the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank in lifting rates since the start of the Middle East conflict.
"The MPC raised Bank Rate two weeks ago to limit how much higher energy costs affect other prices, and will continue to set interest rates to make sure inflation returns to the two-percent target and stays there," the Bank of England said after Wednesday's data.
Analysts said the central bank could increase the rate again as soon as December, with UK households and businesses expected to face large increases to their energy bills from January .
A further rate increase next month "is looking increasingly likely", said Paul Dales, chief UK economist at Capital Economics research group.

noticias.titulo: Italy approves antisemitism law amid protests from left-wing opposition
noticias.resumen: The Chamber finally approved an anti-antisemitism bill using the IHRA definition, splitting the opposition and reviving debate on where criticism of Israel's government ends and antisemitism begins.
noticias.texto:
The Chamber finally approved an anti-antisemitism bill using the IHRA definition, splitting the opposition and reviving debate on where criticism of Israel's government ends and antisemitism begins.
The Chamber of Deputies on Tuesday gave final approval to the antisemitism bill. There were 147 votes in favour, 93 against and 5 abstentions, after Democratic Party MP Piero Fassino announced that he and other Democratic colleagues would not follow the party line.
There has been no shortage of controversy over the definition adopted in the bill.
The text, already approved by the Senate in March, adopts the definition of antisemitism provided by the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA), which has divided the opposition itself.
The Democratic Party voted against, despite defections within its reformist wing, as did the Five Star Movement and AVS, while Italia Viva and Azione backed it. All amendments were rejected.
What the definition of antisemitism approved by Italy says
The text brought before the Chamber (source in Italian), which contains five articles, states in the first that the Republic "rejects all forms of antisemitism, promotes action to counter any expression of it and prevents the spread of antisemitic prejudice in Italy, without prejudice to freedom of political criticism and freedom of expression and to freedom of assembly and association, in compliance with constitutional principles".
The subsequent articles introduce a Coordinator for the national antisemitism strategy, and the lines of action against antisemitic hatred, including educational and training initiatives.
At the heart of the measure and of the political clash, however, is the definition of antisemitism drawn up by IHRA in 2016 and above all the examples provided by the organisation (source in Italian) which, according to critics, in effect extend the definition of hate to include dissent towards the actions of the Israeli government.
Criticism from the opposition and the alternatives
It is a "gag law to cover up the crimes of the Netanyahu government and the ethnic cleansing of the Palestinians. The Meloni government chooses not to disturb those who illegally occupy Palestinian land and at the same time wants to muzzle those who denounce it. It is a disgrace", attacked the co-founder of Avs, Angelo Bonelli.
"The majority does not really want to fight antisemitism, it wants to censor criticism of the Israeli government, which is committing genocide", said Democratic Party MP and former speaker of the Chamber, Laura Boldrini. "If it had really wanted to fight antisemitism, it would have approved our amendments, which replace the IHRA declaration, which is controversial, with the Jerusalem Declaration".
In Tuesday's debate in the chamber, the opposition asked the majority, as it had on the eve of the vote, to amend this definition or replace it with less controversial documents, such as the one adopted by the Council of Europe in 2022 (source in Italian), which focuses more on tools for combating or preventing it, or the Jerusalem Declaration on antisemitism from the previous year.
In particular, the latter distinguishes between antisemitism and criticism of Israel (source in Italian), stating that opposing the Israeli government or Zionism as an ideology is not in itself antisemitic.
The response, for example from Osservatorio Israele, was that the bill "does not limit freedom to criticise the Israeli government, but distinguishes legitimate political dissent from antisemitism".
The debate in the chamber also became heated when the death toll in Gaza since 2023 was brought up, and an amendment that would have banned naming streets and monuments after figures who supported antisemitism was rejected, sparking a clash complete with insults over streets and statues in Italy dedicated to figures from the fascist era.

noticias.titulo: Portuguese families spend 83% of net income on rent, Idealista study finds
noticias.resumen: Idealista's analysis shows rising pressure on households. Faro demands most effort to rent, Funchal to buy, and Lisbon's burden is very high for both.
noticias.texto:
Idealista's analysis shows rising pressure on households. Faro demands most effort to rent, Funchal to buy, and Lisbon's burden is very high for both.
In a context of major social and political unrest in Portugal, largely due to successive demonstrations for the right to housing and the high cost of living, the conclusions of a new analysis by southern Europe's largest property portal, Idealista, are blunt: Portuguese families spend on average 83% of their net annual income on rent. The figure falls to 70% in the case of buying a home.
"Renting or buying a home consumes a large part of household income, reflecting the difficulties that many families face in accessing adequate housing," can be read in the study's conclusions.
This reality is widespread across the country, but in some places the financial burden of housing on families is even greater.
The analysis covered 20 cities: the 18 district capitals in mainland Portugal and the two capitals of the autonomous regions of Madeira and the Azores. Faro is where families spend the highest share of their annual salary on renting, with the effort rate reaching 92% of household income.
Next comes Lisbon, where families spend 88% of their salary on rent, and Funchal, with 85%.
Also in the top five cities where families devote the largest share of their income to rent are Porto (66%) and Setúbal (64%). Coimbra, Viseu, Beja, Vila Real and Bragança appear as the cities where rents weigh least on household income. Only in three cities does the effort rate not exceed the recommended limit of 33%: Castelo Branco and Portalegre, with an effort rate of 32%, and Guarda, with 29%.
Effort rate for buying a home
The idea of buying a home is increasingly utopian for many Portuguese people, even for young people who have seen some government measures targeted at them, notably the controversial public state guarantee.
And those who do manage to buy a home in Portugal are facing an effort rate that is increasingly high.
According to Idealista, Funchal is the city where "buying a home represents the greatest financial effort", with a rate of 96%, followed by Lisbon, with 90%, and Faro, with 79%. This means that almost all of families' net annual income goes on repaying a housing loan.
The recommended effort rate for buying a home, equal to or below 33%, is clearly exceeded in most cities: Porto (76%), Aveiro (68%), Ponta Delgada (59%), Setúbal (57%), Braga (53%), Viana do Castelo (53%), Leiria (51%), Coimbra (47%), Évora (45%), Viseu (45%) and Santarém (43%).
Only in six district capitals does the effort rate for buying a home remain within the recommended level, such as Guarda (20%), Castelo Branco (23%), Portalegre (23%), Bragança (26%), Beja (29%) and Vila Real (30%).
The rise in interest rates has pushed up mortgage repayments, leaving families with ever higher bills to pay. In 2026, in Portugal, three, six and 12 month Euribor rates began to register sharper increases from March 2026.
The Bank of Portugal this year reduced the maximum recommended effort rate from 50% to 45% of net monthly income. This is a maximum threshold and is still above many perceptions of sustainable effort rates.

noticias.titulo: EU pushes methane rules back two years in win for oil and gas industry
noticias.resumen: MEPs and EU governments have agreed to postpone key methane emissions requirements by two years amid pressure from the fossil fuel industry and mounting concerns over energy security and affordability.
noticias.texto:
MEPs and EU governments have agreed to postpone key methane emissions requirements by two years amid pressure from the fossil fuel industry and mounting concerns over energy security and affordability.
EU methane emissions rules will be delayed by two years, until 2029, under a deal struck between MEPs and EU governments, in what critics have decried as another concession to the oil and gas industry at the expense of the bloc's climate ambitions.
The EU's methane rules, first adopted in 2024, require foreign suppliers to provide information about methane emissions associated with the oil, gas and coal they sell to European buyers.
The delay marks another retreat from the EU's climate commitments as governments prioritise energy security, industrial competitiveness and affordability over the swift implementation of green legislation.
EU countries have cited high and volatile oil and gas prices, coupled with potential supply disruptions caused by the US-Israeli war against Iran, to justify delaying the rules.
The political battle over the delay has exposed a difficult relationship between the EU's centre-right and its traditional pro-climate allies.
In October, the European People's Party (EPP), the Parliament's largest political group, pushed through a three-year postponement, winning support from far-right lawmakers after negotiations with the Socialists and Liberals broke down. The proposal passed with 341 votes in favour and 225 against.
The Greens accused conservatives of joining forces with the far right to weaken climate rules and protect the interests of the fossil fuel industry. The EPP, however, argued that the original timetable was unrealistic and risked putting European producers and importers at a disadvantage.
Thursday's compromise reduces Parliament's demand for a three-year delay to two years, but still exceeds the Commission's initial offer and the one-year delay backed by EU governments.
MEP Dimitris Tsiodras (EPP/Greece), the Parliament’s negotiator on the Environment Committee, said the EPP's priority was to ensure energy security, affordability and industrial competitiveness alongside methane reduction commitments.
"We are not suspending the methane regulation but ensuring its effective implementation and that all compliance requirements can be met in practice”, Tsiodras reacted.
Czech First Deputy Prime Minister and Industry and Trade Minister Karel Havlíček said the deal would prevent further increases in oil and gas prices.
"It can be done. When we unite and are determined, we can change even what seemed impossible. The Czech Republic, which won 19 other countries over to its side, achieved a major success in the EU," Havlíček said on X.
Macron's intervention and US pressure
The push to delay the rules has also gathered momentum outside Parliament.
French President Emmanuel Macron wrote to Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in September calling for a delay of the methane rules, arguing that the EU should not weaken its own production capacity at a time of mounting energy insecurity.
Paris had previously backed stronger action to curb methane emissions, but joined governments and industry groups arguing that the rules could make it harder to secure oil and gas supplies during a period of market disruption.
The United States, Europe's largest supplier of liquefied natural gas (LNG), has also repeatedly criticised the EU legislation, warning that its requirements could create additional costs and complicate exports to the EU market.
The EU also relies on the US for between a third and half of its diesel imports (around 180,000 barrels per day).
The pressure comes as the US-Israel war against Iran has disrupted shipping through the critical Strait of Hormuz and has intensified concerns about the bloc's dependence on imported fossil fuels.
But the argument that delaying methane rules will protect supplies and lower prices remains disputed. The rules don't ban imports of fossil fuels that fail to meet EU standards.
Its initial requirements focus on monitoring and reporting emissions, allowing the bloc to obtain information about pollution generated during the production of imported energy.
Environmental groups and experts have questioned whether postponing those obligations will make any meaningful difference to energy prices or supply availability.
Another test for the Green Deal
Methane is responsible for around 30% of global warming and is significantly more potent than CO2 over the short term. Cutting emissions from fossil fuel production is considered one of the fastest ways to slow global warming.
Under the deal struck overnight on Thursday by EU governments and the Parliament, importers of crude oil, natural gas and coal will have until 1 January 2029 to comply with monitoring, reporting and verification requirements, instead of the original January 2027 deadline.
The agreement also pushes back methane-intensity reporting obligations for both European producers and importers by two years, to August 2030.
The provisional deal still needs formal backing from the Parliament and the Council, due by the end of the year.
François-Régis Mouton de Lostalot, managing director at the lobby group the International Association of Oil and Gas Producers (IOGP) Europe, described the delay as a "certain improvement" building on the Commission's proposal.
"But without a review clause, Europe has no margin for error. The Commission and Member States must lead a coordinated effort from day one, with clear milestones and responsibilities, to make the compliance framework fully operational before the obligations apply," Mouton de Lostalot said.
EU lawmakers and climate scientists have previously identified methane as a "low-hanging fruit" because it delivers fast, low-cost reductions in near-term global warming using existing technology.
Inger Andersen, executive director of the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), said methane is the second largest contributor to global heating behind CO2 and warned that cutting its emissions "is our emergency brake to slow warming".
“With the world on course to exceed 1.5°C of warming, we must limit how high temperatures rise and how long they stay high, and then bring them down,” said Andersen.
Environmental activists argue the extended delay will weaken climate goals, criticising Brussels for its strike in softening other parts of its climate agenda, including the EU's carbon market, industrial decarbonisation rules and CO2 emissions in cars.

noticias.titulo: Italian journalist Corrado Augias dies at 91, Senate holds minute of silence
noticias.resumen: Journalist Corrado Augias has died at the age of 91, after decades as a leading figure in Italian journalism.
noticias.texto:
Journalist Corrado Augias has died at the age of 91, after decades as a leading figure in Italian journalism.
Corrado Augias, a historic voice of Italian journalism as well as a writer, populariser, author and television host, died on Thursday at the age of 91. The news was reported by the daily newspaper Repubblica, with which Augias had been a contributor since its foundation.
"With the passing of Corrado Augias, Italian journalism loses an essential point of reference. Journalist, essayist, playwright, presenter, Augias was an intellectual capable of deciphering, in every era, the changes in Italian society, which he was able to narrate with authority," the Usigrai executive said in a statement.
The career of Corrado Augias, from newspapers to television
Born in Rome on 26 January 1935 to parents of French origin, Augias was admitted to the order of journalists on 1 April 1969. Over sixty years of intense activity, in addition to his long-standing collaboration with Repubblica as correspondent and columnist, from 2001 to 2021 he was in charge of the letters column, featuring correspondence sent in by readers.
Not only a print journalist, Augias also became well known as a television presenter, with a style marked by elegant, courteous yet incisive manners and a touch of irony, able to engage with the most diverse guests. His fame on the small screen came with the programme he devised for Rai, Telefono Giallo, dedicated to famous unresolved crime cases, which he presented from 1987 to 1993.
**In recent years Augias worked mainly with the broadcaster La7, on the programme La Torre di Babele.**In addition to his journalistic work, he successfully turned to writing crime novels and essays.
Applause and a minute's silence in the Senate to remember Corrado Augias
After hearing the news of his death, announced in the Senate during the debate on the school decree by Italia Viva group leader Raffaella Paita, senators from both the majority and the opposition joined in prolonged applause.
"We have just learned of the death of Corrado Augias and I would like this chamber to pay him a tribute with applause," Paita said. The President of the Senate, Ignazio La Russa, also joined in expressing condolences, asking for a few minutes of silence.
The Mayor of Rome, Roberto Gualtieri, also paid tribute to the intellectual before the sitting of the city council. "Corrado Augias was a major figure in culture and journalism, a committed intellectual and a citizen of Rome to whom we owe a great deal. I want to express all my personal grief, that of the administration and, I believe I can say, of the entire city. I extend my deepest condolences to his family, friends and relatives," Gualtieri said.
The director of La7, Andrea Salerno, also expressed his condolences on Augias's death and his closeness to the family.

noticias.titulo: Commerzbank welcomes UniCredit commitments after Berlin agreement
noticias.resumen: Commerzbank has welcomed UniCredit's commitments to keep the German lender listed and based in Frankfurt. This comes as Berlin and UniCredit have agreed on key terms of what would be one of Europe's biggest cross-border banking deals in years.
noticias.texto:
Commerzbank has welcomed UniCredit's commitments to keep the German lender listed and based in Frankfurt. This comes as Berlin and UniCredit have agreed on key terms of what would be one of Europe's biggest cross-border banking deals in years.
Commerzbank has welcomed commitments from UniCredit to keep its headquarters in Frankfurt and retain its stock market listing, after the Italian lender and the German government reached an agreement in principle on the proposed takeover.
"We take note of the agreement in principle between the German federal government and UniCredit. We welcome the commitments announced by UniCredit," Commerzbank told Euronews in a statement.
The German bank said the agreement included a commitment to expand its business with mid-sized companies and preserve its ability to serve clients internationally. That was one of Berlin's priorities in the talks, along with keeping the bank in Frankfurt and protecting employees' interests.
"Key decisions will continue to be made in Germany. Employee rights and existing agreements are also explicitly recognised," Commerzbank told Euronews. The bank said its management would work with UniCredit to develop a strategy that builds on the strengths of both banks.
Reuters first reported the agreement. Euronews contacted UniCredit and the German finance ministry for further details. Neither had replied by the time of publication.
A tie-up between Italy's UniCredit and Germany's Commerzbank would create a bank with more than €1.3 trillion ($1.4tn) in assets, making it one of Europe's biggest cross-border banking deals in years.
UniCredit began building a stake in Commerzbank in 2024 and announced an unsolicited bid in March 2026. Despite initial resistance from Berlin and Commerzbank, the Italian lender secured access to just under 50% of the voting rights once the tendered shares are transferred.
Berlin softened its stance in July, when Chancellor Friedrich Merz said his government would not block the takeover, although it opposed the way UniCredit had gone about it.
The European Central Bank gave its approval in October. The European Commission and the US Federal Reserve followed on Monday. UniCredit said it expected the final outstanding regulatory approval by the end of November.
The European Commission examined how the takeover would affect banking services in Germany, where UniCredit already operates through its subsidiary HypoVereinsbank. It found that the banks' combined market shares were moderate in most areas. It identified trade finance as an exception but concluded that the deal raised no competition concerns.
The German government has yet to say whether it will sell its 13.3% stake in Commerzbank.

noticias.titulo: US President Trump rejects global AI regulation as China's Xi calls for cooperation on safety
noticias.resumen: The US and Chinese leaders have set out contrasting approaches to AI governance at talks in Shenzhen, with Trump warning that regulation could hamper innovation while Xi called for the technology to remain under human control.
noticias.texto:
The US and Chinese leaders have set out contrasting approaches to AI governance at talks in Shenzhen, with Trump warning that regulation could hamper innovation while Xi called for the technology to remain under human control.
The leaders of the world’s two pre-eminent artificial intelligence powers, the United States and China, are holding meetings to discuss the future of the technology in Shenzhen this week, with Trump and Xi representing two very different approaches to rein in AI.
President Donald Trump said that the United States opposes "globalist regulation" of AI in any form in a meeting with Xi, who responded that the US and China should cooperate to keep “AI under human control”.
Trump has repeatedly rejected calls for wide-reaching international governance of AI, warning it could hold his country back in its race with China.
"It's super intelligence, but we have to watch it," he told leaders at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting in Shenzhen, using his administration's preferred term for AI.
"We have to be careful. We have to cherish it. It's almost completely good, but it's got some bad elements, and we have to be very careful in managing those bad elements," Trump said.
"So we oppose any form of globalist regulation or anything to control and stifle SI, and we won't allow that to happen, frankly," Trump added.
Xi told his US counterpart that the two countries should cooperate to keep AI "under human control", Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported after the presidents met.
"China and the United States should strengthen communication and coordination to guard against artificial intelligence safety risks and ensure that artificial intelligence always remains under human control", Xinhua reported Xi as saying.
Despite the countries' fierce tech rivalry, AI safety risks of shared concern range from infrastructure hacking to people using the technology to help build bioweapons.
Another problem in the spotlight is out-of-control AI agents, tools that complete real-life tasks online with minimal human input, after the ChatGPT maker OpenAI's bots hacked into websites including an Australian government portal and several US government sites, incidents followed by similar reports by other labs.
Military use and mass surveillance are also potential flashpoints for the world's two leading AI powers.
Looming over the talks is Jensen Huang's resignation as boss of US chip titan Nvidia after revelations of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
Trump and Xi agreed in September to create a channel for urgent communication on AI incidents, with details to be hammered out on Thursday.
Xi this summer said the technology should be "always under human control" — calling for more "laws and regulations, technological monitoring, early warning and emergency response systems".
At APEC on Wednesday, the Chinese leader said leaders should "deepen cooperation in the digital economy and artificial intelligence", without giving details.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney meanwhile said on Wednesday that the lack of global governance on AI poses an "enormous risk".
"It is past time" to develop international frameworks for reining it in, Carney added.

noticias.titulo: Ocean Catalyst Group launched at COP31 to safeguard ‘vital’ coastal and marine tourism
noticias.resumen: At COP31 in Türkiye, the World Travel & Tourism Council and member organisations launched the Ocean Catalyst Group to drive investment, strengthen coastal resilience and protect marine destinations.
noticias.texto:
At COP31 in Türkiye, the World Travel & Tourism Council and member organisations launched the Ocean Catalyst Group to drive investment, strengthen coastal resilience and protect marine destinations.
A new strategy to protect and restore coastal and marine tourism was launched during a spotlight event at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye.
On COP31’s Ocean Day, the World Travel & Tourism Council (WTTC) jointly announced with its members the creation of the “Ocean Catalyst Group”. It was unveiled at an event titled “Delivering and Powering Resilient Coastal Destinations: Accelerating Implementation through Ocean Breakthroughs”.
The Ocean Catalyst Group will bring together the tourism private sector on a voluntary basis to "accelerate collaboration among businesses, governments and other stakeholders, including finance and insurance partners”, the WTTC said.
The goal of the initiative is to bring collective action to protect coastal destinations, whose communities depend on travel and tourism for their livelihoods. Further, investment into these sectors will help protect assets, maintain business continuity, while also supporting livelihoods and sustaining the visitor experience.
As such, the group will be tasked with identifying shared priorities, developing partnerships and helping to drive action and investment in coastal destinations.
Globally in 2023, coastal and marine tourism generated approximately $3.3 trillion (€3 trillion) in GDP, and supported around 100 million jobs, including through supply-chain impacts. However, its “long-term prosperity depends on healthy ecosystems, reliable energy and water, and thriving communities”, the WTTC said.
“Coastal and marine tourism is a vital part of the global travel and tourism sector," Gloria Guevara, President and CEO of the WTTC, said. "The destinations and communities that depend on it are exposed to growing environmental pressures, so taking action is essential. Bringing together businesses, governments and financial institutions can accelerate investment and strengthen resilience."
This comes within the framework of also supporting the goals of the Coastal Tourism Breakthrough (CTB), which forms part of the Ocean Breakthroughs initiative. The CTB has called for $30 billion (€27.31 billion) annually by 2030 to support halving emissions from coastal tourism.
Alongside the launch of the Ocean Catalyst Group, the Coastal & Marine Tourism Public-Private Sector Playbook was also introduced.
Developed by the WTTC with Iberostar Hotels & Resorts, Intrepid Travel and the Ocean & Climate Platform, it provides practical guidance for businesses’ operations and value chains, while also identifying how governments can support the industries.
"Through the Ocean Catalyst Group and this new Playbook, we are helping to turn shared ambitions into practical action, ensuring that coastal tourism can continue to drive economic opportunity while protecting the natural assets on which its future depends," Guevara said.

noticias.titulo: Smooth as silk: how Thai Airways is rebuilding the road between Europe and Asia
noticias.resumen: Thai Airways is growing again, adding more European flights via Bangkok and upgrading cabins, food and service to deliver a smoother, more connected journey.
noticias.texto:
For centuries, the Silk Road connected Asia and Europe through trade, culture and commerce. Thai Airways draws on that history for its ‘Smooth as silk’ promise. For Chief Commercial Officer Kittiphong Sansomboon, the idea goes beyond a slogan.
“We are inspired by the old Silk Road,” he says. “Silk Road connecting people, connecting culture, connecting cities, connecting economies. The only difference is that in the old days they connected by boat. We connect everything by aeroplane.”
Today, that means rebuilding the airline, expanding its network and giving passengers more reasons to choose Thai Airways.
From recovery to expansion
Thai Airways has completed its rehabilitation and is growing again. Having exited its restructuring plan in 2025, the airline is investing in new aircraft, adding routes and building on the momentum of a strong recovery. Sansomboon has had a close view of that journey, from leading corporate communications as the process began to shaping the customer, brand and marketing work that helped win back stakeholder confidence.
“We explored the opportunities. We changed. We made sure the foundation became stronger and better, and we improved the customer experience and the connectivity,” he says.
The airline has returned to Amsterdam with a daily service and plans to operate 66 routes during the winter 2026/27 schedule. Brand Finance has also reported an increase in Thai Airways’ brand value, reflecting progress in its recovery.
“Exiting from the rehabilitation plan doesn’t mean that we are going to stop transforming ourselves,” Sansomboon says. “We continue improving, and perhaps it will be even better.”
Europe remains a key market. Greater financial stability and improved operational efficiency underpin the airline’s plans to strengthen connectivity and build confidence among passengers and business partners.
“The transformation only matters if the passengers feel the difference,” he says.
More choice between Europe and Asia
Thai Airways is increasing frequencies on three key European routes during winter 2026/27: Paris will reach 14 flights a week from 1 December, Munich 10 from 16 December and Zurich 11 from 16 January. Amsterdam will continue to receive a daily service.
The additional flights give leisure and business travellers more flexibility, while Bangkok offers onward connections across Southeast Asia and to Australia.
“We see the huge potential between Europe and Southeast Asia, and onward to Australia,” Sansomboon says.
The airline is also expanding its Asian network, including services to Vietnam, Laos, Myanmar, India, China and Japan, and will return to Danang from 1 December.
Its Silk Hub strategy is designed to make connections through Bangkok more convenient. Southeast Asia feeds traffic into the network, India and China provide passenger volumes, while long-haul routes from Europe and Australia generate value.
“Suvarnabhumi Airport is conveniently located right in the middle of everywhere,” he says.
Sansomboon’s own career has taken him across many of the markets Thai Airways serves. He began in an airline operations control centre before moving into international leadership roles, including Regional Director for ASEAN, based in Singapore, and Greater China, based in Beijing. He also held overseas postings in London, Dubai, Karachi and Shanghai.
Returning to Thailand in 2020, he led corporate communications through the pandemic and the airline’s court-supervised rehabilitation. He later became Director of Customer, Brand & Marketing before taking on his current role. Now, as Chief Commercial Officer, he is focused on turning that experience into growth: expanding Thai Airways’ network, strengthening its commercial performance and improving the experience for passengers.
Designing for the sixth sense
Connectivity gets passengers where they want to go. The experience on board, Sansomboon argues, is what brings them back
His thinking draws on the Buddhist concept of Āyatana, which recognises six sense bases. At Thai Airways, this informs an approach to the passenger experience that considers what people see, hear, smell and taste, how they experience touch and, ultimately, how they feel.
“As long as you design the customer experience around the sixth sense, you will win,” he says.
He divides the experience into functional and emotional elements. The first includes the aircraft, seats and entertainment systems. Thai Airways is developing its cabin offering across travel classes, with features including Business Class privacy doors and more personal space, new-generation Economy seats and upgraded entertainment screens. Its Junior Sky Explorers programme aims to make flying more engaging for children and families.
“Functional benefit is hardware, emotional benefit is software,” Sansomboon says. “We do it simultaneously. That is the key.”
Food is another part of the experience. Through its Taste of Thai Tales programme, the airline works with Michelin-starred Thai chefs on menus featuring local produce. Coffee from Chiang Rai, Thai-sourced chocolate and amenity kits featuring silk brand Jim Thompson bring local products into the journey.
For Sansomboon, the approach also creates opportunities to support Thai businesses and communities.
“We are the big platform. We are the ecosystem,” he says. “So we have to give back to the community.”
“Thai food has a story,” he adds.
The airline’s efforts have earned recognition, including Travel Daily Media’s Guest Experience of the Year award in 2024 and 2025.
Aiming higher
Thai Airways has climbed nine places in the Skytrax World Airline Awards, moving from 29th to 20th in a year. Sansomboon says the result has lifted morale, but sees it as a reason to keep improving rather than a final achievement.
Passenger feedback remains important in identifying where the airline can do better.
“It’s a signal that we have to work harder and improve ourselves,” he says. “Of course, we want to be among the top ten.”
The journey ahead
For European travellers, Sansomboon sums up the offer in three parts: “Better connections, better service and the famous Thai hospitality.”
More flights from key European cities, onward connections through Bangkok and an onboard experience shaped by Thai food and thoughtful service form the basis of the airline’s next chapter.
The Silk Road once carried goods, ideas and people across continents, one trading post at a time. Thai Airways is working to do the same in the air, with more flights from Paris, Munich, Zurich and Amsterdam, a Bangkok hub built for easy connections and a cabin experience shaped by Thai food and hospitality.
For Sansomboon, the test is how the journey feels from the first welcome to the last connection. “We would like to welcome our European passengers on board Thai Airways and to enjoy our renowned Thai hospitality, as smooth as silk.”

noticias.titulo: Spain freezes new foreign degree applications as foreign doctors flood residency exam
noticias.resumen: A Spanish ministry has stopped accepting new applications to recognise foreign university degrees, after years of increases.
noticias.texto:
A Spanish ministry has stopped accepting new applications to recognise foreign university degrees, after years of increases.
A Spanish ministry has stopped accepting new applications to recognise foreign university degrees, amid a controversy over the surge in foreign doctors sitting the country’s medical residency exam.
For the first time, foreign applicants outnumbered Spanish applicants for the national medical residency placement exam, known as the MIR, as highlighted by the Asociación MIR España (AME). Recognitions of foreign medical degrees had been rising for years, though Spaniards still make up the majority of admitted candidates for the exam.
The health ministry reserves a maximum quota of 10% for foreign candidates, meaning they should compete among themselves for just 968 of the positions offered overall. That makes both their chances of admission and their choice of speciality more difficult.
However, this is not how it works in practice. Many foreign doctors apply through the ordinary route thanks to their residence permits. The rules governing the call allow EU citizens and anyone with permanent or temporary residence to apply via the general pool. Only those in Spain on study permits, or who don’t fall into those categories, are left out.
A day after the figures were released, ABC reported that the Ministry of Science, Innovation and Universities, headed by Diana Morant, had blocked new applications to recognise foreign degrees, which is required to sit the exam. Recognitions have been climbing for the past decade, which is at the heart of the controversy.
The ministry said the shutdown of the online portal used for applications is due to a series of attempted cyberattacks on public websites around the world last month. The portal has since partly reopened, but still isn’t accepting new recognition applications.
Potential consequences
In 2025, there were 85,564 applications for recognition and equivalence of foreign university degrees processed, according to the ministry. That is more than twice the figure for 2024 (39,975) and eight times that of 2017 (10,224).
Only 49,906 of last year's cases were recognitions, which is the only category under which a foreign doctor can sit the exam.
The president of the Organización Médica Colegial (OMC) told RTVE that the situation also affects private health care. He warned that private companies could be tempted to hire doctors who have recognised degrees but no specialty training , on lower salaries and with more precarious conditions.
The next round of the competitive exam for health care posts is expected to take place on 23 January.

noticias.titulo: From car parts to drones: German suppliers pivot to defence as auto crisis deepens
noticias.resumen: German car parts makers are moving into drones, defence and space as the country's auto industry crisis deepens, with one Bavarian family firm now able to turn out 1,000 surveillance drones every month as it tries to depend less on carmakers.
noticias.texto:
German car parts makers are moving into drones, defence and space as the country's auto industry crisis deepens, with one Bavarian family firm now able to turn out 1,000 surveillance drones every month as it tries to depend less on carmakers.
Germany's struggling car parts suppliers are branching out into drones, defence and space as the crisis gripping the country's auto industry deepens, with family firm Jopp now having the capacity to make 1,000 surveillance drones every month in a bid to rely less on carmakers.
Jopp, based in Bavaria, one of the heartlands of German carmaking and a growing hub for defence start-ups, came up with the idea as its Porsche contract for gear systems was drawing to a close.
It now builds the drones for Highcat, a young German defence company that sells them on to customers including the military, police and firefighters.
The drone contract fits Jopp's plan to cut the share of its sales that comes from the car industry from 85% today to 60% by 2035.
Germany's once-dominant car industry has been plunged into crisis by intense competition from China and elsewhere, steep US tariffs and sluggish sales in Europe.
The sector has shed more than 140,000 jobs in Germany since 2019, or one in six, according to advisory firm EY.
That has pushed almost 80% of German car suppliers to seek growth in other industries, a survey by consultancy Roland Berger found last year, with defence, space and medical technology the most popular targets.
Holding on to jobs
Moving into drones means the company can at least hold its headcount steady, Martin Buechs, Jopp's managing director, told AFP.
"At some point I hope we'll be able to expand again, but for now it's about keeping the jobs we have," he said.
Its workforce has shrunk to 1,400 from around 2,000 six years ago, and two factories have closed.
"We have been very successful in the past with winning new automotive business," Buechs explained. However, many projects are now pushed back by as much as two years, he added, while customers are ordering far smaller volumes.
Jopp is far from being the only one making the pivot.
Schaeffler, a far bigger German maker of car and industrial components that is set to cut over 8,000 jobs, has also struck partnerships to move into new markets.
In May, Schaeffler announced it would produce spacecraft parts with US satellite data company Spire Global, adding that the pair could one day build satellites together in large numbers.
In June, it unveiled plans to manufacture Damocles attack drones designed by French firm Delair, along with Delair's Aspik Interceptor, which is built to counter hostile drones.
Europe's car sector faces "a continuous downturn", Schaeffler CEO Klaus Rosenfeld warned this month, adding "I don't think this is something that will go away tomorrow".
No cure for the car crisis
Yet diversifying alone will not be enough to save most suppliers, according to Roland Berger car industry expert Felix Mogge.
The markets they are targeting are already fiercely contested, he pointed out, and defence orders come in smaller and less predictable volumes than those from carmakers.
"Finding new product segments can be an interesting addition to a supplier's portfolio, even a small one," Mogge told AFP, adding that "it won't solve the structural problems on the automotive side".
Back at Jopp, Buechs acknowledged that the way defence deals are structured made it hard to know exactly how many posts the drone contract would protect.
Defence firms tend to sign framework contracts, committing to a set quantity with the possibility of ordering more later.
"The defence sector makes orders in small batches," Buechs noted.
Car production, by contrast, runs for years in volumes that are "usually very easy to calculate", he added.
Even so, Jopp had little option but to look beyond cars, he argued, as margins in the car industry are "difficult and indeed rather bad".
"It's already got really difficult for the industry and it looks like that will carry on," he concluded.

noticias.titulo: EU Commission hit by large-scale cyberattack with data leakage unknown
noticias.resumen: The European Commission's internal HR systems have been targeted by a malicious cyberattack, with EU cyber experts still assessing whether sensitive personal information has been compromised.
noticias.texto:
The European Commission's internal HR systems have been targeted by an AI-powered cyberattack, with EU cyber experts still assessing whether sensitive personal information has been compromised.
The European Commission has suffered a major cyberattack, but it is not yet clear who is behind it or whether sensitive staff data was stolen.
For several days, Commission officials could not access Sysper, the internal HR platform where they check salary information, request holidays and sick leave, submit timesheets and sign up for training.
"The investigation is still ongoing. We are taking any necessary steps based on the findings as they come," Thomas Regnier, the Commission's spokesperson for digital, told reporters on Thursday. "We have not detected any evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff as a whole."
Regnier said that the attack was based on a publicly available AI tool; it was first detected on 22 October and confirmed on 22 October, and the Commission did not receive any ransomware request.
However, he declined to confirm whether it was still ongoing, nor to attribute it to a specific actor.
On Thursday, Sysper was working again, whereas the health insurance Joint Sickness Insurance Scheme (JSIS) remained unavailable, two EU officials told Euronews under the condition of anonymity.
Beyond these relatively minor disruptions, most civil servants barely noticed the systems had been compromised. The Commission's IT department, DG DIGIT, is still investigating the incident, trying to assess the damage.
CERT-EU, the cybersecurity service for the EU bodies, and the European Data Protection Supervisor have been informed of the incident.
The key question is whether the attacker, who has yet to be identified, gained access to the data held in Sysper, JSIS and other HR systems. That would not normally open the door to the Commission’s internal documents, which are hosted on a separate system.
Still, the platforms hold sensitive personal details, including officials’ names, pay grades, home addresses and contact details. Such a database could fuel far more sophisticated campaigns targeting individual staff.
EU officials are yet to receive official internal communications about the incident, as the extent of the damage is still being assessed.
"The problem I have with the European Commission is that they keep the information about it internally and don’t disclose it to the public," MEP Bart Groothuis (The Netherlands/Renew) told Euronews.
"Each time they don’t bring information to the public about intrusions that hit EU institutions, bodies and agencies, they miss an opportunity to explain and sell the economic security policy we set out as the EU against our adversaries," he said.
The Commission is not new to cyberattacks. In March, its cloud infrastructure hosting its Europa.eu websites was compromised, resulting in the theft of around 91.7 GB of data, including personal information and email content.
In January, a cyberattack targeted the Commission's central mobile-device infrastructure, potentially exposing staff names and phone numbers.
This article was updated with additional information.

noticias.titulo: Danish lawmakers ratify US-Greenland security pact
noticias.resumen: The deal lets the United States build two new military bases on the Arctic island and stays in force even if Greenland becomes independent.
noticias.texto:
The deal lets the United States build two new military bases on the Arctic island and stays in force even if Greenland becomes independent.
Denmark's parliament has unanimously approved a security agreement with the United States and Greenland, easing a row over US President Donald Trump’s ambition to take control of the island.
All 109 lawmakers present in the 179-seat Folketing voted for the text on Thursday after its second reading, with no debate and no votes against.
Greenland's own parliament approved the agreement in early November, by 16 votes with seven abstentions.
The pact was signed in New York, United States, on 22 September and adds to a 1951 agreement governing the US military presence in Greenland, an autonomous territory of Denmark.
It also shuts countries outside the European Union and NATO out of strategic sectors. The aim is to stop China or Russia from building influence in Greenland, especially through investment.
Since returning to the White House in January 2025, Trump has repeatedly said the United States must control Greenland for strategic reasons. His remarks have alarmed Denmark, a NATO ally, and other partners.

noticias.titulo: The World’s 50 Best Vineyards 2026 have been revealed – and number one is in Germany
noticias.resumen: While Schloss Johannisberg in the Rheingau region took the top spot, three vineyards from France made the top 10.
noticias.texto:
While Schloss Johannisberg in the Rheingau region took the top spot, three vineyards from France made the top 10.
Each year, World’s 50 Best names the top hospitality experiences around the globe from restaurants and bars to hotels.
Now the 50 Best Vineyards have been revealed for 2026, with the top gong going to Schloss Johannisberg in Germany.
Located in the Rheingau region in the state of Hesse, visitors to the historic estate can explore the palace grounds, vineyards and historic cellars, including the Bibliotheca Subterranea.
“Schloss Johannisberg is a truly deserving No.1 winner, combining more than 1,200 years of winemaking heritage with exceptional hospitality, a strong sense of place and an immersive visitor experience that brings the story of riesling to life,” Rikki Tidball, managing director of awards and rankings for The 50 Best Vineyards, said.
The ranking is decided by an academy of more than 700 experts, including sommeliers, wine journalists and grape enthusiasts.
The academy is split into 20 regions, with each voter asked to nominate seven vineyard experiences to be evaluated on their visitor experience, including hospitality, atmosphere, activities and wine offering.
This year, vineyards from 31 regions in 15 countries across six continents made the list.
The best vineyards in Europe for 2026
Europe dominated the rankings, with half of the top 10 coming from the continent.
While Germany took the top spot, three French vineyards made the top 10: Maison Ruinart in Champagne (fourth), Château Smith Haut Lafitte (eighth) and Château d’Yquem (ninth), both of which are in Bordeaux.
Bodegas Ysios in Spain’s Rioja region took second place this year, with World’s 50 Best praising its architecture and panoramic vineyard views.
Five vineyards made their debut in the 1-50 ranking this year, including Champagne Philipponnat in France, which placed 47th.
Aya Estate in Bulgaria’s Struma Valley was given the inaugural One to Watch Award, which is handed to an emerging vineyard that is making “a significant impact within the industry” and will likely make the top 50 in the future.

- Schloss Johannisberg, Rheingau, Germany
- Bodegas Ysios, Rioja, Spain
- Montes, Colchagua Valley, Chile
- Maison Ruinart, Champagne, France
- Creation, Walker Bay, South Africa
- Clos Apalta, Colchagua Valley, Chile
- Klein Constantia, Western Cape, South Africa
- Château Smith Haut Lafitte, Bordeaux, France
- Château d’Yquem, Bordeaux, France

noticias.titulo: International film community join in protest of Iranian filmmaker Jafar Panahi’s prison sentence
noticias.resumen: International film festivals, actors, directors and industry professionals have joined forces in condemning the ongoing persecution of the acclaimed 'It Was Just An Accident' director.
noticias.texto:
International film festivals, actors, directors and industry professionals have joined forces in condemning the ongoing persecution of the acclaimed 'It Was Just An Accident' director.
The international film community is speaking out in support of dissident Iranian filmmaker Jafar Panahi, who was given a prison sentence of five years and one month by the Tehran Revolutionary Court in October.
A letter initiated by the International Coalition for Filmmakers at Risk (and shared with Variety) so far features more than 200 signatories “deeply concerned by reports of the new prison sentence of five years and one month issued by the Tehran Revolutionary Court against Iranian filmmaker Jafar Panhi, in absentia.”
The Oscar-nominated director returned to Iran in the spring following the end of the awards run for his Palme d’Or winning film It Was Just an Accident – which was nominated for Best International Feature and Best Original Screenplay at the 2026 Academy Awards.
“In March 2026, the 66-year-old Mr. Panahi courageously decided to return to Iran, aware of the risks but having always spoken of his deep love for his country, and for his desire to stay and work there," reads the letter.
"In October 2026 he learned of the new court verdict against him after his bank accounts were frozen, his lawyer, Mostafa Nili, said in a statement to the Iranian press. The new charges against him remain unclear, but appear consistent with repeated efforts to intimidate him into ceasing his filmmaking. The case will now go to regional court, and the sentence can be appealed. This requires resources, but all of Mr. Panahi’s accounts have been blocked."
The statement concludes: “We stand in solidarity with Mr. Panahi and all Iranians facing persecution for their work at the hands of their own government. We call on the Tehran Revolutionary Court to rescind all actions to penalize and imprison Mr. Panahi and to abide by the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights to which the Iranian government is a signatory."
"In this exceptionally heightened moment of conflict and political tension, such artists as Mr. Panahi, who create understanding within and across borders are of utmost importance. The international creative community stands together here to bear witness and to protect freedom of artistic expression everywhere.”
Actors and filmmakers who have signed the letter include Tilda Swinton, Mark Ruffalo, Barry Jenkins, Alex Gibney, Jacques Audiard, Kleber Mendonça Filho, Laura Poitras, Catherine Breillat, Michael Moore, Alice Braga, Asif Kapadia, Lucrecia Martel, and many more.
Festival leaders who signed the letter include Berlinale director Tricia Tuttle, Venice’s Alberto Barbera, Telluride head Julie Huntsinger, New York Film Festival artistic director Dennis Lim, and others including representatives for Rotterdam, Locarno, Karlovy Vary, Sydney, Tokyo, Busan film festivals – as well as the German Film Academy, the Austrian Film Academy and the Académie des César.
The statement follows a similar letter of protest published by Cannes this week, which stated that the festival “condemns the judicial persecution of Jafar Panahi and calls for the lifting of all restrictions that prevent him from traveling, creating and expressing himself freely.”
“Like artists, festivals, and cultural institutions around the world, the Festival de Cannes calls on the international community to take action and speak with one voice to prevent his imprisonment. His freedom is not just about one filmmaker, it is about the rights of all artists to think, create, and express themselves without fear of imprisonment,” it said.
Panahi won last year’s Palme d’Or in Cannes for It Was Just An Accident. He was sentenced by Iran’s Revolutionary Court to one year in prison and a two-year travel ban in absentia at the end of 2025.
Panahi was jailed shortly before making It Was Just An Accident and was only released after going on a hunger strike. He spent 86 days in Iran’s notorious Evin prison in 2022 and 2023 on charges of anti-government activity dating back to 2010 and for demonstrating against the imprisonment of his friend and fellow filmmaker Mohammad Rasoulof.
In prison, Panahi met activist and political prisoner Mehdi Mahmoudian. The two collaborated on the screenplay for It Was Just An Accident, a thriller inspired by Panahi’s time in prison.
Mahmoudian was re-arrested earlier this year on accusations of “insulting the Supreme Leader” and “propaganda against the Islamic Republic.”
Panahi has clashed with the repressive Iranian authorities as far back as 2003, has been imprisoned twice in Iran, and was banned from filmmaking for his anti-regime stance and “propaganda against the state”.
He has continued to make films in defiance of the authorities and is best known for films like This Is Not a Film, No Bears and Taxi Tehran, which won the Golden Bear at the Berlin Film Festival in 2015.
It Was Just An Accident follows a group of formerly imprisoned Iranians who contemplate whether to exact revenge on a man they believe to be their former jailer and torturer. It serves as an unflinching condemnation of the Islamist Republic’s repression and is a timeless commentary of the sins of state despotism.
In our review of It Was Just An Accident, we wrote: “Shot in secret, considering Panahi was not allowed filming permission from the authorities, the result is a taut, tense and tightly scripted drama that surprises due to its deft tonal shifts. (...) It’s a powerfully engrossing work that explores the consequences of torture, the price of revenge and whether mercy is possible, as the characters are rattled by the possibility that fighting violence with violence could dehumanize them further.”

noticias.titulo: French policeman jailed for eight years on appeal over 2020 killing of motorist
noticias.resumen: Olivio Gomes' family called the verdict historic as figures show ethnic minorities are four times more likely to be stopped by police in France.
noticias.texto:
Olivio Gomes' family called the verdict historic as figures show ethnic minorities are four times more likely to be stopped by police in France.
A French appeals court has jailed former police officer Gilles Guilbert for eight years for murdering Olivio Gomes, a 28-year-old black man he shot dead at the wheel of his car in 2020. That is two years less than the sentence he was given at his first trial.
The court in the Hauts-de-Seine department, west of Paris, France, ruled late on Wednesday that Guilbert, 35, had not acted in self-defence when he opened fire at close range during a night-time stop on 17 October 2020.
Guilbert was also banned for life from serving as a police officer and may not carry a firearm for 15 years.
Guilbert and two colleagues had followed Gomes's car for about 20 minutes, to outside his home in Poissy, a town in the Paris region. The defence said the officers tailed him because he was speeding, but security camera footage contradicted that account.
When Gomes stopped, Guilbert got out of the police car and aimed his gun at him. As Gomes started the engine to drive away, the officer fired three times, killing the father of three.
A court in Versailles had sentenced Guilbert to 10 years in prison in March. His lawyer appealed straight away.
"It's a relief. All these years of struggle, of fighting, there was a lot of doubt. We can finally breathe, mourn our loss," Leonel Gomes, the victim's younger brother, told AFP.
Damien Vinet, one of the family's lawyers, described the ruling as "historic".
Another high-profile case is due before the courts: a police officer will stand trial over the death of 17-year-old Nahel Merzouk, who was shot at point-blank range in Nanterre, near Paris, in June 2023.
Rights groups and campaigners accuse French police of systemic racism and violence. The government and police unions say abuses are isolated.
A report published last year by France’s Defender of Rights found that young men "perceived as Arab, black or from North Africa" are four times more likely to be stopped by police than the rest of the population.

noticias.titulo: Strasbourg, Birmingham and Baden-Baden: Europe’s top 10 most accessible Christmas markets
noticias.resumen: This new study looked at factors like the distance to step-free public transport and the share of uneven ground in the surrounding area to create the ranking.
noticias.texto:
This new study looked at factors like the distance to step-free public transport and the share of uneven ground in the surrounding area to create the ranking.
The most accessible Christmas markets in Europe have been named – and the top spot went to Strasbourg in France.
Based on a study from British mobility store Muick Sandy, the team looked at five factors: The distance to an accessible toilet, accessible parking, step-free public transport, the share of rough or uneven ground in the surrounding area, and available accessibility facilities.
Each of these was given a weighted score out of 20, which was then turned into an overall accessibility score out of 100 – with Strasbourg earning a rating of 88.49.
The market in the self-declared “capital of Christmas” was praised for being just 23 metres from step-free public transport, while only 5% of the ground assessed was rough or uneven.
“Christmas markets are a huge part of the festive season for millions of people, but something as simple as uneven ground, a long journey from accessible parking or a lack of suitable facilities can make visiting much more difficult for somebody with limited mobility,” Ben Kenny, director at Muick Sandy, said.
“What stands out from the research is that accessibility isn’t determined by one feature alone. A market might have excellent accessible facilities, but if visitors have to travel a significant distance from parking or public transport, that can still create a barrier.”
Europe’s most accessible Christmas markets
While Strasbourg took the top spot, hot on its heels was Birmingham in the UK, with a score of 88.36. The city in the West Midlands was the only one to get full marks for its accessibility facilities, with visitors 110 metres from an accessible toilet, 158 metres from accessible parking and 113 metres from step-free public transport.
Germany, the home of the very first Christmas markets, has four in the top 10, including Baden-Baden in third place. Frankfurt placed fourth, followed by Dresden in eighth and Nuremberg in ninth.
Vienna in Austria rounded out the top five.

- Birmingham, UK – 88.36
