noticias.titulo: EU plans a new €45bn loan to Ukraine. How much will it cost? And will it be repaid?
noticias.resumen: Euronews breaks down the European Commission's new proposal to issue a €45 billion support loan to Ukraine. Here's what you need to know.
noticias.texto:
Euronews breaks down the European Commission's new proposal to issue a €45 billion support loan to Ukraine. Here's what you need to know.
The European Union is "as committed as ever to support Ukraine in war and in peace", Ursula von der Leyen said as she unveiled a €45 billion support loan to help the country address its growing wartime budget deficit.
"We think this is the best way to give Ukraine a strong hand at the negotiation table," the European Commission president said on Wednesday.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy publicly thanked her, saying "strong support for Ukraine is the best signal to Russia that this war must end".
The loan still has to be greenlit by EU leaders, but the urgency is growing. Moscow's non-stop airstrikes have multiplied costs and worsened Kyiv's dependency on foreign aid.
But governments are also wary of the optics of approving fresh cash for Ukraine at a time of high energy bills, tight budgets and popular discontent. After all, any new pledges will fall on European taxpayers.
Here is everything you need to know about the new loan.
Why now?
In December last year, EU leaders agreed on a €90 billion loan to fulfil Ukraine's military and financial needs for 2026 and 2027 combined.
The €90 billion loan, which is still ongoing, was designed under the assumption that Russia's war would end sometime in 2026.
Instead, the opposite has happened: Moscow has escalated its attacks to make Ukraine's winter insufferable and further cripple the country's economy.
The relentless attacks have disrupted business activity, impaired the energy system and diminished Kyiv's capacity to raise public revenue. The blockade in the Black Sea, a vital route for Ukrainian farmers, has further exacerbated the pain.
The devastation has drilled a €70 billion hole in Ukraine's 2027 budget. In their October summit, leaders heard from Zelenskyy and agreed to address the situation.
Why €45 billion?
This is the division of labour between the EU and its allies.
Last year, the bloc committed to cover two-thirds of Ukraine's estimated €135 billion needs. This produced the €90 billion loan.
Now, it repeats the same formula: the €45 billion will cover two-thirds of the €70 billion shortfall. Other allies, such as the UK, Norway, Canada, Japan and Australia, are expected to supply the remaining €25 billion.
In its proposal, the Commission offers two ways for allies to chip in: a €5 billion top-up through AAA-rated guarantees or an extension of a previous G7 loan backed by the windfall profits stemming from the immobilised Russian assets.
There is little hope that the US will contribute financially, despite the Democratic Party's sweeping victory in the midterm elections.
"It would not be wise to budget on hope alone," a senior Commission official quipped.
How will it be raised?
The €45 billion will be raised through joint debt, a straightforward option.
The Commission, which is triple-rated, will issue bonds of different maturities to the markets and gradually borrow the money on behalf of all member states.
This is the same method as in the €90 billion loan.
Combined, the EU will raise €135 billion for Ukraine in 2026 and 2027.
How much will it cost?
Joint debt is always costly – even more so today.
Borrowing costs have soared worldwide in reaction to energy turmoil, geopolitical volatility, high debt concerns and the all-consuming AI race. From Brussels to Washington, public accounting is under strain.
Commission officials estimate an annual bill of roughly €6 billion in interest payments: €3.5 billion from the €90 billion loan (up from €3 billion when it was set up) and somewhere between €2 billion and €2.5 billion from the €45 billion loan.
Member states will subsidise the interest to avoid burdening Ukraine.
As of now, the plan is to pay the annual payments through the €100 billion special envelope that Brussels has allocated for Ukraine in the next seven-year budget. But this will reduce the allocation by €42 billion and slash fungible support for Kyiv.
An alternative plan would be to cover the payments through a separate financial instrument to keep the €100 billion envelope intact.
The question adds yet another link between Ukraine and the budget, which are rapidly becoming one single, politically explosive package. Both depend on unanimity
What about those countries that want an opt-out?
In the lead-up to the presentation, four member states – Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Bulgaria – indicated they will not be part of the new scheme.
"I say a clear no to war, weapons and war loans, and a yes to peace," Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico said in a video message.
Slovakia, the Czech Republic and Hungary are already exempted from the €90 billion and want to continue their opt-out policy. Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev, a vocal critic of weapon deliveries to Ukraine, wants to join the club.
The attitude has infuriated German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who argues that "supporting Ukraine is a matter of our indivisible European security, and so must be the burden sharing for that support".
Merz has threatened to veto the next EU budget, which contains billions in cohesion funds that Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Bulgaria depend on, if the new loan is not backed by all 27 member states.
"I support the Chancellor," von der Leyen said, taking Merz's side. "I'm very confident we will agree by 27."
The Commission has offered the four countries the option to opt in to the loan's budget strand (€20 billion) and opt out of its military strand (€25 billion). But this is unlikely to sway them, as their opposition is intrinsically political.
Will it ever be repaid?
The EU will ask Ukraine to repay either the €90 billion or the €45 billion loans only when Russia agrees to provide war reparations as part of a future peace deal.
Until that day comes, it will roll over the loans indefinitely.
Moscow has repeatedly dismissed such a thing, raising the odds that the EU will have to assume responsibility one way or another.
Brussels says it "reserves the right" to use the immobilised Russian assets, worth €210 billion, to repay the aid provided to Ukraine. But this will deprive Kyiv of a much-needed cash injection to rebuild the country after the war ends.
Ukraine, which is already saddled with debts from other partners and institutions, is not expected to pay out of pocket in any case.
"There can always be a political decision to waive the debt," a senior official said.
"De facto, the EU has become the lender of last resort for Ukraine and is likely to be there for some time."

noticias.titulo: Festive train trips: Europe’s most magical Christmas and winter rail journeys
noticias.resumen: Get the festive season on the right track with these unique European winter and Christmas rail journeys, offering luxury, adventure and slow travel.
noticias.texto:
Get the festive season on the right track with these unique European winter and Christmas rail journeys, offering luxury, adventure and slow travel.
With picture-perfect snowy scenes, twinkling lights, hearty feasts and so many Christmas markets to enjoy, winter is a great time of year to visit Europe.
And what better way to get in the holiday spirit than with a slow rail journey through some of the continent’s most beautiful landscapes?
Here, Euronews Travel rounds up some of the most picturesque and unique festive train journeys to take this winter.
The Santa Claus Express, Finland
This might be one of Europe’s most magical train journeys to take at the end of the year. Venture straight into the heart of Christmas fairy tales with the Santa Claus Express, a Finnish double-decker night train which takes travellers from Helsinki and Turku all the way north into the Arctic Circle. Going past frozen lakes and snow-dusted woods, some lucky travellers may also spot the elusive Northern Lights during certain journeys.
By the time you wake up, you’ll be deep into Finnish Lapland in Rovaniemi, the “official hometown of Santa Claus”. Here, travellers can enjoy attractions such as Santa Claus Village, and go to the Santa Claus Main Post Office to get an Arctic Circle postmark available on letters and postcards. You can also post letters from here.
The train offers standard sleeper cabins, deluxe sleeper cabins and seating carriages. Sleeper cabins usually have two beds, temperature control and private bathroom options with showers. A dining car with breakfast, other meals and snack options is also available.
Cogwheel train to Santa’s House, Switzerland
From the shores of Lake Geneva, a cogwheel train climbs from Montreux to Santa’s House at Rochers-de-Naye, more than 2,000 metres above sea level. The 55-minute ride offers views over the lake and the Swiss Alps, and children can meet Santa and have their photo taken with him at the summit. The festive trips run on selected dates from 20 November to 24 December 2026. A combined ticket covers the return train journey, a reserved seat on the way up and entry to Santa’s House.
La Dolce Vita Orient Express ‘Jingle Route’
Luxury sleeper train La Dolce Vita Orient Express is running a festive round trip from Rome via Venice and Florence. Departing on 19 December 2026, the three-day, two-night “Jingle Route” begins at Ostiense Station in Rome before travelling north through Italy's winter landscapes and arriving in Venice in the early evening.
Here, private boats escort guests through the canals to the recently opened Orient Express Venezia hotel where they can enjoy a festive celebration with live music and dinner in the palazzo before returning to the train just after midnight.
On day two, passengers arrive in Florence in the afternoon and have time to explore the city before returning to the train for dinner and live entertainment. A slow journey will then see the train make its way back to Ostiense Station where the journey ends the following morning. Prices start from €6,560 per passenger.
Majestic Imperator ‘Advent in Prague’
The Majestic Imperator is running a festive round trip from Vienna to Prague from 4-6 December 2026. The luxury train leaves Vienna on the Friday morning, with a champagne brunch and live music on board before arriving in the Czech capital that afternoon. Passengers spend two nights at the five-star Almanac Prague hotel near Wenceslas Square.
On the Saturday, monks lead a private tour of the library at Strahov Monastery, followed by a concert. The train heads back to Vienna on the Sunday evening, with a three-course dinner and live music. The package costs €1,250 per person, including the hotel stay.
British Pullman, UK
On 28 November and 10 December, Belmond’s British Pullman train heads from London to Bath for a day at the city’s Christmas market. Passengers are served brunch on the way out and a four-course dinner with wine on the return, with time in between to browse the market’s craft stalls.
The luxury train’s festive programme also includes a trip to Blenheim Palace in Oxfordshire for its illuminated light trail and a day in Canterbury that pairs a Christmas carol performance with time to explore the city. For a trip centred on the food, the Christmas lunch round trip serves a festive meal as the train rolls through the countryside.
Bergen Railway, Norway
The Bergen Railway, operated by the Norwegian state-owned rail company Vy, is another train line that comes into its own in winter. From Oslo to the city of Bergen on Norway’s west coast, this train travels around 500 kilometres in about seven hours and includes about 180 tunnels. It is also one of Europe’s most high-altitude lines.
Enjoy a magical festive winter adventure, as you pass by frozen vistas and waterfalls, snowfields, dramatic mountains, winding fjords, vast plateaus and fairy tale-like villages with wooden houses.
Some highlights of the route include the Hardangervidda plateau, one of Europe’s largest mountain plateaus, as well as Finse, a high-altitude station with stunning glacier views and Geilo, a popular ski resort town. Travellers can connect to the famous Flåm Railway at Myrdal station for an even more unforgettable descent into the fjords.
Passengers can choose between multiple daily departures, including a sleeper train. The train offers a first and second class, as well as a cafe car, vending machines, and wi-fi. Some carriages are also specially designed for families.
Golden Eagle Danube Express ‘Christmas Markets of Central Europe’
Love Christmas markets? The Golden Eagle Danube Express is for you. Offering a variety of year-round itineraries ranging from eight to 12 days, this train is extra special in winter. It runs a “Christmas Markets of Central Europe” itinerary, which operates between Budapest and Munich, taking in Vienna, the Austrian Alps and Salzburg as well.
Departing on 3 December 2026, this eight-day trip includes a two-night stay at a five-star hotel in Budapest, three nights on the train and two hotel nights in Munich, as well as welcome dinners, guided city tours, champagne receptions, and Christmas market tours.
Highlights include a traditional horse-drawn carriage ride in Vienna, a concert of Viennese Christmas folk songs and a tasting of Pirker gingerbread.
Glacier Express
The Glacier Express route is one of Switzerland’s most famous rail journeys. Dubbed the “slowest express train in the world”, it runs between Zermatt and St. Moritz in an epic eight-hour journey over 291 kilometres. Cross the Swiss Alps, passing through 91 tunnels and 291 bridges, while marvelling at panoramic snow-capped mountain views, icy blue lakes and deep gorges.
Highlights include the dramatic Rhine Gorge, also known as the “Swiss Grand Canyon”, and the Landwasser Viaduct, a UNESCO World Heritage-listed railway. Choose from three classes, including second class, first class and excellence class.
The train includes facilities such as wi-fi access, digital infotainment and audio guides. Excellence class passengers can enjoy luxurious five-course dining, with vegetarian, vegan, gluten-free and lactose-free options as well as a range of regional Swiss wines and digestifs. All meals are freshly prepared on board, with high-quality, seasonal ingredients and are served at your seat. Winter service resumes on 5 December 2026 and seat reservations are mandatory.

noticias.titulo: China: Xi, Trump and Putin gather ahead of trilateral summit
noticias.resumen: Chinese President Xi Jinping, US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin appeared together in Shenzhen, on Thursday 19 November 2026, posing for a group photograph alongside other world leaders ahead of a closely watched trilateral summit.
noticias.texto:
The three presidents stood together for the official group shot ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum’s opening session. The high-level assembly drew leaders from across the Pacific, featuring Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, Canada’s Mark Carney, Australia’s Anthony Albanese and South Korean President Lee Jae Myung.
Taking the podium, Xi Jinping made a plea for closer Asia-Pacific ties in an era of sweeping global upheaval and rapid technological breakthroughs. He challenged member nations to prioritise innovation, openness and deeper integration, framing the goal as a shared regional community rooted in solidarity and inclusive development.
All eyes, however, were fixed on Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, who are slated to join Xi for separate trilateral talks. The rare sight of the Chinese, American and Russian presidents sharing a stage at the opening ceremony threw into sharp relief the diplomatic significance of the Shenzhen meeting.

noticias.titulo: Zelenskyy says he expects debrief from US envoys on Trump’s talks with Xi and Putin
noticias.resumen: The US envoys told Kyiv they would give a debrief on the talks being held by Trump in China during meetings in Berlin on Thursday, Zelenskyy said.
noticias.texto:
The US envoys told Kyiv they would give a debrief on the talks being held by Trump in China during meetings in Berlin on Thursday, Zelenskyy said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Wednesday that he expects US envoys to brief him on the talks taking place in China, as Donald Trump prepares to meet China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin.
Trump has said he plans to raise limits on nuclear weapons and an end to the war in Ukraine in his historic trilateral meeting with Xi and Putin at the APEC summit in Shenzhen.
Speaking in his nightly video address, Zelenskyy said, “We and the Europeans have a clear, shared position: issues concerning Ukraine must be decided with Ukraine’s participation, and issues concerning Europe must be decided with Europe’s participation."
The Ukrainian leader said the US envoys had told Kyiv they would give a debrief on the talks being held by Trump in China during meetings in Berlin on Thursday. Ukraine will also hear from other partners currently in China, he added.
Germany, France and Britain are co-hosting talks in Berlin that begin only hours after Trump, Putin and Xi wrap up their landmark trilateral summit in Shenzhen.
More than 30 European leaders are due to attend the Berlin meeting, along with Zelenskyy and US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, amid fears that Trump, Putin and Xi could make decisions on Ukraine without Kyiv and Europe.
War grinds on amid Kyiv's strained ties with Washington
Trump has often boasted of his rapport with Putin, while relations between Washington and Kyiv appear to have deteriorated recently.
Trump has rejected new sanctions on Russia, and Ukraine has faced disruptions in satellite support for its drones during the war.
But for the first time since February, Russian, Ukrainian and US negotiators held talks on ending the full-scale war in Abu Dhabi earlier this month, with security guarantees topping the agenda.
The two-day session followed previous negotiations early this year that failed to produce any visible progress toward ending Europe’s most devastating conflict since World War II.
Meanwhile, fighting is continuing, despite the Trump administration's renewed diplomatic efforts to end the nearly five-year conflict.
Russian drones attacked Kharkiv Oblast on the evening of Wednesday, hitting an apartment building, Ukrainian media reported, while Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko reported that drone debris fell in the Pecherskyi district of the city on Wednesday afternoon, causing fire.
No injuries were reported, as emergency services were dispatched to the scene.
Earlier, Ukraine struck two oil refineries in southern Russia, something Zelenskyy has praised and described as the "effectiveness of Ukrainian-made weapons."
A strike partly damaged the Kerch Bridge, a strategic crossing linking Russia to the occupied Crimean Peninsula.

noticias.titulo: Anthropic's record IPO lands as Nvidia suffers its worst run since 2008
noticias.resumen: Anthropic priced its record IPO at $83 a share ahead of Thursday's debut, as Nvidia heads for a seventh weekly loss and Washington tightens AI chip exports.
noticias.texto:
Anthropic priced its record IPO at $83 a share ahead of Thursday's debut, as Nvidia heads for a seventh weekly loss and Washington tightens AI chip exports.
For years, Jensen Huang and Dario Amodei could hardly agree on anything.
The Nvidia founder once said he disagreed "with almost everything" the Anthropic chief executive says. Amodei, for his part, compared selling advanced American chips to China to "selling nuclear weapons to North Korea".
This week, their paths split dramatically. Huang is gone from the company he built over 33 years, while Amodei is taking his to Wall Street in what could become the largest stock market debut in history.
Anthropic, the San Francisco company behind the Claude chatbot, priced its shares at $83 each on Wednesday and increased the size of the offering, according to people familiar with the matter. That is well above the $70 to $78 range set in its filings with US regulators.
At that price, the 825 million shares originally on offer alone would raise more than $68bn. A private placement at the same price with investors including Nvidia, Google and AMD adds at least $26bn more, taking the total past the $86.2bn SpaceX raised in June, including extra shares sold to meet demand.
Shares are expected to start trading on Thursday on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. Counting all its shares, the company would be worth about $1.5tn.
A company that grew 45 times in 18 months
In the first quarter of 2025, the company booked $376 million in revenue. In the third quarter of 2026, it booked $16.96bn, an increase of 1,127% compared with the same period a year earlier.
The pace has not slowed. Anthropic's annualised revenue, a company estimate based on recent usage and subscriptions, reached $81bn at the end of October, $10bn more than just a month earlier.
Most of that money comes from businesses, and more than 11,900 customers now spend over $100,000 a year.
The cost of serving them is also falling. A year ago, computing power cost Anthropic one and a half times its revenue. In the third quarter of 2026, it was 58% of revenue.
Its $104bn net loss for the first nine months of the year comes almost entirely from accounting revaluations that disappear with the listing. Excluding stock-based pay and donations, operations made a $2.5bn profit in the third quarter.
Wall Street sees a catalyst, with a price tag
Analysts see the debut as a test for the whole artificial intelligence trade.
"The issue is over six times subscribed, and there's plenty of excitement ahead of the first public offering of a pure frontier lab at the forefront of AI development," David Morrison, senior market analyst at Trade Nation, said in a note on Wednesday.
Thahbib Rahman, research analyst at Block Scholes, sees a familiar pattern. Bitcoin fell 19% in the 50 days before SpaceX began trading in June, and it is down 23% over the same stretch ahead of Anthropic.
Yet Rahman said "there is some evidence to suggest that this latest sell-off is more closely tied to the wider rout in risk assets than to investors rotating out of crypto assets and into the IPO".
Jay Peters, portfolio manager at NewEdge Wealth, considers the price fair. "It's a historic IPO and we think the valuation at $1.2-1.4T is reasonable based on the trajectory of the business," he said in emailed comments.
"Anthropic is coming on Thursday - all aboard!" said Richard Reyle, chief investment officer at Questar Capital Partners, who called Nvidia "the Jenga tower of the whole AI trade".
Nvidia's worst losing streak since 2008
Nvidia shares fell 2.9% on Wednesday to $150.96, the day after its quarterly results. The stock is heading for a seventh straight weekly loss, its longest losing streak since July 2008, and has lost about 35% of its value since the start of October.
The slide deepened after Nvidia announced Huang's resignation on 12 November, following reports about his private life that had prompted an internal investigation. Chief financial officer Colette Kress is now interim CEO.
Its results on Tuesday beat expectations, but did little to calm investors.
"Investors have, repeatedly and ultimately, 'bought the dip' on every occasion since October 2022. So far, this one hasn't worked out so well," Morrison said.
Washington tightens the chip pipeline
Politics is adding to the pressure. On Monday, the US Commerce Department introduced licence requirements for advanced chips shipped to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil, which it considers at higher risk of diversion.
It also requires licences for data centres anywhere that rent large amounts of computing power to Chinese companies.
It is the kind of restriction Amodei has long called for, and one Huang has spent years fighting.
Peters sees the market moving towards "a slower-for-longer buildout", as borrowing costs rise and politics gets tougher.
The buyer becomes the investor
For three years, the AI boom rewarded the companies selling the hardware.
On Thursday, the market will put a price for the first time on a frontier AI lab, one of the handful of companies building the most advanced models.
And one of the buyers lining up next to ordinary investors is Nvidia itself, ready to put more than $10bn into the company whose chief executive its founder spent years arguing with.
Whether Thursday becomes a turning point or a high-water mark will depend less on the first day of trading than on what Anthropic reports in the quarters that follow.

noticias.titulo: Hegseth in Colombia to deepen anti-drug ties after surprise Venezuela stopover
noticias.resumen: Colombian Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora had told his country's parliament that the Pentagon chief would hand over a C-130 Hercules military aircraft during the visit.
noticias.texto:
Colombian Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora had told his country's parliament that the Pentagon chief would hand over a C-130 Hercules military aircraft during the visit.
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth arrived at a military airbase in Bogotá on Wednesday for talks on security cooperation, following an unannounced stopover in Venezuela.
Colombian Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora received Hegseth at the airbase in the country's capital. Mora had told Congress the previous day that the Pentagon chief would hand over a C-130 Hercules military aircraft during the visit.
Hegseth standing alongside Colombian ministers, "In each country, according to each country's laws, but in working together, we are going to find, we are going to hunt, we are going to kill and defeat narcoterrorists." "
He added that "each country wants to deny safe haven to those cartels while respecting the sovereignty, the laws and the constitution and the congress of each individual country, but bonding and working together to take a fight to a common enemy in way that has never happened before."
Following a closed-door meeting with Hegseth, Colombian Foreign Minister Omar Bula said the government will ask Congress to approve joint military operations with the US. Washington has already supported counter-narcotics strikes inside Colombia.
Bula said President Abelardo De la Espriella “has been very clear about his country’s sovereign position, and it is also very clear to the secretary of war after the conversation we had.”
Washington and Bogota, allies in the drug war
Hegseth's visit follows an impeachment attempt in Congress that left him fighting to keep his job less than two years into his tenure.
Thomas Massie, a Republican lawmaker critical of Trump, accused him of mismanaging the war with Iran, overstepping his authority in personnel decisions, and carrying out extrajudicial killings through strikes on boats accused of smuggling drugs in the Caribbean and Pacific. Hegseth has survived the push for now.
Colombia has traditionally been one of the US' closest allies in the region and Washington and Bogotá have long worked together against drug trafficking, linking the world’s largest cocaine market with one of its biggest producers.
Colombia’s new right-wing president, Abelardo de la Espriella, who took office in August vowing to confront the country’s many trafficking groups, has since stepped up military cooperation with the US and intensified the crackdown.
Hegseth’s trip comes after Vice President JD Vance cancelled a planned visit to Colombia this month. Secretary of State Marco Rubio visited in September and pledged to “restore” ties with Bogotá after four years of leftist government.
And most recently, a top US military officer, General Dan Caine, visited Colombia last week to coordinate joint efforts against drug trafficking.
The two countries are carrying out a major offensive against criminal gangs that Washington classifies as terrorist organisations.
More than 300 US soldiers recently trained with 400 Colombian troops in anti-trafficking exercises, which US Southern Command (SOUTHCOM) said highlight “the deep and enduring security partnership between the United States and Colombia.”
US troops have also carried out joint operations against trafficking and violence in other Latin American countries, including Mexico and Ecuador.

noticias.titulo: GTA VI launch sparks celebrations in Miami and Dublin
noticias.resumen: After 13 years of anticipation, Grand Theft Auto VI has finally arrived. Fans celebrated at a launch party in Dublin, while Miami Heat supporters rushed to buy limited-edition Vice City merchandise.
noticias.texto:
Screens displayed images from the game, while mock crime scene tape added to the atmosphere. The excitement was palpable among players eager to explore the latest instalment of Rockstar Games' crime series. Some players told AFP they planned to skip college for two days to play, declaring that nothing else mattered for the next 48 hours.
In Miami, United States, the launch inspired a crossover with the NBA's Miami Heat, whose arena was transformed into Vice City, the fictional metropolis featured in GTA VI and inspired by Miami itself. Fans queued for hours before rushing into the arena shop to purchase limited-edition jerseys and shorts bearing the game's branding.
The release follows the extraordinary success of GTA V, launched in 2013, which became one of the most commercially successful entertainment products ever. The celebrations underline the franchise's cultural reach, extending well beyond gaming into sport, fashion and popular culture.

noticias.titulo: Watch: EU health chief has ‘ashes’ thrown over him in protest at pesticide rules
noticias.resumen: Olivér Várhelyi was about to speak at a cancer summit when he had a grey substance thrown at him.
noticias.texto: BRUSSELS — Activists from a cancer survivor group threw what appeared to be ashes over the EU’s health chief in protest at Europe’s new rules relaxing pesticide use. Commissioner for Health Olivér Várhelyi was about to deliver a speech at a cancer summit on the EU’s work to curb the disease when two protesters got on stage and threw a grey, dusty substance on him. “I am a cancer patient; I’m protesting against omnibus law,” said one of the activists from French group Cancer Colère. “These are the ashes of the people you will kill with the pesticides,” said another. One of the protestors was Fleur Breteau, a French writer and activist. The other could not be identified. The Commission presented the omnibus as a way to clear the backlog of pesticides waiting for approval, to make life easier for farmers. But it is strongly opposed by many civil society groups. More than 2,000 scientists have signed a letter calling for the proposal to be put on hold until an independent impact assessment is carried out. Consumer group Foodwatch took the issue to the European Ombudsman, accusing the Commission of maladministration, and NGOs have organized multiple protests. More than 300 NGOs — including environmental organizations, beekeepers’ associations and pesticide victims’ groups, plus doctors and scientists — from 25 European countries will gather outside the European Parliament in Strasbourg at 2 p.m. on Nov. 24 to express discontent with the omnibus. Video taken at The Hotel in Brussels on November 19, 2026. | Emma Pirnay/POLITICO Várhelyi brushed off the dust, visibly displeased, and continued with his speech as planned. “What sort of people are you?” he remarked. “As I was saying, good morning, I’m a bit surprised that in the name of victims of cancer, they dare to splash the ashes of those who have died.” “This is beyond anything we could have imagined. We are sorry,” Elisabetta Zanon, head of the European Cancer Organisation, told the audience.

noticias.titulo: Spanish election race tightens ahead of campaign’s final week, new poll shows
noticias.resumen: The conservative People's Party and Socialists are neck and neck, with the far-right Vox in position to play kingmaker.
noticias.texto:
MADRID — A new Spanish election poll shows the People’s Party and Socialists locked in a tight race, as conservative leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo and left-wing Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez prepare for a head-to-head debate Thursday night.
According to the poll conducted for POLITICO by PF Global, the PP would win the Nov. 29 snap election with 29.5% of the vote, while the Socialist Party would secure 27.2%.
With a margin of error of 2.6%, the two parties are in a statistical dead heat. The poll surveyed 2,454 Spaniards between Nov. 15 and 17.
Advertisement
The results for the far-right Vox party, in third place, offer a more complete picture of the potential next Spanish government.
The poll shows it is on course to receive 19.6% of the vote, allowing a right wing PP-Vox coalition to net almost 50% of the vote, making Feijóo the clear favorite to be Spain’s next prime minister.
The poll also shows how voters have changed their minds since 2023. For example, 20% of the voters who three years ago supported the PP said they would now back Vox, and 10% of those who voted for the Socialists said they were now switching allegiance to the PP.
Left of the Socialists
One of the Socialists’ biggest hurdles in this election is the collapse of their allies to the left. After three years as the junior partner in government, Sumar has rebranded as Frente Amplio — meaning Broad Front — in an attempt to reenergize its base.
The left may yet find unity of another kind, by rallying behind the Socialist party.
Advertisement
According to the poll, 29% of Frente Amplio and Podemos voters would be willing to back Sánchez on Nov. 29 to keep Vox out of power. But that same tactical vote is shrinking the parliamentary left, making it harder for Sánchez to find the support he needs to have options to stay in office with a coalition. Around 30% of Socialist voters are backing Sánchez only to stop Vox leader Santiago Abascal.
The poll also reveals how personal the campaign has become.
As leftist voters mobilize against Vox and its leader, the conservatives and others are doing the same in respect to Sánchez. Around 30% of those polled explained that ousting the Socialist prime minister was their main goal. In the case of PP and Vox voters, 59% of them said their priority was to kick Sánchez out of power.
The level of distrust in the vote count also loomed large in the poll, especially on the right: 65% of Vox voters and 34% of PP supporters didn’t trust it. By contrast, only 15% of Socialist voters had such fears in the legitimacy of the ballot.
Suspicion is even higher when it comes to mail-in voting. There’s also broad opposition on the right to the so-called grandchildren’s law, which allows descendants of exiles and emigr´és to obtain Spanish citizenship — and with it the right to vote: 63% of Vox supporters and 56% of PP voters are against it.

noticias.titulo: UK Tory chief Badenoch blasts ‘disturbing’ Trump-Putin-Xi trilateral
noticias.resumen: Right-wing Kemi Badenoch says Britain must now look beyond a U.S. 'administration on its way out.'
noticias.texto: LONDON — Kemi Badenoch called Donald Trump’s trilateral meeting in Shenzhen “disturbing” — as she placed significant distance between the U.K.’s opposition Conservatives and the U.S president. “It’s basically an administration on its way out — we should be looking to the future,” the Tory leader told the BBC Thursday morning when pressed on Trump’s White House. The U.S. president is holding three-way talks with his “ friend ” Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese premier Xi Jinping. Trump has defended his decision to engage directly with two leaders whose countries are often at odds with Washington, saying he has “a special responsibility to maintain open, respectful and productive dialogue on issues impacting not just our people, but the entire planet.” “Disturbing is how I would describe it,” Badenoch told the Today program when pressed on the summit. “There are three world leaders who look like they’re trying to carve up the world between them.” She argued that the three leaders are trying to forge a tripolar world where the Chinese president commands Asia, the American the western hemisphere, and the Russian gets Europe. “That is very concerning, especially seeing Donald Trump call president Putin his friend. Russia is not America’s friend,” Badenoch added. It’s another notable break by a British right-wing leader with the U.S. commander-in-chief. Badenoch praised Trump after his return the White House, and even looked enviously at initiatives like DOGE and ICE . But like Nigel Farage , the leader of her right-wing rivals in the Reform UK party, Badenoch has been distancing the Conservatives from Trump as the effects of his foreign policy become apparent in the U.K. Her latest comments come after Trump’s Republicans took a major hit in the U.S. mid-terms. Badenoch called for Britain to strengthen partnerships “with all our allies,” including in the U.S., Canada and Europe — a clear tilt beyond Trump.

noticias.titulo: Revealed: What Britain thinks on free movement
noticias.resumen: Presented by TikTok
noticias.texto:
Listen on
With multiple high-stakes summits taking place across the world – where does Britain stand on the international stage and are we prepared for a new relationship with Europe?
From Trump, Xi and Putin meeting in China to Andy Burnham preparing for the long-awaited UK-EU summit – Sam Coates and Anne McElvoy assess where Britain lies in the world.
Will the future of Ukraine be decided behind closed doors, do the British public favour European freedom of movement, and will we see some dates and timelines?
**A message from TikTok: Did you know TikTok contributed at least £10 billion to the UK economy in 2025? The platform supported 153,000 jobs, turning online discovery into real-world growth, from high streets to bookshops, new research from Public First and EY shows.**

noticias.titulo: Why depth beats breadth in Europe’s hunt for an AI edge
noticias.resumen: At the European Resilience Summit, Mauro Capo, Accenture’s digital sovereignty lead for EMEA, shared the company’s view on Europe’s opportunities in AI’s next phase.
noticias.texto: ​​​An artificial intelligence (AI) system is judged on the job it does, not on how clever it is in general. For European businesses, that is an opening. For example, a pharmaceutical company does not need a model that can discuss biology. It needs one that can flag the rare adverse-event signal in its own trial data. An energy grid operator needs load forecasts built on its own network topology, not generic ones. A defen​s​​​e manufacturer needs a system that can verify a weld against its own specification, and say why it passed or failed. Each needs a system that understands its domain, works on its data, follows its rules and guardrails, and can be trusted to execute in a protected, controlled environment. An edge Europe can’t buy That task-specific fit is Europe’s opening to turn its industrial experti​z​​​e into an AI edge, because that edge was never going to come from outspending anyone. US private AI investment reached ​US​$285.9 billion in 2025 , more than 23 times the ​US​$12.4 billion invested in China​ ​—​​​ ​though looking at just private investment figures likely understates China’s total AI spending, given its government guidance funds. The ​​Stargate​​ venture plans to invest between ​US​$100 billion and ​US​$500 billion to build advanced AI data centers across the US by 2029. Matching that euro for dollar would be a strategic mistake, and Europe’s grids rule it out regardless: connection queues in major hubs already run seven to ​10​​​ years. None of this means Europe should stop building AI factories. They matter for critical workloads and for a credible European alternative. ​ ​The point is not to scale compute, but to invest smartly in the infrastructure needed to run specialist industrial applications. A factory with nothing to run on is just an expensive data cent​er​​​. The number that matters is not compute deployed, but the number of specialist applications built, the tasks addressed and the vertical industry solutions delivered. Breadth first, depth next The same pattern shows up globally in how AI is actually used. Our September 2026 CIO Pulse survey of 300 technology leaders worldwide found that 70​ percent​​​ were using AI for individual productivity: particularly copilots and general-purpose tools adopted across the organi​z​​​ation. Only 37​ percent​​​ were using it to orchestrate processes end-to-end with agents, where AI sits inside a process and solves a real business problem in context, as a specialist. Breadth of adoption is arriving first, and faster​,​ than depth. Depth is harder, because it needs speciali​z​​​ation, context and precision, not just more scale, and that is where Europe can lead. Sovereignty by design Another factor in European AI adoption is non-negotiable: sovereignty. In mid-2025, 61​ percent​​​ of the business leaders we surveyed called it a strategic priority . By early 2026 that figure exceeded 80​ percent​​​. The June 2026 suspension of access to two frontier models under US export controls showed how fast the terms of access can change, and how little say any European company had in the decision. Sovereignty itself has layers: where infrastructure sits, where data lives, which models run, and now, above all three, what knowledge those models are grounded in. It has to be designed in from the start. It cannot be bolted on after a system is already live. Being sovereign while staying part of the global technology landscape is Europe’s real competitive advantage. That balance only works through speciali​z​​​ation: the precision to control what matters most while still drawing on the best of what the world builds. This is a wave Europe is well placed to ride. Specialist AI in practice AI designed with intention. How Europe can win with Specialist AI | via Accenture We call this operating logic Specialist AI in our report, AI designed with intention. How Europe can win with Specialist AI : model size, data, deployment location, inference pathway and governance controls matched deliberately to a defined task. Frontier models suit open-ended reasoning, cross-domain synthesis and genuine exceptions, which we estimate account for roughly 10​ ​percent​​​​ of enterprise workloads. Smaller domain-tuned models suit repetitive, high-volume work where latency, cost, auditability or local control matter most. The strongest architecture uses both, deliberately, not by accident. The point is not to scale compute, but to invest smartly in the infrastructure needed to run specialist industrial applications. A factory with nothing to run on is just an expensive data cent​er​​​. The European Patent Office​ (EPO)​ shows what this looks like in practice . With Mistral AI, it processes 400,000 pages a day on a one-billion-parameter model fine-tuned on 50,000 patents. The error rate is below 1​ percent​​​, and work that used to take five days now takes minutes. The model runs on the EPO’s own domain data, in a sovereign environment. It is not the biggest model in the world. It is the right one. Upcoming regulation​,​ including the proposed Cloud and AI Development Act ​​​ which was put forward​​​ in June, will likely only reinforce this shift and the opportunity it creates, especially through its multi-layer sovereignty definitions. Companies should start shoring up governance that holds across every layer of the stack now and understand that different parts of the stack carry different types of risk, with kill-switch exposure varying by layer. The future needs sophisticated controls, but it also rewards whoever builds them first. Turning ​a​​​dvantage into action Three moves follow for enterprises: Build demand alongside capacity. Develop the pipeline of industrial applications, from predictive maintenance to mission-critical decision support, while infrastructure is provisioned. Design for choice. Classify data, workloads and applications to find the right deployment model and governance for each, and keep the ability to change models as the market moves. Govern the knowledge layer. Set rules for grounding, provenance, evaluation and retention of derived knowledge, and for what any provider may learn from your data. Policymakers can reinforce the shift. Compute investment should connect to sectoral test facilities and adoption cent​er​​​s, not sit apart from them. Procurement should reward task performance, auditability, energy efficiency and portability, not just scale. Standards should enable interoperability and federation, so every provider adds to a single European fabric of capacity rather than ​27​​​ disconnected ones. Europe may not lead on AI breadth, but it can lead on AI depth. By combining generations of industrial experti​z​​​e with sovereign, specialist AI, designed for specific tasks and deployed on Europe’s terms, businesses can turn the potential of AI into lasting competitive advantage. AI Designed with Intention: How Europe Can Win with Specialist AI

noticias.titulo: EU lawmakers accuse Chinese officials of intimidation over Taiwan
noticias.resumen: Parliament President Roberta Metsola is in touch with Chinese authorities “to ensure that further incidents can be avoided”
noticias.texto: BRUSSELS — EU lawmakers from across the political spectrum say they have come under pressure from the Chinese government for traveling to or communicating with Taiwan. Eight MEPs gave accounts of what some described as intimidation inside the European Parliament — including a senior Chinese diplomat turning up unannounced at one MEP’s office — detentions at the Chinese border and threatening letters. The incidents come a little over a year after the European Parliament and Beijing restored ties following years of fraught relations over European criticism of China’s treatment of ethnic and religious minorities, and against the backdrop of European manufacturers creaking under the competitive pressure of Chinese imports. Taiwan has been politically separate from China since 1949, but Beijing views the island, home to 23 million people, as part of its territory and has long criticized Western governments for maintaining relations with Taipei — although the EU and its member countries do not recognize Taiwan as a separate country. But MEPs allege they have faced more than just criticism for taking a pro-Taiwanese independence stance. “I have never encountered such behavior from foreign diplomats,” said Engin Eroglu, a German liberal MEP who chairs the Parliament’s delegation to China. Eroglu said he had received “fierce” pushback from Beijing, without specifying what that entailed, and that he was troubled by Chinese officials’ actions toward other members of Parliament. The Chinese mission to the EU did not reply to requests for comment for this article. Markéta Gregorová, vice-chair of the China delegation — which manages relations between the European Parliament and China’s National People’s Congress — said she would ask Parliament President Roberta Metsola to bar Chinese officials from Parliament if Beijing doesn’t explain why she was stopped at the border during a recent visit. Metsola, who helped broker the deal to lift sanctions and restart diplomatic engagements with China, has been in close contact with the MEPs concerned and “has conveyed our questions and concerns directly to the Chinese authorities,” her spokesperson, Juri Laas, said. “Diplomatic contacts are ongoing in an effort to ensure that further incidents can be avoided.” “MEPs concerned must be able to exercise their freedom of mandate, and the Parliament expects that members traveling with an official European Parliament delegation should not have problems when entering their host country,” he added. Escalating pushback The far-right Patriots group vice-chair António Tânger Corrêa said that, before a June 2025 visit to Taiwan, a senior Chinese diplomat visited his office unannounced, warning that they “could not ensure” his safety and “didn’t know what could happen” if he made the trip. He said Metsola offered to warn the Chinese mission to the EU or take tougher action, but he urged her to pursue diplomacy first. Lawmakers who attended a forum in Taipei in October this year received letters, seen by POLITICO , from China’s EU mission urging them to “refrain from any official exchange in whatever form with the Taiwan authorities.” Chinese ships patrol as military drills take place on Pingtan Island on Dec. 30, 2025. | Adek Berry/AFP via Getty Images “China has no right to intimidate elected representatives or interfere with their parliamentary work,” said one of the MEPs who received the letter, Czechia’s Ondřej Krutílek. “We should make it clear that no one can dictate where MEPs travel, whom they meet or whom they engage with. These are decisions for elected representatives themselves, not for Beijing.” Others who also received the letter include Polish liberal MEP Michal Kobosko, Latvian conservative Rihard Kols, French liberal Bernard Guetta, and German center-right MEP Michael Gahler. “We cannot accept acts of direct pressure against us,” said Kobosko, calling the letter “bizarre.” Meetings with China are usually “completely polite,” said Guetta, but the letter was sent “to try pressure.” “There’s nothing particularly new about the approach,” said Kols. “The tone is quite aggressive, but then the message comes from a generic email address, with no named official attached to it. You could quite reasonably mistake it for spam. I don’t know whether that’s deliberate, but it makes the letter easier to dismiss.” He added that “coming from Latvia, there is something distinctly Soviet about the tone” but “MEPs deal with attempts to put pressure on us every day, in one form or another. We can handle a letter like this ourselves. I don’t see it as grounds to tighten access rules for Chinese officials or ask President Metsola to intervene.” Border incident Gregorová, a member of the Greens, said that on Sept. 26 she had an uncomfortable encounter with Chinese officials when she landed in Beijing as part of the Parliament’s trade committee delegation to China. The Czech MEP said she was stopped at border control, had her passport confiscated, and was forbidden from using her phone. “I was surrounded by police officers and held for approximately an hour and a half,” she told POLITICO. “It was an extremely unpleasant experience and, without my colleagues there to help me, it would have been frightening.” Gregorová is the lead MEP on the revision of the Cybersecurity Act, a legal proposal that could see Chinese telecom suppliers excluded from European networks. It has drawn Beijing’s ire, and Chinese officials have threatened “countermeasures” if the bill is passed. Gregorová said she didn’t know whether what happened to her was an administrative error or a “deliberate intimidation tactic.” She said she was sending a letter to the Chinese National People’s Congress — the national legislature — demanding an explanation, and that she’d ask Metsola to bar Chinese representatives from entering the Parliament unless an explanation is provided. Earlier this year, POLITICO reported that Chinese officials had told MEPs in the Socialists and Democrats group not to vote for a report critical of Beijing, warning there could be consequences. A troubled relationship In 2021, Beijing sanctioned five MEPs following EU sanctions targeting alleged Uyghur rights abuses. Parliament responded by freezing ratification of an EU-China investment deal and halting diplomatic contact with Beijing. The outer wall of a complex that includes what is believed to be a reeducation camp where mostly Muslim ethnic minorities are detained, outside Hotan, China, on May 31, 2019. | Greg Baker/AFP via Getty Images Beijing and the Parliament lifted those sanctions in April 2025. The Parliament will host the 44th EU-China interparliamentary meeting in Strasbourg in June, the second such meeting since relations were unfrozen, according to an internal note. The Chinese Mission to the EU organized a briefing on Taiwan in Brussels on Tuesday. As attendees entered, they had their invitations checked by staff sitting at a table decorated with panda bear plushies. Neatly stacked beside them were copies of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s tome, “The Governance of China.” Liu Jieyi, the former director of China’s Taiwan Affairs Office, spoke for most of the session, flanked by Ambassador Cai Run, head of the EU mission. Liu, who is now vice-chairman of the Foreign Affairs Committee of China’s top political advisory body, spent much of the session discussing the historical intricacies of China’s claim over Taiwan. While Beijing preferred to pursue peaceful reunification with Taiwan, Liu said China “will not renounce the use of non-peaceful means or the option to take all necessary measures to safeguard our sovereignty and territorial integrity.” The Chinese official also obliquely addressed some of the recent tensions with the European Parliament. “Certain institutions have adopted Taiwan-related resolutions and provided a venue for political theatrics staged by Taiwan independence secessionists, sending wrong signals to these elements,” he said. Liu added that the EU “must realize that such statements and actions severely erode China–EU relations and mutual political trust.” Beijing’s diplomatic push comes as Chinese President Xi Jinping on Nov. 12 called for “reunification” with Taiwan. In October, the Parliament passed a resolution condemning any attempt to change the situation in Taiwan by force. German MEP Eroglu said Beijing’s pressure was linked to warming ties between the Parliament and Taiwan, calling it “unimaginable” that China could dictate who lawmakers meet. “If we were to allow that, [Russian President Vladimir] Putin would probably be next to tell us that we should or can no longer meet,” he said.

noticias.titulo: Germany presses to make Ukraine aid Le Pen-proof
noticias.resumen: Berlin wants to lock future increases of aid to Kyiv into an EU budget framework that can't be vetoed by any single country.
noticias.texto: BERLIN — Germany is pushing to lock a durable funding scheme for Ukraine into the EU’s next long-term budget that will be difficult for potential opponents such as Marine Le Pen to veto should she win next year’s French presidential election. Berlin’s plan is to give the EU “headroom,” or financial leeway, to raise additional money for Ukraine beyond the €100 billion the Commission has already proposed, according to a senior European official with knowledge of the negotiations. The borrowing mechanism would allow for future funding without committing to massive — and politically unpalatable — upfront spending. “Ukraine funding is more disputed than it’s ever been,” said the senior European official who, like others who spoke to POLITICO about the negotiations, was granted anonymity to discuss sensitive budget plans. This will become “even more the case” if Le Pen from the far-right National Rally wins the French presidential election in April, the official added. Speaking after publication of this article on Thursday morning, Germany’s Europe Minister Gunther Krichbaum said: “ The financing of Ukraine is in our common interest, and it has to be reliable in the future, and therefore it is necessary to integrate a mechanism in the multiannual financial framework .” Whereas passing the bloc’s next long-term budget — and the headroom plan Germany wants to attach to it — would require unanimous support among EU member countries, future decisions to raise money for Ukraine under the scheme would require only a qualified majority if Germany gets its way. That would make it harder for any single government to block EU support, according to an EU diplomat with knowledge of the discussions. “In today’s geopolitical world, this [need for unanimity] doesn’t make sense,” the diplomat said. The German proposal is likely to run into opposition from countries such as Hungary, Czechia and Slovakia — which have demanded opt-outs for Ukraine aid — and further complicate already tough negotiations over Europe’s seven-year budget ahead of a special EU summit set for Nov. 26-27. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy attend a press conference at the Chancellery on November 3, 2026 in Berlin. | Pool photo by Filip Singer/Getty Images German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, however, is attempting to get his way on Ukraine aid by using the immense leverage his country derives from being the biggest contributor by far to the EU’s €2 trillion budget . In a letter sent to European Council President António Costa earlier this month, Merz issued an ultimatum that made German support for the next budget contingent on the bloc’s agreeing to raise a further €45 billion for Ukraine for 2027, as well as a “financing perspective for Ukraine from 2028 onwards.” In doing so, Merz was also implicitly threatening to cut German contributions to regional development funds that benefit Central European sceptics of Ukraine aid, should those countries attempt to block the headroom plan or opt out of aid for Kyiv. German officials worry that allowing smaller countries such as Slovakia to opt out of funding Ukraine could set a precedent, giving larger countries like France — if governed by Le Pen — a way to avoid future commitments. ‘A truly European endeavor’ From the German perspective, the need for a comprehensive EU funding plan for Ukraine is all the more urgent given that Merz wants the EU budget to cover the over €40 billion in interest coming due on existing loans, according to figures provided by a European Commission official. Those interest payments alone would consume a substantial share of the €100 billion the Commission has proposed for Ukraine in its seven-year budget, likely forcing the EU to seek additional aid soon after closing the current funding gaps. That’s not a debate Merz wants to keep having, however. Berlin isn’t just worried about Central European opponents of Ukraine aid and a potential Le Pen victory in France, but also about politics at home. The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won historic victories in eastern state elections last fall and has opened a wide polling lead over Merz’s conservatives, in part by attacking him for spending money on Ukraine instead of at home. The AfD’s success and Merz’s low popularity are leaving the chancellor with less political capital to justify bilateral aid to Ukraine, particularly as Germany is already Ukraine’s biggest EU backer. Hence Berlin’s broader effort to fold Ukraine aid into the EU’s next long-term budget and expand what Merz calls “burden sharing” across the bloc . “We must fully incorporate Ukraine policy into the EU budget,” Merz said last week in Berlin alongside Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar. For Merz, who suffers from dismal approval ratings at home, the headroom scheme could help shore up his political standing while securing long-term financing for Ukraine. “They don’t want to be the only ones who will continue to finance Ukraine given elections in other countries,” a European diplomat said of the German position. “Ukraine funding in Germany is also a sensitive topic,” the diplomat added, so Berlin wants “to show they’ve managed to transform the Ukraine issue into a truly European endeavor.” Nicholas Vinocur contributed reporting. This article has been updated.

noticias.resumen: Nuclear weapons are at the top of Donald Trump’s agenda at the trilateral summit in Beijing. noticias.titulo: Listen: Is the EU’s Digital Services Act actually working?
noticias.resumen: Earlier this week, the European Commission stepped up its action against Chinese online marketplace Temu. It announced that the platform was once again in breach of the Digital Services Act (DSA), and could face further fines.
noticias.texto: Production: By Europod , in co-production with Sphera Network . EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms . Find the full transcript below : Earlier this week, the European Commission stepped up its action against Chinese online marketplace Temu. It announced that the platform was once again in breach of the Digital Services Act (DSA), and could face further fines. Is the EU finally managing to rein in the tech giants? The commission first opened an investigation into Temu in October 2024. It was looking into several issues: the sale of illegal products, potentially addictive design, the way the platform recommends products to users, and the lack of access to data for researchers. In May this year, the commission fined Temu €200mln. The reason? The platform had failed to properly assess the risks associated with its services, particularly the likelihood of consumers encountering illegal products. And on 17 November, the commission announced new preliminary findings. This time, the problem is not just that Temu failed to assess the risks. It’s that it has also failed to put effective measures in place to address them. The commission points to inadequate product checks, weak content moderation and an ineffective system for sanctioning sellers. Read more EU Commission again rebukes Temu over failure to stop illegal product sales, exposing Chinese giant to another hefty fine In other words, illegal and unsafe products are still making their way onto the platform. Temu can still respond to these preliminary findings, and no new fine has been imposed at this stage. But beyond Temu, is the Digital Services Act actually delivering results? Since 2024, the commission has imposed three fines under the DSA: one on Elon Musk’s social network X , one on Temu , and one on AliExpress . That’s a total of €870mln in fines. And that’s only part of the picture. The commission has also opened investigations into more than a dozen issues involving major platforms. Some are still ongoing, while others have ended after platforms made legally binding commitments to change their practices. So the fact that some investigations have been settled through commitments is already a sign that the system can work. Platforms sometimes agree to change their practices before the commission even reaches a final decision. And when it comes to fines, the enforcement mechanism is clearly being used. Even if the process can be rather slow, and sometimes imperfect. Now, what changes did DSA bring to platforms? Take TikTok, for example. The commission launched an investigation into its potentially addictive design, including features that encourage users to spend more time on the app. In 2024, after the commission raised concerns about TikTok Lite’s rewards programme, the platform agreed to permanently withdraw it from the EU. Read more Consumers pay the price for online manipulation, and the EU Digital Fairness Act can put a stop to it That’s a concrete change. But the broader issue of addictive design is far from settled. In February this year, the commission issued preliminary findings that TikTok’s design itself could breach the DSA. Then there’s X. In December 2025, the platform was fined €120mln over three issues: its misleading blue verification checkmark, its lack of transparency around advertising, and its failure to provide researchers with access to public data. Since then, X has taken steps to address some of these issues. It has introduced a dedicated procedure for researchers who want access to public data, with a catalogue of available data and instructions on how to apply. But that doesn’t necessarily mean that access is now working smoothly in practice. And the blue checkmark issue also needs some nuance: in the EU, it is no longer supposed to be understood as proof that someone’s identity has been verified. It essentially signals a Premium subscription. These are rather easy issues to solve. What about the more delicate ones? Just look at Temu. Despite investigations and a 200-million-euro fine earlier this year, the commission still believes that illegal and unsafe products are being offered on the platform. Read more EU should use Digital Services Act against online tormentors of Belarusian and Russian exiles in Europe That doesn’t mean the DSA is useless. The battle is ongoing, and every commitment or change that can be secured is worth having. Whenever a platform is fined, there is criticism that the amount is too small compared with its global turnover. Under the DSA, fines can reach up to 6 percent of a company’s worldwide annual turnover. And in X’s case, there was also debate about whether the commission had deliberately kept the fine relatively low to avoid provoking Donald Trump and risking political or economic retaliation. The commission rejects that interpretation. It says its calculations are based on objective criteria, including the seriousness and duration of the infringements, and their impact on users. To conclude, having those tools is one thing. Making sure they actually change how these companies operate is another.

noticias.titulo: The same EU Parliament that built the Ethics Body is now killing it, in violation of European law
noticias.resumen: Two and a half years after signing the agreement, the EU Parliament is blocking its own ethics body before it has met even once, but EU law does not allow it to walk away so easily, and nor should parliament president Metsola.
noticias.texto: No EU institution did more than the European Parliament to bring about the Union’s first common Ethics Body . Decades of scandals, from the resignation of the Santer Commission in 1999 to Qatargate in 2022, had exposed conflicts of interest, revolving doors, and the influence of private interests. In response, the parliament championed an unprecedented attempt to reform the fragmented and largely self-policed ethics systems of the EU institutions. It pushed for the body, negotiated its creation, approved the agreement and signed it, but today, it is the same institution quietly killing it. Two and a half years after the agreement was signed, the Interinstitutional Body for Ethical Standards has yet to hold its first meeting. It was presented as a landmark step towards restoring public trust in the EU. The political families that make up parliament’s right-wing majority are now deliberately preventing it from starting work: the European People’s Party (EPP), together with the European Conservatives and Reformists (ECR), Patriots for Europe (PfE), and Europe of Sovereign Nations (ESN) groups. The story began long before Qatargate, arguably the most damaging corruption scandal in the history of European integration. After the Santer commission collapsed, commission vice-president Neil Kinnock proposed an advisory group on standards in public life. The initiative was later quietly shelved. Academia and civil society subsequently revived the idea. In 2019, Daniel Freund, a former Transparency International EU campaigner newly elected as a German Green MEP, helped secure commission president Ursula von der Leyen’s commitment to a common independent ethics body in her political programme. In 2020, the Greens in the European Parliament asked me to develop a legal blueprint for such a body, drawing on France’s High Authority for Transparency in Public Life. Parliament adopted that blueprint in September 2021. It called for an independent body with investigative powers and the power to recommend sanctions. Yet it took Qatargate, which erupted in December 2022, to turn this long-standing proposal into an institutional priority. The scandal exposed the vulnerability of a system in which EU institutions largely policed their own members. Read more Socialist leader accuses EPP of ‘allying with far-right’ on new EU ethics body More critically, it unveiled how in the EU Parliament, seven in 10 MEPs have outside activities , and roughly a quarter are paid for them, under limited scrutiny. The pressure to show that the EU was serious about cleaning up its act became irresistible : Within a week, Parliament voted by 541 to two to demand the ethics body. When the EU Commission presented its proposal in June 2023, parliament called it “unsatisfactory” and pushed for a stronger role for independent experts and closer scrutiny of declarations of interest. Negotiations among eight EU institutions and bodies eventually produced a compromise. It fell far short of parliament’s original vision, but was still a significant achievement . The body would develop common minimum standards on financial and non-financial interests, outside activities, gifts, hospitality, travel, and contacts with lobbyists. Five independent experts would advise the participating institutions. Each institution would assess its own rules against the common standards and explain publicly how it intended to close the gaps. On 25 April 2024, MEPs approved the deal by 301 votes to 216. Three weeks later, it was signed in parliament’s name. EU parliament president Roberta Metsola called it “a starting point”. The text is not just a declaration of good intentions, but – as it states plainly – it is binding. How the EPP stalled it For its part, the EPP never liked it. Most of its MEPs had voted against the deal, and, after the 2024 EU elections, the party found the allies it needed to stall it: the three groups to its right. Read more Far-right opposed EU ethics body to fight corruption In February 2025, parliament told its partners it could not move until it had updated its internal rules. In May, the EPP and its allies voted down the very report that would have made those amendments. Now even the appointment of the body’s five independent experts has become a battleground. The Irish EU Council presidency has formally asked the EU Parliament to endorse the nominees and attend a first meeting in December. They are Věra Jourová, Erkki Liikanen, Leo Brincat, Dagmar Roth-Behrendt, and Élisabeth Morin-Chartier. Every other participating institution has approved them, including the EU Commission. Yet the EPP has blocked a fast-track endorsement in parliament. Lóránt Vincze, the EPP’s lead MEP on the file, now says the Ethics Body “cannot be revived”. But it has never met only because his own party blocked it. Parliament is still legally bound Slow-walking the Ethics Body, however, runs into one obstacle: EU law. Parliament formed the body by a plenary vote, and only another plenary vote can undo it. No political group, committee or Conference of Presidents can do so by stalling. The agreement is legally binding, and its text says so explicitly. Parliament remains bound by it unless it lawfully withdraws, and must cooperate in good faith with the other institutions that signed it. By refusing to take the steps necessary to make the agreement operational, the EU Parliament risks exposing itself to legal action for failure to act. Under Article 265 of TFEU [EU treaty] , another EU institution, or a member state can formally call on parliament to act and, if it fails to define its position within two months, bring the matter before the EU Court of Justice in Luxembourg. The EU’s only directly elected institution could thus find itself condemned by its own court for failing to honour a commitment it voluntarily undertook. And where, in all this, is the parliament’s president? Metsola signed the agreement. She chairs the Conference of Presidents and, under parliament’s rules of procedure, is the institution’s legal representative. She cannot treat the agreement as a political project her own party is free to abandon. Her responsibility is to ensure that parliament honours its commitments. If the EPP wants out, it must make its case to the plenary, where it can be debated and voted on openly. How can the president allow a group of MEPs to walk away from parliament’s legal obligation without even putting it to a vote? That this group happens to be her own political family makes her silence all the harder to explain. MEPs are entitled to oppose the Ethics Body. They are not entitled to kill it through manufactured procedural delays that evade public scrutiny and accountability. Paradoxically, MEPs have remarkably little to fear from this agreement. Even the EPP, the group with the highest share of MEPs declaring paid outside activities , should not be afraid. The body has no power to investigate or sanction MEPs. It does not replace parliament’s own rules. It sets common standards and brings independent expertise into a system that has long relied on self-regulation. If even this modest step towards accountability is unacceptable, the real question is whether parliament is willing to accept even the most basic common standards of probity. Those who want to kill the Ethics Body should say so openly, put the EU Parliament’s withdrawal to a plenary vote, and defend that decision before European voters. Their refusal to do so tells us everything. They know what voters would think of MEPs who voted down an ethics watchdog, so they prefer to work in the dark. It is now up to Metsola, and the rest of us, to drag the situation into the light.

noticias.titulo: EU should tax Big Tech and crypto to help farmers in next budget, Spanish socialist MEP says
noticias.resumen: As EU leaders wrangle over Europe’s next long-term budget, socialist MEP Sandra Gómez López warns that unless Big Tech, online gambling, and crypto start paying more, farmers and poorer regions will be the ones footing the bill.
noticias.texto: Europe’s next long-term budget may seem far removed from everyday life. Yet the decisions being debated in Brussels will shape the support available to our farmers, investment in our regions, and Europe’s ability to respond to an increasingly uncertain world. The European Commission’s proposal for the 2028–2034 Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) would significantly change both the structure of the budget and the balance between its priorities, shifting resources from policies such as cohesion and agriculture towards security and competitiveness. The European Parliament recognises that changing circumstances require a different budget. Europe needs the means to deliver what it promises to its citizens and businesses. But we cannot finance every new priority by cutting another. Cohesion and agriculture deliver tangible benefits across Europe. Asking the people who depend on them to bear the cost of new responsibilities is a political choice, not an inevitability. There is a way forward: genuine new sources of revenue for the EU budget. As negotiations advance, European leaders must give this question the same attention as the debate over spending. Read more Cut the EU budget and we all lose Own resources in practice “Own resources” may sound like Brussels jargon. The question behind it is straightforward: how do we pay for what Europe needs? Some member states want to cut the commission’s proposed budget, while others believe it already falls short of what Europe needs to meet its challenges. New own resources could help break this deadlock by funding our common priorities without relying solely on higher national contributions. The aim is to bring in at least €60bn a year for the next EU budget. We must repay the money borrowed together under NextGenerationEU to help our economies and societies recover from the pandemic. We must also fund the responsibilities we are asking the EU to take on. Without new revenue, these demands will place further pressure on existing programmes and national budgets. That is why an agreement on new own resources must go hand in hand with the next MFF. Read more Von der Leyen joins MEPs in defence of EU’s €2 trillion spending plan ahead of summit Where should the money come from? The EU Parliament proposes levies on digital services, online gambling and crypto-assets. These would complement the Commission’s proposed basket of revenues, rather than replace it. That basket includes a contribution from large companies operating in the EU, known as Corporate Resource for Europe (CORE); a tobacco excise duty-based own resource (TEDOR); a revised share of revenues from the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS); revenue from the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM); and a contribution based on non-collected electronic waste, intended both to raise revenue and to encourage better collection and recycling. Read more [Interview] Czech MEP Niedermayer slams Babiš opposition to new EU budget revenue: ‘It’s short-sighted’ Parliament’s proposals broaden the options available for reaching an agreement. They would help finance our common priorities while limiting the pressure to increase national contributions or cut programmes. Why Big Tech, gambling, and crypto Large multinational companies earn substantial revenues from Europe’s digital market. It is only fair that they contribute to the public investment and shared prosperity that help sustain it. Some member states already apply digital services taxes. Their experience provides a starting point for action at European level. For online gambling and betting , there is also a compelling social argument. Addiction carries a cost for those affected, their families and the public services that respond to its consequences. It is only fair that an industry profiting from this activity should help bear that cost. Existing national taxes provide a basis for a coordinated European approach that would also generate revenue for the EU budget. Crypto-assets also deserve attention. As governments work to address the challenges of this relatively new sector, a levy on its profits could provide another source of revenue. A common approach would help avoid a patchwork of national measures. These proposals reflect a simple principle: sectors that benefit from the European market should make a fair contribution to its future. Take MEPs’ proposals seriously National governments have a central role in shaping the next long-term budget, but the European Parliament’s consent is also essential. Reaching an agreement will require a shared effort. For us in the Socialists and Democrats Group, genuine new own resources are an essential part of that agreement. European leaders cannot keep asking the Union to do more while refusing to discuss how to pay for it. Nor should farmers, local communities, and families be left to absorb the cost through cuts to the policies they rely on. Those who earn substantial profits from our single market must also contribute. That is the choice at the heart of this budget debate.

noticias.titulo: Xi, Trump y Putin abogan por la paz mundial y reducir el arsenal nuclear sin concretar medidas
noticias.texto:
Xi, Trump y Putin abogan por la paz mundial y reducir el arsenal nuclear sin concretar medidas
- Coinciden en que una "guerra nuclear" no es "ni factible ni deseable"
- Los líderes de las principales potencias nucleares han firmado una breve 'Declaración de paz' sin medidas concretas
Los presidentes de Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, Rusia, Vladímir Putin, y China, Xi Jinping, han abogado por la paz mundial y por reducir el arsenal nuclear en un esperado encuentro trilateral celebrado este jueves en la ciudad china de Shenzhen, en los márgenes del Foro de Cooperación Económica Asia-Pacífico (APEC).
