noticias.titulo: 'Frustrated' - Democrats remain a divided party despite winning big in midterms
noticias.resumen: After winning power in Congress, a Democratic conference in Denver was animated with talk on the best way forward.
noticias.texto:
'Frustrated' - Democrats remain a divided party despite winning big in midterms
- Published
When James Talarico - who recently became the first Democrat to win election to the US Senate for Texas since 1988 - appeared onstage at a Democratic political conference, he was greeted by a chorus of cheers and a standing ovation.
But the audience's enthusiasm dimmed when he suggested working in tandem with the Republican Trump administration.
"We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any presidency in American history," said Talarico, who at 37 will become the youngest member of the Senate when he takes his oath of office in January. "Because this moment is so much bigger and so much more important than the red team or the blue team."
He was just one of many rising stars speaking last week during a political conference in Denver, titled "What's Next: investigating strategies and priorities for the future of the Democratic Party".
And the answer to what's next? No one's sure.
Those present, who included activists and political organisers, were invigorated and celebratory the week after a "blue tsunami" saw Democrats win in Republican heartlands in the midterm elections.
The party took control of both chambers of Congress, winning a majority in the House by over 80 seats and gaining nine seats in the Senate.
But the atmosphere in Denver was also introspective and forward-looking, as discussions focused on how those victories were won, which issues did not resonate, and what would be needed to continue the party's seat-winning momentum.
Some, like Talarico, suggested working alongside Republicans to push forward an economic agenda that would resonate with Americans, such as extending health coverage and reducing inflation.
Alabama Congressman Shomari Figures - who surprised many pollsters when he held his seat despite Republicans redrawing his district months before the election - cautioned against going after Trump, when there were more pressing concerns for Americans.
Previous Democratic-led efforts to impeach Trump both ended in Senate acquittals.
"We impeached him twice and got him back - with a Republican majority," Figures said.
Yet others, like Maryland Congresswoman Angela Alsobrooks, insisted that voters wanted to see accountability.
Voters "realised the smash-and-grab that occurred, and they want people to account for it", she said, pushing for transparent investigations into the Trump administration.
The two-day event was staged by Majority Democrats, a political action committee launched last year to address tensions between the left and centrist factions of the party, with some of the biggest divisions forming over how to deliver health care and the war in Gaza.
Prominent left-wing members of the party - such as Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Senator-elect Abdul El Sayed - were not in attendance.
In Denver, it was clear those tensions weren't going away, as protesters waving Palestinian flags shouted as people walked past and armed police looked on.
Some in attendance made a point to criticise Chuck Schumer, the long-time Democratic Senate minority leader who is seen as a part of the party's centrist establishment.
He has been challenged for the role of Senate majority leader by Chris Van Hollen, a senator from Maryland who is considered a left-wing populist.
Democrats have not been "strong enough in their displeasure with what's been happening with Trump, and I think that's one of the reasons that people are asking for new leadership," said Vicki Saxe, holding a sign criticising Schumer.
"I'm frustrated with the lack of urgency that I feel coming from the party leadership," said Tami Butters, 65, standing beside her with a "Vote Yes for Chris Van Hollen" sign. She cited the absence of 11 Democrats last week, when the House voted on whether to consider impeaching US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The effort failed.
Hakeem Jeffries, a centrist Democrat who is poised to become the country's first black speaker of the House, faced similar pushback, as protesters heckled his speech.
One of the biggest issues of division is the war in Gaza, with both Schumer and Jeffries backing continued military assistance for Israel, while some new members of Congress, like El-Sayed, support ending unconditional US military aid to Israel.
Non-profit founder Shiva Saram, who also chairs the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund, travelled from Connecticut to the conference despite having "almost left my party over Gaza and the Iran War".
Saram has been newly encouraged, however, by the "real depth in our bench of new and young leaders".
"What my party has done wrong for too long is we did not listen," she said.
Many speakers and guests stressed that the Democrats won because they focused on real policies that would impact their constituents' daily lives - and that failing to do so in previous years might have been why they lost on those occasions.
Delaware Senator Chris Coons told BBC News that he had advised newly elected members to "under-promise and over-deliver".
"We got hired because the average American wants us to help make their lives better - lower their costs, end the cruelty and the corruption and give them more reason for hope," he said. "That's going to require hard work, and it isn't going to be easy to get done."
Michigan Representative Kristen McDonald Rivet agreed, saying she did not care "if we have to put Donald Trump's name" on legislation to gain the president's support for efforts to help her district.
Tahra Hoops, the 28-year-old senior director of economic analysis at the Chamber of Progress, a "left-of-centre" tech think tank, suggested that the party's divisions be embraced, not paved over.
"I think Democrats can look different wherever they are," she said.
While "very progressive" candidates can win in her home town of New York City, she said it made sense that Talarico held more centrist views because running in Texas "is not going to be the same".
"America is a very diverse country; our politicians and their views should also be diverse," she added.
Carlos Repetto-Ayala, a campaign consultant, made a similar point. The 25-year-old Texan travelled with two friends to the What's Next? event, wearing a cowboy hat and a red-white-and-blue pin on his lapel in the shape of the Lone Star State.
"It is a big tent party, but I think, as long as everyone that's in the party is laser-focused on addressing the issues that people would like for them to fix, I think Democrats will be successful," he said.

noticias.titulo: Trump’s case against NYT and Penguin Random House may proceed: Judge
noticias.resumen: The lawsuit cited a book about Trump by two NYT reporters and what it said were 'false, malicious, defamatory' articles.
noticias.texto:
Trump’s case against NYT and Penguin Random House may proceed: Judge
The lawsuit cited a book about Trump by two NYT reporters and what it said were ‘false, malicious, defamatory’ articles.
A federal judge has said United States President Donald Trump’s defamation lawsuit against The New York Times and book publisher Penguin Random House may proceed, a victory for Trump in his legal campaign against media companies he accuses of treating him unfairly.
US District Judge Steven Merryday, an appointee of former President George HW Bush, handed down the ruling in federal court in Tampa, Florida, on Thursday.
Trump has filed several lawsuits against media companies since 2024, alleging they defamed him or fraudulently misled the public with false coverage. His critics have denounced the lawsuits as attacks on the free press.
The lawsuit against The New York Times and Penguin Random House cited a book about Trump by two New York Times reporters and what it characterised as “false, malicious, defamatory, and disparaging” articles that he says were aimed at sabotaging his chances in the 2024 presidential election, which he won.
The Times and Penguin have denied defaming Trump and said in a court filing that his case is legally flawed and aimed at scoring political points.
Representatives for The New York Times, Penguin Random House and Trump’s personal lawyers did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Merryday threw out two of Trump’s claims but said the rest of his complaint plausibly alleged that statements accusing Trump of “planning and perpetrating complex crimes” were “based on incomplete, minimal information”.
The lawsuit against The Times and Penguin concerned two articles and a book that cast doubts on his origin story as a savvy businessman who ascended in the real estate and entertainment industries.
Trump cited 22 statements from the book by Times journalist Peter Baker titled For Trump, a Lifetime of Scandals Heads Toward a Moment of Judgment, and 12 from the articles by Susanne Craig and Russ Buettner.
They include assertions about Trump’s role in creating his hit reality TV show The Apprentice, his inheritance from his father, his business ventures and upbringing in New York City.
The Times and Penguin said in a motion to dismiss that Trump’s lawsuit failed to explain how the statements were defamatory and included subjective opinions that cannot be proven true or false.
‘Press freedom crisis’
The latest victory comes days after another judge allowed Trump’s $10bn defamation lawsuit against the BBC to move forward. That civil case alleges that the British broadcaster deceptively edited a documentary on the January 6, 2021, riots on Capitol Hill to damage Trump’s reputation.
Trump, since resuming office last year, has undertaken a wider pressure campaign against the media and coverage he disagrees with. He has an ongoing $10bn lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal that he refiled in May after it had been dismissed. In September, he moved to bar CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House and its press pool – a blanket ban a federal judge later blocked.
The US has fallen to a “historic low” in the Reporters Without Borders (RSF) annual press freedom tracker, continuing a decade-long decline, the organisation said earlier this year in its annual report.
While the US, during the first year of Trump’s second term, remained in the “problematic” category, it dropped seven places from 57th in the world to 64th.
In a statement, Clayton Weimers, executive director of RSF’s North America office, said at the time that the US was experiencing a “press freedom crisis”.
“Trump and his administration have carried out a coordinated war on press freedom since the day he took office, and we will live with the consequences for years to come,” he said.

noticias.texto:
Senate Republicans in US reject measure to limit Trump’s war powers in Iran
The resolution was defeated 51-48. Three Republicans broke rank, voting against the measure.
United States Senate Republicans have voted against a measure that would have required President Donald Trump to end the war in Iran or seek congressional approval to continue military action, reaffirming their support for the conflict despite recent electoral losses widely attributed in part to public opposition to the war.
The resolution was defeated on Thursday 51 to 48. Senators voted largely along party lines. In June, the House of Representatives passed it 215 to 208.
Three Republicans – Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky – voted with Democrats in favour of the measure. Only one Democrat, Senator John Fetterman of Pennsylvania, voted against it.
Democratic Senator Tim Kaine of Virginia, a longtime advocate for restoring Congress’s constitutional authority over decisions to go to war, urged lawmakers to support the resolution. He argued that the election results reflected widespread dissatisfaction with the conflict and the rising cost of food, fuel and other goods.
“The unpopularity was made absolutely, manifestly clear in the election results of November 3,” Kaine said ahead of the vote.

noticias.titulo: ‘On the same page’: Hegseth hails US ties with Colombia’s de la Espriella
noticias.resumen: The US defence secretary praised security cooperation with Colombia as country joins Americas Counter Cartel Coalition.
noticias.texto:
‘On the same page’: Hegseth hails US ties with Colombia’s de la Espriella
The US defence secretary praised security cooperation with Colombia as the country joins the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition.
Bogota, Colombia – United States Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has hailed the White House’s close alliance with far-right Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella during a brief visit to the capital, Bogota.
The US envoy met with top officials on Wednesday to discuss cooperation against organised crime and drug trafficking in the region.
They also announced Colombia as the likely host of next year’s meeting of the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition (AC3).
“It was an excellent meeting, and we’re completely on the same page. And I think the reason we’re on the same page is because both of our countries are led by strong, clear leaders,” Hegseth told reporters on Wednesday.
The US defence secretary landed at an Air Force base in Bogota around 1pm local time (18:00 GMT) Wednesday, before having a closed-door meeting with Colombian Defence Minister Jorge Mora and the General Commander of the Armed Forces Erik Rodriguez.
The military leaders discussed the difficulties of combatting the armed groups active in Colombia, particularly along the border with Venezuela, and the mounting challenge posed by their use of advanced drones, according to local media reports.
De la Espriella, a political outsider, was elected on a promise to crush Colombia’s cartels through military force. Sergio Guzman, director of Colombia Risk Analysis, a political risk consultancy, said the president will require US support to achieve his goals.
“Colombia’s fiscal situation suggests that the government needs as much assistance as it can get,” argued the analyst.
Though no new funding commitments materialised during the visit, Hegseth presided over the formal delivery of a Lockheed C-130 Hercules plane, used to transport troops and cargo, to the Colombian Air Force.
“We’ve partnered more deeply with Colombia than ever before, and now we are just enhancing that cooperation and that partnership,” Hegseth told reporters.
Standing next to Hegseth at a news conference, Mora also announced that Colombia would host next year’s meeting of the AC3, also known as the Shield of the Americas.
Launched in March, the AC3 serves as an alliance of US-aligned nations in Latin America and the Caribbean, aimed at combatting organised crime through a military-centred approach.
Colombia only recently joined the coalition when de la Espriella – who was endorsed by Trump – took power in August, replacing leftist Gustavo Petro, who regularly clashed with the White House.
The Trump administration has been pressuring members of the alliance to allow US strikes on their territory, as it seeks to expand its bombing campaign against suspected drug vessels in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific to land operations.
Though Hegseth announced at an August AC3 summit in Panama that de la Espriella had authorised joint military operations, The New York Times reported yesterday that the Colombian president had since shot down the idea of direct US intervention in Colombia.
The New York Times also reported that Hegseth shortened his visit to Colombia as a result of the rejection of a bilateral military agreement.
Both Hegseth and de la Espriella described the report as “false”, highlighting ongoing close collaboration between the two militaries.
But de la Espriella noted that the move would require congressional approval, something that would be difficult, given unfavourable public opinion.
Guzman noted that Colombia’s rejection of direct US strikes likely deals a blow to the White House’s hopes for direct intervention against drug traffickers.
“Colombia is at the centre, the keystone of the strategy. So that’s quite a disappointment for [the Trump administration], I can imagine,” he said.
Hegseth also visited Venezuela on Wednesday, where he signed a bilateral deal pledging US military support for Caracas. He later departed Colombia for Ecuador and is also scheduled to make a brief stop in Honduras.

noticias.titulo: European leaders unite in Berlin to reaffirm support for Ukraine
noticias.resumen: German chancellor warns peace talks without Europe's involvement are doomed to fail, urging unity with Ukraine.
noticias.texto:
European leaders unite in Berlin to reaffirm support for Ukraine
German chancellor warns peace talks without Europe’s involvement are doomed to fail, urging unity with Ukraine.
European leaders of the so-called “Coalition of the Willing” gathered in the German capital for talks intended to signal a united front in support of Ukraine.
The Berlin meeting happened hours after an unprecedented three-way summit in Shenzhen, China, between US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin.
Germany’s Chancellor Friedrich Merz called the Shenzhen meeting a “photo op”, warning that any deal made without Europe at the table would fail.
Merz said that “if it comes to peace negotiations, then we will be involved”, adding that such talks “can only be successful with Ukraine and Europe”.
Merz said he hoped to work as a “team with Kyiv and Washington” when they hold talks with Russia on ending the Ukraine war, although no announcement of when that would be has been made.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Europe is “ready to enter negotiations”, insisting that “a peace agreement between Ukraine and Russia must come first”.
“Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position,” Burnham added.
European countries have been angered after the European Union was largely sidelined in the United States’ stop-start negotiations with Russia and Ukraine.
However, Donald Trump’s son-in-law and peace envoy Jared Kushner said, “Trump wants to make a deal with Europe by his side.”
Kushner said, “We do believe that Russia having Europe at the table will be essential for ending the war.”
The British prime minister welcomed the US presence at talks in Berlin, saying it added momentum to end the war.
“This clearly has got to be a moment to move towards peace because of the US involvement that we’ve seen today and the progress clearly that is being made,” Burnham said.
Meanwhile, French President Emmanuel Macron called on Ukraine’s allies to ramp up efforts to end the war.
“Everyone who has the capacity to provide the means to defend and protect Ukrainian citizens must do so now,” he insisted, adding the priority was to deploy anti-missile systems and interceptors.
“Faced with the maximalist nature of the Russian position, I believe we need to reopen the question of Ukraine’s accession to NATO,” Macron said. NATO membership for Ukraine is among the issues holding back a peace deal for Ukraine.
In a post on X, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, “We do not want Russia to drag all of this out into the winter. Pressure is needed. Europe is ready with new sanctions and new steps to support Ukraine and the Ukrainian people. It is important that the United States of America exert its influence on Russia.”

noticias.titulo: Photos: Genocide ruling spotlights human toll of 2017 Rohingya crisis
noticias.resumen: Nearly a million Rohingya fled to Bangladesh in 2017, forming one of the world's largest refugee camps near Cox's Bazar.
noticias.texto:
Photos: Genocide ruling spotlights human toll of 2017 Rohingya crisis
Nearly a million Rohingya fled to Bangladesh in 2017, forming one of the world’s largest refugee camps near Cox’s Bazar.
Save
Share Photos: Genocide ruling spotlights human toll of 2017 Rohingya crisis on social media
Share
Add Al Jazeera on Google
Rohingya refugee women with their children stand in line outside a food distribution centre at Balukhali refugee camp, about 50km (32 miles) from Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, on September 17, 2017, after fleeing Myanmar. [Showkat Shafi/Al Jazeera]
The United Nations’ top court has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, finding the military acted with “genocidal intent” and killed about 10,000 people during its 2017 operations in Rakhine state.
In a landmark judgement under the 1948 Genocide Convention, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) found Myanmar in breach of its obligations — a decision Rohingya activists hope will finally bring accountability for years of mass killings, rapes and the burning of villages.
Nearly a million Rohingya fled those attacks, crossing into Bangladesh and building one of the world’s largest refugee settlements around Cox’s Bazar.
Today, many remain confined to overcrowded, fragile camps, stateless and with little prospect of safe return, even as the ICJ ruling sharpens pressure on Myanmar’s military and raises wider questions about justice for victims of mass atrocities.
This photo story returns to the early months of the crisis in 2017, documenting Rohingya families arriving exhausted and traumatised, queuing for food and trying to rebuild a semblance of community in the makeshift camps.
Through these images, all captured in September 2017, we see how the violence now recognised as genocide reshaped countless lives – and why, for Rohingya still living in limbo, the court’s judgement is only one step in a much longer struggle for safety, rights and a home.
Rohingya refugees arrive in Bangladesh, carrying the few possessions they managed to take during a last-minute escape from Myanmar soldiers who attacked their village, killing and raping residents and burning their homes. [Showkat Shafi/Al Jazeera]
Advertisement
A Rohingya girl and her mother rest by the roadside after crossing the Bangladesh–Myanmar border, exhausted from days of walking along muddy tracks while carrying the few belongings they could salvage from their village. [Showkat Shafi/Al Jazeera]
Newly arrived Rohingya refugees who crossed from Myanmar into Bangladesh’s Teknaf area carry their belongings towards the nearest refugee camp, about 40km (25 miles) away. [Showkat Shafi/Al Jazeera]
A Rohingya mother and her two children rest on the roadside after crossing into Bangladesh with their family. [Showkat Shafi/Al Jazeera]
A Rohingya family finds temporary shelter at a local school after a long journey from Rakhine state in Myanmar. At dawn, they must continue towards refugee camps further north along the road. [Showkat Shafi/Al Jazeera]
Rohingya refugees stand aside as an aid agency truck drives into a makeshift camp to deliver supplies for thousands sheltering there. [Showkat Shafi/Al Jazeera]
Advertisement
A Rohingya family finds temporary shelter at a local school after a long journey from Rakhine state in Myanmar. At dawn, they must continue towards refugee camps further north along the road. [Showkat Shafi/Al Jazeera]
Rohingya refugees who have crossed into Bangladesh find shelter in a local school for the night before continuing their journey to camps located about 40km (25 miles) away. [Showkat Shafi/Al Jazeera]
Two Rohingya children, separated from their mother while crossing the border from Myanmar, rest by the roadside. Soldiers killed their father, and the dehydrated girl lost consciousness for several hours before passers-by revived her with water. [Showkat Shafi/Al Jazeera]
Sixteen-year-old Bushra Begum rests with her three-month-old son Mohammad Kaisar. "We crossed over to Bangladesh on foot. It took us 10 days to reach this refugee camp in Kutupalong," she said. "I am worried for my son. I think this journey has emotionally traumatised him. He has drunk only a little milk since the day we escaped from our home. The journey was tough and there were days we went without food, and this also affected his health." [Showkat Shafi/Al Jazeera]
Rohingya refugees line up for aid at Balukhali makeshift camp. With supplies limited, tensions run high and men scuffle to grab packages at the distribution point. [Showkat Shafi/Al Jazeera]
Yaemeena Ara, 30, holds her six-month-old daughter Rohana. "Our village was attacked on Eid last month, and we escaped that day. It took us five days and nights to reach here," she said. "I have six children, including her. My husband and I had to carry each child in our arms and on our shoulders, in order to cross into Bangladesh, as they could not walk for so long." [Showkat Shafi/Al Jazeera]
A Rohingya boy carries a parcel of food supplies he received from an aid agency at Balukhali makeshift camp, where most refugees are completely dependent on humanitarian assistance. [Showkat Shafi/Al Jazeera]
Continuous rain floods the camps where the Rohingya live, leaving mud-soaked paths and damp shelters without sanitation or basic infrastructure. [Showkat Shafi/Al Jazeera]
Hamida, 33, stands in the camp with her four-month-old nephew Yousuf. "His parents were killed," she said. "I grabbed him and brought him with me, [or] else he would have just died there alone. I have six children of my own and one of them is six months old. I have to breastfeed both of them because they cannot be given this food. It is hard for me because even I hardly get to eat one meal in a day." [Showkat Shafi/Al Jazeera]
Rohingya refugees queue to receive aid outside an unofficial settlement near Balukhali in Bangladesh, where agencies distribute food and other supplies. [Showkat Shafi/Al Jazeera]
Hamida, 35, holds her one-year-old son, Mohammad Alam. "They murdered my husband," she said. "I had to run to save the lives of my five small children. I have nobody to help me get the relief material and food. I need the food packets desperately to feed my children. I have been waiting in a queue for the past three hours and haven't been able to secure anything. The men are healthy and stronger and they jump and grab any aid that is thrown towards us, while women like me keep waiting." [Showkat Shafi/Al Jazeera]
Heavy rain complicates aid distribution in a muddy field crowded with thousands of Rohingya refugees desperate for food. [Showkat Shafi/Al Jazeera]
A Rohingya woman pleads with aid workers for food and supplies at a distribution point. [Showkat Shafi/Al Jazeera]
Shahida Begum, 40, lies in a hospital bed, her body covered in burns after soldiers set fire to her home in Myanmar. “The army came and burned down my house. I was inside,” she said. “The pain is unbearable. It would have been better to die than suffer like this.” [Showkat Shafi/Al Jazeera]
Dildar Begum sits beside her injured 10-year-old daughter, Noor. They are the only members of their family who survived the violence. [Showkat Shafi/Al Jazeera]
Suffering from severe burns, Mohammad Haris lies in the lap of his mother, Khursheeda Begum, in a hospital ward. They fled Thami village in Myanmar’s Buthidaung District. Khursheeda’s husband and five other children are missing. “I have no idea where they are, but I have a strong feeling they are alive,” she said. [Showkat Shafi/Al Jazeera]
Newly constructed plastic-and-bamboo tents cover a hillside at Balukhali refugee camp in Bangladesh. Many Rohingya buy the materials from local villagers. [Showkat Shafi/Al Jazeera]
Twenty-five-year-old Haseena rests with her 18-month-old daughter, Muneera. "I came here with my husband and two children," she said. "We had only managed to take enough food to last us for two days. The rest of the days we walked hungry. I had to leave my cow behind, when we ran to save our lives. I wish I could have brought her with me." [Showkat Shafi/Al Jazeera]
Sudden heavy rain floods an area where Rohingya refugees had set up a makeshift camp. A bamboo bridge they built to evacuate people and belongings from a shrinking island in the river stands partially collapsed. [Showkat Shafi/Al Jazeera]
Khalida, 20, with her one-year-old daughter, Shahana. "It took us five days to reach here and I consider myself fortunate that my entire family is with me," she said. "The army had invaded our village and was burning houses and killing people. We also ran to save our lives and crossed over to Bangladesh on a boat. My husband goes out in the day to get relief material and food for us. I would want to go with him and get more food, but it's tough to stand in a queue with an infant and struggle to find food." [Showkat Shafi/Al Jazeera]
An elderly Rohingya man waits in line to receive food and other essentials at an aid distribution centre. [Showkat Shafi/Al Jazeera]
Heavily pregnant 20-year-old Rohingya refugee Sameron walked through the night with her husband Anwar and three-year-old daughter Sabiha after Myanmar soldiers attacked their village in Rajarbill, forcing her into labour during the journey. [Showkat Shafi/Al Jazeera]
As rain pours down and crowds surge towards an aid truck, many Rohingya refugees leave a distribution point empty-handed. [Showkat Shafi/Al Jazeera]
Shams-un-Nehar, 35, holds her two-month-old twins, Eesa and MusaI. "I have 10 more children apart from these two and we walked for three days to reach the border," she said. "We did not get to eat a single morsel of food in these three days and I was as a result not able to breastfeed my twins. They kept wailing in thirst and hunger. It was so frustrating and painful to see them starve like this in front of me." [Showkat Shafi/Al Jazeera]
Trapped on an island by rising floodwaters, Rohingya refugees wade across a swollen river to higher ground. The bamboo bridge they built the previous day now lies underwater. [Showkat Shafi/Al Jazeera]
Twenty-four-year-old Tahira with her seven-month-old daughter Rusma Akhtar. "We were sleeping in the night at our home when we heard screams outside," she said. "We saw fire everywhere outside and people screaming and running around. My husband grabbed my daughter and we ran out with others. All my belongings must have been destroyed. I wish I had managed to get our big family photo from the wall." [Showkat Shafi/Al Jazeera]
A Rohingya woman holds her son as she waits for her husband to return with aid from a nearby distribution point. The family has covered their few belongings with a plastic sheet to protect them from the rain and mud. [Showkat Shafi/Al Jazeera]
Sona Mehar, 45, with her three-month-old daughter, Mirana Begum. "I am taking care of my seven children alone," she said. "My husband was shot with a bullet in the shoulder and is getting treated in the hospital. I stand in the queue for the entire day with this baby in my arms to secure a meal." [Showkat Shafi/Al Jazeera]

noticias.titulo: Blockbuster GTA VI release shows cultural, economic heft of video games
noticias.resumen: Runaway success of popular franchise comes as video game industry has struggled with mass layoffs in recent years.
noticias.texto:
Blockbuster GTA VI release shows cultural, economic heft of video games
Runaway success of popular franchise comes as video game industry has struggled with mass layoffs in recent years.
Even before its release, Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA VI) was a cultural phenomenon that cemented the status of video games as the undisputed champion of the vaunted United States entertainment sector.
The game racked up more than $1.5bn in pre-sales before Thursday’s launch and attracted nonstop buzz and anticipation on social media, where players have waited more than 13 years since the last edition of the popular franchise was released.
“The launch of GTA VI is a reminder that games aren’t just niche entertainment—they’re now at the centre of global culture,” Mark DeLoura, Vice President of Strategy for GDC Festival of Gaming, told Al Jazeera in an email.
In GTA VI, players follow the journey of two characters, Jason and Lucia, as they explore the underworld of Vice City, a fictionalised version of Miami, Florida.
Almost impossibly, the newest addition seems to have lived up to more than a decade of hype: critics are nearly unanimous in their praise, with the latest GTA becoming the best-reviewed video game of all time.
That success is partly explained by the nostalgia that the game evokes for those who grew up playing it with friends, along with meticulous worldbuilding and attention to detail, memorable soundtracks, and the transgressive thrill of running pedestrians over in a semi-truck.
GTA’s appeal was only heightened by the fact that, for an earlier generation of gamers, parents, media coverage, and politicians were united in stern disapproval.
While most critics of violent video games have long since abandoned the field or switched sides in a bid for relevance with young voters, a few holdouts remain.
“I really am going to say I’m not thinking this is a good thing for our culture and society,” a member of a recent Fox News programme said of the game.
“They’ll have a documentary on how best to steal a car at gunpoint or shoot a cop,” Republican Representative Tim Burchett told the outlet TMZ, arguing that GTA encourages violence and lawbreaking. “I mean, what in the world!”
But across US culture and politics, the taboo has largely faded away.
Once the subject of television segments asking if it would corrupt impressionable youths by exposing them to a seedy underworld of carjackings and police shootouts, everyone from the US military and the White House to the Weather Channel has tapped into the runaway popularity of the game’s sixth instalment.
The US military outlet Task and Purpose reported that 43 soldiers took advantage of a reenlistment incentive that gave them a four-day weekend to enjoy the game’s release.
Assessments of GTA’s cultural impact have also shifted, with critics lauding the franchise’s ability to capture the pulse of life in the US and its exploration of themes such as the hardships faced by immigrants and minorities.
“When a release like this becomes a major cultural event in the US and a shared global conversation, it says a lot about both the scale of the games industry and the place games now hold in people’s lives,” said DeLoura from GDC Festival of Gaming.
According to the Entertainment Software Association, an industry group, about two-thirds of people in the US play video games, and the sector generated more than $95bn in economic activity in 2025, with US consumers spending more than $60bn on games.
By comparison, the 2025 North American box office for movie ticket sales was just under $9bn.
Industry challenges
The runaway success of GTA VI comes, counterintuitively, at a time when the gaming industry is struggling to cope with a challenging financial environment and mass layoffs.
“The industry hired for a pandemic that ended. Demand stopped growing in 2022, costs didn’t, and the average blockbuster now costs $440m, up from $47m in 2000,” Joost van Dreunen, an adjunct assistant professor at NYU Stern and writer of the SuperJoost Playlist newsletter on Substack, said in an email.
“GTA VI proves that the model works for exactly one company,” he added, noting that the developer, Rockstar Games, spent a billion dollars and leaned on thousands of employees to create a level of attention to detail that few others can hope to match.
According to the tracker website Gaming Layoffs, 40 video game studios have shuttered in 2026 alone, with nearly 13,000 workers laid off. That figure represents a nearly 150 percent increase over the same time last year.
Life for some workers in the industry has also become more precarious.
A survey of industry workers by the GDC Festival of Gaming, compiled in a state-of-the-industry report in 2026, found that about 39 percent of US respondents had been laid off at least once in the last two years.
About 77 percent of US respondents also said they were “not hopeful” about the direction of the industry, and about 30 percent said they were considering leaving.
DeLoura from the GDC Festival of Gaming said the industry’s challenges have had “a real impact on a lot of very talented people”, but he remains optimistic the industry will weather the storm.
“The long arc of the game industry is one of strong growth,” he said.
“More people play games than ever, more people have access to them on the devices in their pockets, and more people can make and share games than at any point in history! To me, that’s the clearest way to understand this moment: not as a contradiction, but as a sign of how big, global, and varied games have become.”

noticias.titulo: Save the Children: Gaza’s children face ‘unmatched dangers’
noticias.resumen: Aid group says one third of violations against children worldwide were in occupied Palestinian territory.
noticias.texto:
Save the Children: Gaza’s children face ‘unmatched dangers’
Aid group says one third of violations against children worldwide were in occupied Palestinian territory.
Children in Gaza face dangers “unmatched” anywhere in the world after three years of war, with at least 20,000 killed, according to the aid group Save the Children.
The warning came in the group’s annual global report on Thursday – the same day Israel’s military told the AFP news agency it had finished a ground operation in central Gaza that began a day earlier, despite a “ceasefire” that took effect more than a year ago.
Save the Children said almost one third of the tens of thousands of attacks and violations against children recorded worldwide last year took place in the occupied Palestinian territory.
It counted nearly 12,500 cases – mostly attacks on hospitals and schools, and denial of aid.
“This report is showing very clearly that what happened and what continues to happen in Gaza are violations at a scale that we haven’t seen,” Regional Director Ahmad Alhendawi told the AP news agency.
He said conditions have shown little improvement this year, and that many surviving children are injured and have lost their parents.
The report found that denial of humanitarian aid is the fastest-growing violation against children worldwide. Verified incidents rose from 509 in 2015 to 8,322 in 2025 – almost one per hour on average – and more than 70 percent of them targeted Palestinian children.
Killings and maimings made up the largest share of violations since 2005, with 171,712 verified cases, and more than 70 percent were recorded in four countries, plus the occupied Palestinian territory.
Children waiting for treatment
Gaza’s Health Ministry said at least 300 children have died while waiting for Israeli permission to leave for life-saving treatment, including at least 90 with cancer. Another 5,400 are on medical travel lists awaiting approval. In February, it reported that 1,360 patients had died awaiting permits since the Rafah crossing between Gaza and Egypt closed in May 2024.
Displaced resident Riad Abou Shamel, 65, told AP that Gaza’s children “are deprived of the bare minimum in life”.
“They go to the market and can barely bring back half a cucumber or half an apple,” he said.
Israel ends incursion
Israel’s military told AFP that its first broad ground offensive since a “ceasefire” was signed more than a year ago “is complete”.
The new operation was launched in central Gaza on Wednesday, and went beyond the “Yellow Line” to dismantle a tunnel the Israelis claimed posed an “immediate and direct threat” to its troops.
The “Yellow Line” demarcates the Israeli-occupied area of Gaza, and was established under the truce agreed by Israel and Hamas in October 2025.
Hamas called the two-day operation a “blatant ceasefire violation”.
More than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the “ceasefire” began, according to an AFP tally of Gaza Health Ministry data.
Israel did not immediately comment on Save the Children’s report, the AP said.

noticias.titulo: World reacts to ICJ finding Myanmar guilty of genocide against Rohingya
noticias.resumen: Landmark judgement in The Hague is the first time a state has been held responsible for genocide at the ICJ.
noticias.texto:
World reacts to ICJ finding Myanmar guilty of genocide against Rohingya
landmark judgement in The Hague is the first time a state has been held responsible for genocide at the ICJ.
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the predominantly Muslim Rohingya minority in 2017.
The landmark judgement in The Hague on Thursday is the first time a state has been held responsible for genocide at the ICJ.
The case filed by Gambia in 2019 has been closely watched by governments, lawyers, rights groups and Rohingya communities for its implications for how states are judged under the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The court said Myanmar has an obligation to compensate the Rohingya for the violations it committed, with the terms to be determined at a later date.
Here’s how key parties and world leaders reacted to the landmark verdict:
Myanmar’s shadow National Unity Government
The National Unity Government, which includes remnants of former leader Aung San Suu Kyi’s National League for Democracy party, said it respects the authority of the International Court of Justice and its judgement.
It pledged to consider the court’s findings and orders, reaffirming its commitment to accountability and preventing further atrocities.
The Gambia
The Gambia, which brought the case against Myanmar in November 2019 with the support of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, welcomed the ruling with “profound satisfaction”, calling it “a historic day for international justice”.
The government said the obligation to prevent and punish genocide is shared by all states party to the 1948 Genocide Convention and called on Myanmar to comply with the judgement “fully and without delay”.
Organisation of Islamic Cooperation
In a post shared on X, the OIC commended the ICJ’s judgement, saying it offered “redress for victims and [upholds] the principle of no impunity”.
United Nations Secretary-General
Antonio Guterres described the ruling as a “demonstration of international justice” and a reaffirmation that impunity for “such horrific acts must not stand”.
He noted that it marked the first time the court had found a state responsible for committing genocide and called on Myanmar to comply with its decision.
UN Human Rights Chief
Volker Turk said the judgement “clearly concludes” that Myanmar is responsible for “one of the most egregious crimes known to humankind.”
In a post shared on X, he added that the Rohingya people’s “suffering is a stain” on humanity.
UK Foreign Secretary
Ed Miliband said the United Kingdom ordered the expulsion of Myanmar’s defence attache and summoned the country’s charge d’affaires. He also called for an urgent UN Security Council session to discuss the ruling.
He said further measures would be announced in the coming days to ensure those responsible are held accountable.
UN Special Rapporteur on Myanmar
Yanghee Lee called it a “deeply emotional day for all Rohingya people”, adding that “justice has been decided, but not yet delivered”.
Rohingya activist and co-chair of the Arakan Rohingya National Council
Activist Nay San Lwin said justice for the Rohingya means the restoration of their citizenship, recognition of their identity and their safe and dignified return home.
He added that their struggle would continue until those demands are met.
Rohingya activist and executive director of Women’s Peace Network
Activist Wai Wai Nu said the ruling had shattered the military’s decades-long efforts to erase Rohingya identity, deny their existence and dismiss their suffering.
“By finding that Myanmar committed genocide, ordering a guarantee of non-repetition, and ordering restitution and compensation, the world’s highest court has permanently shattered that state-sponsored lie,” she said.
Amnesty International
Human Rights Watch senior international justice counsel
Maria Elena Vignoli welcomed the court’s decision, calling it a “long-awaited recognition of the suffering the Rohingya have endured from Myanmar’s military”.

noticias.titulo: France awaits verdict six years after police beat Black music producer
noticias.resumen: Three officers are accused of assaulting Michel Zecler in an incident that was filmed by surveillance cameras.
noticias.texto:
France awaits verdict six years after police beat Black music producer
Three officers are accused of assaulting Michel Zecler in an incident that was filmed by surveillance cameras.
Paris, France – Six years ago, Michel Zecler was assaulted by the three officers at his Parisian music studio.
Surveillance camera footage shows the officers pushing Zecler, who is Black, inside his studio and beating him until other musicians intervened on November 21, 2020.
Aurelien Lapersonne, Pierre Plantier and Philippe Tondeux are accused of striking the music producer 29 times in four minutes, and an additional six times in the face after Zecler was already handcuffed.
The verdict is expected on Friday.
The case fuelled wider concerns in France about police brutality and caught the public’s attention. At the time, football star Kylian Mbappe shared an image of a heavily injured Zecler, blood running from his face, with the words: “Unbearable video. Unacceptable violence”.
The three French police officers are also accused of forging a public document.
During the attack, the officers allegedly made multiple racist remarks towards Zecler. All three signed a falsified police report stating that Zecler hit the police officers – a claim refuted by surveillance footage.
“It’s pretty obvious that this case is about institutional racism, systemic discrimination and police violence. Everything is connected. Not only are we dealing with police violence against a Black man, but that’s on top of attempting to conceal evidence and falsify a report,” Rim-Sarah Alouane, a legal scholar and an associate researcher in public law at the University of Toulouse Capitole, told Al Jazeera. “When these reports are falsified, we’re questioning the integrity of the entire system.”
The prosecution’s office requested a permanent ban on all three officers, along with prison sentences.
The prosecutor called for a jail sentence of six years without parole for Lapersonne, the officer who initiated the police identity check and submitted the falsified report, a five-year sentence for the trio’s leader, Tondeux, the most experienced officer present, and four years for the third police officer, Plantier.
“There is no room for a symbolic sentence,” a representative of the public prosecutor’s office said in a statement. “We are talking about crimes, violence and racial slurs. About a complete lack of control over what was done and an absolute determination to get away with it in the end.”
‘If there was no footage, we would not be here today’
A series of court cases has identified the systemic discrimination among the police in France.
Last year, the European Court of Human Rights condemned France for racial profiling of Karim Touil, a young French national of North African origin who was stopped by police three times within 10 days in November and December 2011.
In October 2023, France’s high court acknowledged racial profiling during police identity checks but did not require French authorities to take the “necessary measures to end this longstanding, abusive practice”, Human Rights Watch (HRW) noted.
In 2021, the French government was condemned for “gross negligence” in an identity check of three high school students in at Gare du Nord in Paris.
Although concerns about police violence in France are not new, this trial is pivotal because of the surveillance footage and attempted cover-up, Alouane noted.
“This trial brings to light those issues that human rights organisations have been documenting for years. It gives an illustration, through a proper case, about the use of force and systemic violence that we’ve known about for years,” Alouane said. “If there was no footage, we would not be here today. The police would have gotten away with it.”
Police officer Lapersonne, who submitted the report, initially claimed that Zecler attacked the officers and “struck out with his arms and legs”. When the presiding judge asked if he had “made that up”, Lapersonne responded, “Absolutely.” Lapersonne’s initial police report also failed to mention that the officers landed blows on Zecler.
“I deliberately omitted them. I think out of fear. It was stupid of me,” Lapersonne told the presiding judge.
For Alouane, this case revealed the tactics behind systemic police violence in France.
“The falsified documents aspect is crucial to illustrate why this case advanced and the public attention it received. In this case, the footage directly contradicted the police’s claims. The cops knew they did something wrong,” she said. “This is a serious accusation and not an isolated incident.”
The trial comes as France’s Senate considers a controversial bill that would presume police officers and gendarmes acted in self-defence when using firearms in the line of duty, which would place the burden of proof on the complainant. Critics call the proposal a “licence to kill”. The National Assembly approved the measure in July.
“It’s a very dangerous piece of legislation. It’s liberticide. It would create a sense of impunity amongst police officers — which already exists, but this would strengthen that. It would undermine investigations and make access to the justice system even more difficult for victims and their families,” Alouane said. “It raises serious issues regarding equality under the law because it puts a presumption of innocence in favour of people because of their profession as cops.”
Legislation like the self-defence law could inhibit cases like Zecler’s in the future, Alouane noted.
“If this proposal were in place, we would not have this case. It would have been dismissed today,” she said.
French police are also under scrutiny for their tactics during recent student protests. A 15-year-old lost a hand from a police stun grenade, and another officer threw a tear gas canister at close range, shattering a 14-year-old’s jaw and several teeth.

noticias.titulo: Palestinians in Gaza face new displacement after Israeli army operation
noticias.resumen: Families in Nuseirat spend the night without shelter, while many fear returning despite Israel ending offensive.
noticias.texto:
Palestinians in Gaza face new displacement after Israeli army operation
Families in Nuseirat spend the night without shelter, while many fear returning despite Israel announcing the end of its raid.
Nuseirat, Gaza Strip – For the 13th time, Suhail al-Mashharawi has been forced to flee. The 50-year-old Palestinian and his family of eight spent the night in a schoolyard in central Gaza, without blankets, bedding or enough clothing to protect his children from the cold.
Thousands of Palestinians have once again been forced to abandon their makeshift shelters as Israeli forces launched a major ground operation in the enclave, the first major offensive publicly announced by the military since a ceasefire was agreed in October 2025.
On Wednesday, the Israeli military issued forced evacuation orders covering three blocks north of the Nuseirat refugee camp, saying its troops were targeting a suspected Hamas tunnel.
The military announced on Thursday that it had completed its operation and reopened Salah al-Din Street, Gaza’s main north-south thoroughfare.
While some Palestinians began returning to check on their belongings, others stayed away, saying that sporadic gunfire continued and the road remained unsafe.
For al-Mashharawi, the operation ended a year of relative stability, forcing him and his family to abandon their tent and seek refuge at a nearby educational centre.
He described the conditions there as “dire”, saying his family had received no humanitarian assistance and had no idea how long they would have to stay.
‘Fleeing death into the unknown’
About 6,000 Palestinians fled the area on Wednesday, Gaza’s Government Media Office said.
Israel said the operation targeted a tunnel that threatened its troops. Hamas condemned the incursion as a violation of the ceasefire, while the Israeli military accused the group of violating the agreement.
More than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire took effect, according to Gaza health authorities.
About 1.4 million Palestinians across Gaza now live in tents or makeshift shelters, according to United Nations humanitarian figures.
Ismail Younis, who manages a camp for displaced people in the al-Mufti area, said bullets penetrated the tents during the operation, with a quadcopter flying over the camp, prompting families to flee quickly.
“The families left without having a specific destination, or an alternative place for them to take refuge,” he said. “Their main concern was to save their lives and the lives of their children, in light of the escalating gunfire and continued shelling.”
Amna al-Qassas, 49, was one of those who had to rapidly flee her camp in Nuseirat when the forced evacuation came. She had time to pack only a small bag containing her family’s identification documents.
Al-Qassas fled with 10 family members, leaving behind the tent and possessions she had managed to salvage during an earlier displacement from the Tuffah neighbourhood in eastern Gaza City.
She told Al Jazeera that displacement had become a “recurring nightmare”, taking her family back to square one and destroying what little sense of security they had regained.
Now, they were being forced to leave again. “We have not had time to think … our only concern was to escape death, even if it meant fleeing into the unknown,” she said.
Unable to find a vehicle to transport her belongings, al-Qassas left everything behind. She fears the destruction of her shelter could leave her with nothing to return to.

noticias.titulo: Iraq reaches compromise with Kataib Hezbollah over armed group’s stronghold
noticias.resumen: The compromise reached will unite forces that include brigades from the Popular Mobilisation Forces.
noticias.texto:
Iraq reaches compromise with Kataib Hezbollah over armed group’s stronghold
The compromise reached will station forces that include brigades from the Popular Mobilisation Forces.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi says his country’s security forces will establish a joint operations centre in the town of Jurf al-Sakhar, in a compromise with the Iranian-backed Kataib Hezbollah armed group over control of a strategic area south of Baghdad.
The Jurf al-Sakhar area has long been a stronghold of Kataib Hezbollah, and the new agreement comes after the Iraqi government announced plans to send in security forces amid allegations that the group was smuggling oil.
The compromise reached late on Thursday will see a new combined force deployed to the area, consisting of a brigade from the Iraqi army, a brigade from the Federal Police, a regiment from the Energy Police to provide protection for oil pipelines in the area, and two brigades from the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) Commission, a collection of armed groups that are officially part of Iraq’s security forces, including some Kataib Hezbollah fighters.
A military spokesman said the new joint operations centre will open at 6am local time (03:00 GMT) on Friday morning.
In a statement, the PMF said their forces will begin replacing the military units stationed in Jurf al-Sakhar on Friday, in accordance with the directives from Prime Minister al-Zaidi.
Earlier in the week, an Iraqi official told Al Jazeera that the commander of the Quds Force of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), Esmail Qaani, arrived in Iraq to push for a solution due to the simmering tensions with Iran.
A Kataib Hezbollah spokesman confirmed that Qaani met with senior members of their organisation, as well as the head of PMF and a representative from the Badr Organization, an Iranian-backed political group that also contributes armed fighters to the PMF.
In a statement, Kataib Hezbollah said the talks addressed the current crisis and described the outcomes of the discussions as positive.
Separately, in a news conference on Thursday, Kataib Hezbollah expressed appreciation for the PMF and Iraqi security forces for preventing escalating tensions that serve “the enemies”. The group also affirmed that any existing issues would be resolved through private channels.
A senior Iraqi official previously told Al Jazeera that Kataib Hezbollah had until Friday to leave Jurf al-Sakhar. The group had threatened to confront government troops and had rejected the government’s efforts to disarm non-state militias.

noticias.titulo: ‘Not an acquittal’: After impeachment vote, Hegseth still under microscope
noticias.resumen: A week after a fizzled impeachment bid, analysts say Hegseth continues to face backlash for his leadership at Pentagon.
noticias.texto:
‘Not an acquittal’: After impeachment vote, Hegseth still under microscope
A week after a fizzled impeachment bid, analysts say Hegseth continues to face backlash for his leadership at Pentagon.
In the wake of the United States midterm elections, attention has turned to whether Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth will be able to preserve his cabinet-level position once Congress’s new Democratic majorities are sworn in.
Already, the Fox News host-turned-military-chief has faced mounting calls for his removal from office.
But analysts question the extent to which Hegseth’s impeachment would affect military policy under President Donald Trump.
“Ultimately, the secretary of defence is a powerful participant in shaping a war,” said Jasmine El-Gamal, a former Middle East adviser in the Pentagon.
El-Gamal, however, believes targeting Hegseth alone would not be enough to secure accountability for decisions like launching the US-Israel war on Iran.
Hegseth holds significant power in directing the US war effort, she explained, but he also works hand-in-hand with the president and his advisers.
“Calling him merely an ‘executor’ understates that power, while calling him its sole architect understates the president’s power and obscures where particular decisions were actually made,” El-Gamal said.
Facing impeachment
Since he was sworn in on January 25, 2025, Hegseth has overseen some of Trump’s most controversial international campaigns, including the war on Iran and a series of deadly boat strikes in the Caribbean Sea and eastern Pacific Ocean.
Both campaigns have been accused of violating international law. The Iran war, in particular, became a political albatross for Trump’s Republican Party during the midterm race.
A poll earlier this month found that 44 percent of US voters said they were less likely to vote for a midterm candidate who supported the war.
That number dwarfed the 13 percent who said they were more inclined to vote for such a candidate, by a ratio of more than three to one.
The Democratic Party scored a thumping victory in the November 3 midterms, flipping both the House of Representatives and the Senate from Republican control.
Less than a week later, Hegseth faced a push for impeachment, led by outgoing Republican Congressman Thomas Massie.
Among the eight articles of impeachment Massie filed were accusations that Hegseth had dismantled fundamental safeguards to protect civilian lives, leading to incidents like the bombing of an elementary school in Minab, Iran, that killed at least 120 children.
But the impeachment proceedings were shelved on November 10, after the Republicans’ lame-duck majority in the House voted 211 to 204 to block the measure. Eleven Democrats were absent for the vote.
Scrutiny of Pentagon chiefs
Hegseth is hardly the first Pentagon chief to face pressure to leave office following a dismal election for his party.
In November 2006, Republicans likewise suffered a midterm rout amid a groundswell of voter ire over the US-led wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. Both chambers of Congress that year flipped to Democratic control.
Within a day of the vote, then-President George W Bush announced that his defence secretary, the late Donald Rumsfeld, would resign. He cited the Iraq war in his remarks.
“I recognise that many Americans voted last night to register their displeasure with the lack of progress being made there,” Bush said of the conflict.
Hegseth, however, has resisted calls for his resignation. In a five-minute video posted two days after the midterms, Hegseth dismissed his critics as “deep-state radicals” obsessed with “political theatre”.
“They attack us because we are effective. It’s not going to work. We will not back down,” Hegseth said. “We put America and the war-fighter first, always and without apology. And that fight continues in the lame-duck Congress.”
His message of defiance included an appeal for the military to “stay the course”, including in the war against Iran.
“I’ll assure you, we have only just begun to fight,” Hegseth added. “We are more determined than ever, more resolute than ever to finish what we have started.”
A key role in the war
Some of the criticism, however, has come from within Hegseth’s own party. Vice President JD Vance, for instance, said the “real reason” the Republicans lost the midterms is “obvious to almost everyone”.
“The reason we lost is the war,” he wrote on social media.
Hala Rharrit, a former US diplomat who spent 18 years in the State Department, was among the officials who resigned before Trump took office for his second term, in protest of the US involvement in Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
She explained that Hegseth would have been critical in guiding some of the Iran war’s most divisive moments.
The bombing of the Minab elementary school, for example, took place on February 28, the first day of the conflict.
Rharrit said Hegseth and other senior Department of Defense (DOD) officials would have drawn up the initial strike lists before advising Trump on the targets for final approval.
“I suspect that Trump would not get into the granularities of which targets to strike on day one,” Rharrit told Al Jazeera.
“Hegseth and others in DOD had a lot to do with those precise decisions, which also runs through lawyers.”
She also drew a line between decisions taken by Hegseth and Trump and the losses the US and its allies have endured since the war began.
Iran has retaliated against US and Israeli attacks with strikes across the Middle East. At least 23 US service members have died in the conflict, and 865 were wounded.
“Ultimately, they are both responsible, not just for the strikes in Iran, but also for making American service members and diplomats throughout the region sitting ducks,” said Rharrit.
Congress reasserting its authority?
Throughout the war, Congress has had the power to pull the emergency cord and stop the fighting, according to Brian Finucane, who served as a legal adviser in the State Department from 2011 to 2021.
Under the Constitution, “the overwhelming bulk of war powers belong” to the members of Congress, he said.
He sees the midterm results, in part, as a backlash to the Trump administration’s expansive use of executive power.
After all, critics say officials like Hegseth have offered Congress relatively little transparency in the military’s overseas actions.
“We’ve seen sort of the apex of presidential unilateralism under Trump,” Finucane said. “I think it has reminded Americans of why the Constitution gives Congress, not one man, the power to take the country to war.”
The incoming Democrat-led Congress has pledged to use its power to check Trump’s war-making powers and confront Hegseth over his policies.
In the final days of the midterm race, Democratic Congressman Hakeem Jeffries, who is now in line to become the first Black speaker of the House, told supporters that Hegseth’s days were numbered.
“In the majority, one of the first things we’re going to do is run Pete Hegseth out of town,” Jeffries said.
He has since described himself as a “hard yes” on impeachment proceedings against the Pentagon chief.
But El-Gamal cautioned against treating the impeachment vote as the only path to accountability.
“Impeachment is just one constitutional accountability mechanism,” said El-Gamal.
She pointed to congressional investigations and the legislature’s “power of the purse” — its authority over federal spending — as two other avenues for reining in Hegseth and Trump.
El-Gamal added that November’s blocked impeachment motion “was not an acquittal nor a vote resolving the allegations” of war crimes in Iran and elsewhere. She anticipates the new Congress, once sworn in, will continue to pursue those allegations.
