noticias.titulo: Yemen’s besieged city of Taiz faces a deepening water crisis
noticias.resumen: Fuel shortages and the loss of access to wells have left residents dependent on unsafe water.
noticias.texto:
Yemen’s besieged city of Taiz faces a deepening water crisis
Fuel shortages and the loss of access to wells have left residents dependent on unsafe water.
Taiz, Yemen – Qaid al-Sharaabi waited three days before it was his turn to receive a tanker of clean water.
But the delay is not the only problem. He says he now has to pay more – the result of the Houthi siege on Taiz, in southwestern Yemen.
“This is the second time since the siege began a month-and-a-half ago that I’ve had to pay twice the price for a water tanker,” al-Sharaabi told Al Jazeera. “I’m afraid that if things continue like this, more residents will resort to using unsafe water.”
The United Nations children’s agency (UNICEF) says that water production in Taiz has nearly halved, while more than 800,000 people are reported to be cut off from humanitarian assistance.
The crisis has left the city reeling, even as government soldiers try to defend it, in the latest round of fighting to hit the area since the war in Yemen started in 2014.
Hospital administrators are warning of a public health disaster, while government officials are unsure how much longer they will have the funds needed to carry out even limited services.
Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city, has long suffered from severe water shortages.
But, according to Wafiq al-Aghbari, director-general of Taiz governorate’s Local Water and Sanitation Corporation, the crisis “intensified in 2015, with the first siege imposed on the city by the Houthis, and continued to worsen year after year, as the suffering of the city’s residents grew”.
He said the crisis has deepened since the Houthis laid siege to the city again in October, after they made advances against government forces in the countryside around Taiz.
Before the war started in 2014, al-Aghbari explained, Taiz received about 20,000 cubic metres (700,000 cubic feet) of water per day from six large wellfields, which had supplied the city and its immediate surroundings for years.
But only one of those wellfields is inside the city limits, and before the war, it had only been used in emergencies.
By 2015, Taiz had lost access to all five of its external wellfields, which had either fallen under Houthi control or were on the front lines, leaving the city reliant on its emergency wells.
But work in the past few years to dig additional wells and rehabilitate existing sources had brought daily production capacity up to 5,000 cubic metres (175,000 cubic feet) – still just 14 percent of the city’s estimated daily needs.
Tightening siege
The Houthi encirclement of Taiz in October led to the Iranian-backed group seizing control of Hadhran al-Dhabab, an external wellfield that had been partially restored in August 2025.
The situation has led to the water corporation losing 3,200 cubic metres (112,000 cubic feet) of daily production capacity – 1,200 cubic metres (42,000 cubic feet) after pumping stopped from the Hadhran al-Dhabab wellfield, and a further 2,000 cubic metres (70,000 cubic feet) after wells inside the city stopped operating because of a shortage of diesel. The corporation is now able to produce only 1,800 cubic metres (63,180 cubic feet) a day from the emergency wells that it can still operate.
Al-Aghbari said the consequences of the siege had extended beyond the widening gap between water supplies and demand.
Funding and supplies for the city’s charitable water distribution points, known as “sabeel”, have also been disrupted, because of shortages of fuel and water.
According to al-Aghbari, the subsidised distribution points had previously provided up to 1.5 million litres (396,000 gallons) of fresh water a day, alongside a further 1 million litres (264,000 gallons) of untreated water.
“The water corporation has entered a major financial crisis as a result of the loss of most international and local funding for its operations, at a time when the corporation is also under immense pressure because of the growing shortfall in meeting local water needs,” al-Aghbari said.
He added that this was especially problematic because more residents cannot afford to buy commercially-supplied water as a result of the worsening economic situation, and become more dependent on the free water distribution points.
The owner of one commercial water tanker, who did not want to give his name for security reasons, said that prices had risen sharply at the beginning of the siege, from 18,000 riyals per tanker (about $12 at parallel market rates) to 30,000 riyals (about $20).
He continues to try to pick up water from the Hadhran al-Dhabab wellfield, but said that the process had become difficult.
“[That is] because of the consequences of the siege, including the inspection procedures imposed by the Houthi group … which last for hours,” he said. “Sometimes we are prevented from entering and remain outside the city for more than a day, on the grounds that there are risks because of heightened military and security tensions.”
The Houthis have denied responsibility for the closure of roads into Taiz. Human Rights Watch has said that residents, aid workers, and UN officials had blamed the armed group for shortages in the city.
Contaminated water
The consequences of the siege have gone beyond its humanitarian and economic impact, with serious implications for public health, according to Dr Abdulqawi al-Shamiri, the director of Taiz’s al-Taawun Hospital.
He warned of “serious health disasters because of the interruption of safe water supplies that residents used to obtain from groundwater fields outside the city”.
Al-Shamiri said water from the emergency wells within the city had “long been unfit for human use, as a large proportion of it has become contaminated, or is hard water containing high concentrations of salts”.
He explained that the contamination was the result of sewage mixing with water because of poorly maintained sewage networks, and rubbish dumped in streets and floodwater channels. The Houthis, al-Shamiri said, have prevented waste from being transported to a landfill outside the city.
According to an internal report from the governorate’s Cleaning and Improvement Fund, close to half of the city’s rubbish is going uncollected.
Residents are contracting illnesses such as cholera and acute diarrhoea as a result, Al-Shamiri said.
“The rubbish quickly decomposes into extremely dangerous bacteria and chemicals that increase the existing contamination of the city’s well water, making it unfit for human use,” al-Shamiri said. “Unfortunately, however, most people are being forced to use it under the current circumstances because of the difficulty of accessing clean, safe water.”

noticias.titulo: Anthropic starts trading in the US after blockbuster IPO
noticias.resumen: Anthropic’s IPO surpasses SpaceX, marking the largest initial public offering in US history at $81bn.
noticias.texto:
Anthropic starts trading in the US after blockbuster IPO
Anthropic’s IPO surpasses SpaceX, marking the largest initial public offering in US history at $81bn.
Anthropic, the maker of the Claude AI assistant, is now trading on the Nasdaq through the largest initial public offering in history, surpassing the debut of Elon Musk’s SpaceX.
The stock began trading on the ticker ANT midday on Thursday.
The artificial intelligence (AI) lab, valued at $2 trillion, said last week that it would offer 825 million shares with its initial public offering (IPO) at a price range of $70 to $78 per share. However, that changed on Wednesday when the Dario Amodei-led company announced it would sell 980 million shares at $83 each.
By the time the stock ultimately went live, at 11:50am in New York (16:50 GMT), it was trading at $111.50 per share, a 34 percent rise. It dipped below $100 in midday trading, hitting $95.69 by 1:55pm (18:55 GMT).
The tech-heavy Nasdaq is down 1.5 percent in midday trading, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average is down by 1.8 percent and the S&P 500 is down 1.5 percent.
Other tech giants are also trending downwards, with Microsoft down 1 percent, Nvidia tumbling 1.7 percent, Meta down 2.5 percent, Apple by 0.9 percent, Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) by 9.2 percent and Micron Technology by 0.5 percent.
The high-profile IPO has fuelled excitement across the board, including among industry insiders such as Michael Monaghan, founder and portfolio manager at Founders ETF.
“We have indicated our intention to buy in the IPO and hope to get an allocation. The books are well oversubscribed with high-quality orders, according to our trading counterparts,” he told Al Jazeera.
Anthropic’s listing is the first of the two major AI labs to go public on US markets, as competitor OpenAI has also eyed an IPO. However, it comes at a rocky time for the AI industry, amid the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Nvidia invested a combined $20bn in Anthropic, including $10bn in a partnership announced in November 2025 and another $10bn in a share purchase tied to its IPO.
The massive IPO also comes amid backlash from voters in the recently concluded midterm elections, where all but one ballot initiative restricted expansion of data centres, and a sweep by Democrats who ran on platforms of reining in the AI industry.
“Some of the demand may simply reflect investors not wanting to miss out on the rare opportunity to gain exposure to a leading AI company, even if its long-term profitability remains uncertain,” IPOX associate Lukas Muehlbauer told the Reuters news agency.
That has not dented analysts’ assessments of the sector.
“Anthropic’s IPO [is] a big near-term win for the tech sector and should help restore some investor confidence that the AI Revolution growth thesis is not waning,” Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director of Yorkville Ives, said in a note.
Anthropic is also closely watched for how intertwined it is with other tech companies, including Amazon and Google.
Anthropic has committed $110bn to Amazon for computing infrastructure over long-term agreements and at least $121.3bn to Google.
Underscored concerns
Anthropic’s Wall Street debut comes amid growing concerns about the safety of its technology. The company’s more than 300-page US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filing devoted approximately 90 pages to outlining potential risks, including warnings that its AI systems could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”.
The company also disclosed a net loss of $104bn in the first nine months of 2026 in its SEC filing.
The concerns come as a group of AI safety experts has criticised Anthropic in a new statement released in the days surrounding its IPO. Dubbed the “Misanthropic Statement”, it challenges the company’s claims about its commitment to developing safe AI.
“Anthropic is not a safe AI company, and we must reject its reckless attempt to amass power in the name of the greater good,” the statement said.
Amid the concerns, the company put out a lengthy statement on the social media platform X.
“We will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control,” the statement quoted Anthropic CEO Amodei as saying. “We will not bend to either business or political pressure. Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing.”

noticias.titulo: As Burnham heads to Brussels, are new Brexit wars about to begin?
noticias.resumen: The UK premier is heading to Brussels for the second round of EU talks aimed at deepening post-Brexit cooperation.
noticias.texto:
As Burnham heads to Brussels, are new Brexit wars about to begin?
The UK premier is heading to Brussels for the second round of EU talks aimed at deepening post-Brexit cooperation.
Lincolnshire, United Kingdom – A decade is a short time in cheesemaking. Barrels of Tim Jones’ “Lincolnshire Poachers” cheese rest on their racks for months and years, disturbed only by Florence, the robot cheese turner.
Complexity, depth and flavour develop with patience.
The most mature cheese in Tim’s Lincolnshire dairy, in the English midlands, is five years old. By that measure, it was only a couple of cheeses ago that 52 percent of the British public voted for the country’s most tumultuous constitutional revolt in living memory.
Jones was one of them. But he is under no illusion that it went well – particularly for his exports.
“It suddenly made life much harder. We lost certain customers, and it became more expensive to get the cheese there. It definitely harmed our business,” he told Al Jazeera.
Ten years after the UK voted to leave the European Union, few are happy with what they got.
Remainers are still heartbroken that a majority of the country did not look on EU membership with approval. Leavers, by and large, think many of Brexit’s promised benefits were never delivered.
“I did vote to leave,” said Jones. “But I didn’t vote to leave in the way that we did.”
Recent polling tells a consistent story: A majority of Britons now view Brexit as a mistake.
In September, 55 percent of respondents told YouGov that leaving the EU was a wrong turn for the UK. Only 21 percent think it was the right decision.
Fifty-nine percent of Britons now support rejoining the EU.
Where does Burnham stand?
The relatively new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, has noticed the shift in public mood. Less cautious than his predecessor, Keir Starmer, Burnham reignited the Brexit debate shortly after taking office in July.
He has ruled out major changes to the UK’s relationship with the EU before the next general election. But he would like to see the country back in the bloc within his lifetime, and has suggested that a future Labour manifesto could promise a new referendum.
The changing mood is only part of the logic. A government searching for growth would naturally prioritise what is still its biggest trade partner. Geopolitics matter too. The UK’s bond with the United States is less reliable than it was.
Unsurprisingly, Brexit talk has swept through media in Britain and, to a lesser extent, in Europe. Burnham insists he will not get ahead of the public on this. His immediate concern, he says, is improving the current UK-EU relationship.
On Friday, Burnham will be in Brussels for the second UK-EU Summit – a vehicle established under Starmer to deepen post-Brexit cooperation.
Among the deals being worked on are a youth mobility scheme, an emissions trading agreement, and a food and drink trade deal.
Jones, the Lincolnshire cheesemaker, is hopeful.
“If he can reduce the red tape and the cost of sending cheese to Europe – and for us that means across the world – that would be a huge positive for us,” he said – although he was less certain which way he would vote in another referendum.
“Gosh, I genuinely don’t know. I think it would depend entirely on a critical view on the arguments that were presented at the time. A much more critical view than I had the first time around.”
It is an issue familiar to anyone who has lived through the Brexit years: the terms matter.
Former premier Theresa May used the motto, “Brexit means Brexit”. But the slogan was vague. What kind of Brexit? Hard? Soft? Norway Plus? Canada Plus?
There were many potential Brexits – as there might be many possible ways to rejoin.
Some are more popular than others.
A new YouGov survey gave people a menu of 18 options.
In the most popular scenario, 58 percent said they would vote to rejoin if the UK stayed out of the euro, joined the border-free Schengen Zone, and kept its previous rebate from the EU budget. But if the UK lost the rebate, did not join Schengen, and adopted the euro, only 35 percent of people said they would be interested in EU membership.
Anticipating the battles ahead, two pro-Brexit campaign groups are relaunching under new names: Stay Out and Enough Official.
Burnham says he will begin talks with the EU about options for the long-term relationship after this week’s summit.
Buckle up, the Brexit wars may be starting again.

noticias.titulo: Putin pitches Arctic route, calls for investment: Will it work?
noticias.resumen: Analysts say some Asian investors may show interest, but the route is unlikely to be a viable global shipping lane.
noticias.texto:
Putin pitches Arctic route, calls for investment: Will it work?
Analysts say some Asian investors may show interest, but the route is unlikely to be a viable global shipping lane.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has used his speech at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit to pitch investments in the country’s Arctic regions, as Moscow hopes to spearhead year-round navigation on the Northern Sea Route (NSR), which is currently confined to the summer months.
“I am confident that the business community and investors from APEC economies will fully appreciate the opportunities emerging in the Russian market – and, naturally, will take advantage of them,” Putin said on Wednesday in Shenzhen, China, according to Russian media.
The package proposed by the Russian president to support this includes tax breaks on profits, property and land, as well as reduced payroll contributions and preferential leases, Russian media reported.
His APEC speech follows Putin’s remarks at the Eastern Economic Forum in the Russian city of Vladivostok in September, when he also outlined plans to make navigation along the NSR year-round as well as to introduce new measures to expand transport, energy and technological infrastructure.
Russia has been developing the Arctic shipping corridor which connects its northern ports to the Pacific region. But Putin’s efforts to turn the NSR into an important artery of global trade have raised concerns about geopolitical and security challenges, as well as environmental risks for the fragile Arctic environment.
What is the Arctic route and why is Russia betting on it?
The Arctic shipping lane runs for about 5,600km (3,480 miles) along Russia’s northern coast, from the Novaya Zemlya archipelago in the west to the Bering Strait in the east. But it is only navigable for a few weeks of the year when the ice melts during the summer.
A more reliable shipping route through the Arctic could ease global trade, which is currently hampered by the Middle East crisis that has paralysed critical waterways, including the Bab al-Mandeb strait on the edge of the Red Sea, which feeds into the Suez Canal, and the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf. Shipping companies have become increasingly interested in alternative trade routes amid these heightened security concerns.
China announced its own new shipping route through the Arctic Ocean in August, dubbed the “Ice Silk Road”, which also takes in Russia’s NSR.
Climate change, which has contributed to major melting in the Arctic, is making the route more navigable for longer stretches of the year, raising its prospects as a viable alternative to existing shipping corridors.
The layer of frozen seawater that caps the Arctic Ocean, which melts through the summer to its annual low in September, has reached record lows. This year, according to NASA, it shrank to its lowest on satellite record.
Can Putin succeed in turning the Russian Arctic into a global trade route?
It might be trickier than it seems. While a changing climate is slowly transforming the Arctic, experts say the region remains largely impervious.
“Harsh climate, low visibility, short windows of navigation opportunities, drifting ice will remain serious obstacles for a large-scale commercial traffic,” Andrey Todorov, a researcher at the Netherlands Institute for the Law of the Sea (NILOS), told Al Jazeera.
“Any serious consideration of shipping through NSR will require not only investing in ice-capable vessels, which will be not as efficient and commercially viable in non-polar waters, but also experienced and knowledgeable masters, crew and operators.”
Todorov said he expects navigation along this route to remain “very niche and limited”, serving mainly Russia’s goal of transporting mineral resources extracted in the Arctic to the world market. At most, the analyst predicted, “a very small portion of transit container traffic, on a scale far from comparable to that of the traditional southern routes”.
Ksenia Vakhrusheva, Arctic project adviser at the Bellona Environmental Transparency Center in Vilnius, Lithuania, said Putin has been seeking to attract Chinese investments in the Arctic because Moscow doesn’t have the financial resources to carry the project through.
European sanctions on Russia’s energy sector have made it more urgent for Moscow to ship oil and gas to Asian markets through alternative shipping lanes, as Russian and Ukrainian forces target cargo ships in the Black Sea.
While China has been keen to “keep an eye” on the Arctic, Vakhrusheva said turning the NSR into a global maritime trade route does not appear realistic. “Everyone understands that route is under full control of Russia,” she said. “I don’t think that other players, including China, want to be dependent on a single country.”
Pavel Devyatkin, senior associate and leadership group member at The Arctic Institute, however, said he is confident that Asia-Pacific partners like China, Japan and South Korea would take up Putin’s call to increase participation and further route development.
“At the same time, the concerns are real: there is limited search-and-rescue capacity, environmental risks from heavier traffic, and the danger of the Arctic being drawn into geopolitical confrontation,” he said.
What could opening up the Northern Sea Route mean for the Arctic?
From an environmental point of view, more shipping could increase black carbon emissions and exacerbate the effects of climate change, pollution and biodiversity loss in the fragile Arctic.
A 2024 review by the Ocean & Coastal Management journal on the impact of Arctic shipping on the region’s environment showed a negative impact on water bodies, air emissions and wildlife.
The melting ice is also exposing a new geopolitical fault line.
Much of the NSR runs through Russia’s economic zone, where it regulates navigation. Russia and China are strengthening cooperation to develop the route, while United States President Donald Trump has repeatedly said that Washington must take over Greenland to prevent Moscow and Beijing from dominating the Arctic. In September, the US, Denmark and Greenland signed a deal on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, granting Washington a greater military presence on the continent-sized Arctic island.
Trump’s repeated threats to take over the Danish territory in the lead-up to that have strained US relations with European allies.

noticias.titulo: A geography of hearts: Turkiye and Lebanon, building the Levant together
noticias.resumen: Turkiye and Lebanon can build a stronger Levant through partnership, sovereignty and mutual respect.
noticias.texto:
A geography of hearts: Turkiye and Lebanon, building the Levant together
Some journeys feel less like a first visit and more like a homecoming. That is how I felt during my three days in Lebanon — my first ever visit to a country I had long known through its history, its poets and its people, but had never walked through myself.
I came at the kind invitation of Dr Tarek Mitri, Deputy Prime Minister of Lebanon, who proved the most gracious of hosts. I came in a spirit of friendship and partnership, and I leave with gratitude. In every conversation — in Beirut, in Tripoli, in Akkar and beyond — I heard the same quiet determination: Lebanon wants to stand on its own feet, and it wants partners, not patrons.
I also leave with a full heart and, I must admit, a fuller stomach. From a za’atar breakfast on the road to Akkar to the sweets of Hallab in Tripoli and shawarma at Barbar in Beirut, Lebanese hospitality is everything people promise. Around shared tables, over strong coffee and long conversations, I was reminded that the bonds between our peoples were never only about diplomacy. Distance on a map tells you very little. What matters is the geography of hearts — and by that measure, Beirut and Istanbul have always been neighbours.
That warmth carries a responsibility, for friendship is proved not in words but in what we do together. Five convictions stayed with me throughout the visit.
1. Unity is Lebanon’s greatest strength
Lebanon’s diversity of faiths, communities and traditions is not a weakness to be managed; it is a richness to be protected. I was honoured to meet leaders from across the country’s political and spiritual life: President Joseph Aoun, Prime Minister Nawaf Salam and the veteran Speaker of Parliament, Nabih Berri; the Grand Mufti of the Lebanese Republic, Sheikh Abdul Latif Derian, and the Greek Orthodox Metropolitan of Beirut, His Eminence Elias Audi; Mrs Bahia Hariri, Vice President of the Future Movement; and Mr Walid Jumblatt, former leader of the Progressive Socialist Party. Different as their paths have been, each spoke of the same hope: a state that serves all its citizens, institutions that work and a future their children will not have to leave the country to find. National unity is the foundation on which everything else — security, recovery, prosperity — must be built. Turkiye’s interest is in a strong, whole and united Lebanon.
2. Lebanon’s decisions belong to the Lebanese
For too long, Lebanon has paid the price of being treated as an arena for the rivalries of others. That has to end. Nowhere is this felt more deeply than in the south, whose towns, farmland and families have borne the heaviest cost of this year’s war. Lebanon’s sovereignty and territorial integrity are not negotiable — and they must extend to every inch of its land. Occupation in the south must end, and the Lebanese state must be able to protect all of its citizens, from Beirut to the southern border. The choices about Lebanon’s future must be made in Beirut, by Lebanese, for Lebanese. Foreign states — near or far — should respect that. Real friends offer support when it is asked for and step back when it is not. That is the principle Turkiye seeks to live by.
3. A Levant-driven future, built on trade
The problems of our region will not be solved one capital at a time, and they will not be solved from outside. The Levant must think and act as a region, as it once did. The Greek historian Diodorus Siculus records that the Phoenician cities held their common council in Tripoli, gathering there to deliberate on matters of the greatest importance. More than 2,000 years later, our region urgently needs to recover that tradition of meeting, talking and deciding together, and Tripoli, which welcomed me so warmly, is a fitting place to begin. Our economies are natural complements: Lebanon’s entrepreneurial talent, its banking and services heritage and its ports; Turkiye’s manufacturing base, logistics networks and access to Europe and Central Asia. As Syria recovers, a corridor of trade, transport and energy linking our countries can become the backbone of a new regional economy. Let goods, investment and young people’s ideas move freely across our region, and stability will follow prosperity.
4. A record, not a promise
Turkiye does not come to Lebanon with new slogans; we come with a track record. We have stood behind UNIFIL’s peacekeeping mission in the south. Through TİKA and the Turkish Red Crescent, we have delivered humanitarian aid in Lebanon’s hardest hours. Now the task is to rebuild the south — its homes and schools, its hospitals and roads and its olive groves — so that every displaced family can return home with dignity. Turkiye stands ready to play its full part in that effort, and to help strengthen the Lebanese institutions that must lead it. We have consistently defended Lebanon’s sovereignty in every international forum, and we will continue to do so. Through the foundations and educational institutions I work with, we have seen firsthand how much Lebanese students and young people have to offer — and how much our two societies gain when they learn side by side.
5. Interdependence is not dependence
In a fragile world, no country prospers alone. Cooperation between Turkiye and Lebanon is not charity flowing in one direction; it is interdependence that strengthens both. When Lebanon is stable, Turkiye and the whole region are safer. When Lebanese businesses grow, Turkish businesses gain partners. When our universities, civil society and young people connect, both nations gain. The goal is a partnership of equals — one where each side brings its strengths and neither loses its independence.
The road ahead
I leave Lebanon convinced that the moment for deeper partnership is now. Lebanon has endured more than its share of war, economic hardship and loss — especially this year, and the south most of all. Yet what I saw was not a country defeated but a people ready to rebuild. Turkiye will be there — not as a distant benefactor, but as a neighbour in the geography of hearts — until the last family has returned to its village in the south and the last school has reopened its doors. I hope this was the first of many visits, and that the friendships begun over these three days grow into lasting partnerships between our institutions, our businesses and, above all, our young people.
Shukran, Lebanon. Tesekkurler. Until we meet again.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

noticias.titulo: China, Russia and US agree peace declaration with no mention of Ukraine and Iran wars
noticias.resumen: Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’ China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants. The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.
The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.
The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.
The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.
“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”
Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and now had a “mutual understanding”.
Some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed Trump’s advances to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.
The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK.
“The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” said Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.
Analysts had said that the meeting’s primary significance was in its optics. “Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,” said Prof William Hurst, from the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back at the suggestion the summit had just been a photo-op. “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said.
In the declaration, the men “committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security”.
First among their concerns was “promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”. Sun said this was a favourite topic of China’s and showed that Beijing was “flexing its diplomatic muscles”. She said: “It is able to set the agenda and the deliverables according to its priorities … and make other great powers accept them.”
The declaration also agreed that “the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant and so the clause added to the perception that he has done well from the summit. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian president has been treated as an international pariah by Kyiv’s allies and he has not been to an Apec summit in years.
Hurst said: “This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power. It’s yet another example of Putin playing a poor hand to maximum effect.”
Xi, his status as a global power broker now assured, began the morning by addressing Apec leaders, reiterating the themes of trade openness and innovation he has emphasised throughout the summit. However, Apec affairs appeared to take a back seat for most of the day, with business dominating the discussions. For all the camaraderie on display, relations are complex. Russia is under US sanctions over the Ukraine war, while China and the US spent much of the last year engaged in an escalating tit-for-tat trade war before Trump and Xi called a truce.
Trump and Putin earlier held a separate meeting – their first since August 2025 – where the US president called his Russian counterpart his “friend”.
European allies meeting in Berlin to show their support for Ukraine expressed indignation at the cosy optics. “Mr Putin is not our friend and will never be,” the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said in a rejoinder to Trump. The Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, said she found it “very incomprehensible” that a US president would want to sit down with Putin.
The peace declaration in Shenzhen said the three countries planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. That was important, said Shan Guo from Hutong Research, a Shanghai-based advisory firm, but “now let’s see if the US will lift sanctions”.
Trump and Xi then held their third bilateral of this year. Xi said the US-China relationship was “generally stable and positive”, according to state media. But he cautioned Washington over Taiwan, saying the US “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in US-China relations”.
Another watched-for topic lacking detailed findings was that of AI. Xi said the two countries should “enhance communication and coordination to guard against security risks … and ensure that AI remains under human control at all times”.
Ultimately, the lack of breakthroughs might suit China, which has no appetite to move beyond the role of convener, said Kim. “Beijing has little interest in taking on the diplomatic risks of brokering an actual peace agreement in Ukraine or resolving the conflict with Iran. That would entangle China in conflicts it would rather avoid,” she said.

noticias.titulo: Trump accused of falling asleep during Xi Jinping speech at Apec summit in China
noticias.resumen: US president appeared to doze off while Chinese leader made speech, but White House insisted he was awake Donald Trump was, again, accused of falling asleep during a televised event, this time during the speech of the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in China. The US president appeared to close his eyes for roughly 10 seconds on Thursday. As his eyes closed, Trump’s head tilted downward, and his hands remained clasped in front of him. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Donald Trump was, again, accused of falling asleep during a televised event, this time during the speech of the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in China.
The US president appeared to close his eyes for roughly 10 seconds on Thursday. As his eyes closed, Trump’s head tilted downward, and his hands remained clasped in front of him.
Several prominent Trump critics on social media alleged that the US president was asleep, including Republicans Against Trump, California governor Gavin Newsom’s press office and conservative lawyer George Conway.
White House officials denied the allegations, claiming the 80-year-old US president was looking down at papers in front of him.
“Fake News! President Trump was looking at papers in front of him while the speaker made remarks. You can clearly see his eyes move back and forth,” Steven Cheung, the White House director of communications, wrote on X in response to a Newsweek article.
“This is why the people despise media so much. They constantly lie,” Cheung added.
Trump often faces accusations of falling asleep during televised events such as Oval Office press conferences, cabinet meetings and sporting events.
Occasionally, while listening to other people speak, the US president will close his eyes for several seconds, appearing as though he is falling asleep. Despite footage of the instances going viral, the White House and Trump allies have insisted the US president does not fall asleep during meetings.
Administration officials have excused Trump’s apparent drowsiness as blinking or an example of the president listening intently. They consistently claim Trump “doesn’t sleep”.
Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, testified to lawmakers earlier this year that he had “never seen” Trump fall asleep.
“On the contrary, the guy doesn’t sleep, which is a big problem because he calls me at two in the morning,” Rubio said in June.
Last year, JD Vance said that Trump hardly ever sleeps, even while traveling overnight.
“If we go on a 20-hour trip somewhere, he doesn’t sleep the entire time. And of course, if he’s not sleeping, if he’s working, he expects everybody else to be working too,” Vance told Fox News.
Trump became the oldest US president ever inaugurated when he was sworn in nearly two years ago. Despite his age, Trump often claims he is in near-perfect health, often bragging about his “perfect” cognitive test results and insisting he has a lot of energy.

noticias.titulo: New page in history? Xi, Trump and Putin summit was more of a footnote
noticias.resumen: Far from the grand ambitions declared in Yalta in 1945, Shenzhen felt like a meeting in search of an agenda It is arguably true, given it was the first such meeting of the leaders of China, Russia and the US, that Thursday’s gathering in Shenzhen deserved the description of “historic”. But in terms of tangible outcomes, it is unlikely to warrant the “new page in the history of diplomacy” that Vladimir Putin claimed had been written, and will instead be consigned to a smallish footnote in any future volume of the 21st century. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
It is arguably true, given it was the first such meeting of the leaders of China, Russia and the US, that Thursday’s gathering in Shenzhen deserved the description of “historic”.
But in terms of tangible outcomes, it is unlikely to warrant the “new page in the history of diplomacy” that Vladimir Putin claimed had been written, and will instead be consigned to a smallish footnote in any future volume of the 21st century.
It’s true that the meeting could yet be an icebreaker and the start of a permanent new dialogue. It’s also true that each leader can return home with something from the 90 minutes they spent together.
Despite falling asleep during the main Apec summit, Donald Trump had a chance to show his proximity to two authoritarian leaders he admires. With Ukraine having destroyed Russia’s bridge into Crimea, the US president greeted Putin as not just a friend but almost a wartime ally.
The Russian president, although occasionally pushed to one side by protocol during the early photo opportunities, will be able to show back home that it is Moscow, and not his adversary Europe, let alone Ukraine, that commands the respect and attention of Trump and Xi Jinping. As such, the summit was a free gift to Putin, and underlined that Trump was no longer the leader of the free world, as the former British foreign secretary Jeremy Hunt commented.
From Putin’s perspective, a meeting in Berlin of the coalition of the willing was a sideshow. Europe’s attempts to isolate Russia had failed and the Asia-Pacific region had become the centre of the global economy, Putin boasted. His relationship with Trump, he said, despite the difficulties, was founded on “similar civilisational values”.
For Xi, it was a prestigious chance to play host and implicitly demonstrate that the era of American hegemony is over. No longer the sole arbiter in world affairs, the US, the consumer economy, must share the stage with China, the manufacturing giant, and Russia, the energy bank.
The trio’s brief joint statement covered four pretty disparate topics: boosting energy supply, reforming the United Nations, limiting the powers of the international criminal court (ICC) and a tentative commitment to discuss nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation.
For grandeur at a time of various global crises, these ambitions hardly matched Yalta in 1945 or even the declaration after the Tehran summit in 1943, when the leaders of the UK, US and Russia sat on the veranda of the British embassy and pledged that their countries would work together after the war to build a “world family of democratic nations” free of tyranny and oppression. Winston Churchill declaimed in Tehran: “In our hands we have the future of mankind.” Joseph Stalin went further. “History has spoiled us,” he said. “She has given us very great power and very great opportunities.”
Shenzhen, by contrast, felt like a meeting in search of an agenda. The vacuum was filled with platitudinous commitments to “maintain strategic stability and international security”, a task that – looking around the world – none of those in attendance are currently pursuing with great effect.
Perhaps technology, multipolarity and their own divisions mean even they do not have “very great power”. Certainly there were no accompanying plans for how to reform the UN, let alone boost energy production or show respect for international law – a subject Trump’s current favoured successor, Marco Rubio, had just disparaged in a speech as a plaything of the global elite.
It was the summit’s chief instigator, Putin, who was the most eager of the three to set the meeting in a historic context, describing China, Russia and the US as the victors of the second world war, in a deliberate slight to Britain. A pledge to “preserve and strengthen the system of international law” seemingly referred to ensuring certain world leaders were freed from the prospect of the ICC serving them with arrest warrants.
By coincidence, the other world court, the international court of justice (ICJ), found a state – Myanmar – guilty of genocide for the first time on the same day. The Shenzen statement did not name the ICJ as a target, beyond an oblique reference to the ICC and “other similar institutions”. Doubtless that is only because ICJ rulings can be dismissed with near impunity.
Xi, nervous that China’s status as protector of the global south might be damaged by being involved in a global superpower carve-up, stuck to a familiar script: “History tells us that when major powers are at peace, the world is secure. When they clash, there is chaos.”
It may be that behind the scenes, or at other events, serious progress is being made on how China might act as a guarantor of a peace deal with Iran, or on who should lead the UN through its coming phase of reform, or even on how Putin might bring himself to seek peace in Ukraine in a way that protects Ukrainian sovereignty.
For the moment, though, it looks as if what little history was made in Shenzhen was made for exclusively the wrong reasons.

noticias.titulo: Howard-era minister Sharman Stone dies via voluntary assisted dying, aged 75
noticias.resumen: The former Liberal MP had fought a long battle against glioblastoma, an aggressive form of brain cancer Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast Former Liberal MP Sharman Stone has died via voluntary assisted dying after spending much of her political career advocating that people should have autonomy over their bodies. Stone died aged 75 on Wednesday surrounded by family after a long fight against glioblastoma, an aggressive form of brain cancer. She was minister for workforce participation from 2006-07. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Former Liberal MP Sharman Stone has died via voluntary assisted dying after spending much of her political career advocating that people should have autonomy over their bodies.
Stone died aged 75 on Wednesday surrounded by family after a long fight against glioblastoma, an aggressive form of brain cancer. She was minister for workforce participation from 2006-07.
During her political career, Stone championed contentious medical research and supported access to abortion, and readily – and publicly – disagreed with former leader Tony Abbott on both topics.
Stone was one of the first female superintendents in the Victorian Office of Corrections, the first female director of the Victorian Farmers Federation, and the recipient of an economics PhD.
She was elected to federal parliament in 1996, serving through the Howard years in what was then the seat of Murray in northern Victoria.
Stone was remembered as a strong voice for her local community, right up to her late days.
“She was born and bred in the heart of the electorate she served – a sixth-generation northern Victorian from a farming family,” the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, said after her death.
“She understood the rugged and regenerative nature of the land and what makes regional Australia tick.”
Stone spent two decades in parliament and was characterised by her independence.
She held several roles during the Howard government, including as parliamentary secretary to the environment and finance ministers.
She also held the shadow environment portfolio after the Liberals’ defeat to Kevin Rudd.
Stone retired from politics in 2016, and served as the Australian ambassador for women and girls until 2020.
Her celebration of life is expected to be held after the 28 November Victorian election.

noticias.titulo: Australian music industry rejects ‘divide and conquer’ proposal to give musicians exemption from AI scraping
noticias.resumen: Reported proposal to give musicians special treatment is ‘unworkable’, Aria CEO says, vowing to stand with other creatives Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast The music industry will not accept an AI carveout deal that leaves other creative sectors behind, rejecting a reported proposal to give musicians special treatment while allowing big tech to train on other copyrighted material – described by David Pocock as a “divide and conquer strategy”. The trade union representing writers and creatives is “alarmed” at a proposal to let AI companies train on Australian data
noticias.texto:
The music industry will not accept an AI carveout deal that leaves other creative sectors behind, rejecting a reported proposal to give musicians special treatment while allowing big tech to train on other copyrighted material – described by David Pocock as a “divide and conquer strategy”.
The trade union representing writers and creatives is “alarmed” at a proposal to let AI companies train on Australian data if they buy a permit, an idea also strongly rebuffed by the Coalition and Greens.
The Albanese government would not comment on the reported proposal, but senior ministers have raised concerns about current copyright law in recent days, hinting reforms were needed.
Annabelle Herd, the CEO of the Australian Recording Industry Association (Aria), and Claire Pullen, the CEO of the Australian Writers’ Guild, said the creative community – which this week launched a major AI campaign – would remain united in rejecting such changes.
“I can’t see any creative workers leaving their colleagues behind,” Pullen said.
The Australian Financial Review reported on Thursday the government was considering a copyright change under which AI companies would buy permits to train on Australian content, but that music may be exempted. Such a proposal would be more in line with AI companies, after Anthropic suggested a model of “conditional approval” to scrape content unless a rightsholder objected, and OpenAI told a parliamentary committee it would “potentially” support paying into a fund for creators.
Guardian Australia was not able to independently verify details of the proposal. One senior member of the creative community, involved in copyright discussions with government, said they had heard some details of such an idea, but others said they had not and doubted the Albanese government would seriously entertain it. One source in the AI industry, who declined to be named, said they would welcome such a plan.
Herd said she was unaware of the proposal before Thursday, but the music industry would not desert other creatives.
“Had we been consulted, we would have advised this scheme is unnecessary, unworkable and designed to suit the commercial interests of AI companies, not protect creators,” she told Guardian Australia.
“Our position is unchanged: we stand with the rest of the creative and media industries.”
Herd and Pullen said such a scheme would be difficult to implement technically, questioning how content like movies or TV shows – which combine copyrighted elements such as music, video and screenwriting – would be treated if just one element was exempted from AI scraping.
“This just seems like such a convoluted path, when AI companies have had an open invitation to sit down and negotiate for years. We have been working with government to come up with a model since 2024. We’ve come up with solutions and tech has steadfastly refused to even talk,” Pullen said.
While the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has declared it would be “theft” if creatives weren’t paid for their work, and that artists “need to be compensated”, some AI companies have argued it is too difficult to make individual licensing deals under existing copyright law.
The Media, Entertainment & Arts Alliance said it would be “alarmed” at the reported proposal, and demanded protections promised by Albanese “must apply to all creative sectors”.
While government MPs declined to comment on the report, senior Labor figures have recently begun more forcefully pointing to what they claim are shortfalls in copyright law in the AI age – despite major rightsholder groups rejecting the need for change. The industry minister, Tim Ayres, on Tuesday said “the status quo is no good” for creative workers, a line repeated by the acting prime minister, Richard Marles, on Thursday. Marles added on News24: “People are being ripped off”.
The attorney general, Michelle Rowland, also used newly strengthened language when contacted, promising “certainty and strong protections for Australian artists”.
“Right now, the work of Australian creatives is being used without their consent or payment,” a spokesperson for Rowland said.
“The Government has long advocated for tech companies to strike commercial deals with Australian artists, and we will continue to do so.”
Potentially carving out musicians did not win support among parliamentarians, either.
The shadow attorney general, Michaelia Cash, claimed such a proposal would “divide the rightsholders”.
“This ham-fisted tactic should be strongly resisted. Everyone who owns property should have the same right for it not to be stolen.”
Pocock also described it as “some sort of divide and conquer strategy”.
“It’s hard to know what [Labor] are actually doing at the moment. The joint select committee hasn’t even given its report to the government, and we’re hearing all sorts of whispers about what the government is planning.”
Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young urged the government not to meet copyright demands requested by big tech.
“What they’re asking Australia to do actually is to undermine copyright the world over. Australia will become known as the Cayman Islands for AI if we allow this loophole to happen,” she told News24.
“I say, don’t be that stupid. Stand up to them.”

noticias.titulo: An elevator, a brick wall and a bathroom: scientists use gravity to send ‘practically unblockable’ message
noticias.resumen: Australian physicists chose to transmit the word ‘gravity’ in binary code through brick wall Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Australian scientists have used gravity as a means of communication, in a proof-of-concept experiment involving a snail-paced 1950s elevator, a brick wall and a men’s bathroom. Physicists at the University of Queensland have used gravity to transmit a “practically unblockable” message about 70cm through a brick wall, by sending an elevator up and down between two floors and measuring changes in the gravitational field as a result of the movem
noticias.texto:
Australian scientists have used gravity as a means of communication, in a proof-of-concept experiment involving a snail-paced 1950s elevator, a brick wall and a men’s bathroom.
Physicists at the University of Queensland have used gravity to transmit a “practically unblockable” message about 70cm through a brick wall, by sending an elevator up and down between two floors and measuring changes in the gravitational field as a result of the movement.
The research, published in the journal Science Advances, involved a sensitive detection device known as a gravimeter, which was set up on the floor of a men’s bathroom adjacent to the lift.
The gravimeter was able to detect the position of the elevator’s 1.8-tonne counterweight as it moved between two levels – representing 0 and 1 in binary code – which enabled the scientists to send a message.
The researchers chose to transmit the word “gravity”, or 1000111 1110010 1100001 1110110 1101001 1110100 1111001 in binary code. At a transmission rate of one bit (digit) per minute, the single word took nearly an hour to send.
The scientists say that while gravitational communication is currently far from usable given its extremely slow speed, an advantage is that it is a “practically unblockable wireless communication scheme”.
“Unlike the electromagnetic signals used in modern wireless communication, a gravitational signal cannot simply be screened out by placing ordinary material in its path,” said co-author Dr Charles Woffinden, of UQ’s school of mathematics and physics. “Anyone who has lost phone reception in a tunnel or struggled with wifi through a solid wall will understand the appeal.”
Study co-author Prof Matthew Davis told Guardian Australia: “At the moment, it’s very hard to imagine how it could be practically useful.” But he added that the experiment was “theoretically interesting enough that it was worth doing”.
To put into perspective how slow the message transmission was, Davis said that Nasa’s Voyager 1 spacecraft, which after 49 years of travel had just reached a distance of one light-day away, could “communicate with Earth at a faster data rate than our communication concept”.
According to Davis, the new method of communicating could theoretically occur at ranges of up to 500 metres and at a rate 15 times faster, if more sensitive quantum gravity sensors were used.
The idea for the elevator study arose from a project to develop a contactless weighbridge – which would use quantum sensors to detect changes in the strength of gravity due to a passing truck, allowing scientists to determine the mass of a large vehicle.
Classical gravimeters can be thought of as a mass on a spring. “If you stretch the spring, the mass bounces up and down at a certain rate, which is determined by the spring and the gravitational field,” Davis said. “If the gravitational field changes ever so slightly, the rate at which it bounces back and forth changes.
“Quantum sensors are still under development
“Sometimes doing physics leads in unexpected ways and it’s a bit of fun … you get to do quirky things on the side. It’s one of the great joys of science to have stuff like this happen.”
Other near-unblockable methods of communication – involving neutrinos or gravitational waves – have been proposed “but these approaches are somewhat hindered by the difficulty in generating a measurable signal”, the scientists note.
The physicists conducted the research in UQ’s Parnell physics building, which is also home to the world’s longest-running science experiment – the pitch drop experiment, which began in 1927.

noticias.titulo: UK and EU plan first talks on sending refused asylum seekers to third countries
noticias.resumen: Two sides to commit to discussing third-country hubs as part of reset pact after five-country deal with Rwanda The UK and the EU plan to establish formal talks for the first time about sending rejected asylum seekers to third-country hubs, according to a leaked document. A draft of a joint statement expected to be signed by Andy Burnham and Ursula von der Leyen at a summit on Friday morning states that both sides will establish “a structured dialogue” to discuss “returns to third countries”. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
The UK and the EU plan to establish formal talks for the first time about sending rejected asylum seekers to third-country hubs, according to a leaked document.
A draft of a joint statement expected to be signed by Andy Burnham and Ursula von der Leyen at a summit on Friday morning states that both sides will establish “a structured dialogue” to discuss “returns to third countries”.
Until now, the Home Office has been seeking bilateral agreements with third countries allowing the removal of migrants, but with no obvious success.
Last week, five EU countries – Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands – announced an agreement in principle with Rwanda to establish a migrant “return hub” there in 2027.
Burnham hinted at possible cooperation with EU countries last week when he told reporters that the UK had not had direct discussions with European governments involved in return hubs but “we will watch that [the five-country deal] with interest, learning from what went on in the past”. He said: “The public want us to do whatever we can to deal with illegal immigration.”
The UK has been fighting for deeper cooperation with the EU on migration, with the new deal on a “strategic dialogue” secured in the last two weeks by negotiators in Brussels.
It is a key part of the UK-EU reset pact, which also covers a youth mobility scheme, tariffs on Chinese imports, food and drink exports to the EU and a wider restatement of commitment on defence and security.
Informed sources confirmed this was the first time the UK and the EU had agreed to “open a dialogue on returns” after the launch of the bloc’s Channel action plan in June this year.
Whitehall sources said the UK was now open to the possibility of sending rejected claimants to Rwanda – a recent pivot from the position under Keir Starmer’s government, which rejected the move.
According to a draft of the joint agreement, negotiations over third-country hubs will be part of increased cooperation to tackle irregular migration.
The document states: “The EU and UK … will establish a structured dialogue on migration covering in particular the joint activities under the Channel action plan, action against irregular migration and migrant smuggling networks, strategic communication and border management, upstream cooperation and engagement with third countries, returns to third countries, pull factors for irregular migrants and legal pathway.”
In May, the UK and 45 other European countries signed an agreement that explicitly endorsed plans to send unwanted asylum seekers to third-country hubs.
A political declaration from the 46 members of the Council of Europe, the body that oversees the European convention on human rights (ECHR), said states had an “undeniable sovereign right” to control their borders.
It is understood that the UK has been seeking a deal with an unnamed third country, similar to the Italy-Albania agreement that allowed Rome to place detention centres in Albania. Albania has ruled out a bilateral agreement on a return hub with the UK.
Previous discussions have reportedly centred on 11 countries: Armenia, Egypt, Ethiopia, Ghana, Libya, Mauritania, Rwanda, Senegal, Tunisia, Uganda and Uzbekistan. Montenegro has denied reports that it is considering housing refused asylum seekers.
Starmer scrapped a Tory plan to forcibly send small-boat arrivals to Rwanda where their asylum claims would have been processed.
Before the election, the Conservative government had spent £700m on its Rwanda returns policy, which was meant to deter Channel crossings. The scheme hit legal and political obstacles from the start, with the UK supreme court eventually ruling it illegal.
Under Burnham, the Home Office has refused to close down the possibility of sending asylum seekers to Rwanda. This week, when asked if the UK might ever send asylum seekers to Rwanda, a Home Office spokesperson said: “The UK, like other European countries, is exploring innovative approaches including returns hubs to tackle illegal migration.”
The UK has been looking for years to strengthen cooperation with France and other EU member states to tackle small boats carrying asylum seekers across the Channel.
But sources say it is only in recent months that there has been a change of mood in the EU, with member states realising that the intensity of criminal trafficking across the Channel is “proving [to be] a pull factor” to enter the EU. Those that fail to make it to British shores remain in the EU’s migrant support system.
Responding to the planned cooperation on migrant hubs, Madeleine Sumption, the head of the Migration Observatory at Oxford University, said: “Its inclusion in the statement would confirm the now relatively widespread interest in ‘third country’ options.”
In response, Imran Hussain, the director of external affairs at the Refugee Council, said return hubs were likely to be difficult and costly to run.
“Removing people to places they have never stepped foot will be difficult and distressing,” he said.
“The last decade has shown that working with people to support their return to their countries is far more successful.”
A Home Office spokesperson said: “While we are not part of this EU member state initiative, there is widespread international agreement on the need to have practical and workable solutions to deal with the global challenge of illegal migration.
“We continue to explore innovative approaches, including returns hubs, to build on the 80,000 people with no right to be in the UK returned or deported since July 2024. We have consistently made clear that we support the principle of returns hubs.”
