noticias.titulo: UK-EU reset talks will go ‘down to the wire’ as crunch summit approaches
noticias.resumen: Britain understood to have made concessions on youth mobility scheme as negotiations on wider deal continue British and EU negotiators have provisionally agreed to allow 100,000 young EU citizens to come to the UK every year under a new mobility scheme, as negotiations on the UK-EU reset talks go “down to the wire”. Tensions in Brussels remained high on Thursday afternoon as ambassadors began crunch talks on the latest draft of the wider agreement, with sources confirming both sides were still battling over the exact nature of the UK’s role in shaping future European food and farming rules, in
noticias.texto:
British and EU negotiators have provisionally agreed to allow 100,000 young EU citizens to come to the UK every year under a new mobility scheme, as negotiations on the UK-EU reset talks go “down to the wire”.
Tensions in Brussels remained high on Thursday afternoon as ambassadors began crunch talks on the latest draft of the wider agreement, with sources confirming both sides were still battling over the exact nature of the UK’s role in shaping future European food and farming rules, in a second part of the deal.
It is understood the UK made concessions in meetings on Thursday to increase the quota of EU citizens who could take part in a new youth mobility scheme, from 50,000-80,000 to a new cap of 100,000.
It was also agreed to raise the age cap from 30 to 31.
The number of young British people allowed to go to the EU under the scheme will be matched but could be higher, with some countries, including Germany, being prepared to take unlimited numbers each year.
With less than 24 hours to go before Andy Burnham is due in Brussels for a summit with EU leaders, the two sides still need to resolve some central sticking points, including how much of a say Britain will have in new EU food rules.
France is perceived by other member states to be the main barrier to greater UK involvement in EU working groups on food and drink laws. “They are super principled on that point,” said one EU diplomat.
Speaking in general terms about the disagreements, also including tuition fees for EU students in the UK, another EU diplomat said: “It will go down to the wire. Our feeling is that the Brits have to move if they want a deal.”
A spokesperson for the British prime minister also described the talks as close, saying if an agreement was reached, the government would bring forward legislation, the cutting costs bill, to parliament next week.
Another EU diplomat said ambassadors representing the EU member states would meet at 5pm and “will go until agreement is reached tonight”.
Sources said the UK was still resisting pressure from the EU on tuition fees for EU students coming to Britain under the youth mobility scheme.
“We are fighting hard on this and think we will get there,” said an EU insider. “But for us, one of the hardest discussions centres on this question of the UK being a rule taker or rule maker.”
At the long-awaited summit, the EU and UK hope to sign three agreements, including a highly prized food and drink deal that was a Labour manifesto commitment and is expected to add 0.4% to British GDP.
The deal, expected to come into force on 1 March 2028, requires the UK to align with EU rules on sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) standards, making Britain a rule taker.
Asked about Britain’s status as a rule taker, No 10 said the Labour manifesto had aimed to build closer ties with the EU, adding: “We were obviously elected on a manifesto that promised to reset the relationship and seek to deepen ties with our European friends.”
According to EU sources, the UK has been pushing to have a formal role in EU committees involved in implementing existing and setting new SPS rules.
But after a meeting of EU ambassadors that ended late on Wednesday, the issue remained unresolved. The EU diplomat said: “They want to be able to shape decisions, not only implementation, but future decisions. That has always been a red line.”
Under the SPS proposal, the UK will agree to dynamically align with EU laws and will have a “voice” but “not be in the room” when laws are drafted.
A second diplomat from a country sympathetic to the British position said the European Commission had proposed an “extremely restrictive consultation mechanism” for the UK.
In contrast, the EU diplomat thought it was reasonable for a British representative to take part in the implementation of SPS legislation affecting the UK.
“Of course the UK cannot vote in the council as a non-member state, but we feel that we need to be pragmatic about coordination and implementation,” they said.
The issue raises the tensions at the heart of the UK’s status as a rule taker, and would be many times magnified were Britain to choose to enter the single market as a non-EU member state.
The precise details of how the UK would be consulted on future food and farming rules remain unclear.
Separately, the EU and UK remain deadlocked over whether EU students in Britain should pay the British or international tuition fee rate.
The draft proposal gives the UK two options: to agree to significantly reduced undergraduate fees or equal treatment with nationals.
Burnham’s spokesperson suggested there was an UK-EU consensus that there would be no further incremental reset summits beyond the one on Friday until a full negotiation commenced on a longer-term, more stable relationship, such as rejoining the single market.
“After the summit, we will begin those discussions with our European partners about the realistic options for our longer-term relationship,” he said.
The UK has prioritised seeking commitments on Britain’s position relating to the EU’s Made in Europe legislation. The trade defence policy will include tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles but will also affect British manufacturing. The sides are believed to be close to an agreement to language at the summit that would point towards UK inclusion, but nothing can be formalised until the EU passes its own legislation.
Burnham’s spokesperson said: “[The UK is] engaging constructively with the EU on that, and we’ve been clear about the challenges it could represent for British industries. We have deeply integrated supply chains with Europe, and we want to keep working together to boost growth and open up trade.
“The UK and Europe have shared economic challenges, and we believe shared challenges are best met with a collective approach that is in Britain’s best interests, and in Europe’s too.”

noticias.titulo: What is at stake at the EU-UK summit in Brussels?
noticias.resumen: Leaders will wrestle with easing Brexit red tape, restoring emissions trading and opening up youth mobility UK politics live – latest updates The EU and UK will hold a long-awaited summit in Brussels on Friday – the second since Brexit – to hammer out the UK’s longer-term relationship with the bloc. It will be attended by the prime minister, Andy Burnham, the head of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, and the president of the European Council, António Costa. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
The EU and UK will hold a long-awaited summit in Brussels on Friday – the second since Brexit – to hammer out the UK’s longer-term relationship with the bloc.
It will be attended by the prime minister, Andy Burnham, the head of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, and the president of the European Council, António Costa.
The gathering, which follows up last year’s inaugural EU-UK summit in London, was scheduled for July but postponed when Keir Starmer resigned.
What is on the table?
The two sides hope to announce three deals, which were initiated under Starmer’s government.
First, a food and drink agreement that will remove a lot of Brexit red tape on animal and plant products, making it easier to trade meats, cheese, wine and flowers. To secure the deal, which is not expected to take effect until 2028, the UK will align with EU standards, meaning the government, for example, must abandon a planned ban on foie gras imports.
A second agreement will link the British emissions trading system with its bigger EU cousin, restoring a link severed by Brexit. It is a significant step for industry because EU and UK businesses will be exempt from each other’s charges on high-carbon imports such as steel, cement and electricity. This agreement also requires alignment with relevant EU rules.
The third deal is the most contentious: a youth mobility scheme that will give those aged 18-30 the right to live, work, travel and study on both sides of the Channel for up to three years. The scheme may not be up and running until 2030 – bad news for anyone in their late 20s.
With less than 24 hours before the summit begins, two big issues remain open. EU negotiators want to ensure EU students pay the UK rate of university tuition, around four or five times lower than international fees. The two sides also disagree over how many people would be allowed to take part: the EU wants 100,000 visas a year, but the UK is looking at 50,000 to 80,000 to keep migration numbers down.
To maximise its leverage on tuition fees, the EU is linking the three agreements, warning they must come into force together.
EU negotiators want their students to pay tuition fees at UK levels instead of the much higher international rate. Photograph: Chris Ison/PA
Will the UK be included in Made in Europe?
Not on Friday. The UK has been pushing for inclusion in the EU’s Made in Europe plan, a protectionist scheme to favour EU companies when public money is being spent on goods such as electric cars, renewable energy and nuclear technology. Inclusion in Made in Europe is a big priority for the Burnham government, which has dangled major concessions on tuition fees to make sure British firms are not shut out.
The problem for London is that the EU lawmakers have not finalised the Made in Europe law, known as the Industrial Accelerator Act. Many EU member states want to include the UK, but France and the European parliament take a stricter position.
The EU law is not expected to be agreed until spring 2027. To help the British government, which has linked a generous offer on youth mobility with Made in Europe, the European Commission proposed delaying agreement on tuition fees by six months. But member states want precise guarantees now about equal treatment for EU students.
Another problem is that British inclusion in Made in Europe requires the UK to sign up to EU trade-defence policies. The EU, for instance, has imposed high tariffs on “unfairly subsidised” Chinese electric cars and fears the UK, which has not followed suit, could become an alternative route into the EU if Chinese companies set up in Britain and sell into the bloc. The EU is calling on the UK to align with its trade-defence policies, but the UK insists it can guard against circumvention without copying the EU.
In a sign of possible tensions, an earlier summit text proposing a trusted partnership on economic security has been downgraded to a partnership.
An agreement expected next year will bring the UK back into the EU’s internal electricity market. Photograph: CW Images/Alamy
What happens next?
Beyond the headline deals, the EU-UK draft summit statement opens the door to British integration in European policies on energy, crime-fighting, educational exchange, tech and foreign policy cooperation.
The next major agreement, targeted for next year, is bringing the UK back into the EU’s internal electricity market. This is a priority for five EU member states: Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark and Luxembourg. They argue that Britain’s inclusion in the EU electricity market is essential to take advantage of the nascent green power boom in the North Sea. In return for market access, the UK will be required to contribute to the EU budget to aid the development of poorer EU regions.
Beyond that, the two sides will “explore opportunities” for the UK to join the Erasmus student exchange programme after 2027; the current arrangement applies only for the 2027-8 academic year.
In a win for the UK, the EU appears ready to expand talks on the mutual recognition of professional qualifications, beyond existing negotiations on architects. The sides will sign a digital partnership, which includes joint work on AI safety, and examine how to share data on law enforcement and border management.
Is this joining the EU by the back door?
Far from it. A lot of diplomatic plates are spinning, but the UK remains outside the EU’s biggest economic clubs: the single market and the customs union. It also has no decision-making powers inside the EU.
Burnham says he will set out the long-term options for the future relationship after this week’s summit. “The hard Brexit we were given is not good enough for Britain,” he said on Monday in a major speech. But amid concerns among some cabinet ministers about reopening Brexit divides, the prime minister appears to be taking a more cautious approach. He said the process would take time and insisted that “at every stage the British people will be the boss”.
The EU has welcomed Britain’s interest in rejoining but is wary of a protracted negotiation that could be reversed by an anti-EU British government.
In an echo of the Brexit years, EU insiders say, once again, that it is up to Britain to define what it wants.

noticias.titulo: Myanmar ruling gives new relevance to genocide convention and is ‘full of messages’ for Israel
noticias.resumen: Hailed as ‘a rare moment of justice’, judges’ decision sets out a roadmap for assessing the question of intent The international court of justice (ICJ) verdict making Myanmar the first country in history to be found guilty of committing genocide does not just deliver justice for Rohingya victims. It also gives the 1948 genocide convention new relevance in governing the actions of nation states. In their nine votes to six majority ruling, the panel of judges in The Hague set out a detailed roadmap for how the convention should be applied to real-world situations in which a government is accused
noticias.texto:
The international court of justice (ICJ) verdict making Myanmar the first country in history to be found guilty of committing genocide does not just deliver justice for Rohingya victims. It also gives the 1948 genocide convention new relevance in governing the actions of nation states.
In their nine votes to six majority ruling, the panel of judges in The Hague set out a detailed roadmap for how the convention should be applied to real-world situations in which a government is accused of committing genocide against a whole population group, especially when it comes to assessing the question of intent.
The lengthy judgment will have been read particularly carefully by Israel, the only other country currently before the ICJ accused of genocide.
It is also relevant to Germany, which has been brought before the court by Nicaragua on the accusation it has facilitated and failed to prevent genocide in Gaza.
“I think it’s a judgment that brings the genocide convention alive,” said Philippe Sands, a leading human rights lawyer who was part of the Gambian legal team. “It gives the convention practical, real meaning. And if the alternative view had been taken, the convention would essentially become a dead letter.”
Amnesty International’s secretary general, Agnès Callamard, called the ruling “a rare moment of justice for survivors, victims and their families”. But it was also an assertion of humanitarian law in an increasingly lawless world.
“This is a good day for international law. We needed it,” said Dr Iva Vukušić, an assistant professor in international History at Utrecht University and a war crimes expert. “It is really important, clarifying a lot of law, and that’s going to be very helpful going forward.”
There will be a spillover from this ruling to its sister tribunal in The Hague, the international criminal court (ICC), providing a benchmark for when genocide charges could be made against individual perpetrators.
The Trump administration, instinctively hostile to international legal institutions, is also watching critically. The US ambassador to the UN told the ICJ before this judgment not to “lower the legal threshold for proving genocide” lest it be “weaponised” against US and allied soldiers.
The court did not directly lower the standard for demonstrating genocide, and the Gambia – which brought the case to The Hague – did not ask it to.
The judges kept the existing benchmark for judging genocide intent as the “only reasonable inference” of Myanmar’s actions and referred extensively to prior case law. But it went a long way towards clarifying how that standard should be applied in assessing atrocity crimes committed by states.
Before this case, only Serbia had faced the charge of genocide at the ICJ, in cases brought by Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the Bosnian ruling in 2007, Belgrade was found to have failed to prevent the 1995 genocide in Srebrenica, but in both cases it was cleared of committing the genocide directly.
The new ICJ judgment finds the Myanmar military directly responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, a Muslim minority targeted in a ferocious counterinsurgency campaign that reached its peak in 2017.
In assessing the Myanmar campaign, the ICJ looked not just at the death toll of about 10,000 in assessing the scale of the atrocities, but at the total Rohingya population targeted in northern Rakhine state, 815,000 people. Significantly, it cast its net wider than just the death toll, considering mental damage done to the survivors, particularly victims of sexual violence, and the impact on reproduction in the Rohingya community.
Most importantly, the ICJ judgment provided a guide to interpreting the standard set by Serbian cases, in which a finding of genocide could be made only if there were not other plausible motives for mass killing.
In this judgment, the court ruled that Myanmar could have had other motives, such as the desire to displace or punish the Rohingya population, but that those motives could exist alongside genocidal intent. The judges said genocidal intent was the “only reasonable inference” from the “totality” of evidence.
In justifying that conclusion the judges pointed to several factors that international law experts say are relevant to the Gaza case, which is now hearing written pleadings and is expected to take at least another three years.
The common factors include the targeting of children, which the court described as striking at the “foundation” of the Rohingya as a group – the ICJ said up to 2,109 Rohingya children under the age of five had been killed, while more than 5,000 Palestinian children under five years old have been killed in the Gaza war.
Another incriminating factor cited by the court was the “bulldozing and large-scale terrain clearance” after the destruction of villages, followed by “rapid construction” including security installations, which has been the hallmark of Israeli army occupation of over 60% of the Gaza Strip.
“It’s full of messages for Israel,” said William Schabas, an international law professor and expert on genocide at Middlesex University. “There are obvious differences, of course, the evidence will be different, but if you exchanged the word Myanmar with Israel, you wouldn’t have to change much in the judgment.”
The fact that there were six dissenting voices on the bench suggested that substantial parts of the majority’s reasoning were not beyond dispute, and lawyers involved in the case cautioned that it did not necessarily mean that the same bench would find Israel guilty of genocide in Gaza. But the same lawyers added that the opposite was almost certainly true. If this case had failed, the case brought by South Africa against Israel would have been all but over.

noticias.titulo: Eight injured after driver in Israel repeatedly rams car into Palestinians
noticias.resumen: Arab MPs accuse politicians of fuelling hostility as footage shows driver accelerating towards Palestinians at four locations in Kafr Qasim Eight people were injured on Wednesday evening when a driver struck Palestinian residents at four separate locations in Kafr Qasim, a city in central Israel. Footage shared on social media appears to show the car accelerating towards people, all Palestinians, at several locations in the city, striking them before driving away. Three of those injured were in moderate condition, and several of the victims were women leaving a nearby wedding, the Times of Isr
noticias.texto:
Eight people were injured on Wednesday evening when a driver struck Palestinian residents at four separate locations in Kafr Qasim, a city in central Israel.
Footage shared on social media appears to show the car accelerating towards people, all Palestinians, at several locations in the city, striking them before driving away. Three of those injured were in moderate condition, and several of the victims were women leaving a nearby wedding, the Times of Israel reported.
Haaretz has reported that investigators are examining whether the driver struck people deliberately. Avi Levy, a police district commander, said the incident appeared to be a hit-and-run and that the driver had tested positive for drugs. He said the Shin Bet security service was taking part in the investigation and said: “As of this moment, nothing is coming up. The suspect has no criminal record.”
The incident prompted Arab lawmakers and activists to accuse Israeli politicians of fuelling hostility towards Arab citizens. Benjamin Netanyahu has called Arab parties “terror supporters” and said partnering with them would put Israel’s security at risk. The parties won a record 19 seats in the Knesset in the country’s recent election.
Yousef Jabareen, the chair of the Joint List, said the incident “raises difficult questions about the claim that the driver lost control”. He said: “I’ve been warning for weeks that the incitement against Arab citizens will turn into assaults and even assassinations.”
Said Issa, a community activist in Kafr Qasim, described the incident as an “act of terror”. “Someone who loses control of his vehicle might hit one or two vehicles, but not multiple people in several different places,” Issa said. “The attacker struck at four locations, one after the other.”
In a separate incident in the occupied West Bank, the Palestinian foreign ministry called on Monday for an Israeli settler to be held accountable after eight Palestinians were run over and injured in Tuqu, south-east of Bethlehem. Local sources told the Anadolu news agency that the driver had first struck three young men, then returned and ran over five others who had gathered to help them.

noticias.titulo: ‘Everyone struggled for this justice’: tears in court as Rohingya vindicated in Myanmar genocide ruling
noticias.resumen: Relief in the immediate aftermath of a landmark ruling, but what happens next is in the hands of governments around the world There were tears in the halls of The Hague in the Netherlands and an eruption of applause in the refugee camps of Bangladesh as the scattered communities of Rohingya watched the UN’s top court rule the Myanmar military had committed genocide against them. For almost a decade, the Rohingya have awaited this moment; recognition from the international court of justice (ICJ) that Myanmar in 2017 intentionally tried to destroy the mostly Muslim minority group through a campa
noticias.texto:
There were tears in the halls of The Hague in the Netherlands and an eruption of applause in the refugee camps of Bangladesh as the scattered communities of Rohingya watched the UN’s top court rule the Myanmar military had committed genocide against them.
For almost a decade, the Rohingya have awaited this moment; recognition from the international court of justice (ICJ) that Myanmar in 2017 intentionally tried to destroy the mostly Muslim minority group through a campaign of mass killings and rape. More than 10,000 Rohingya were killed and 700,000 fled to neighbouring Bangladesh.
By the time they spilled into the court’s halls, the relief was evident. A Rohingya community leader threw a big thumbs up as he left the courtroom and others immediately took out their phones to call family in the refugee camps.
Salma, 30, a Rohingya survivor who lost family members in the 2017 genocide, said: “Everyone worked hard and struggled for this justice, for this cause. When they hear it today, everyone will be happy, thank God. I don’t know how to express it or even what to do with myself.”
Another Rohingya present, who cannot be named because of safety concerns, said they cried as the judge went through each of the rulings.
“During the last few minutes I couldn’t even sit down any more, I had to move to the back because I didn’t know how I’d react,” they said. “I saw some of the other Rohingya around me crying. They were so emotional.
“Now the responsibility is with the international governments. It has been declared genocide now and they have to act.”
In Bangladesh, where most of the Rohingya population have lived – in the world’s largest refugee camp – since being forced to flee in 2017, the verdict was translated into the Rohingya language for the crowds who had gathered to watch on screens specially set up for the purpose.
They immediately leapt up, cheering, applauding and shouting gratitude for the Gambia – the faraway African nation that brought the case to the ICJ on behalf of the stateless minority. Many held posters that read “Thank You Gambia” and “Justice = Safe Return”.
“Since we arrived here, we have been waiting and looking forward to this justice,” said Farida Khatun, 50, who has been a refugee in Bangladesh since 2017, when her village, Tula Toli, was targeted by soldiers. The village in north-western Myanmar, near the Bangladesh border, was the scene of a massacre in August of that year, with reports of mass killings and gang rapes.
She said, however, that she does not expect to be able to return home. Tula Toli was completely destroyed by Myanmar’s forces and no longer exists. “Even though today’s verdict makes us happy, my heart still cannot believe that they will take us back in true peace.”
The case has taken seven years to reach this point, with Rohingya researchers working to collect testimony from survivors. The initial hope for justice had faded during the long wait for a ruling. Many were also left deflated during early hearings when the one-time pro-democracy hero Aung San Suu Kyi defended the Myanmar military at The Hague.
Before today’s ruling, some were optimistic, others were prepared to be disappointed, but all said they knew themselves that they were victims of genocide.
The tension was finally released when the court declared Myanmar was responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, highlighting the use of sexual violence and attacks on children alongside the killing of Rohingya who tried to flee violence, which it said meant the violence amounted to more than ethnic cleansing.
The court ordered Myanmar to provide reparations for the Rohingya and end continuing breaches of the genocide convention.
There is now also an international criminal court investigation into the violence of 2017, looking specifically at the crime of mass deportation, and for which prosecutors in 2024 sought an arrest warrant for Myanmar’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing.
With continuing violence against the Rohingya, the possibility of a return to Myanmar, as happened after previous exoduses to Bangladesh in 1978 and the early 1990s, remains unlikely.
But many hope the ICJ ruling will be the start of a process of ensuring justice and lead to real international pressure to ensure their safety in Myanmar.
“We will be able to return to our homeland – with our rights, with our citizenship, and having received our full security. We will be able to return,” says Salma.

noticias.titulo: Grand Theft Auto fans skip work and pull all-nighters to play new instalment
noticias.resumen: Hotly anticipated Bonnie and Clyde-inspired adventure GTA VI has gamers glued to their screens around the world Grand Theft Auto fans around the world pulled all-nighters, skipped work and school, and attended overnight launch parties to vicariously embark on police chases and coordinate robberies as the latest instalment of the eagerly anticipated series arrived. GTA VI, a Bonnie and Clyde-inspired crime adventure game set in the fictional US state of Leonida, was launched at midnight on Wednesday after a 13-year wait. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Grand Theft Auto fans around the world pulled all-nighters, skipped work and school, and attended overnight launch parties to vicariously embark on police chases and coordinate robberies as the latest instalment of the eagerly anticipated series arrived.
GTA VI, a Bonnie and Clyde-inspired crime adventure game set in the fictional US state of Leonida, was launched at midnight on Wednesday after a 13-year wait.
The hype around the release led to schools encouraging pupils not to miss lessons in anticipation of “GTA flu”, a term coined for the swathe of absences when GTA V was released in 2013, which is expected to recur over the coming weeks. The human resources platform Remote said there had been a 32% increase in leave requests worldwide on Thursday.
Birchgrove comprehensive school in Swansea, south Wales, had warned parents and carers that despite the “considerable excitement”, studies should remain a priority.
The Sandon secondary school in Essex entered students into a raffle for £10 Amazon vouchers, a lunchtime queue-jump pass and free Christmas dinners as incentives to stop them bunking off to play as the game’s dual protagonists, Jason and Lucia.
Narendra Modi, India’s prime minister, took a different approach in a country with an estimated 550 million gamers. Modi posted 10 images on X modelled on the game’s artwork that compared India today with the time of GTA V’s release.
The Indian politician, who has stepped up efforts to appeal to younger voters since youth-led protests over jobs and education, wrote: “India is playing a whole new game!”
Downing Street said Andy Burnham would not be playing the new instalment. Asked whether the UK prime minister would be exploring Vice City, the Grand Theft Auto maker Rockstar’s fictional take on Miami, a spokesperson said: “His diary is very full.”
The launch of GTA VI generated more than 2.6m posts on social media in 24 hours, according to social media monitor Visibrain.
Approximately 1,850 messages about the game were published per minute – 7% more than the number of posts at the start of the 2026 men’s Fifa World Cup.
Among the game’s fans is Sean Little, a self-employed painter and decorator. He persuaded his wife and daughter to sign a “non-interference contract”, giving him a week off dad duties to play in peace in Dumfries and Galloway, Scotland.
Myles_Away, a UK-based streamer on the Twitch platform, told the BBC he planned to play for “13 or 14 hours” on Thursday.
He said: “I played all last night, and then I slept, woke up, and [came] right into this interview,” adding: “Obviously not everybody is able to drop the money required. [Consoles] are very expensive at the moment, so they are able to experience the story through streamers.”
Jacob Joel, a 30-year-old IT professional in Bengaluru, southern India, took the day off to play in a gaming cafe. “We waited around 13 long years to get into GTA VI,” he said. “That is a nostalgic feeling.”
In Bangkok, British tourists Kyle McKee and Emily Todd reserved a PS5 console, TV and a sofa at a gaming centre. McKee, 27, told the AFP news agency: “It’s the fear of missing out, honestly.”
The launch also surpassed broadband records in the UK. Virgin Media O2 said its evening traffic between 8pm and 10pm on Wednesday was 9.4% higher than the previous record, set last week by “pre-loading” for GTA VI.
BT and EE networks also recorded their highest-ever home broadband traffic peak in the lead-up to the release.
Data from the two brands found that Fort Augustus, in Loch Ness, Scotland, recorded the biggest percentage uplift in gaming download traffic anywhere in the UK since the start of the pre-downloads last week.
Sony’s shares were up 2.92% on the Tokyo stock exchange after the global launch, with the analytics firm Omdia estimating that GTA VI could generate $3.2bn (£2.4bn) in sales by the end of the year.

noticias.titulo: ‘Welsh can tell any story’: Cymraeg dub of Star Wars premieres in Cardiff
noticias.resumen: Actors Mark Lewis Jones and Osian Morgan, who voiced characters in dub of 1977 film, among guests on red carpet It has been a memorable few days for Wales. At the weekend, the men’s rugby team secured a historic win against New Zealand – their first victory over the All Blacks in more than 70 years. Then on Thursday evening came another culturally significant moment when Cardiff rolled out the red carpet to celebrate the first Welsh-language dub of the Star Wars franchise. Stars of stage and screen who voiced the words of Luke Skywalker, Darth Vader, C-3PO et al in Welsh (Cymraeg) over the ori
noticias.texto:
It has been a memorable few days for Wales. At the weekend, the men’s rugby team secured a historic win against New Zealand – their first victory over the All Blacks in more than 70 years. Then on Thursday evening came another culturally significant moment when Cardiff rolled out the red carpet to celebrate the first Welsh-language dub of the Star Wars franchise.
Stars of stage and screen who voiced the words of Luke Skywalker, Darth Vader, C-3PO et al in Welsh (Cymraeg) over the original 1977 Star Wars film took the plaudits at the Cineworld Cardiff screening.
Among those on the red carpet was Mark Lewis Jones, who has appeared in shows ranging from The Crown to Game of Thrones and had a role in the 2017 Star Wars film The Last Jedi. In this version of Star Wars, he is a Welsh Darth Vader.
He said he thought Welsh was a good language for Vader. “It has an ancient, poetic sense. It gives him that status, that authority,” said Jones, who hails from the Wrexham area in north-east Wales. “I give all my characters north-east Wales accents,” he said.
Also taking a bow was Osian Morgan – well known in Wales for his appearances in the Welsh-language soap opera Pobol y Cwm – who voices Luke Skywalker.
“There’s so much excitement about this project and the cast is unbelievable,” Morgan said. “I think in Wales we’re on an upward trajectory and this instils a lot of hope. The future is exciting for Wales, particularly in the creative arts. The talent is vast.”
Asked if he felt the pressure of being Luke Skywalker, he said he was thrilled rather than nervous. “He’s had such an important impact on my life,” he said. Morgan was also pleased that his 10-year-old brother’s first experience of Star Wars would be in the medium of Welsh. “The fact that Luke tonight in the Welsh language can have that impact on kids here is fantastic.”
Rhys Ifans, who has appeared in Harry Potter and Spider-Man films, had the tough job of standing in for Alec Guinness as the Jedi master Obi-Wan Kenobi. Sadly, he did not make it to Cardiff for the event.
His brother, Llŷr Ifans, the Welsh voice of the droid C-3PO, was present, however, which was apposite as C-3PO is “fluent in over 6 million forms of communication” – including, clearly, Welsh.
Ifans said: “When I first heard about it, I thought: wow, what are we doing – Star Wars in Welsh? The idea has settled. C-3PO is a genius who speaks over 6 million languages. Now he speaks 6 million and one. He speaks the best language in the world.”
Asked what accent he used for his C-3PO, Ifans said: “There are no accents in space. But it’s more about the character. He lives on his nerves and speaks staccato. I had to bring in those aspects.”
The Welsh-language version of the 1977 film (subsequently retitled Star Wars: Episode IV – A New Hope) has been produced by Lucasfilm and Disney in collaboration with the Welsh-language broadcaster S4C and the Welsh government via its Creative Wales agency.
Its Welsh title is Star Wars: Gobaith Newydd (New Hope). Those not lucky enough to be at the screening in Cardiff will be able to hear the immortal line “May the Force be with you” in Welsh (“A boed i’r Grym fod gyda chi”) when the version is broadcast on S4C platforms on Christmas Day.
Thursday’s screening wasn’t as glitzy as a London or Los Angeles premiere, but it had charm. Côr Bechgyn Glantaf, a schoolboys’ choir from Cardiff, performed as the crowds – including many children – arrived and made their way up the escalators of the multiplex to screens eight and nine. Band Pres Llareggub, which bills itself as a Bronx hip-hop-inspired, New Orleans-tinged brass band with attitude from north Wales, also provided a musical backdrop.
S4C’s chief executive, Geraint Evans, described the screening as a “hugely proud moment”. He said: “Most importantly, it will give Welsh-speaking children the thrill of hearing some of cinema’s most beloved characters speak their language for the very first time, showing that Welsh can tell any story.”
There are a few connections linking Wales and Star Wars, not least that a version of the Millennium Falcon was built in south-west Wales.
Mark Williams, who oversaw an exhibition about the Millennium Falcon, said he felt the Welsh-language version of the film was long overdue. “I’ve been saying for years it should be done, especially with the ties that Wales has with the franchise,” he said.
Also at the screening was the cabinet minister for enterprise, connectivity and energy in the Welsh government, Adam Price, who said it was an excellent opportunity for Welsh actors and production staff to work with a major Hollywood studio.
“Seeing one of the most iconic films of all time in Welsh is a great way to make the language more accessible and introduces it to new audiences beyond our shores,” he said.
The Welsh government is aiming to have a million people speaking Cymraeg by 2050. A spokesperson for the Welsh language commissioner’s office said one of its key aims was to increase the use of the language on a community level.
The spokesperson said: “In order to do this, the language must be seen and heard in all aspects of our daily lives. The use of Welsh in such a high-profile film as Star Wars has the potential to attract new audiences and raise awareness of the language.”

noticias.titulo: Prison authorities consider whether Russell Brand harassed victims with YouTube message
noticias.resumen: Ministry of Justice weighs up comments issued through rapist’s wife as PM asks: ‘Why are we having to hear from him?’ The prison authorities are weighing up whether Russell Brand harassed his victims by issuing comments through his wife insisting he was not guilty of rape and sexual assault. After Andy Burnham called on Google to take down the statement from YouTube, a continuing Ministry of Justice inquiry is focusing on whether Brand has broken rules that are supposed to prevent “serious distress” to the victims of crime. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
The prison authorities are weighing up whether Russell Brand harassed his victims by issuing comments through his wife insisting he was not guilty of rape and sexual assault.
After Andy Burnham called on Google to take down the statement from YouTube, a continuing Ministry of Justice inquiry is focusing on whether Brand has broken rules that are supposed to prevent “serious distress” to the victims of crime.
Other factors that will help to decide whether he has broken a rule include the “notoriety” of the crimes and the length of time between the verdict and the statement.
A video in which Brand’s wife, Laura Gallacher, read out a message from the jailed sex offender protesting he was not guilty has remained on YouTube days after ministers asked for it to be removed.
Brand is serving a 10-and-a-half-year term after he was convicted of one count of rape and three sexual assaults at Southwark crown court on 5 November.
On Thursday night, the UK prime minister said he “wouldn’t leap” to changing the law to force social media companies to take down the content. But he added: “I would call on those social media companies to take these interviews down.
“You know, why are we having to hear from from him? We shouldn’t be, and certainly [the victims] shouldn’t be hearing from him.”
According to official guidance on prisoner access to the media, a prison governor must decide whether to permit it, and must consider that “serious distress to victims of the prisoner and/or outrage to public sensibilities is not likely to result from the broadcast. This is likely to occur if, for example, the prisoner’s crimes or conduct are recent, notorious or horrific.”
The rules state that correspondence likely to be published or broadcast “must not contain material about the prisoner’s own crime or past offences or those of others, except where it consists of serious representations about conviction or sentence”.
It is understood that the inquiry is taking into account the right of prisoners to protest their innocence. However, there is a strict protocol governing the way such statements are issued and whether permission has been sought beforehand.
Recent reports have claimed that Brand, who is jailed in the category C HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire, is likely to be moved to a category A or B prison instead after protesting his innocence.
It is understood that there has been no such proposal, and he is likely to remain in Littlehey, a specialist prison for sex offenders.
The government has no power to compel YouTube’s direct owner, Google, to remove the video, but has been in “dialogue” with the tech firm over it.
“We trust that they will do the right thing,” a Downing Street spokesperson said when asked about the standoff. They said: “The prime minister’s position on this is that Russell Brand’s victims deserve peace, and we’ve heard enough from him.
“We’ve asked YouTube to remove the content. I would also just point out that they acted before when they suspended Brand’s account from making money. Given he has been convicted of rape by a jury of his peers, we trust that they will act again.”
No 10 was repeatedly asked whether Burnham would personally welcome the video being removed, as well as Brand’s YouTube channel being disabled. It told reporters: “Removal ultimately depends on YouTube and the platform’s terms and conditions.”
A spokesperson for Google said: “We’re aware of the new content and our teams are investigating. We suspended Russell Brand’s channel from the YouTube partner programme in September 2023. The channel has not been able to monetise on YouTube since then.”
Kemi Badenoch said if she was in power she would not immediately demand Google remove the video.
The Conservative leader told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “My personal opinion is that Russell Brand has been convicted. He is guilty under the law. His wife is a separate person. She can make the protestations that she likes.
“I think that immediately demanding the private platforms take things down without looking at exactly whether a law has been broken is not where I would start from. If we want to make legislation for that, then we can look at that.”

noticias.titulo: Man arrested after ‘horrific’ knife attack on Bradford councillor
noticias.resumen: Politicians call attack on independent councillor Ibrar Ali canvassing in Bradford Moor ward ‘deeply disturbing’ Politicians have described an attack on a councillor who was canvassing in Bradford as “horrific” and “deeply disturbing”, after a man was arrested on suspicion of attempted murder. A 32-year-old man is in custody suspected of attacking Ibrar Ali at about 11am on Thursday as the independent councillor was door-knocking in his Bradford Moor ward, leaving him with a stab wound in the leg. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Politicians have described an attack on a councillor who was canvassing in Bradford as “horrific” and “deeply disturbing”, after a man was arrested on suspicion of attempted murder.
A 32-year-old man is in custody suspected of attacking Ibrar Ali at about 11am on Thursday as the independent councillor was door-knocking in his Bradford Moor ward, leaving him with a stab wound in the leg.
West Yorkshire police said there was nothing to suggest the incident was politically motivated, although the investigation was at an early stage.
Jim McMahon, the MP for Oldham West, described the attack as “horrific” and said: “Our thoughts are with [Ali], his family, councillors in Bradford and, of course, our members of parliament too.
“Our thoughts are very much with you all at this time.”
Imran Hussain, the MP for Bradford East, said: “This horrific attack is deeply disturbing. My thoughts and prayers are with councillor Ibrar Ali and his family.
“No elected politician should feel under threat or fear for their safety while carrying out their duties and serving their community. I am receiving regular updates from the police as they deal with this extremely serious incident, and I understand a suspect is in police custody.”
Officers were called just after 11am to reports that a 52-year-old man, a serving Bradford councillor, had been found seriously injured on Manse Street.
Police said: “The man is believed to have first been injured on Thornbury Avenue, before being driven to Manse Street where emergency services attended. He was taken to hospital where his condition is described as serious but not life-threatening.”
A 32-year-old man fled to the roof of a property on Thornbury Avenue but was brought down some time later and arrested on suspicion of attempted murder.
He remains in custody.
Sharon Taylor, a local government minister, named Ali in the House of Lords. Lady Taylor said: “I am afraid I have to mention a very tragic incident that’s occurred in Bradford … where an independent councillor who was out canvassing has been stabbed.
“I would want to send the wishes, that I’m sure noble lords would agree, of the whole house to councillor Ibrar Ali for a speedy recovery, and our thoughts are with all of those in Bradford who are affected by this awful incident.”
Police cordons were in place on Manse Street, Leeds Road and Thornbury Avenue while inquiries are carried out.
Adam, who works in the area and did not want to give his surname, said: “I know the councillor on a personal level and it’s shocking. I just know he’s a very kind, warm-hearted man whose goal is to serve, his life is to help out everyone.
“He just wants everyone to succeed. He definitely didn’t deserve what’s happened.
“The world’s not a nice place.”
Chris Herd, the lord mayor of Bradford, said: “It is deeply distressing that this incident has occurred.
“Councillors work tirelessly on behalf of residents across the district and should be able to carry out their duties safely.
“We will continue to work closely with our colleagues at West Yorkshire police as they investigate this matter and seek to bring those responsible to justice, and would like to thank those who provided aid and support at the time.”
Press Association contributed to this report

noticias.titulo: Woman raped by strangers after being drugged by husband calls for consent law changes

noticias.texto:
A woman who was raped by strangers after being drugged by her husband has warned of “serious questions about how the law deals with consent”, as four men who abused her were convicted on Thursday.
Philip Young, 50, advertised his then wife, Joanne Young, on dating and swinging websites, presenting it as a “kink” for both of them, Winchester crown court heard. In fact, he had been sedating her, plunging her into an “inanimate state” in which anything could be done to her by the men who answered the adverts, jurors were told.
The former Conservative councillor pleaded guilty earlier in the year to dozens of charges of abuse against his former wife, who has waived her right to anonymity.
On Thursday, Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32; Richard Wilkins, 62; Norman Macksoni, 48; and Mohammed Hassan, 38, were convicted of various offences against Joanne Young after a three-week trial.
The case has drawn comparisons to that of Gisèle Pelicot, who was drugged by her husband and raped by dozens of strangers in France. It can now be revealed that Wiltshire police received advice from the Pelicot investigators on how to approach their inquiries.
The Crown Prosecution Service said it was the first time a jury had convicted multiple defendants relating to organised drug-facilitated sexual assault in England.
After the verdicts, Wiltshire police said that although rare, the true scale of drug-facilitated sexual offences in the UK could be significantly underreported.
In a statement outside court, Joanne Young – whose bravery was praised by the judge – said the convictions meant “that those who find themselves facing what I have are more likely to come forward, and more likely to have faith in the criminal justice system”.
Saying that she now lives “with a pain that’s hard to put into words”, she added: “Consent has to come from the person themselves. No one should be able to give it on your behalf, and no one should be able to rely on someone else’s word that you agreed.
“At no point did anyone ask me for my consent. I urge the government to look at this as a priority so that women are properly protected in the future.”
Sanderson-Doyle, a Ministry of Defence contractor from Swindon, was convicted of sexual assault and assault by penetration; Wilkins, a taxi driver from Swindon, was found guilty of assault by penetration and rape; Macksoni, a former DJ and waste management worker from Bedfordshire, was convicted of rape; and Hassan, also from Swindon, was found guilty of sexual assault.
A further defendant, Dean Hamilton, 47, from Somerset, had admitted one charge of assault by penetration, two of sexual assault and one of rape.
A spokesperson for Wiltshire police, which investigated Young’s offending, said other victims in similar cases may not know they had been targeted.
He added: “While cases involving organised drug-facilitated sexual assault remain relatively rare compared to other forms of sexual offending, intelligence and other recent cases would suggest this may be a significantly underreported crime type.
“Victims are often unaware they have been drugged, may have fragmented memories of events, or may initially attribute symptoms to alcohol consumption. These factors make detection and reporting particularly challenging.”
Joanne said the abuse had had a devastating impact on her life and the lives of her children but that she hoped the verdict would give other victims of abuse the confidence to come forward.
“The court has today shown that there will be consequences for those who make the choice to abuse,” she said. “I’m determined that their choices will not define me, and I will now use my experience to try to help others. I also owe it to myself to live the best life I can with my children and loved ones as we move forward.”
Mr Justice Saini refused bail applications for the four men convicted on Thursday, telling them they all faced “significant custodial sentences”.
All of the men, including Young and Hamilton, will be sentenced on 21 and 22 December at Winchester crown court.
Young, a father of three, pleaded guilty in January to a total of 56 charges made up of 14 counts of voyeurism, 11 of rape, 11 of administering a substance with intent, seven of assault by penetration, four of sexual assault and one of publishing obscene articles in relation to his wife. He also admitted three charges of making indecent images of children, one of possessing prohibited images of children in July 2024 and four counts of possessing an extreme pornographic image between January 2019 and January 2024.
Over more than a decade, Young – who served as a Swindon borough councillor between 2007 and 2010 – drugged and raped his wife and invited other men on websites and apps such as Craigslist, Grindr and FabSwingers to have sex with her without her knowledge.
Prosecutors told the court the case was about whether it was ever reasonable to have sex with an unknown woman without checking with her first.
Sanderson-Doyle responded to an online advert in 2015 and visited the couple’s home in June 2016. Young filmed him sexually assaulting Joanne as she was drugged, blindfolded and restrained, and heard saying “No”.
Wilkins went to the home in July 2016. Young filmed Wilkins abusing Joanne who again was blindfolded, restrained and seemingly asleep, without obtaining her consent. Police footage of his arrest shows the officers identifying him through distinctive tattoos.
Macksoni visited and raped Joanne in February 2017, while Hassan sexually assaulted her in February 2023. Messages and digital evidence showed Young arranged for Hassan to visit and Hassan had sexual contact with her while she believed he was her husband.
Speaking after the verdicts, James Foster, a specialist prosecutor at the CPS, said: “These men chose to commit unspeakable acts of abuse against Joanne Young without bothering to check if she was consenting.
“By building the case with a suspect-centric approach, we could prove to a jury that Philip Young could not provide consent on the victim’s behalf and each defendant played a part in this horrific sexual abuse.
“During the trial, Macksoni, Wilkins, Sanderson-Doyle and Hassan hid behind the claim that they believed she was freely entering into a sexual relationship with them, despite never seeking reassurances that this was in fact the case.”

noticias.titulo: Senate Republicans rejects war powers bill to halt fighting in Iran
noticias.resumen: Measure fails 48-51 with GOP members again defending war that played a role in costing them midterm elections The Senate on Thursday rejected a war powers resolution aimed at forcing Donald Trump to halt fighting with Iran, with Republicans once again defending a conflict that played a major role in their sweeping midterm election losses. The House of Representatives had approved the resolution in September, and it was the first to be voted on by either chamber since the 3 November vote in which the GOP lost control of both chambers of Congress beginning next year. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
The Senate on Thursday rejected a war powers resolution aimed at forcing Donald Trump to halt fighting with Iran, with Republicans once again defending a conflict that played a major role in their sweeping midterm election losses.
The House of Representatives had approved the resolution in September, and it was the first to be voted on by either chamber since the 3 November vote in which the GOP lost control of both chambers of Congress beginning next year.
The measure failed in a 48-51 vote that broke largely along party lines, with John Fetterman of Pennsylvania the sole Democrat to oppose it, and Susan Collins of Maine, Rand Paul of Kentucky and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska the only Republicans to vote in favor.
Democrats have introduced a steady stream of war powers resolutions since the war began in February with a joint US-Israel attack on Iran. While Trump’s Republican allies have succeeded in voting many of them down, one passed both chambers in June.
However Trump ignored that resolution, prompting Democrats to continue their efforts to make use of the 1973 law to force an end to a conflict that polls indicate is unpopular with the public and has caused prices for gasoline and diesel to increase across the US.
All House Democrats along with seven Republicans – several of whom lost re-election in the midterms – had supported the measure that came up for consideration before the Senate on Thursday. But Republicans largely stood behind the conflict, including Thom Tillis, a North Carolina senator, who is retiring at the end of the year after supporting previous resolutions, and Bill Cassidy, an outgoing senator of Louisiana, whose support was crucial for the June measure’s passage.
Chris Murphy, a Democratic senator, missed the vote, after recently suffering a stroke.

noticias.titulo: John Cornyn blocks Trump judicial nominee after Senate shouting match with Ted Cruz
noticias.resumen: Outgoing senator withheld ‘blue slip’ from T Elliot Gaiser, blocking his appointment to northern Texas district court An outgoing Republican senator blocked one of Donald Trump ’s judicial nominations on Wednesday, throwing a wrench in the party’s plans to approve the US president’s picks before Democrats take control of Congress. John Cornyn of Texas, who is leaving the US Senate after nearly 24 years following his primary loss to a Trump-backed challenger, told the Associated Press he would not support T Elliot Gaiser, a 37-year-old official in the justice department, to serve on a district
noticias.texto:
An outgoing Republican senator blocked one of Donald Trump’s judicial nominations on Wednesday, throwing a wrench in the party’s plans to approve the US president’s picks before Democrats take control of Congress.
John Cornyn of Texas, who is leaving the US Senate after nearly 24 years following his primary loss to a Trump-backed challenger, told the Associated Press he would not support T Elliot Gaiser, a 37-year-old official in the justice department, to serve on a district court in northern Texas.
“He’s not from Texas. He hasn’t been vetted. And this is a lifetime job, and there’s better-qualified people to hold that job,” Cornyn said on Wednesday.
Cornyn’s refusal to support Gaiser came a day after he got into a heated verbal argument with a fellow Texas Republican senator, Ted Cruz, on the Senate floor over Gaiser’s nomination, according to the Washington Sun.
The two men’s yelling match was reportedly so loud that those in the press gallery could hear Cornyn tell Cruz: “I don’t find you credible. I’m mad at you.”
At one point, Cornyn told Cruz he was upset at someone “for ending my career”, though it is unclear whether Cornyn was referring to Trump or Cruz.
In a statement obtained by Reuters, Cruz said: “If the Senate Judiciary Committee does not move Gaiser forward, the people of Texas will pay the price because it will effectively give the judicial seat to the Democrats, who will keep it vacant in perpetuity.”
Cruz said the White House indicated it would be “impossible” to get a new nominee confirmed because the FBI’s background check would take too long.
Republicans are trying to approve as many of Trump’s judicial nominations before Congress recesses for the rest of the year and Democrats take over in January.
But Cornyn withheld his “blue slip”, derailing that plan.
As part of a longstanding tradition, the Senate judiciary committee chair will only support a president’s judicial nominee when the senators of the state in which the nomination is occurring approve. That approval is known as a “blue slip”.
While Cornyn justified his decision by pointing to the fact that Gaiser is not from Texas, there has been tension between Cornyn and the White House after Trump refused to endorse Cornyn for re-election and instead backed Ken Paxton in the Senate race. Ultimately, Paxton lost to Democrat James Talarico.
Cornyn told reporters he recommended Steve Fahey, a federal prosecutor in Texas, for the empty seat on the northern district of Texas court
Gaiser ultimately did not appear before the Senate judiciary committee on Wednesday.
The justice department said in a statement obtained by the AP that it was “deeply disappointing that Senator Cornyn would choose political obstruction over advancing a highly qualified nominee”.
Kevin Roberts, the president of the Heritage Foundation – the conservative thinktank behind Project 2025 – called out Cornyn on social media for refusing to support Gaiser.
“John Cornyn is going out as the Republican Texas Senator who helped get radical leftist James Talarico’s agenda started early. What a legacy,” Roberts wrote on X.
Cornyn responded by calling Roberts “irrelevant” and claiming his “sycophancy has destroyed the credibility of a once great institution”.

noticias.titulo: Judge bans Trump’s restrictions on HIV funds for transgender patients
noticias.resumen: Federal court rules providers can acknowledge gender identity and provide gender-affirming care The Trump administration cannot impose restrictions barring healthcare providers that receive certain federal HIV-treatment ⁠funds from acknowledging the gender identity ⁠of their transgender patients ​or from providing them with gender-affirming care, a federal judge ruled on Thursday. US district judge William Young in Boston sided with a group of national HIV medical associations and ⁠healthcare providers that challenged grant funding conditions imposed by the administration last year after Trump
noticias.texto:
The Trump administration cannot impose restrictions barring healthcare providers that receive certain federal HIV-treatment funds from acknowledging the gender identity of their transgender patients or from providing them with gender-affirming care, a federal judge ruled on Thursday.
US district judge William Young in Boston sided with a group of national HIV medical associations and healthcare providers that challenged grant funding conditions imposed by the administration last year after Trump signed an executive order prohibiting federal funding for what he calls “gender ideology”.
Those conditions were adopted by a division of the US Department of Health and Human Services for funding provided by the Ryan White HIV/Aids Program, which was created in 1990 by Congress to provide medical care for low-income and uninsured people living with HIV.
Young said the conditions were designed to suppress what the administration considered to be “dangerous ideas” in violation of the US constitution’s first amendment by penalizing doctors for acknowledging that transgender people exist and referring to their patients by their preferred pronouns.
Young, who was appointed by the Republican president Ronald Reagan, said the restrictions additionally reflected unconstitutional discrimination on the basis of sex in violation of the constitution’s fifth amendment.
“They are based in animus, loathing, and discrimination,” Young wrote. “They do not stand for justice – in fact, they defy it. They are contrary to the laws of this nation and cannot continue to stand.”
The judge issued the 165-page ruling following a non-jury trial in September.
HHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Lawyers for the plaintiffs, who include the American Academy of HIV Medicine, also did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Beginning in March, the Health Resources and Services Administration, a division of HHS that administers the Ryan White program, added funding conditions designed to implement the Republican president’s executive order directing the US government to recognize only two sexes, male and female.
The new grant conditions required providers to ensure funding would support activities using “sex-based definitions grounded in biological reality” and not “social or medical experimentation”, the lawsuit said.
The plaintiffs contend the policy was unconstitutional and conflicted with the Ryan White program’s statutory mandate to provide comprehensive medical services to HIV patients, which historically has included hormone therapy for transgender people.
The Trump administration also moved to restrict gender-affirming care for transgender inmates in federal prisons, and backed state laws banning transgender athletes from participating on female sports teams at public schools, including universities.

noticias.titulo: Fierce storm lashes southern California after record rain in San Francisco

Los Angeles authorities had urged residents in the Palisades, Hurst and Sunset burn scar areas to be prepared to leave before the storm’s arrival on Thursday, and warned of a risk of debris flows and flooding. Flash flood warnings were issued from Eastern Malibu to Beverly Hills to Hollywood, with heightened risk until noon on Thursd
noticias.texto:
An atmospheric river pounded southern California with heavy rain and winds, one day after the fierce storm set records for rainfall in the north of the state.
Los Angeles authorities had urged residents in the Palisades, Hurst and Sunset burn scar areas to be prepared to leave before the storm’s arrival on Thursday, and warned of a risk of debris flows and flooding. Flash flood warnings were issued from Eastern Malibu to Beverly Hills to Hollywood, with heightened risk until noon on Thursday, while flood warnings were issued across the region through Thursday afternoon.
Heavy rainfall started hitting the region on Wednesday night and through Thursday morning. Multiple drivers had to be rescued from submerged vehicles in flooded city streets near the Burbank airport, KTLA5 News reported.
Karen Bass, Los Angeles’s mayor, said in a press release that city crews had been deployed to address localized flooding on roadways and other storm-related impacts.
The downfall slowed by midmorning in central Los Angeles, and the National Weather Service predicted lighter rain and less intense flooding risk in the afternoon.
The atmospheric river first hit the San Francisco region on Wednesday, bringing heavy rain and fierce winds.
San Francisco broke a rain record previously set in 1917. The city’s fire department said it responded to hundreds of calls, many of which related to flooding, along with downed trees and electrical wires. Flights at San Francisco airport were delayed hours because of wind. The self-driving car service Waymo temporarily halted operations in San Francisco on Wednesday, amid reports and video of Waymo cars stuck in floodwaters and blocking traffic.
Areas along the city’s Embarcadero were flooded as waves crashed over barricades recently installed to prevent flooding near the Ferry Building, a waterfront landmark. Officials canceled several ferries leading from the city due to the storm.
Tens of thousands of households lost power across the region.
Several highways were blocked by flooding or debris in nearby Napa, Marin, San Mateo and Santa Clara counties.
As the storm moved south, a segment of Highway 1 near Big Sur was forced to close.
Several roads in San Luis Obispo and Santa Barbara counties were inundated overnight.
In the mountains, heavy snows forced the closure of highways in the Tahoe area. Snow accumulations of up to 4ft (1.2 meters) were forecast through Friday in the highest portions of the Sierra Nevada.
Atmospheric rivers, huge currents of water vapor that can carry as much or even more water than an actual river, have been growing stronger and deadlier in recent years. In the relatively dry western US, atmospheric river storms provide both essential precipitation and flood risk.
The Golden state is bracing for more weather challenges in the week ahead, when fresh rain is set to coincide with high tides.

noticias.titulo: Uganda minister at COP31: 'We need a just transition'
noticias.resumen: Funding from wealthy countries to help deal with the impacts of climate change hasn't materialized, says Uganda's environment minister. The East African country is hoping oil and carbon credits will help boost finances.
noticias.texto:
Uganda minister at COP31: 'We need a just transition'
November 19, 2026
Ugandan Environment Minister Beatrice Atim Anywar has come to the UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, seeking to secure more funding for her country as it grapples with climate change.
"This is a thing we are living with," she told DW on the sidelines of the COP31 summit, where she's leading the Ugandan delegation. "People are displaced, people are dying of harm, hunger. It has implications on food security and livelihoods."
In recent years, the East African nation has been hit by a series of climate-related disasters, from deadly landslides and floods washing away villages, to droughts damaging harvests and hydroelectricity production.
"When we come to COP and we talk of what the reality is on the ground, we Ugandans have suffered it," Anywar said, referring to the effects of climate change.
"It has an implication for the health of our people, on national budgets," she added.
Climate financing for developing countries to deal with the impacts of a warming planet has become a major sticking point at this year's climate talks. The gathering of some 200 states is seeking to close gaps on how to scale up financing from developed states and whether support should be provided through grants or loans.
Africa contributes less than 4% of the global greenhouse emissions that drive rising temperatures globally, but the continent is among the most vulnerable to climate impacts.
Ramping up electricity production
As it deals with the affects of climate change, including extreme weather, Uganda is also rapidly expanding investment in electricity production from renewables such as hydropower and solar.
In the country of some 53 million people, more than 90% of Ugandan households still rely on wood and charcoal as the most affordable fuel for things like cooking. Biomass accounts for 90% of the country's final energy consumption.
While using wood and charcoal leads to deforestation, Ugandans have little choice. Only around 2% of the country's energy comes from electricity — which is largely derived from hydropower — and less than half of the population has access to electricity.
"Now we are deliberately going into scaling up the production of electricity — hydropower electricity — and making it cheaper for cooking," Anywar said. "We have other alternative energy sources... to mitigate this charcoal use. But the use needs to be phased out in a systematic manner by giving them alternatives."
Drilling for oil
At the same time, the country is seeking to boost economic development by becoming an oil producer. Due to open in 2027, a controversial 1,443-kilometer (897-mile) pipeline is nearly complete. It connects two oil sites in eastern Uganda with a port on the Tanzanian coast.
Environmentalists have criticized the East African Crude Oil Pipeline project, which can transport up to 246,000 barrels per day. Environmentalists say it runs counter to the goal of limiting global temperature rise and could damage fragile ecosystems.
The Climate Accountability Institute said it would release 379 million tons of climate-heating pollution over its 20-year lifetime.
Oil wells for the project, operated by French energy giant TotalEnergies, are also located in Uganda's largest and oldest national park, Murchison Falls.
"That has been also a sticky issue. And actually, that is one of the challenges we are facing at COPs," Anywar said. She stressed that measures have been taken to limit emissions, and that the project was progressing in a "very deliberate way."
The minister also urged developed countries to cut less wealthy nations some slack for using the resources they have to drive much-needed development, saying oil revenues could help fund the transition to cleaner energy.
"You cannot tell us to cut off the umbilical cord that feeds us, as much as it has to be cut off," Anywar said, criticizing the lack of financing from developed countries to deal with climate change. "We are here begging for funds that are not forthcoming."
Anywar added that developing countries "need a just transition," referring to an equitable shift away from fossil fuels that focuses on protecting workers and communities.
Carbon trading 'breakthrough?'
Another way Uganda is looking to finance climate change adaptation is through carbon credits, Anywar said, describing them as a potential "breakthrough."
Carbon credits are tradeable permits representing one ton of carbon dioxide that has been reduced or removed from the atmosphere through initiatives such as forest protection, renewable energy projects or tree planting schemes. Companies or governments can buy them to offset emissions they have not cut themselves.
"Our country is rich with biodiversity. And that is what we are looking forward to — attracting investors into our natural setup so that we earn some finances," Anywar said.
Carbon credits have been promoted as an important source of income for developing countries. But they have also faced criticism, for a lack of transparency and allowing polluting activities to continue.
"We need to have a bankable approach to all interventions. Otherwise… it's not going to work for us," Anywar said, adding that her country also wants to attract investment and build partnerships in smart agriculture and the energy transition.
"If we rely on begging for funds which are not forthcoming, we shall go back empty handed."
This interview also appeared as a video.

noticias.titulo: Germany news: Pistorius visits Auschwitz memorial in Poland trip
noticias.resumen: Germany's defense minister's first stop in Poland was the memorial site of the former Nazi extermination camp Auschwitz-Birkenau. Follow DW for more.
noticias.texto:
Germany news: Pistorius visits Auschwitz memorial in Poland trip
Published November 19, 2026last updated November 19, 2026
What you need to know
- Defense Minister Boris Pistorius talks security in Poland
- Germany warns of cyber security risks in gadgets
- UniCredit and Germany reach Commerzbank takeover agreement
Here is a roundup of the biggest headlines from Germany on Thursday, November 19:
IG Metall blasts VW 'catalog of horrors' ahead of collective bargaining talks
IG Metall, Germany's largest union, railed against automaker Volkswagen's latest demands on its workforce days before both sides are set to begin collective bargaining talks next Tuesday.
The union described VW's vision for the future of work at the Wolfsburg-based giant as a "catalog of horrors."
VW, the world's second-largest car company by both sales and production, has seen profits nosedive — it announced quarterly losses of €5.8 billion ($6.5 billion) in October — for a number of reasons, ranging from increased competition to tariffs and soft sales. Now the company plans to slash 120,000 jobs at 10 brands by 2030.
Arguing that its financial outlook has "deteriorated," VW management says it has no choice but to make deeper cuts faster than expected.
VW wants to scrap the current contract's 35-hour week and is demanding employees work overtime without pay if needed and went so far as to announce that pay would be "adjusted" if workers were forced to work fewer than 35 hours. Moreover, it is calling for a pay freeze for 2027-2028, as well as cuts to benefits for long-term employees.
IG Metall says workers haven't seen a raise since May 2024 and is calling for a 5% hike now, citing ever-rising living costs.
Regional IG representative Thorsten Gröger said, "VW management is stabbing its employees the back." He added that negotiations will be "tenacious, bitter and exhausting" and that they "will leave deep scars at the company."
Workers are primed for walkouts, with the union warning that the battle may be far larger than anything VW has ever seen.
VW works council chairwoman Daniela Cavallo, who represents employees within the company, said, "Management's promises are obviously worthless." Cavallo said workers felt "betrayed" after they agreed to major job cuts for the health of the company two years ago.
The current contract applies to some 130,000 employees at German production sites in Braunschweig, Chemnitz, Dresden, Emden, Hanover, Kassel, Salzgitter, Wolfsburg and Zwickau.
German defense minister call Auschwitz a 'warning' to all of us
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius on Thursday called on Europeans to be vigilant against far-right extremism and warned of divisions and labels in society.
Speaking during a visit to Auschwitz-Birkenau, a former concentration camp, Pistorius said the site bore witness to the worst of Nazi Germany's crimes, calling it an absolute low point.
"It all started with defining what made a life unworthy; by dividing according to race, origin, faith, sexual orientation," Pistorius warned, saying that such marginalization was experiencing a "renaissance" and "gaining ground with far-right extremist parties across Europe."
The defense minister said Auschwitz provides all people, but particularly Germans, with a "symbol warning that we all bear responsibility for what happens and what must not be allowed to happen."
During his tour of the camp, Pistorius laid a wreath at its death wall, where Nazi soldiers shot roughly 5,000 prisoners dead, and lit a candle at the victims' memorial.
Before he departed the site, Pistorius expressed his wish that more German students and travel groups would visit the camp "than appears to be the case at present."
AfD politician accuses Le Pen of abandoning party 'core'
The deputy chairman of Germany's right-wing populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) has accused French presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen of deserting her core values in her bid to achieve wider popularity and improve her chance of victory in French presidential elections.
For years, Le Pen claimed to be embarking on a policy of what's often called "de-demonization," trying to shed the extreme-right image of her father and predecessor, Jean-Marie Le Pen, and soften the stance of the party now called the National Rally or RN.
"Mrs. Le Pen, whom we all once admired greatly, now seems to have one fundamental principle: I say whatever the polls demand of me," Sven Tristschler told the right-leaning website The Pioneer.
France is headed into the last months of a presidential election campaign, with incumbent Emmanuel Macron's second and final term coming to an end and no clear candidate emerging as a main challenger to Le Pen as yet.
"At the end of the day, her victory would likely be even more catastrophic for the right than her defeat," Tritscher asserted. "The citizens would think they were voting to the right, only to get another Macron in the end."
He said that in hindsight, he was glad the AfD and RN parties had fallen out in European politics in recent years, and said AfD supporters should not anticipate a similar move toward moderation.
"A hollowing-out will not take place with us," he said, using the German scientific term for enucleation, the removal of the internal nucleus or core of a cell.
The AfD has made similar complaints about Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, accusing her party of a process of "Melonization" involving a softening of its core policy stances in a bid to retain power.
A similar power struggle is thought to be brewing within the AfD itself as it remains far adrift of majority support despite regularly polling as the largest single party in Germany at present.
Bundesbank expects inflation to rise in 2027
Germany's central bank, the Bundesbank, said in its monthly report that inflation in Germany will rise "sharply" at the beginning of 2027.
Inflation could remain stable through the end of the year, given that a fuel tax cut is still keeping a lid on prices.
Inflation had fallen to 2.9% from 3.3% in September after the German government introduced the fuel discount.
But the central bank said the expiration of that fuel tax cut, along with other government measures, would drive inflation higher.
The report also highlighted that natural gas prices are expected to rise.
"On top of this, higher energy and input costs are expected to gradually feed through into the prices of other goods and certain services," the Bundesbank said.
Deutche Telekom to invest in French AI company
