German telecommunications firm, Deutsche Telekom, announced that it will invest €100 million ($109.75 million) in French start-up Mistral AI, Europe's largest artificial intelligence company.
The investment will pour into Mistral from Telekom's subsidiary T.Capital Tech Fund.
Telekom said the move is a first step toward a strategic partnership, where the two firms plan to jointly support companies and the public sector in Germany in introducing tailored AI.
"Europe’s competitiveness depends on our ability to develop and use powerful AI," Telekom board member Ferri Abolhassan said in a statement announcing the deal. "Businesses must be able to trust this technology while retaining control over their data."
The move is the latest investment by Telekom in the AI space. In February, Telekom built an AI factory in Munich, which has since been expanded due to high demand.
Ukraine's allies meet in Berlin
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrived in Berlin for a summit of the "Coalition of the Willing." The group, which represents Kyiv's allies, is expected to push for a deeper European role in any efforts to end the war.
The process has so far been dominated by the US, Russia and Ukraine.
Zelenskyy wrote on X that "we are doing everything we can to ensure that Europe's presence in the negotiation process is fully represented."
US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff flew to Germany to attend the summit at the Chancellery.
German teen suspected of planning mosque attack with 3D printer weapons
An 18-year-old in western Germany has been held in pre-trial detention in Germany since August over the alleged plot to carry out a terrorist attack on a mosque, prosecutors have said.
The teen, who is from the town of Eslohe in North Rhine-Westphalia, allegedly held far-right extremist views and was planning the attack for late 2026 or early 2027, senior public prosecutor Alexandra Wiese said.
"He also directed his racist ideology against people of the Muslim faith," Wiese told public broadcaster WDR.
A search of the suspect's home led investigators to find numerous weapons, weapon parts and ammunition, including items manufactured using a 3D printer.
Wiese did not provide details of potential targets in order to protect possible victims.
No charges have yet been filed against the teen and Wiese stressed that the presumption of innocence applies as the investigation continues.
UniCredit and Germany reach agreement on Commerzbank takeover
Italian commercial bank UniCredit and the German government reached agreement on the big sticking points of its takeover of Commerzbank.
The EU greenlit UniCredit's takeover of Germany's Commerzbank earlier this week.
The merging of UniCredit and Commerzbank would create a bank with more than €1.3 trillion ($1.4 trillion) in assets
across two of the eurozone's largest economies.
It would be one of the most significant cross-border European banking deals in years.
In a statement to Reuters news agency, Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil said Germany "supports a swift process and an orderly transition of control."
"We have reached common ground and UniCredit has made clear commitments to Germany as a business location, to the rights of
Commerzbank employees and to a continued constructive dialogue with the works council," Klingbeil said, referring to a body of elected employee representatives.
Among the concessions, Germany is said to have given up its insistence on naming two supervisory board members to Commerzbank.
Meanwhile, UniCredit agreed to the key German demand to keep UniCredit's enlarged German business headquartered and listed in Frankfurt.
UniCredit also reportedly pledged to put German nationals on UniCredit's board of directors.
Defense Minister Boris Pistorius heads to Poland
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius will travel to Poland for a two-day visit.
Pistorius is scheduled to meet his Polish counterpart, Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, in the capital, Warsaw, for talks on defense policy.
Poland is a member of both the EU and NATO and is one of the most important political and military allies of Ukraine.
The trip to Germany's neighbor to the east will begin with a stop at the memorial site of the former Nazi extermination camp Auschwitz-Birkenau, which was built during the German occupation of Poland during World War II.
Auschwitz-Birkenau is one of the biggest symbols of the Holocaust and Germany's Nazi regime, with some 1.1 million people having died in the camp between 1940 and 1945, most of them Jews.
The camp's victims were shot, murdered in gas chambers or died of starvation and disease.
Correction: An earlier version of this update misidentified the German defense minister. We apologize for the error.
Germany warns of cyber security risks in gadgets
The German Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) said in a report that cheap gadgets such as streaming boxes are increasingly being hijacked by cybercriminals.
According to the report, the number of hacked systems has nearly doubled within a year, with BSI reporting some 75,400 infected systems in Germany to internet providers every day, an 89% increase. Some of the gadgets were found to be already infected at the factory, the report says.
The vast majority of cases involved Android devices, particularly consumer electronics connected to the so-called "Internet of Things."
BSI said criminals rent the hijacked devices as proxy botnets on the dark web to hide their own attacks, which would allow for consumers themselves to unknowingly come under investigators' scrutiny.
BSI President Claudia Plattner has also warned of AI-driven attacks.
"The disruption coming in particular from high-performance, agentic AI has set new benchmarks," she said.
Welcome to our coverage
Guten Tag from the DW newsroom in Bonn!
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius will head to Poland today to talk security with one the most important political and military allies of Ukraine.
His trip will begin with a stop at the memorial site of the former Nazi extermination camp Auschwitz-Birkenau, which was built during the German occupation of Poland during World War II.
Meanwhile, Germany's Federal Office for Information Security has warned that cheap gadgets such as streaming boxes are increasingly being hijacked by cybercriminals
Follow this blog for more on that and other stories from Germany!

noticias.titulo: Iraq's risky standoff: The state vs. Iran-allied militias
noticias.resumen: This week, Iraqi security forces surrounded an area run by the Kataib Hezbollah militia. Onlookers describe it as the most dangerous confrontation between the Iraqi state and Iran-allied militias in decades.
noticias.texto:
Iraq's risky standoff: Government vs. Iran-allied militias
November 19, 2026
For years, there have all kinds of rumors about Jurf al-Sakhar, an area around 50 kilometers (31 miles) south of the Iraqi capital Baghdad. It is controlled by an Iraqi militia called Kataib Hezbollah, that's closely allied with Iran, and no Iraqi government troops or news media outlets have been allowed inside for around 12 years.
Rumors about what's happening in the area include allegations about secret prisons, mass graves, drone and weapons manufacturing and storage, as well as criminal activity such as oil smuggling. Jurf al-Sakhar is also allegedly a base for foreign, Hezbollah-supporting nationals from Iran, Yemen, Bahrain and Lebanon.
Recently two people — an Israeli researcherand a US journalist — who were kidnapped by an Iraqi militia are thought to have been held captive in this area.
Jurf al-Sakhar previously had an estimated 89,000 residents but after the extremist group known as the "Islamic State," or IS, rose to power in Iraq in 2014, much of the population was displaced in fighting. The area was eventually taken over by Kataib Hezbollah, a militia that had fought IS alongside other armed groups.
As a collective, the armed groups are referred to as the Popular Mobilization Forces, or PMF. Not all of them have pledged allegiance to Iran but Kataib Hezbollah, a Shiite Muslim majority group, has.
In the past 12 years, tens of thousands of the displaced people from here, mostly Sunni Muslims, have not been allowed to return and the area has been described as militarized.
Its name was even changed by Kataib Hezbollah fighters, from Jurf al-Sakhar ("rocky bank") to Jurf al-Nasr ("bank of victory").
'Not even over our dead bodies'
But recent events may shake Kataib Hezbollah's hold on this area.
An early November report for the Iraqi government says that since 2021, the group has smuggled hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of state-owned oil, siphoned from pipelines around Jurf al-Sakhar.
Kataib Hezbollah denies this.
Iraq's new government, headed by Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, made several arrests based on the report and demanded that Kataib Hezbollah leave Jurf al-Sakhar by Friday, Nov. 20.
Kataib Hezbollah rejected al-Zaidi's ultimatum, with a spokesperson saying the group would not withdraw "not even over our dead bodies."
Al-Zaidi then ordered state security forces to surround the area, while Hezbollah reportedly brought in reinforcements.
Observers have described the standoff as one of the most consequential and riskiest confrontations between an Iraqi government and Iranian-backed militiasin Iraq in more than two decades.
"It is a political signal that things will change, that he [al-Zaidi] wants to disarm militias, integrate them into state and claim back the state's authority," Ulf Laessing, head of the Syria and Iraq project for Germany's Konrad Adenauer Foundation, or KAS, told DW. "But it's a minefield and he needs to navigate carefully."
The standoff is also the result of long-running political tensions in Iraq, where the state is torn between its US allies on the one hand and Iranian allies on the other. Both hold sway in Iraq and are considered important relationships.
During Donald Trump's presidency of the US, and thanks to the US and Israel's war with Iran, there's been more pressure on Iraq to disarm Iran's allies inside the country. Al-Zaidi has set a deadline of next June to bring all weapons under the state's control.
Tensions, fears grow
The situation in Jurf al-Sakhar became even more tense this week. Al-Zaidi announced a new security plan for the area that involves other members of the PMF, state security forces and the police. Kataib Hezbollah rejected the plan.
"Al-Zaidi appears serious about ending Kataib Hezbollah's autonomous control of Jurf al-Sakhar," Hayder al-Shakeri, a research fellow at the British think tank Chatham House told DW. "Deploying federal forces and now establishing a new security command there shows this has moved beyond rhetoric."
But how dangerous is Kataib Hezbollah really? After all, al-Zaidi was actually nominated for the prime minister's job by a political bloc known as the Coalition Framework, or CF — these are the politicians who represent the PMF in parliament. Kataib Hezbollah's political party, Harakat Huqooq, is part of the CF.
And other researchers have been critical on social media, noting that the PMF troops that will be given partial control over Jurf al-Sakhar (should Kataib Hezbollah withdraw) are associated with that group anyway.
But Iraqi news media have also reported that there are divisions inside the CF, and apparently even within Kataib Hezbollah, about how to deal with the current standoff. Reportedly, some senior officials think that parts of Jurf al-Sakhar could be handed to federal forces in a gradual withdrawal, the London-based outlet Amwaj Media reported earlier this week, while some senior members of Kataib Hezbollah would seemingly prefer to hand the territory over to certain PMF brigades rather than to state security forces.
What will happen next?
Late Thursday afternoon, the news agency Reuters reported that, according to three anonymous officials, all parties had come to an agreement that would allow government forces to enter Jurf al-Sakhar on Friday.
A compromise is good because it avoids violence, KAS' Laessing said. "It might not be what al-Zaidi initially hoped for but it's still a political signal."
If it did come to actual fighting, the Iraqi military has more resources than Kataib Hezbollah, al-Shakeri explained. "[It] could probably take Jurf al-Sakhar if the political leadership and security institutions remained united," he said. "But there would be no easy victory. Kataib Hezbollah does not need to defeat the Iraqi army conventionally. It can impose costs through asymmetric attacks, political pressure and its networks inside the state."
How the reported compromise plays out in the coming days, will also impact other Iraqi militias and they will be watching closely. Because "the core issue is whether a faction can continue controlling territory and economic activity beyond effective government oversight," al-Shakeri explained.
"The most likely compromise may be to remove Kataib Hezbollah's monopoly rather than remove the PMF from Jurf al-Sakhar altogether," he continued. "That would still matter if it opened the area to regular state forces, if it protects the oil infrastructure and places security under a clearer government command structure."
It could also lead to displaced residents being allowed back to their homes.
"But if one PMF faction simply replaces another while retaining its own networks and autonomy, then Zaidi has redistributed armed influence rather than fundamentally resolved the problem," al-Shakeri concluded.

noticias.titulo: European leaders present united front in push for peace in Ukraine
noticias.resumen: Talks in Berlin end with reaffirmed support for Kyiv and a concerted push for European representation at future peace talks to end Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
noticias.texto:
European leaders present united front in push for peace in Ukraine
Published November 19, 2026last updated November 19, 2026
What you need to know
These updates have been closed.
Below, you can review the top news from the Coalition of the Willing meeting in Berlin on Thursday, 19th November, below:
- Ukraine's main European allies met in Berlin for 'Coalition of the Willing' talks
- Leaders of Germany, France, the UK, Poland and Italy gathered following talks involving President Donald Trump, Russia's Vladimir Putin and China's Xi Jinping in China
- US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were also at the meeting to brief allies about discussions in China
- Ukraine's European allies are pushing to be included in US-backed negotiations with Russia
Leaders of Germany, France, UK, Ukraine issue joint statement
Ukraine and three of its key European allies have reiterated their commitment "towards a comprehensive, just and lasting peace for Ukraine," which they described as being "vital for the security of Europe."
In a joint statement issued after Coalition of the Willing talks in Berlin, the leaders of Germany, France, the UK and Ukraine condemned Russia's "systematic escalation of its deliberate and indiscriminate missile and drone attacks against Ukraine's civilians and civilian infrastructure."
Ukraine's right to defend itself was highlighted, as were Russia's battlefield losses.
The four leaders condemned "Russian hybrid attacks across Europe" and said they "would increase their resolve to strengthen the defence of Ukraine, Europe and NATO."
Leaders pledged "long-term and comprehensive support" for Kyiv and said that Ukraineäs air defense capability was a priority.
Russia's funding of its war effort would be targeted through sanctions and "pressure on Russian oil and gas revenues," while efforts to impede Russia's shadow fleet would continue.
On Ukraine's security, the leaders said the country needed "robust and legally binding security guarantees in place, once a ceasefire enters into force."
The statement mentioned "a European-led Multinational Force Ukraine composed of contributions from willing nations and supported by the US," something that has proven to be a sticking point for Russia.
The leaders said they supported "direct dialogue" between Kyiv and Moscow with US and European participation.
Ukraine's right to choose its own security arrangements needed to be "fully respected," the joint statement said.
"As a first step towards a cessation of hostilities, the leaders called on Russia to agree to an energy ceasefire for the duration of the winter," the statement read.
Message of European unity 'relayed to President Trump' — Jared Kushner
US special envoy Jared Kushner said unity in Europe was clear in the talks and that support for Ukraine remained strong.
"What we came away from today with is really seeing that Europe is very united and very, very strong in their support of Ukraine," Kushner said. "We relayed this to President Trump."
Kushner said this would also be relayed to the Russian delegation and that there was "a real desire for peace."
Kushner said that Trump had joined the Berlin meeting by phone and provided an update on the talks in Shenzhen with President Putin and President Xi.
"He sent a very strong message to both of them on the desire for peace and would like to engage with both of them very aggressively to get there," Kushner said.
Kushner told reporters the talks with European leaders and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had "made a lot of progress on what those security guarantees can look like," as well as a post-war prosperity plan.
He also said Russia was "comfortable" with NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine to end the war.
Macron says question of Ukraine's NATO accession should be reopened
French President Emmanuel Macron said that amid Russia's continued attacks on infrastructure and "maximalist demands," the first priority was for Ukraine to be able to defend itself.
Macron said allies needed to ensure that Ukraine had everything it needed to resist and defend itself from Russian attacks.
"Faced with the maximalist nature of the Russian position, I believe we need to reopen the question of Ukraine's accession to NATO," Macron said in Berlin.
"Everyone who has the capacity to provide the means to defend and protect Ukrainian citizens must do so now," the French leader insisted, adding the priority was to deploy anti-missile systems and interceptors.
Macron said security guarantees were a "key element for our long-term negotiations" and the security plan it had already submitted should remain.
Zelenskyy says next round of talks must include Europe
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Europe should be part of talks going forward.
"America fully understands why strong and coordinated European participation at the negotiations is necessary," Zelenskyy said.
Zelenskyy said his country needed international support ahead of another winter and added that more work was needed to "push Russia to be more constructive in any negotiations."
He also said much work was done to make the Berlin meeting "as concrete as possible."
Zelenskyy thanked all partners and expressed gratitude to Germany, France, the UK, the US along with those who had come out in support of Ukraine.
Zelenskyy highlighted the importance of air defense and said that Russia's aerial bombardments were steadily intensifying.
Zelenskyy said there was no sign this would change as "the Russians have rejected every single proposal for de-escalation."
Zelenskyy said that it was "crucial" that the US "exerts influence on Russia."
Merz pushes for European representation in peace talks
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has pushed for Europe to play a role in helping secure peace in the war in Ukraine.
"Today we prepared for ourselves for possible peace talks," Merz said.
"These talks should comprise Ukraine, Russia, the United States and Europe," Merz said, adding that this format offered the best chance of securing peace.
The German leader said Germany, France, the UK, Poland and Italy would speak on behalf of Europe.
He went on to call the trilateral talks between the president of the United States, Russia and China today at an APEC summit a "photo op" and said such a "Yalta format cannot bring peace" to Ukraine.
Merz pledged "powerful support" for Ukraine in 2027 and mentioned the €45 billion earmarked for next year by the European Commission.
Merz said the level of support was being provided in order for Ukraine to be able to protect itself and that allies wanted the war to end.
Outcome of Ukraine war will 'shape security in Europe' — Merz
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the future of European security would be molded by what was happening in Ukraine.
"The outcome of this war will shape security in Europe for a long time to come," Merz said in a post on social media platform X.
"Together with our partners, we continue our support for peace in Ukraine. That's why we came together today for the Coalition of the Willing," Merz said.
He accompanied his comments with pictures from roundtable talks of the "Coalition of the Willing" in Berlin.
Zelenskyy says he discussed 'key issues' with German, French and British leaders
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he went over "key issues and needs" with German, French and British leaders.
Zelenskyy shared a video on X of his meeting with France's Emmanuel Macron, Britain's Andy Burnham and Germany's Friedrich Merz.
He said they discussed "countering Russian shahed drones and missiles, protecting the energy sector and infrastructure, as well as the diplomatic efforts."
"It is important that today's Coalition of the Willing meeting and bilateral meetings with leaders deliver results," he added.
'Coalition of the Willing' meeting in Berlin
Ukraine's European allies are gathering in Berlin in a show of support just hours after three-way talks took place involving the presidents of the US, Russia and China at the APEC summit.
European leaders are pushing to be included in US-backed talks to end the fighting in Ukraine with US special envoy Steve Witkoff and the US president's son-in-law Jared Kushner in Berlin for Thursday's meeting.
"Mr. Putin is not our friend and will never be," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said in a comment aimed at US President Donald Trump, who referred to Putin as "my friend" at a meeting on Wednesday.
"I find it very incomprehensible that a US president wants to sit down with President Putin," Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen told reporters.
"I think Putin will be even more emboldened after today's meeting. He looks happy," she added. "Unfortunately, that is not a good sign for world peace. That is not a good sign for Ukraine ... And therefore I think that what will come out of this is that he will hit us Europeans even harder, unfortunately."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen promised the EU was united in its support for Ukraine.
"Only through strength can we achieve a just and durable peace," she wrote on X. "We will maintain our support for Ukraine. And maintain full pressure on Russia. Europe stands strong and united."
WATCH: Can Germany make Europe pay more for Ukraine?
Germany's push for more European aid for Ukraine is triggering a backlash.
Michaela Küfner discusses charges of "blackmail" against Chancellor Merz together with DW colleagues Nina Haase, Max Hofmann and Teri Schultz.
Putin not considering Black Sea truce after Kerch bridge strikes
Russian President Vladimir Putin said that Moscow would not hold off on strikes in the Black Sea region or on energy infrastructure following strikes by Ukraine on the Kerch bridge.
The crucial road and railway crossing linking the Crimean peninsula with mainland Russia was put out of action by a series of Ukrainian strikes.
"But after the strikes on the Crimean Bridge, there will be no agreements. We will respond to these strikes. And I want everyone to know this: I believe our response will be far more painful than what the Kyiv regime did to the bridge," he said.
Putin said the bridge was used exclusively for civilian purposes and not to transport military equipment, as Kyiv has alleged.
"We will, of course, restore the bridge. The road section suffered serious damage," Putin said.
Putin calls any European-Ukraine military ties 'a problem' for Russia
Russian President Vladimir Putin said it would be unacceptable for there to be military cooperation between Ukraine and the EU, including any potential deployment of European troops to the country.
"Military cooperation in any form is, of course, a problem," Putin said at a press conference in China.
Putin also said European officials have been invited to Moscow to discuss the potential structure of talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine.
"The American side is urging us to agree to the involvement of the Europeans ... Through diplomatic channels, we suggested to the Europeans to come to Moscow. And after that we will decide in what format the talks can continue," Putin told reporters.
"We understand that discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without the Europeans," Putin added.
For months, European politicians have emphasized that they should be present at any talks on the future of Ukraine.
Leaders start to arrive
Leaders such as Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelenskyy, France's Emmanuel Macron, the UK's Andy Burnham, as well as US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff arrived Thursday at the chancellery in Berlin for the talks.
They were received by Chancellor Friedrich Merz ahead of discussions on providing support to Ukraine against Russia's war.
The “Coalition of the Willing” was established in early 2025 to back Ukraine. It has since grown to include nearly 40 countries, from Japan and Canada to Poland.
Zelenskyy arrives in Berlin for summit
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrived in Berlin on Thursday for the so-called "Coalition of the Willing" meeting.
"Ukraine's priorities are strengthening our air defense, energy and financial support, the diplomatic track, and the next steps toward ending the war and guaranteeing security," he said in an online post.
He said different forms of meeting will take place, with a format involving the US side and European national security advisors.
The coalition is a grouping of countries that provide support to Ukraine against Russian aggression.
Leaders of Germany, France, Britain, Poland and Italy, as well as NATO head Mark Rutte and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will attend the meeting today.
Ukraine claims responsibility for third attack on Kerch bridge
The Ukrainian military on Thursday claimed responsibility for a strike on the Kerch Bridge.
The bridge was attacked on Wednesday for a third time this week, halting rail traffic briefly and damaging some sections.
In an online post, the Ukrainian military said that the strike had been carried out by its forces using Neptune coastal missiles.
It stated that the strikes on Russian bridges hamper Moscow's ability to transport military supplies to the front line.
The bridge, which supports a four-lane roadway and a railroad, is the only bridge linking mainland Russia with occupied Crimea.
Prince Harry says he would return to military service to fight Russia if needed
The United Kingdom's Prince Harry said on Thursday he would rejoin the military to fight against Russia if needed.
"If asked to sign up again, if the need is there, then I will 100% be there to serve my country alongside my fellow veterans and service personnel," he said in an interview from Ukraine with The Telegraph.
"I think there's a lot that the whole world can learn from Ukraine," the prince said during an unannounced visit to the western city of Lviv over the weekend.
Prince Harry, a former British Army officer and the younger son of King Charles III, traveled to Ukraine for his fourth visit since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022, where he met with wounded veterans and medical staff.
"Just because there's not drones, bullets, and rockets flying at us, that doesn't mean that we're not at war," he told the UK newspaper.
He emphasized that "Ukraine are winning" and "there is no version where Russia is making any more advances"

noticias.titulo: Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin have held trilateral talks ― but what did they achieve?
noticias.resumen: The presidents of China, the US and Russia have held an unprecedented summit. While Trump said the three leaders were "making history," Xi described the talks as "fruitful" and Putin called them "open and candid."
noticias.texto:
Xi-Trump-Putin summit: What did it achieve?
November 19, 2026
Chinese President Xi Jinping hosted US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday for an unprecedented trilateral summit in Shenzhen, bringing together the leaders of the world's three most powerful military powers amid heightened geopolitical tensions.
Xi hailed the talks as "groundbreaking," saying discussions ranged from global governance and denuclearization to the war in Ukraine and energy security.
The "peace declaration" released after their meeting made no mention of Russia's war in Ukraine or the US-led war in Iran.
Instead, the three leaders agreed to pursue reforms of the United Nations, limit the role of the International Criminal Court and reaffirm their commitment to avoiding nuclear war. They also pledged to boost supplies of refined petroleum products to address global energy challenges.
The tightly choreographed meeting fueled concerns that Beijing, Washington and Moscow could seek to reshape the international order around competing spheres of influence.
While Xi said the talks with Trump and Putin were "positive, constructive and fruitful," Trump heralded the gathering as "really making history."
Who gained the most from the meeting?
For Putin, the three-way talks, and his meetings with both leaders separately earlier, offered a chance to show the world that he was on par with the leaders of the US and China, despite Western efforts to isolate him since he launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Emma Chanlett-Avery, senior director for Political-Security Affairs at the Asia Society Policy Institute (ASPI), said Putin had the most to gain from the meeting as "he appeared on the world stage as one of the dominant players in the world."
Chim Lee, a senior analyst with The Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU), echoed this view.
The meeting itself is a "major outcome for Russia," he told DW, pointing to Russian media coverage that has cast it as "reinforcing Russia's standing in the world."
Beijing reluctant to accept nuclear limits
The joint statement also said the leaders are committed to work to reduce nuclear risks and prevent nuclear proliferation.
The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States, known as New START, expired in February.
Trump has said he wants "a new, improved and modernized" deal that includes China.
But Beijing has so far been reluctant to accept limits as its estimated arsenal of around 500 warheads remains far smaller than those of Russia and the US.
Moscow and Washington are believed to possess more than 5,000 warheads each.
Lee said China is unlikely to participate in a trilateral institutionalized setting to control nuclear arms.
"The gap between China's nuclear arsenal and those of Russia and US is still quite large. From China's perspective, it doesn't seem to make a lot of sense to put the three powers in the same bucket in this area."
The expert believes Trump attended the meeting as he is "actively thinking about his legacy in the final two years in office."
"So, in this context, the idea of setting up a trilateral nuclear arms control arrangement would have been a very big achievement," Lee said.
But, in the end, the declaration said the countries would merely engage in "dialogue" on the issue, avoiding any explicit commitments to downsize their nuclear stockpiles.
A reluctant host?
China initially hesitated to organize the trilateral summit as it did not want to be explicitly tied to Russia's war in Ukraine and harm Beijing's efforts to present itself as a long-term force for global stability.
The Chinese government, which is working to rebalance economic ties with the EU, was also wary of appearing to form a G3 club with Washington and Moscow, which could alienate other global partners.
Chanlett-Avery said that China had some degree of discomfort in convening this meeting, worried about getting involved in Ukraine issues.
But Beijing eventually "managed to get the outcome they wanted" and kept the European conflict out of the meeting's focus, she noted.
"China was able to show off Shenzhen and all of its sparkling high-tech features. They convened a successful international meeting that grabbed lots of headlines," she added. "So, I think China probably came out feeling okay."
Warnings of a 'second Yalta'
Prior to the summit, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had warned of a "second Yalta," referring to the Yalta Conference held in Crimea in 1945.
That meeting saw the Allied powers decide on the post-war European order following the end of World War II.
In Shenzhen, Putin stressed that Russia, the US and China, as victors in World War II and veto-wielding members of the UN Security Council, bore a "joint responsibility for maintaining international peace."
But Ying-Yu Lin, Associate Professor at Graduate Institute of International Affairs and Strategic Studies at Taiwan's Tamkang University, said the Yalta comparison "is a bit of a stretch," given the vast differences between 1945 and now.
Will there be more such trilaterals?
Putin also said that all three leaders "agree that it's a useful format," and such meetings could take place again.
Lee, the EIU expert, said the trilateral setup "is unlikely to be just a one-off" and there will probably be more such meetings in the coming years.
"Especially from the US side to have this kind of setup, there will be some interest in maintaining warm relations with both China and Russia," he underlined.

noticias.titulo: No mention of fossil fuels in latest COP31 draft deal
noticias.resumen: One of the most fraught debates at the UN climate talks in Turkey has revolved around the future of coal, oil and gas. Now, all mention of fossil fuels has been removed from the summit's new draft agreement.
noticias.texto:
Fossil fuels dropped from latest COP31 draft deal
Published November 19, 2026last updated November 19, 2026
Climate negotiators have removed any mention of fossil fuels — the main source of greenhouse gas emissions heating the planet — in a new draft deal published by COP31 summit co-host Australia.
The latest text released Thursday at the UN climate conference in Turkey stripped out two references to a transition away from coal, oil and gas and a call for an accelerated phaseout that had been in an earlier draft.
This slimmed down version follows days of tough negotiations, with representatives from nearly 200 nations debating issues such as the future of fossil fuels and climate funding for developing countries.
The text still includes a call to increase the global share of final energy demand met by electricity to 35% by 2035 — up from around 20% today — a proposal that was pushed by host Turkey.
It did not specify whether that additional electricity needs to come from clean sources rather than fossil fuels, a point that has drawn criticism from some countries.
The draft did mention the electrification target alongside efforts to triple renewable energy capacity globally as well as other energy efficiency measures. But Jan Kowalzig, a climate finance expert with Oxfam Germany, said negotiators had failed to "meaningfully" link them.
Kowalzig also criticized the text for not referencing a transition away from fossil fuels in a gradual manner — something that had been mentioned in the final decision out of the COP28 in Dubai several years ago.
"This is insufficient for a climate conference that already decided several years ago to phase out fossil fuels and that presents itself as a conference focused on implementation," he said in a statement.
'Worst fears' on climate financing
Another hotly contested issue at the talks has been financial support to help developing countries deal with climate change. Divisions largely revolve around who should bear the costs and whether funding should come in the form of grants or loans.
The second draft called for further discussions on a tripling of funding for climate adaptation measures in developing countries to at least $120 billion (€109 billion). It also noted "with concern the gap between climate finance flows and needs," with the adaptation costs in developing countries estimated at $305 billion annually up to 2035.
The wording on finance prompted criticism from Meenakshi Raman, the coordinator of the climate change program at the Third World Network, who had been "hoping to see much more ambition on the side of finance from the developed world."
"Coming here really confirmed the worst fears that developed countries are not only backsliding but putting nothing in terms of real meaning on the table," said Raman.
The European Union has said it won't agree to higher climate financing pledges because it pays its "fair share" while others don't.
What else is in the draft text?
The draft text also expressed "deep concern" that global warming is projected to exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels — the threshold outlined in the 2015 Paris Agreement to avoid runaway climate change.
It acknowledged that every increment of warming above current levels would "result in increasingly adverse, and in some cases irreversible, impacts and risks to human and natural systems."
Australian Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen said the text aimed to communicate that "1.5 degrees of warming is not acceptable and will not be allowed to stand."
The draft also recognized the need for "deep, rapid and sustained" cuts to greenhouse gas emissions and called for efforts to ramp up action targeting the potent greenhouse gas methane.
The greenhouse gas emissions heating the planet are largely caused by burning fossil fuels.
The text additionally calls for the deployment of technologies that can remove carbon from the atmosphere to be sped up, many of which have yet to be tested and proven on a large scale.
Harjeet Singh of the Fill the Fund campaign to boost climate finance for developing countries said the second draft "trims away inconvenient mandates and accountability while leaving behind lofty rhetoric that won't protect a single vulnerable community."
Talks in crunch time
The climate conference officially ends on Friday, but it's not uncommon for the annual talks to run on for longer than expected. The latest text is expected to face further revisions before it can be adopted.
Decisions on the language need approval from all countries, meaning an objection from one party is enough to scupper a deal.
On Thursday, Panama said it would block any agreement that does not meet its demand for a cap on oil production and steps to eliminate the potent greenhouse gas methane.
The country's environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, said Panama would "not lend its name" to "complacent or ineffective language" in the final pact.
Australian Energy Minister Bowen said he expected countries to bring forward their concerns, feedback and questions in the coming hours and overnight.
"We won't be leaving the rooms of Antalya until we have that consensus, until we have a plan we can put to the parties on behalf of the countries and governments they represent, and they can say, yes, we can do this: we can keep the world to 1.5 degrees of warming."
The stakes are high for this edition of the COP summit, which comes in a year of major climate-related disasters, from wildfires and deadly heat waves in Europe to a glacier collapse in Nepal that killed more than 1,400 people.
It's also taking place against the backdrop of an intensifying "super" El Nino weather pattern, and geopolitical shocks that have sent energy prices rising globally.
The conference is the first to be held under the acknowledgement by the UN that keeping the average global temperature under 1.5C is no longer realistic. Instead, scientists are talking about limiting the time spent above this threshold and bringing temperatures back down rapidly by the end of the century.
Countries are at odds about how to acknowledge overshoot of the temperature threshold in the final agreement, with some worrying that fossil fuel producing countries such asa Saudi Arabia and Iran are seeking to jettison 1.5C entirely, which could lead to "backsliding" on climate action, according to AFP.
"It's critically important for this COP to recognize, and this is really the first COP that will likely do so, that we are on the way to overshooting 1.5 degrees," said David Waskow, the director of the World Resources Institute's International Climate Initiative.

noticias.titulo: Anthropic trading tests investors' appetite for AI
noticias.resumen: Anthropic was valued at $2 trillion after shares started trading on the Nasdaq following a record $81 billion IPO. Its performance will put investor confidence in AI to the test.
noticias.texto:
Anthropic trading tests investors' appetite for AI
November 19, 2026
Shares of US artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic saw their first day of trading on Thursday on the US tech-heavy Nasdaq stock exchange.
Anthropic is one of the global leaders in AI technology and is best known for its Claude chatbot.
The stock opened at $111.50 — that's 34% higher than the IPO price of $83 and puts the company's valuation at $2 trillion.
The company's share performance is being seen as a key test of investor appetite for AI, as stock prices have swung wildly in recent months.
The San Francisco-based company behind the Claude AI tool has offered 980 million shares at $83 per share, raising a record $81 billion.
This valued the firm at $1.5 trillion, well above market estimates of around $1.3 trillion.
First of the AI giants to go public
Anthropic is the first big AI company to go public. Its main competitor, ChatGPT-maker OpenAI, has reportedly pushed its IPO to 2027.
Issuing shares on the stock market is essentially a way to raise money and avoid taking on debt.
Anthropic has already taken on $6.2 billion in debt and is not yet making a profit. At the same time, it faces massive bills for computer power and data centers.
That specific financial situation is one of the reasons for persistent concern that the AI boom might be a bubble that will eventually burst.

noticias.titulo: Alexander Zverev faces fresh lawsuit from ex-girlfriend
noticias.resumen: World No. 1 tennis player Alexander Zverev is facing a new lawsuit related to a domestic abuse trial. The lawyer for his ex-girlfriend, Brenda Patea, told DW what the allegations are against the German player.
noticias.texto:
Alexander Zverev faces fresh lawsuit from ex-girlfriend
November 19, 2026
Alexander Zverev misrepresented the result of his 2024 domestic abuse trial, causing harm to his former partner and the mother of his child, Brenda Patea's lawyer has told DW.
The case ended without a verdict after both sides reached an out-of-court settlement. Zverev, who won the French and US Open in 2026, is alleged to have told French publication L'Equipe that: "I did everything I could, and my innocence has been proven."
As Zverev's lawyers noted in a statement sent to DW: "The criminal proceedings were discontinued...without any finding of guilt, and the presumption of innocence remains unaffected."
However, Zverev's statement has harmed Patea's standing and her career as an influencer, according to her lawyer, Michael Scheele.
"What she suffered after this interview in L'Equipe was published is nothing but a shitstorm. It's also detrimental to her business," Scheele told DW.
"We still don't know the truth objectively and we have an agreement in which he committed not to talk about the incident and the case at all," he added.
However, in the statement sent to DW, Zverev's lawyers asserted that "there has been no breach of any contractual obligations or violation of Ms. Patea’s personality rights."
Zverev's lawyers: 'permissible expression of opinion'
Zverev had made similar comments before. On the day the settlement was reached, the tennis pro spoke to reporters at the 2024 French Open.
"That's what dropping the case is: That is innocence. They're not going to drop the case if you're guilty at the end of the day," he said.
The lawsuit, seen by DW, states that Zverev should be subject to "a fine of up to €250,000 ($275,000) to be determined for each instance of violation — and, in the event that such fine cannot be collected, substitute custodial detention of up to six months," should he be found guilty.
Zverev's lawyers reject the allegations.
"Our client will defend himself against the lawsuit. If the statement attributed to him was indeed made in the form alleged, we consider it to be a permissible expression of opinion protected by Article 5(1) of the German Basic Law," they said.
"Our client would merely have expressed his personal conviction that he had done everything in his power to refute the allegations made against him and that he considers his innocence to have been confirmed by the outcome of the criminal proceedings. "He is fully entitled to hold and express this view."
The law firm, Schertz Bergmann, added that: "Unlike the opposing counsel, we intend to conduct these proceedings in court rather than in the press."
Patea's lawyer: 'We had no choice' but court
Scheele said he and his client did not want to go back to court but were frustrated in their efforts to resolve matters in other ways.
"We went forward writing to him in a polite way, asking him to sign and to declare that he's not going to repeat what he said. And he didn't reply. So we wrote twice more, no reply.
"That's when we had to decide to go to court, which was not the aim at the beginning. We wanted to avoid it, but we had no other choice."
Zverev, now resident in Monaco, is currently playing in the season-ending ATP Finals tournament in Turin.

noticias.titulo: EU Commission confirms it was targeted in cyberattack using AI tools
noticias.resumen: The European Commission was targeted by an "AI-generated cybercampaign," a spokesperson has said. This is the first time the bloc has publicly reported an AI-based cyberattack.
noticias.texto:
EU targeted in an AI-assisted cyberattack, spokesperson says
November 19, 2026
The European Commission confirmed on Thursday that it was targeted by a cyberattack through the use of AI tools.
The incident was detected on October 22 and there was no evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff as a whole, European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier told reporters.
"This was an AI-generated cybercampaign," he added.
Regnier did not elaborate on the attack or name a perpetrator. He said the Commission "has taken the necessary steps in response."
This is the first time the bloc reported an AI-assisted cyberattack.
Disruption reportedly lasted 10 days
Regnier's statement came after Politico reported earlier on Thursday that the Commission had been targeted. The report said the cyberattack disrupted several systems for 10 days and might have compromised large amounts of personal data. The European Commission has roughly 33,000 employees.
The Commission then convened its highest-level internal crisis management body for an urgent meeting about the cyber incidents, according to Politico.
"We temporarily took down several applications, and most of them have since then been restored," Regnier said. He also stated that they did not detect any evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff.
Recent hybrid attacks on supermarkets, air traffic controllers, blood banks and broadcasters across Europe have raised worries among leaders that this may be part of a coordinated attempt at hybrid warfare.
France summoned the Iranian ambassador last week over cyberattacks that caused supermarket freezers to defrost, but Tehran has denied any involvement.

noticias.titulo: Wadephul: 'Coalition of the Willing' talks in Berlin send strong signal to Moscow
noticias.resumen: German Foreign Minister Wadephul has said the Coalition of the Willing meeting in Berlin sends a clear message to Moscow to take peace talks seriously. He also warned Ukraine should be prepared for peace talks to fail.
noticias.texto:
Germany's Wadephul: Berlin talks send strong signal to Moscow
November 19, 2026
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Thursday's meeting of the "Coalition of the Willing" in Berlin sent a strong signal to Moscow that it was time to take negotiations to end the war in Ukraine seriously.
Speaking to DW during a visit to the South Caucasus, Wadephul described the summit as the largest meeting of Ukraine's supporters so far. The meeting represents the 18th set of high-level talks among the coalition's members.
He said it demonstrated that allies remained firmly behind Kyiv in the fifth year of Russia's war and were ready to do "what was necessary to ensure Ukraine could negotiate from a position of strength."
"The summit itself is already a success," he told DW.
Wadephul also welcomed the US initiative to restart peace negotiations. After nine months without progress, an initial meeting had taken place in Abu Dhabi, with a follow-up round planned and European participation expected.
Wadephul promises future support for Ukraine
"We are also preparing for the possibility that the negotiations will not be successful and that, over the coming winter, we will have to continue supplying Ukraine with heating, electricity and all essential supplies, including water," he said.
"And we will continue to stand by Ukraine militarily."
He stressed that any peace agreement must include security guarantees to protect Ukraine against future Russian attacks.
In earlier comments during his trip to the South Caucasus, Wadephul said that Ukraine and Europe must be involved in any negotiations over the future of Ukraine.
Wadephul did, however, welcome the trilateral meeting between US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen.
"Every conversation that takes place is a good conversation," he told DW during a visit to Azerbaijan on Wednesday.
Later on Thursday, Russian President Vladimir Putin said he had invited Europeans to Moscow for talks on the potential structure of future talks to end the war.

noticias.titulo: Pakistan minister to visit India, but no breakthrough expected
noticias.resumen: A Pakistani minister's visit to India for a Shanghai Cooperation Organization forum marks a rare high-level contact between the two archrivals, but analysts say it does not signal a resumption of bilateral engagement.
noticias.texto:
Pakistan minister to visit India, but no breakthrough expected
November 19, 2026
Pakistan's Climate Change Minister Musadik Masood Malik will travel to India from November 20 to 22 to participate in the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Civilizational Dialogue in New Delhi.
It marks the first India visit by a Pakistani federal minister since the two nuclear-armed archrivals fought a four-day war last year.
The fighting erupted after armed gunmen killed over two dozen tourists, mostly Hindus, in India-administered Kashmir in April 2025. New Delhi accused Islamabad of backing the attack, a charge Pakistan denied.
Since the military confrontation, diplomatic tensions have remained high, leaving little room for official engagement between the two sides.
The SCO Civilizational Dialogue was proposed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi at the SCO summit in Tianjin in September 2025.
As the forum's host, India has invited all member states to participate in the event.
The SCO is a political, economic, and security alliance established in 2001. Its current members are Belarus, China, India, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Russia, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan.
India-Pakistan meeting a 'good sign'
Ajay Bisaria, a former Indian ambassador to Pakistan, sees significance in the fact that neither side sought to avoid the engagement. "The real takeaway is that the relationship isn't so broken that India won't invite Pakistan, or that Pakistan won't come. That alone is a good sign," he told DW.
But Bisaria cautions against assuming that the invitation followed a diplomatic breakthrough.
"The trigger was procedural. This forum grew out of Modi's proposal at the 2025 SCO summit in Tianjin, and as host, New Delhi invited every SCO member. I see no evidence of a back channel or outside mediation, and I wouldn't read much into that either way," he said.
'Being pragmatic' within SCO framework
The multilateral setting serves both countries, though for different reasons.
Pakistan wants to retain its influence within the organization. It currently holds the chairmanship of the SCO Council of Heads of State for 2026–27 and is due to host the next leaders' summit in Islamabad in August 2027.
Ayesha Siddiqa, a Pakistani expert on military and security affairs at King's College London, argues that Islamabad's decision to send a senior minister should be understood primarily in terms of its position in the grouping.
"Pakistan is keen to maintain its position and influence within the SCO and does not want to relinquish its role in the organization. The minister's visit should therefore be seen primarily in the context of Pakistan fulfilling its commitments under the SCO Charter, rather than as a gesture towards India," Siddiqa told DW.
T C A Raghavan, another former Indian ambassador to Pakistan, shares a similar sentiment.
"Both India and Pakistan attach importance to the SCO, and Pakistan currently holds its chairmanship. This visit should be seen primarily in the context of the SCO, rather than as a development in India-Pakistan bilateral relations," Raghavan told DW.
"Islamabad is also being pragmatic in keeping channels open during its SCO chairmanship by participating in an initiative championed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. There will be no real impact on the India-Pakistan bilateral."
The freeze in India-Pakistan ties
Since the April 2025 attack, India has maintained that terrorism and talks cannot go hand in hand.
"Post the Pahalgam attack, we have a Pakistan policy. That Pakistan policy remains in place. There has been no change," Randhir Jaiswal, spokesperson for India's Foreign Ministry, said at the end of October.
Pakistan, meanwhile, continues to raise the issues of Kashmir and the Indus Waters Treaty, which New Delhi placed "in abeyance" following the attack.
Malik, the climate change minister traveling to India, has been a prominent voice in Pakistan's campaign over water rights. In June, he warned: "We will protect ourselves... if anyone lays a hand over our share of water, we'll cut off that hand."
Sanjay Kumar Bhardwaj, professor at the Center for South Asian Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University, said the SCO is part of India's "multi-aligned foreign policy."
He noted that the forum "doesn't provide any space to normalize relations with Pakistan."
Unofficial channels, no formal dialogue
The absence of official talks, however, does not mean all bilateral communication has stopped.
Since the May 2025 confrontation, Indian and Pakistani former diplomats, strategic experts, parliamentarians and retired military officers have reportedly taken part in a series of informal or semi-official back-channel meetings.
Such exchanges allow participants to assess the other side's thinking, keep informal lines of communication open and reduce the risk of miscalculation.
But they do not amount to formal negotiations. New Delhi has said retired officials attending such meetings do so in their personal capacities.
An assessment by the International Institute for Strategic Studies in November said both governments appeared reluctant to resume secret talks, despite the role earlier back-channel contacts had played in stabilizing relations.
Bisaria described the visit by a Pakistani minister to India as "a modest step forward, not a breakthrough."
What happens next, he said, "depends on Pakistan."
"If it avoids grandstanding in Delhi and offers credible assurances on terrorism, publicly or quietly, it becomes more likely that Indian leaders will attend next year's SCO summit in Islamabad. That will be the real test."

noticias.titulo: APEC summit: Trump, Xi, Putin talks end with 'peace declaration'
noticias.resumen: The three world leaders discussed the Russian invasion of Ukraine as well as nuclear arms controls. Following the trilateral talks, President Trump reportedly headed to the airport.
noticias.texto:
APEC summit: Trump, Xi, Putin talks end with 'peace declaration'
Published November 17, 2026last updated November 19, 2026
What you need to know
These updates have been closed.
Here are the biggest headlines from the APEC summit and Trump's Asia tour:
- US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping held historic three-way talks
- The discussion took place on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit held in China's Shenzhen
- Trump held bilateral talks with 'friend' Putin as well as separate talks with Xi ahead of the main event
APEC trilateral meet ends with photos and promises
The APEC sideline summit between the leaders of the United States, Russia and China, the first trilateral meeting of the three, ended with much talk about the responsibility that they share for "maintaining and safeguarding peace," but produced rhetoric and symbolism rather than concrete agreements.
The "historic peace declaration" released after the meeting made no mention of extremely disruptive wars currently being waged by two of the three — Russian President Vladimir Putin in Ukraine and US President Donald Trump in Iran. Nor was Taiwan, which Chinese host President Xi Jinping says belongs to Beijing and may have to be taken by force one day.
After agreeing to respect one another's own security concerns, they emphasized that any differences between them must be hashed out in dialogue, not conflict.
Xi said of the summit: "As long as dialogue does not stop, doors remain open, there is hope for peace. The seeds planted at today's trilateral meeting will surely take root, sprout, blossom and bear fruit."
"History tells us," said Xi, "that when major powers live in harmony, the world is at peace. When major powers clash, the world falls into turmoil."
Readouts noted that the three had agreed to work on reducing nuclear risk, increasing global oil supplies and reforming the UN. Further, they agreed that the International Criminal Court — which issued a global arrest warrant for Putin on war crimes charges in March 2023 — should not "abuse its jurisdiction."
Analysis: No more than crumbs of comfort on nuclear weapons
Donald Trump's big theme going into the three-way summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin was "denuclearization" — saying in his opening remarks that they were "uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth."
But there are no signs that that will happen.
China has long resisted US calls for three-way talks on arms control, and Xi's reported call during the summit for a world without nuclear weapons was merely a reaffirmation of longstanding policy.
In fact, as signatories of the global Nonproliferation Treaty, all nuclear states are committed to pursuing nuclear disarmament. So the fact that the final "Heads of State Declaration toward Peace" fails to indicate any steps towards disarmament could be read by critics as just the latest failure to take that seriously.
China is engaged in a rapid buildup of its nuclear forces, from warheads to advanced theater missiles; Russia has made repeated threats to use nuclear weapons in its war in Ukraine; and the United States, despite Trump's calls for "denuclearization," is working on as many as four new theater missiles of its own to try to catch up with the other two in what could be the decisive nukes of this era.
Neither should the Declaration's reaffirmation of the Reagan-Gorbachev mantra "a nuclear war can never be won and must never be fought" be seen as much source of comfort — all three states last retook this oath in January 2022, just weeks before Putin launched his war.
And yet — the Declaration does have some crumbs of comfort for anyone seeking positive nuclear news. It says the three powers will "conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks." Possible areas for progress here would include commitments to notify other states when doing test launches of nuclear missiles (China has no such commitment), or keeping AI out of nuclear command and control (so far only the US and China have a very broad commitment that only humans should order a launch).
This would be the lowest of low-hanging fruit — after all, does anyone want AI to launch nuclear weapons? – but an optimist might say, it would be better than nothing. Let's see.
European officials invited to Moscow to discuss involvement in Ukraine talks, says Putin
Russian President Vladimir Putin said European officials have been invited to Moscow to discuss the potential structure of talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine.
"The American side is urging us to agree to the involvement of the Europeans ... Through diplomatic channels, we suggested to the Europeans to come to Moscow. And after that we will decide in what format the talks can continue," Putin said at a press conference in China.
"We understand that discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without the Europeans," Putin added.
For months, European politicians have emphasized that they should be present at any talks on the future of Ukraine.
The Russian leader also said it would be unacceptable for there to be military cooperation between Ukraine and the EU and that included any potential deployment of troops to the country.
"Military cooperation in any form is, of course, a problem," Putin told reporters.
Allies of Ukraine, the "Coalition of the Willing," are meeting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy today in Berlin.
What do we know about agreements at the trilateral summit?
The highly anticipated three-way talks between US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday have ended.
Ahead of the talks, Trump said they would be about "all problems that are being discussed in the world"
Here are quotes from the leaders and from a joint statement on the topics they addressed:
Nuclear arms
- Trump: "The United States, Russia and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth and also to lessen the risk of those weapons being used."
- Xi: "A nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought. Every effort must be made to prevent nuclear war, adhere to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, and maintain global strategic stability."
International Criminal Court and UN
- In a joint statement reported by Chinese state media and the Kremlin, the leaders agreed that "the International Criminal Court and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction."
- The leaders also "acknowledged the vital importance of the principle of state consent and the respect for (diplomatic) immunity enjoyed by state officials."
- The statement added that all three countries were "committed" to advancing reform of the United Nations.
Energy
- The joint statement said the countries "plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products."
- It reaffirmed "the importance of the stable flow of energy."
Neither the war in Ukraine nor the conflict in Iran were directly mentioned at the talks, according to the Russian and Chinese accounts.
China and Russia report on 'peace declaration' from trilateral summit
Chinese state media and Russian officials have been summarizing a declaration issued by the US, Chinese and Russian presidents at their trilateral summit, which US President Donald Trump billed as history-making.
According to the accounts of what was dubbed a "peace declaration," the three leaders reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.
The three presidents of major nuclear powers are quoted as saying they would hold a dialogue on the reduction of nuclear risks and the prevention of nuclear proliferation.
The three men also "reaffirmed the importance of stable energy flows," saying they plan to up the production and supply of refined petroleum products, according to the Chinese Xinhua news agency.
In addition, Chinese state media said the three had agreed that the International Criminal Court (ICC) — of which neither the US, China nor Russia are signatories — and similar institutions should not abuse their jurisdiction.
Putin himself is subject to an ICC arrest warrant for suspected war crimes in Ukraine.
The summary of the meeting did not mention the wars in Ukraine, triggered by Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion, or Iran, which began in late February with US-Israeli attacks on the country.
Both conflicts were expected to feature in the discussions.
WATCH: US; Russian, Chinese leaders in historic summit
US President Donald Trump has met with his Russian and Chinese counterparts for an unprecedented meeting on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China.
Trump said they were "making history" with the talks, which lasted around an hour and 20 minutes.
Watch here to see how the meeting began:
Historic Trump-Xi-Putin summit comes to an end
An unprecedented three-way meeting of US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin has ended after more than an hour of discussion.
Trump reportedly left the venue of the talks in Kylin Villa for the airport in the southeastern city of Shenzhen directly after the talks ended.
We will be bringing you details on anything concrete that emerged from the talks in further entries.
Xi calls for nuclear-free world
Chinese President Xi Jinping has told his US and Russian counterparts at the three-way that nuclear weapons should be comprehensively banned and thoroughly destroyed, the state-run Xinhua news agency said.
It quoted Xi as saying nuclear war should be prevented by all means and a nuclear-free world created.
"A nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought. Every effort must be made to prevent nuclear war, adhere to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, and maintain global strategic stability," the agency cited Xi as saying.
Ukraine war being discussed at trilateral meeting — Trump
US President Donald Trump said that the war in Ukraine would feature in the talks with his Russian and Chinese counterparts in China on Thursday.
"We are going to discuss the war between Russia and Ukraine," Trump said as the historic summit in Shenzhen got underway.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said all three countries had a shared "interest" to resolve the war in Ukraine, triggered by Moscow's 2022 full-scale invasion of its neighbor.
"Our countries have many converging interests when it comes to resolving regional conflicts, including, of course, the conflict in Ukraine," Putin said in opening remarks.
He added they had a "shared responsibility for maintaining international peace and security" and that closed-door discussions would also touch on food and energy security.
The global security of both food and energy has been weakened both by the war in Ukraine and the conflict in Iran, unleashed by US-Israel attacks on the Islamic Republic at the end of February.
Trilateral meeting to cover all the world's problems — Trump
As the trilateral summit got underway, US President Donald Trump said he would be talking about "all problems that are being discussed in the world."
Among other things, he said, the talks would cover the issue of nuclear arms.
"The United States, Russia and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth and also to lessen the risk of those weapons being used," he said.
Both Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin emphasized a focus on peace in the world.
"We will be having discussions on the theme of promoting world peace," Xi said, adding that China, the US and Russia should "jointly safeguard" international peace.
Putin echoed Xi's statement, saying that the three countries were "the victors in WWII, and we hold joint responsibility for maintaining international peace."
Trump, Putin and Xi begin historic trilateral talks
US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping have started three-way talks, with Trump saying the meeting was "making history."
The talks in the Kylin Villa on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, are expected to cover the issues of nuclear arms and the wars in Ukraine and Iran.
The talks, which ended up being delayed, were preceded by two-way talks between Trump and each of the two other leaders.
Japan wants 'constructive and stable relationship' with China
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said on Thursday that she intends to build a "constructive and stable relationship" with Beijing, in comments made at a time when Japan-China relations are at a low point over a remark she made on Taiwan.
"We intend to comprehensively advance our strategic and mutually beneficial relationship ... pursuing dialogue to safeguard the national interests of both sides, and build a constructive and stable relationship," Takaichi said at a news conference on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen.
She said that Japan's position on Taiwan had not changed from that stated in its 1972 Japan-China Joint Communique, which established diplomatic relations between Tokyo and Beijing and severed those previously held with Taiwan.
China considers the democractically-run Taiwan part of its sovereign territory and has threatened to take it by force if necessary.
Beijing reacted angrily after Takaichi said in November 2025 that a Taiwan Strait crisis could threaten Japan's survival and thus justified a self-defense response.
Takaichi's welcome to the APEC summit was very low-key, which has been seen by observers as a sign that Beijing's ire at the remark has not subsided.
Unlike other world leaders, including US President Donald Trump, Takaichi also did not hold a bilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the summit in Shenzhen.
Xi says China-US relations have remained 'stable and improved' in bilateral talks with Trump
Chinese President Xi said he was committed to working with President Trump to steer ties between the two superpowers to the "correct course," after a brief bilateral meeting with the US President ahead of the trilateral talks.
"During this period, China-US relations have remained generally stable and improved, bringing tangible benefits to the people of both countries and injecting stability and certainty into the world," Xi told Trump at their third meeting this year.
"We have established a new definition of a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability, giving it new substance based on respect, fairness and reciprocity," Xi said.
The leaders reportedly also discussed the possibility of China buying US farm goods, the Iran war and Russia's war in Ukraine.
"We're looking to both help with respect to the war with Russia and Ukraine. I'd like to see it ended, I think I can speak for both of us, very much," Trump said after the meeting concluded.
Trump calls Putin 'my friend' after bilateral talks
Presidents Trump and Putin have concluded bilateral talks that lasted around 40 minutes.
"Wonderful things can come out of this — or at least start," Trump said after joining Putin for the one-on-one meeting on the sidelines of the APEC summit, calling Putin "my friend."
"We've had a great relationship for many years," Trump said after shaking hands with his Russian counterpart.
The two last met in Alaska last year, but the warmer — in comparison to the previous administration — relationship between Trump and Putin has so far failed to bring an end to the war in Ukraine, despite a pledge by the US president to end it on "day one" of his second term in office.
Meanwhile, Russian news agency TASS reported that the leaders discussed the war in Ukraine, US-Russia bilateral ties and the upcoming trilateral meeting.
Trump: US opposes 'any form of globalist regulation' of AI
The United States is against "globalist regulation" of artificial intelligence in any form, President Trump said on Thursday, ahead of the trilateral talks with China's Xi and Russia's Putin.
"It's super intelligence [SI], but we have to watch it," he said, using the term mandated by his administration to refer to AI. "We oppose any form of globalist regulation or anything to control and stifle SI, and we won't allow that to happen," he told leaders at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting in Shenzhen.
Trump and Xi, the leaders of the two main rivals in the AI race, are expected to discuss the issue later on Thursday. The Chinese president on Wednesday called for leaders to "deepen cooperation in the digital economy and artificial intelligence", without giving details.

noticias.titulo: Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya, top UN court rules
noticias.resumen: The International Court of Justice has upheld large parts of a genocide case against Myanmar linked to the 2017 conflict with its Rohingya minority. It called for it to pay reparations and let refugees return safely.
noticias.texto:
Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya, top UN court rules
November 19, 2026
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) on Thursday found Myanmar in breach of several of its obligations under international treaties to prevent and not to commit genocide.
The ICJ's president, Judge Yuji Iwasawa said that the panel of 15 judges had decided by nine votes to six that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya in Rakhine state.
The judges also found the country guilty of a series of other more specific violations by majority rulings.
"On the basis of all the evidence taken together, the Court is of the view that the only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar's actions is an intention to destroy a substantial part of... the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine State," ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said.
Iwasawa said that Myanmar should make efforts to pay reparations to victims or their associates where possible and appropriate.
He also called for it to facilitate the safe return of refugees, and to take measures to investigate and, if necessary, prosecute individual wrongdoing by its nationals and security forces.
What Judge Iwasawa said as he read out the verdict against Myanmar
The ICJ said in its consideration, the Rohingya constituted a distinct ethnic group with their own defining language and culture, as well as self-identifying as such. This means they qualified as a protected group for the purposes of international laws against genocide.
Myanmar's security forces "killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated acts of sexual violence, as well as extreme violence against children," and also attacked Rohingya as they tried to flee the fighting, the ICJ's Iwasawa said.
"The court is fully convinced that the 2017 clearance operations caused serious bodily and mental harm to a significant number of the protected group," Judge Iwasawa said.
Iwasawa also said that some civilian participation in the clearance operations could not necessarily be considered state-ordered or state-sanctioned behavior. But the court found that the government and security forces also made no meaningful efforts to prevent non-Rohingya civilian atrocities and fanned the flames of ethnic and religious tension.
At one point, reading the details of the findings, Iwasawa noted "Myanmar's failure, genuinely to investigate the alleged atrocities, and its refusal to facilitate access to evidence and witnesses, or provide information requested."
He said this meant it was possible the court did not have reliable knowledge of information available only from within Myanmar to which it was not given access.
How did groups from Myanmar respond?
There was no immediate response from the government in Myanmar or the military, which is regarded as the real underlying power.
Rohingya activist Yasmin Ullah — a Canadian citizen since 2016 but who was born in Rakhine state and who was a member of Gambia's delegation that filed the ICJ case — called the verdict more important for the world than for her community.
"The Rohingya never needed a court to tell us what happened to us," she said. "We needed the world to hear it, and today it has."
Wai Wai Nu, a Rohingya activist who directs the Women's Peace Network NGO, said the world's highest court's finding followed "decades" when "the Burmese military tried to erase our identity, deny our existence and dismiss our suffering."
And the co-chair of the Arakan Rohingya National Council, Nay San Lwin, said that for Rohingya people, "justice means the restoration of our citizenship, recognition of our identity and our safe and dignified return home."
Myanmar's shadow national unity government, which includes remnants of former President Aung San Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy Party, said it "respects the authority" of the ICJ.
It said that since the beginning of the "revolution against military dictatorship" in 2021, it had affirmed its "commitment to the rule of law, human rights, justice and states' obligations to prevent and punish genocide."
Myanmar was under nominally civilian rule at the time of the atrocities, but the extent to which Suu Kyi's government held sway over the military and its actions is debatable.
How did the international community react?
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres welcomed Thursday's verdict, calling it a "powerful recognition of the Rohingya victims of genocide" and noting it was the first verdict of its kind against a state.
"Myanmar must act in accordance with its obligation to comply with the Court's decision," Guterres said in a statement, adding that this includes "the safe, voluntary and dignified return [of Rohingya] to their place of residence nad reunification of families."
Gambia's Justice Minister Dawda Jallow, who attended the hearing, spoke to reporters afterward at the Peace Palace in The Hague.
"The victory belongs to the Rohingya," Jallow said. "They survived. They testified. And today, they will believe."
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband issued a statement saying the former colonial power was "taking immediate action today in light of this judgment."
Miliband said Britain would expel Myanmar's defense attache in London and was calling for a special UN Security Council session in response. He called on Myanmar to "comply fully with the judgment," and on the international community to "play its part in supporting implementation, accountability, and justice for the Rohingya."
UN human rights chief Volker Türk said the ruling "clearly concludes the State of Myanmar stands responsible for one of the most egregious crimes known to humankind."
What is the genocide case against Myanmar?
The case centers around the military crackdown in Rakhine state on the country's western coastline against the predominantly Muslim Rohingya minority in 2017.
Violence had been brewing for several years beforehand, but the most intense phase of the military crackdown in the north of region was triggered by a coordinated attack by a Muslim militia group against several police and military installations and personnel in August 2017.
