A UN fact finding mission later concluded that some 10,000 people likely died in the military clearance operations that followed. Around 700,000 people fled to Bangladesh, where most still reside in the world's largest refugee camp.
Gambia filed the complaint at The Hague in 2019, alleging a deliberate campaign of arson, rape and murder designed to wipe out the Rohingya minority in whole or in part.
Myanmar's influential military, now back in full de facto control of the country albeit amid a long-running civil war, has maintained that it was engaged in a legitimate counterinsurgency.
Aung San Suu Kyi, who was the civilian president at the time, took a slightly more nuanced stance, but nevertheless traveled to The Hague to contest the charges, calling them "incomplete and incorrect."
The case is likely to draw close attention from those pursuing ICJ prosecutions against Israel and Benjamin Netanyahu for the war in Gaza and against Russia and Vladimir Putin for the invasion of Ukraine.

noticias.titulo: Judges have put Trump's arch and golf course on hold, but only for a matter of days
noticias.resumen: A federal judge has twice delayed construction of Trump's arch. Another is keeping East Potomac Park open. The proposed golf course redesign got mixed feedback from a federal arts panel on Thursday.
noticias.texto:
Judges have put Trump's arch and golf course on hold, but only for a matter of days
A federal judge has extended her block on construction of President Trump's D.C. arch for two weeks, another short-term victory for those who don't want to see the 250-foot structure break ground.
D.C. District Judge Tanya Chutkan extended her temporary restraining order on Wednesday, the day before it was set to expire. She originally stepped in to block construction on the night of Nov. 5, after the National Capital Planning Commission and National Park Service gave the arch final approval and the Trump administration said construction could begin imminently.
Chutkan's new five-page order prevents the administration from "initiating, making, or otherwise effectuating any construction, excavation, demolition, land-disturbance, utility-installation, or roadway-closure activity, or any other construction-related activity" at Memorial Circle through Dec. 3.
"The judge's order recognizes that the conditions that called for emergency relief two weeks ago remain unchanged," Nick Sansone, the Public Citizen attorney representing the original plaintiffs in the lawsuit, said in a statement.
The extension gives Chutkan more time to consider plaintiffs' request for a longer-term preliminary injunction, which would prohibit construction as the lawsuit against the arch plays out.
That lawsuit started earlier this year with a challenge from a group of Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian, but has expanded in recent weeks.
In late October, the governments of D.C. and Virginia filed another lawsuit, which was combined with the original. And nine members of the Kennedy family joined the fight last week, saying the arch will block historic sightlines and cast shadows over the graves of John F. Kennedy and others at nearby Arlington National Cemetery.
"This is one man who wants to build this arch. He's violated every rule. If this is a great idea, then bring it before Congress, follow the rules and get it approved," Max Kennedy, a son of Robert F. Kennedy, told NPR's All Things Considered.
Opposition to the arch — from area residents, veterans, local officials, Democratic lawmakers and more — has grown in recent months as the structure hurtled through the federal approval process.
Critics take issue with the arch's scale and location, saying it would interrupt the solemn and historic vista between Arlington National Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial. Plaintiffs argue the structure violates several laws — including the Commemorative Works Act and D.C.'s Height of Buildings Act — and is fundamentally illegal without approval from Congress.
The Trump administration has not sought that approval, arguing the arch is covered by Congress' authorization in 1925 of a pair of 166-foot columns at the same location, which were never built.
In court filings and a recently unveiled website, the administration characterizes building the arch as a matter of urgency — both to complete that century-old vision and to facilitate national security. Trump said in September that the arch would double as a military complex, but the plans that got final approval this month don't include any details to that effect.
In a declaration this week, Ricky Buria, chief of staff to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, told the court that the agency is "currently in the planning process to determine how to integrate national defense uses … into the Arch without changing the existing plans for the Arch."
White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told NPR on Thursday that the administration will "continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds."
The arch is one of several construction projects that Trump has pursued with vigor in his second term. Some of them, like the White House ballroom and Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, are well underway. Others, like the Kennedy Center closure and East Potomac golf course redevelopment, are held up by various legal challenges.
Democrats have said they will use their forthcoming majority in Congress to push back on Trump's construction agenda, including by blocking federal funding. But experts say the fate of many of these projects will ultimately be up to the court.
'Time is of the essence' at East Potomac
Trump's dream of redeveloping a municipal D.C. golf course into a championship-level venue is also temporarily on hold, despite his repeated social media pronouncements that the park would close and work would begin on Nov. 15.
Another D.C. district judge, Ana Reyes, intervened Saturday to order the administration to keep East Potomac Park open for two weeks, on the eve of its indefinite closure.
But the golf course itself is currently unstaffed, since its operator lease expired on Sunday. That hasn't stopped locals from showing up and teeing off, finding creative ways to mark the holes after the flagsticks were removed from the course.
Reyes has ordered both parties to weigh in on whether she has the authority to order the government to keep the golf course open.
On Wednesday, the Trump administration officially appealed Reyes' restraining order as it had promised. That order is currently set to expire on Nov. 28, the Saturday after Thanksgiving.
Noting that timing, the plaintiffs in the case — local golfers and historic preservationists — have asked Reyes to extend her order by another two weeks, until Dec. 12, while she considers the underlying legal issues and decides whether to issue a longer preliminary injunction.
The government, on the other hand, said "the court already has everything it needs to promptly consider a motion for preliminary injunction" and has proposed a schedule that would enable her to issue a final ruling by Nov. 28.
In the meantime, the administration took another step forward in the federal review process on Thursday. The Interior Department presented its plan for the golf course to the Commission of Fine Arts, one of two federal agencies which would need to approve the project.
Commission Secretary Thomas Luebke said some 700 members of the public submitted comments ahead of the meeting, all but three in opposition to the golf course proposal.
The biggest concerns had to do with making the park less accessible to golfers of all levels, as well as cyclists, runners and picnickers who use the park's perimeter loop, which would be eliminated. There were other concerns about the impact of major road races — like the Marine Corps Marathon — that use that road, the loss of historic cherry trees and the cost of the project (the Interior Department said deferred maintenance alone would cost $43 million but did not specify how much the renovations would cost).
Over a dozen other people spoke out in the room, sharing their personal experiences with the park, raising questions about gaps in the presentation and urging the commission to defer or outright reject any plan that does not leave the perimeter loop intact.
Commissioners — all of whom were appointed by Trump — did not have the quorum needed to vote on preliminary approval. Several offered praise for the idea of beautifying the space and overhauling the golf course, but questioned whether this plan is the best way to do it.
Vice Chair Rodney Mims Cook, Jr., a Trump ally, said there seems to be enough space in the park to accommodate the aspects that people care about, like preserving the historic mini-golf course. His comments prompted applause from many of the people who had crowded into the meeting room.
Cook asked the Interior Department to bring alternative designs to its next meeting, in late January. The administration has said it plans to present the same proposal to the National Capital Planning Commission at its meeting in early December.
Administration officials said in Thursday's meeting, as they have in previous court hearings, that their plan is not yet finalized. Judge Reyes, however, is not convinced and accused the administration of already taking steps to carry it out, like cutting down hundreds of trees.
Plaintiffs in the case argue the administration has violated federal environmental law by splitting the project into smaller parts, like the tree removal, to bypass necessary reviews. And they say the administration skipped required legal steps in its rush to close off most of the park, which Reyes seemed to agree with in her order.
"In its haste to meet an arbitrary deadline, the Government has likely violated at least the National Environmental Policy Act and the Administrative Procedure Act," she wrote.
Trump has repeatedly described the East Potomac golf course as decrepit and dangerous, and challenged Reyes' authority over the project. Over the weekend, he reiterated that Reyes was appointed by President Biden and slammed her decision as "highly destructive and political."
"Why would a judge want to delay taking a terrible and very unsafe golf course, one that is mocked all over D.C.(and far beyond!), instead of quickly turning it into a great and admired one?" Trump wrote on Truth Social. "Time is of the essence, or golf seasons, jobs, prestige, and much money, will be lost!"
Government lawyers asked Reyes to recuse herself from the case in mid-October, accusing her of bias and hostility. She denied that request on legal grounds. Tensions between Reyes and the administration have dominated this case so far, with the judge ordering a misconduct inquiry into whether government officials and lawyers misled the court about its plans for the park.
Government lawyers have pushed back, telling the court Thursday that such an inquiry is "not necessary."

noticias.titulo: The 'Magic Six': How to strengthen your marriage in midlife
noticias.resumen: How do we maintain healthy romantic relationships as we age? Allison Aubrey and Scott Detrow talk about about the science of healthy, later-in-life relationships.
noticias.texto:
The 'Magic Six': How to strengthen your marriage in midlife
Ever argued with your spouse in the car? NPR's Nina Totenberg can relate.
She and her husband, David Reines, have been married for 26 years, and it's on the road where they're most likely to have a spat. "The car is awful," Totenberg told me, laughing. It comes down partly to the brakes. She taps them "way before" Reines does. And when another driver cuts him off, he sometimes wants to return the favor. Totenberg's advice from the passenger seat: "Don't take the bait."
It's so relatable. And as Reines put it, "You can't not have some conflict after 26 years. I think the secret is how you deal with it." (They began our interview for this episode of Your Turn by giving each other a kiss!)
As we ask "What comes next?" in midlife, who's standing beside us matters a lot. Kids leave home, careers shift, and relationships can change, too. So what does a good partnership look like at this stage?
David and Nina's Four L's
When people ask Reines why their marriage works, he points to four L's:
Love. "You gotta love each other."
Like. Do you actually like each other? For Reines, respect is part of this. He says he has total respect for her work, and she respects his career, too. He is a retired trauma surgeon and now keeps busy as a volunteer at the Library of Congress and serves on boards. Each of them also keeps a strong sense of self. "Although we meld," Reines says. "I still have me, and she still has her."
Lust. Physical intimacy matters. They kiss every day, hold hands, "all the time," and have held off on buying a king-size bed. In hotel beds, they joke, they can't find each other if the bed is too big.
Laugh. He says she has one of the best senses of humor he knows. They laugh together every day.
The Magic Six
I also talked with clinical psychologist Julie Schwartz Gottman who I interviewed for my book, Your Turn. She and her husband, John Gottman, co-founded the Gottman Institute and are two of the best-known names in relationship science, and co-authors of Fight Right: How Successful Couples Turn Conflict Into Connection, where they describe the "Four Horseman" which are four destructive communication patterns that can help predict the breakdown of a relationship.
Gottman points to research that shows many dual-career couples spend little time together and much of the communication can be transactional. Did you call the plumber? Did you walk the dog?
The Gottmans found that couples can improve their relationships by intentionally carving out about six hours a week together, and making changes to small, daily and weekly habits. They call it the Magic Six.
Some of these things may sound obvious, yet oftentimes these are the very things that can fall away when couples are too busy or distracted. And she says it's illuminating when couples actually track progress.
Partings (a few minutes each day). Before you leave in the morning, spend a few minutes communicating about what's happening in your partner's day.
Reunions (about 20 minutes a day). At the end of the workday, share a kiss or physical affection. Then have a 20-minute stress-reducing conversation about your day.
Admiration and appreciation (35 minutes a week). Spend about five minutes a day expressing genuine gratitude or naming a trait you admire in your partner. Or tell a story to remind each other.
Affection (35 minutes a week). That works out to about five minutes a day on physical touch, such as holding hands or cuddling before sleep.
Date night (2 hours a week). Have distraction-free time together to enjoy being together. It doesn't need to be dinner and a show. It can be a low-key hike, a museum visit or any activity you enjoy.
State of the union meeting (1 hour a week). Review what's going well as well as concerns or things that are not working, and then talk things out.
Listen. Don't Fix.
Many partners fall into the trap of trying to "fix" the other person's problems or tell them how to proceed. But the point of the daily conversation is to step away from this mentality.
"Most of us just wanna be seen," Gottman told me. "We wanna be witnessed." Jumping in with advice can cut off the conversation before your partner gets the chance to describe what's bothering them.
Instead, she suggests three simple words: "Tell me more."
It's an invitation, Gottman says. It tells your partner, "I really am interested in what you're saying." It shows them that you care.
Nina Totenberg and David Reines have their own version. Every night at dinner, they sit down and ask, "How'd your day go?" He calls Nina a good listener and she says she enjoys connecting this way and spending time together. They keep each other in check and serve as each other's confidant.
Find Your Rhythm
Gottman also had good news for couples who don't share every hobby. You can pursue different passions as long as you bring them back to the table and stay curious about each other. Some couples want lots of independence, and others want to do everything together. The key is to keep asking: Are you missing me? Do we need more time together, or less?
Totenberg and Reins have found their balance. They agree on watching British murder mysteries together. And when he wants a shoot-'em-up, she heads upstairs for Law & Order. Summer vacations on Cape Cod are friends-only, where they spend days doing what they each enjoy. Winter holidays are for her sisters and family.
As Totenberg put it: "If you find somebody that you really love who loves you back, you should grab that and run for all the world because it's ... an enormous gift."
So, if you'd like: give this a try: Ask your partner one open-ended question. Then say, "Tell me more."
For more, follow the Your Turn newsletter and listen to the Your Turn podcast on the NPR app or wherever you get your podcasts.

noticias.titulo: The midterms were the largest win for either party in 50 years
noticias.resumen: Some 56% of people cast votes for Democrats in House races, compared to 42% who voted Republican. That 14-point spread is the widest win for either party in 50 years, since after Watergate.
noticias.texto:
The midterms were the largest win for either party in 50 years
With vote counts concluding and the closest House races being decided, we now have a clearer picture of Democrats' dominant midterms.
Some 56% of people cast votes for Democrats in House races, compared to 42% who voted Republican. That's a 14-point spread on the House ballot.
It's the biggest win for either party in 50 years, since after Watergate.
Loading...
Democrats' wins in 2018 and 2006 — the earlier of which then-President George W. Bush described as a "thumping" — and the 2010 "shellacking" that Democrats took, as former President Barack Obama called it, were all less-than-10-point House margins. Obama's 2008 election comes the closest at almost 11 points.
Nearly 50 House seats flipped
So far, Democrats have flipped 46 House seats currently held by Republicans.
That number could rise to 49, as Democrats lead in three other races that have not yet been called.
It's the second-most number of flipped seats this century. The first was in 2010 when Republicans flipped 66 seats, netting 64, a backlash to the passage of the Affordable Care Act, which has since become more popular.
Loading...
The biggest House majority in a generation
This year's drubbing was so resounding that when all the votes are counted, Democrats will likely have the largest majority in Congress since the early 1990s.
If Democrats win all the races where they are leading, they will have 260 seats, the most since the 102nd Congress, which spanned 1991 to 1993.
Loading...
Democrats controlled the House for 40 years until the 1994 Republican Revolution that ushered in GOP control of Congress.
This century has seen some of the slimmest House majorities in American history and the most changes of party control of the chamber in 130 years. Starting in January, control of the House will have changed hands five times in the last 20 years. In a 20-year stretch in the post-Reconstruction era after the Civil War, there were six changeovers of the House, beginning in 1875.
Now, three decades after former House Speaker Newt Gingrich's "Contract with America" — and a decade into Trump's grip on the Republican Party — House Republicans are back to where they were before the Republican Revolution.

noticias.titulo: The U.N.'s top court rules Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya
noticias.resumen: The International Court of Justice found that Myanmar security forces "acted with genocidal intent" against the Rohingya during military operations in the northern Rakhine state in 2017.
noticias.texto:
The U.N.'s top court rules Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya
International Court of Justice issues ruling on Myanmar genocide case
The United Nations' top court ruled Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, the first time in the court's 80-year history that it has held a state responsible for the crime.
Judges of the International Court of Justice voted 9-6 that the military's 2017 crackdown was carried out with intent to destroy the long-persecuted Muslim minority. Myanmar's military-backed government has not yet responded to the ruling at the time of writing.
Brought by Gambia under the 1948 Genocide Convention, the ruling will have repercussions far beyond Myanmar, according to a legal expert.
But for Ma Roga Bibi, a Rohingya who fled Maungdaw township in northern Rakhine state, the impact was immediate.
"I feel wonderful and grateful," said the 18-year-old, who lives in the world's largest refugee settlement in Bangladesh. "It was an emotional, historic day."
Genocidal campaign
For several weeks in August and September 2017, the Myanmar military attacked and burned to the ground hundreds of Rohingya villages. Soldiers committed rapes and massacred women, men as well as children.
The court estimated that about 10,000 Rohingya were killed. It cited estimates that up to 2,109 Rohingya children younger than 5 died, and found the violence was systematic, including the burning of all or parts of 392 villages.
Ma Roga Bibi, then age 9, was one of about 700,000 people to flee to Bangladesh, joining earlier refugee waves. The camps sprawl across a narrow coastal strip a few miles from Cox's Bazar, a busy beach town near Myanmar. Rohingya are denied citizenship on both sides of the border.
"Recognition alone is not enough," she said. "We need justice, accountability, and the opportunity to return home with dignity."
She wants to be a doctor, adding, "in our Rohingya community, there is no girl doctor."
Khin Khin Myint, 18, a refugee leader in activist group Rohingya Youth Voice from Buthidaung Township, also in Camp 16, said Rohingya women and girls have experienced "unimaginable suffering."
"We want the world to listen to survivors, recognize their courage, and include women in decisions about our future," she said. "We expect the international community to move beyond a statement of sympathy."
Rejected defense
Myanmar had argued its military was conducting counterinsurgency operations against an armed group, the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army. The court said the military failed to distinguish between civilians and alleged insurgents, and that the scale and nature of the violence could not be explained by counterterrorism.
"The execution of Rohingya men and boys in some locations, the widespread sexual violence, the targeting of children and babies, the methodical burning of villages, and attacks on fleeing civilians are not consistent with an intent to conduct counterinsurgency operations," said ICJ president, Judge Yuji Iwasawa.
Antonia Mulvey, executive director of Legal Action Worldwide, a human rights group based in Geneva, said the court found evidence from the U.N. and rights organizations credible, and that counterterrorism operations were not a defense to Myanmar's argument.
She said the ruling will affect future genocide cases, including South Africa's case against Israel, on questions such as genocidal intent and state responsibility.
"Although every case must ultimately be decided on its own evidence," she said.
The judgment is binding on Myanmar and on all states that have ratified the Genocide Convention, she explained. All countries should review trade agreements, including arms and jet fuel supplies, and financial and economic ties with the junta, she said, while supporting accountability and reparations for the Rohingya. But the court, which hears disputes between states, can't enforce its decisions.
A group long denied recognition
In Myanmar, Rohingya are widely regarded as interlopers from Bangladesh, despite generations of roots in Myanmar.
Iwasawa, however, identified the Rohingya as a distinct ethnic group, saying their language and art set them apart, and that they self-identify as such. He said they have been discriminated against by Myanmar "for decades" and qualify as a protected group.
The United States had previously reached a similar conclusion. In 2022, the Biden administration formally determined that Myanmar's military had committed genocide and crimes against humanity against the Rohingya during its 2016 and 2017 operations.
But tensions have mounted between the Trump administration and international justice bodies. In a statement to NPR on Thursday, the State Department expressed support for Rohingya refugees but raised doubts about the International Court of Justice. "The proper interpretation of the Genocide Convention is of paramount importance, as is preventing politicization of the ICJ. We are studying the decision to fully assess its implications," the State Department said.
In October, U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz wrote online, "The ICJ must not be allowed to lower the legal threshold for proving genocide" so it can later be weaponized against U.S. and allied soldiers.
Yet international human rights organizations and the United Nations applauded the court's judgment.
U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres called it "a powerful recognition of the Rohingya victims of genocide" and said it reaffirms that "impunity for such horrific acts must not stand."
The judgment does not order Myanmar to grant citizenship, saying such the issue fell outside the scope of the measures being considered to prevent future atrocities.
However, Myanmar must take steps to investigate people suspected of involvement in the crimes and prosecute them if warranted, said the court. It also found Myanmar must provide restitution and compensation, with the amount to be set in future proceedings.
The order to enable displaced Rohingya to return runs into a hard reality: The territory is now controlled by ethnic Rakhine armed group the Arakan Army.
Rakhine state has been ravaged by conflict between the military and the group, which now controls most of it.
Su Mon, a senior analyst at the independent conflict monitor Armed Conflict Location & Event Data, said the Rohingya in Myanmar and in the camps are "threatened by multiple armed groups," including Rohingya armed groups, the Arakan Army and the military.
Nearly all are stateless, she said, with few viable ways to earn a living or get food. Many are "on the verge of acute famine" because of aid shortfalls in the camps and a junta blockade in Rakhine.
"Unless the broader conflict dynamics in Rakhine state improve or credible guarantees of safety are secured from all armed actors, the prospects for displaced Rohingya to return to their homes remain bleak," she added.
She urged the military to halt airstrikes, drone attacks and the use of advanced weaponry in northern Rakhine, lift its blockade and give humanitarian groups full access, including in Arakan Army-controlled areas.
Lorcán Lovett reported from Thailand. Michele Kelemen contributed reporting from Washington, D.C.

noticias.titulo: World Toilet Day is a funny idea with a serious goal: A world awash in toilets
noticias.resumen: Yahoo for the loo! November 19 marks the 25th anniversary of World Toilet Day. The theme this year: "Sanitation and Gender Equality: Safe Toilets, Equal Futures."
noticias.texto:
World Toilet Day is a funny idea with a serious goal: A world awash in toilets
Twenty-five years ago, Jack Sim was flush with excitement. (Please pardon the pun.)
The Singapore entrepreneur was looking for a meaningful project and came upon this thought from the prime minister: "He said we should measure our graciousness according to the cleanliness of our public toilets," Sim recalls.
Thus was born World Toilet Day. The goal was more than cleanliness. It was access, too — billions of people do not have a safe and sanitary toilet to use.
Enshrined as an official U.N. day in 2013, World Toilet Day aims to get people talking and thinking about a topic that maybe is a taboo in polite conversation.
Let's eschew the euphemisms
World Toilet Day is all about peeing, pooping and addressing menstrual hygiene in a clean and safe manner — followed by the "conveyance" of excreta to a sanitary disposal system, notes Kate Olive Medlicott, the sanitation and waste team leader within the WASH team at the World Health Organization. Human diseases are shed in sewage, so a top-notch sanitation system is critical, says Medlicott. Cholera is linked to sewage. Polio is, too.
This year's World Toilet Day theme is "Sanitation and Gender Equality: Safe Toilets, Equal Futures." Even though everyone suffers when they can't find a toilet, the menstrual cycle creates additional complications. If schools or offices lack a safe and sanitary place to attend to period needs and to dispose of period products, girls and women may opt to stay home.
There is another gender issue. Sofia Calltorp, the U.N. Women global head of humanitarian action, says: "When women and girls do not have access to safe toilets," they leave their home and look for a public toilet or a secluded space to do their business, often venturing into unsafe areas. "There is a huge impact in terms of being exposed to harassment or violence," Calltorp says. She points to refugee camps as a place where this issue often arises, with unlit toilets that aren't differentiated by gender.
Now you might well ask: Has World Toilet Day made a difference?
The toilet titans we interviewed say yes, it has, just by talking about toilets in the public arena. The U.N. has stated that access to safe sanitation is a human right. And in just about every country, progress has been made in improving access to sanitary facilities. Since 2015, 1.2 billion people have become part of the world of safely managed sanitation systems.
What are the next steps? Kellogg Schwab, who specializes in water and wastewater contaminants of public health concern at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, stresses that governments should be a force for change but that it shouldn't be top down. It should also be … oh, forgive me again … bottom up. Schwab suggests giving money to communities to figure out what solutions they can come up with to improve the toilet and sanitation situation. There will be flops. But there will be successes that can be scaled up.
So maybe one day — Medlicott of WHO thinks in 50 years or so —- Earthlings will look back and say, How curious that in a world of wealth there were not enough safe and secure toilets.
A toast to toilets
Let's end by reflecting on the present day.
"World Toilet Day is my favorite day of the year," says Medlicott. "People find it fun and funny but it's really important to celebrate and act on something we take for granted."
If you're among the population where toilets are plentiful, she suggests pausing to think of a moment — it's happened to all of us — when you needed a bathroom and couldn't find one. Maybe that incident has turned into a funny story you share with friends. Now imagine if it were to happen every day.
I am deeply thankful that all I need to do is walk down the office hallway to find a clean and private loo.
For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

noticias.titulo: Anthropic raises more than $100B in IPO. And, Dems nominate Jeffries for House speaker
noticias.resumen: Despite growing concern over a possible AI bubble, Anthropic had a record-breaking initial public offering. And, Hakeem Jeffries could become the first Black Speaker of the House.
noticias.texto:
Anthropic raises more than $100B in IPO. And, Dems nominate Jeffries for House speaker
Trump Trilateral Summit In China, House Democratic Leadership, Anthropic IPO
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.
Today's top stories
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has received the House Democrats' nomination to become speaker when the party regains the majority in the new year. This nomination, confirmed by a closed-door vote of 251 to 11, marks the start of the formal selection process for speaker. It will culminate in a House floor vote on Jan. 3, at the start of the new Congress. If successful, Jeffries will make history as the first Black Speaker of the House. Jeffries said after the closed door vote that he is committed to addressing cost-of-living issues, pledging to fight for lower costs in groceries, gas, housing and healthcare.
- 🎧 Jeffries, who has served as the top Democrat in the minority since 2023, ran unopposed for the speaker position. But that is not the case in the Senate, NPR's Elena Moore tells Up First. Current minority leader Sen. Chuck Schumer faces a challenge from Sen. Chris Van Hollen for majority leader. Van Hollen has positioned himself as an anti-status quo, progressive leader. Both Van Hollen and Schumer have served in Congress for decades. The vote for that Senate position is set for early December.
- ➡️ Rep. Robert Garcia, poised to chair the House Oversight Committee, sent document-preservation letters to more than a dozen of President Trump's allies and family members in preparation for investigations starting in January. These letters focus on four main areas: "Trump family corruption, corporate corruption, DHS misconduct and the White House Epstein cover-up."
Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping met today in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum. Xi and Putin met separately the night before the trilateral meeting. Trump also had one-on-one meetings with Putin and Xi. It's the first time the three leaders have held a summit together.
- 🎧 The three leaders had different agendas as they went into their meeting, NPR's Jennifer Pak says. Trump aimed to prioritize nuclear arms control. He said that they had a unique opportunity to reduce nuclear weapons, a stance Beijing has typically resisted due to its smaller stockpile compared to the U.S. and Russia. Putin sought discussions to end the war in Ukraine, but on Moscow's terms. The complexity of these issues makes substantial outcomes unlikely, Pak says. Xi aimed to position China as a stabilizing global force by bringing together Russia, its old ally, and the U.S., its direct competitor.
Anthropic is set to debut on the Nasdaq exchange today. The company raised more than $100 billion in a record-breaking initial public offering that valued the company at around $1.5 trillion. The company sold 956 million shares at $83 each, surpassing its initial target range of $70 to $78. The seven founders sold over 23 million shares as part of the IPO, and the company's prospectus outlines plans to introduce an extra $26 billion in shares through private placements with Google, Microsoft and Nvidia.
- 🎧 In its IPO filing, Anthropic was optimistic that AI would have a bigger impact on the economy than industrialization, electricity, semiconductors and the internet, NPR's John Ruwitch says. The company's paperwork suggested that the addressable market for Anthropic's products could be as big as $40 trillion annually, exceeding the GDP of the United States. But CEO Dario Amodei has been outspoken about the danger of losing control over AI. The prospectus flagged some political risks, including the company's current dispute with the Pentagon over how its models can be used. Ruwitch says that now that Anthropic and SpaceX are on the market, OpenAI could potentially join next year.
Watch this
Go face-to-face with the person of the moment. NPR's Newsmakers video podcast brings the biggest names in politics, business, sports, arts, and culture out of the headlines and into the interview chair to discuss the mark they're making on the world. Follow the Newsmakers podcast or subscribe to NPR's YouTube channel to get new episodes as soon as they're available.
Ben Shapiro says he remains committed to his values during Trump's turbulent presidency. The conservative podcast host voted against Trump in 2016, but actively campaigned for him in 2024. Shapiro expressed disappointment in the president's tariffs, alleged corruption and the handling of the war in Iran. He says that Trump's strict immigration policies and the "whiff of corruption" surrounding the White House contributed to the GOP's midterm losses. The co-founder of the media company The Daily Wire warns that Republicans face an "uphill road in 2028," and he doesn't see Vice President JD Vance as the right GOP presidential candidate. Shapiro argues that Vance could alienate key voter groups like Hispanics, the working class, women and the college-educated. In conversation with Morning Edition's Steve Inskeep, Shapiro discussed who he thinks could be a potential 2028 GOP candidate, his new movie, Confession, and the recent decline in his show's YouTube subscriptions.
Watch or listen to the interview or read the article about their discussion.
Today's listen
The West-Eastern Divan Orchestra is an ensemble founded by Edward Said and Daniel Barenboim nearly 30 years ago in Germany to unite Middle Eastern musicians. Despite the deep personal grief and heightened tensions following the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, and the Gaza war, members of the orchestra strive to confront, rather than sidestep, political realities. Longtime musicians say Barenboim has helped them bridge painful cultural divides and foster enduring cross-border friendships. The space has also given some participants a safe space to discuss Gaza, allowing music to resolve the dissonance.
3 things to know before you go
- Abdelrahman ElGendy has won the National Book Awards' non-fiction prize for his memoir, Huna, which recounts his six years as a political prisoner in Egypt.
- "Choosin' Texas" singer Ella Langley won six of the seven categories she was nominated for, including song of the year, at the Country Music Awards.
- In this week's edition of Far-Flung Postcards, NPR's Esme Nicholson sends greetings from a Berlin square, where children play around a Käthe Kollwitz bronze cast. In the wake of World War I, the German artist's work often portrayed undernourished children in their mothers' arms.
This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

noticias.titulo: Incoming House majority leader Katherine Clark stresses Democratic unity
noticias.resumen: As Democrats prepare to take control of the House, incoming majority leader Katherine Clark discusses the party's ambitious agenda and divisions within its ranks.
noticias.texto:
Incoming House majority leader Katherine Clark stresses Democratic unity
Rep. Katherine Clark, D-Mass., on the Democratic Party's agenda for the new Congress
House Democrats needed a bigger room Wednesday to accommodate their newly expanded caucus, according to Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts.
Nominated to become the first woman to serve as House majority leader next year, Clark reflected on the moment in an interview with Morning Edition on Thursday.
"It was really looking at the diversity of that caucus, people who have been sent to Congress from all walks of life, that gives me the optimism and the energy that we can really deliver for the American people," she said.
Clark, who is currently the House minority whip, was nominated for House majority leader by a unanimous voice vote. Democrats also nominated Hakeem Jeffries for speaker and Pete Aguilar for majority whip.
The incoming leadership faces the challenge of lowering living costs while investigating alleged corruption in the Trump administration.
"Of course we can," she said when asked whether Democrats could accomplish both. "That's our responsibility."
She also called President Trump's description of himself as "Mr. Veto" a "stunning statement," expressing hope for bipartisan cooperation on healthcare.
But Democrats face divisions within their own ranks.
Jeffries won his nomination 251-11. Opposition came from incoming progressives including Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York and Adam Hamawy of New Jersey. They have pressed for Medicare for All, immigration enforcement reforms and an end to the war in Gaza.
The two leaders have differed over U.S. aid to Israel. In July, Clark voted for a Republican amendment that would have cut aid to Israel, while Jeffries opposed it.
Despite that disagreement and concerns among other Democrats about Jeffries' leadership, she emphasized party unity when asked whether the 11 votes against him could complicate Democrats' agenda.
"We are having conversations with every part of our new caucus, and they are united behind making life better for working people," she said.
Listen to the full interview by clicking on the blue button above.
The radio interview was edited by Ally Schweitzer. The web copy was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

noticias.titulo: Muslims will outnumber Christians worldwide by 2035, report says
noticias.resumen: By 2070, the Democratic Republic of the Congo will surpass the United States as the country with the largest total number of Christians.
noticias.texto:
Muslims will outnumber Christians worldwide by 2035, report says
Muslims will soon become the largest religious group on the planet, according to a new report by the Pew Research Center released today.
Christians will be the second-largest cohort by 2035. The Muslim and Christian populations are both expected to grow, but researchers anticipate Muslims will grow faster.
If recent demographic trends continue, Pew expects the world's Muslim population will reach 3.6 billion by 2070 while the Christian population will be just under 3 billion.
The Pew Research Center arrived at its projections using data from national censuses worldwide, combined with data on fertility rates and religious switching patterns. The projections also use findings from United Nations reports and global migration estimates, along with Pew Research Center's earlier studies on religious migration.
Hindus and Jews are projected to grow in absolute numbers but decline as an overall percentage of the world population. Buddhists, meanwhile, are expected to shrink in both number and portion of the global population in the coming decades.
Some of these trends, according to Pew, can be explained by population growth trends. For instance, most of the population growth in the 21st century is expected to occur in Africa.
By 2070, more than a quarter of the global population will live in sub-Saharan Africa. The vast majority of those who live there are either Christian or Muslim. The region's high fertility rate and lengthening lifespans mean the numbers of both faiths there are expected to grow, with the Muslim population growing faster than the Christian one.
In fact, Pew projects that by 2070, the Democratic Republic of the Congo in sub-Saharan Africa will surpass the United States as the country with the largest total number of Christians. The Pew Center's religion research director Alan Cooperman calls this a "global change in what one might think of as the center of gravity of Christianity."
Birth rates drive religious shifts
Pew points out that differences in fertility rates have major effects on religious populations. Around the world, Muslims tend to have more children than people of other faiths. In recent years, the fertility rate for Muslims has been 3.1 children per woman. The average rate for non-Muslim women has been about 2 per woman.
Among the other religious trends anticipated by 2070 in the Pew Research Center's report: The overall populations of China, Japan, and South Korea will shrink, and their Buddhist populations will shrink by half. And, an increasing portion of the world's Jews will live in Israel. In 2020, 46% of global Jewry lived there, but Pew projects that by 2070, 62% of Jews will live in Israel.
One of the more surprising projections is that while the percentage of people who identify as having no religious affiliation will increase in many countries, the global population of "nones" is expected to drop. The reason for this is that a very large portion of the religiously unaffiliated live in China, and that country is expected to have dramatic population losses in the coming decades due to dropping birth rates there.
U.S. religious trends reflect overall global patterns
The report also details how religious change will affect the United States. Pew says the U.S. will no longer have a Christian majority by 2070, yet Christians will remain the largest single religious group in the country. Christians are expected to decline to just under 48% of the population. (They currently make up 62% of the U.S.) During this same period, the percentage of the population of those who are religiously unaffiliated is expected to rise to 41%.
The anticipated population change in the U.S. among Christians and the religiously unaffiliated will be driven mostly by people changing their religion rather than by birth rates, according to the report. Christians tend to shed more adherents than they gain through what demographers call "religious switching," most of whom switch to being religious "nones" rather than taking on another tradition.
The U.S. is expected to become increasingly religiously diverse, with Pew projecting that both Muslims and Hindus in the country will outnumber Jews by 2070 if current demographic trends continue. 
Correction Nov. 18, 2026
A previous version of this headline incorrectly said Muslims would outnumber Christians by 2070. They will outnumber Christians by 2035.

noticias.titulo: US defence secretary Pete Hegseth lands in Ecuador on Latin America anti-narcotics tour
noticias.resumen: The US defence secretary, under fire for his role in the Iran war and illegal bombings in the Caribbean and Pacific, has announced a military pact with Venezuela. His next stop is Honduras.
noticias.texto:
The US defence secretary, under fire for his role in the Iran war and illegal bombings in the Caribbean and Pacific, has announced a military pact with Venezuela. His next stop is Honduras.
United States Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth landed in Ecuador on Thursday as part of his South American tour, after brief visits to Colombia and Venezuela, where he pledged to eliminate and defeat narcoterrorists.
Ecuador's president, Daniel Noboa, is ideologically aligned with the Trump administration and has driven a growing militarisation of the country's cities, in line with other conservative populist leaders in the region.
Hegseth's trip to Latin America comes after an attempt by United States lawmakers, including a Republican representative, to remove him from office, prompted by the war against Iran and by air strikes without legal backing on several vessels suspected of drug trafficking over the past year, causing the deaths of more than 200 people.
The Defence Secretary will later make a brief visit to Honduras, according to the country's press office, where he will meet at a nearby air base with Nasry Asfura, another leader allied with Trump. This is the Pentagon chief's first official visit to South America, which has included a meeting with Venezuela's interim president, Delcy Rodríguez.
As part of his trip to Venezuela, Hegseth announced that he would increase military cooperation with the post-Maduro regime and promised to hunt down drug traffickers.

noticias.titulo: At least one dead and dozens missing after migrant boat capsizes off Senegal en route to Spain
noticias.resumen: The latest sinking comes amid a sharp rise in departures towards the Canary Islands, with more than 11,000 people reaching the Spanish archipelago in the first two weeks of November.
noticias.texto:
The latest sinking comes amid a sharp rise in departures towards the Canary Islands, with more than 11,000 people reaching the Spanish archipelago in the first two weeks of November.
At least one person has died, and dozens more are missing after a boat carrying around 100 migrants capsized off the coast of Senegal while attempting to reach Spain, local officials have said.
The latest incident, which is thought to have happened in the early hours of Wednesday morning, comes amid a surge in departures towards the Canary Islands, with more than 11,000 people reaching the archipelago in the first half of November alone.
The boat, described by some sources as “rickety”, sank off the coast of Yenne, a town south of the Senegalese capital, Dakar.
“The accident happened around 3 a.m.," said Ousmane Sène, secretary general of the Yenne mayor's office.
“When we went to the scene, we saw the boat on the shore.”
Sène added that firefighters recovered one body while police arrested one survivor.
According to other survivors, there were around 100 people on board at the time it sank.
Sène confirmed that two other bodies were also recovered in nearby villages, but it’s not clear if they were people who drowned in this particular incident.
Recently, Senegalese coastal areas have become major departure points for migrants attempting the treacherous sea journey to Europe. Many of them are hoping to reach Spain’s Canary Islands, an archipelago off West Africa which lies more than 1,000 kilometres south of the European mainland.
According to Spanish government figures, more than 11,000 migrants reached the Canaries in the first half of November – that number was more than half the total for all of 2025.
This week’s sinking comes shortly after a disaster which saw at least 39 people die after a migrant boat sank near the town of Kébémer in northern Senegal.
Senegalese authorities are making efforts to crack down on people attempting the dangerous migration route and have made dozens of arrests.
On Wednesday, the country’s navy said it had “rescued” over 1,400 migrants at sea in just 48 hours.
Also on Wednesday, Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye spoke out against the resurgence of migrant departures toward Europe and called for strengthened controls along Senegal's coasts, too.
“The acceleration and complexity of irregular migration demonstrate the urgency for the government to intensify... the diligent and efficient implementation of public policies concerning youth, education, vocational training, youth employment and entrepreneurship, as well as the economic empowerment of women,” said Faye.

noticias.titulo: France to monitor YouTubers for political bias ahead of 2027 election
noticias.resumen: France will hold its presidential election on 18 April and 2 May next year, with far-right leader Marine Le Pen currently leading in opinion polls. Parliamentary elections are expected to follow in June.
noticias.texto:
France will hold its presidential election on 18 April and 2 May next year, with far-right leader Marine Le Pen currently leading in opinion polls. Parliamentary elections are expected to follow in June.
France's media regulator, Arcom, announced on Thursday that it will monitor online influencers and content creators for political bias ahead of next year's presidential election, marking a major expansion of its powers.
The change reflects the growing influence of YouTubers and other content creators, whose audiences, particularly among young people, can sometimes be larger than those of traditional media outlets.
"There's a new phenomenon, it’s here and it's massive," Arcom president Martin Ajdari announced at a press conference in Paris.
Under Arcom's rules, presidential candidates must receive airtime proportionate to their projected electoral support during the initial phase of the campaign. However, from 5 to 30 April, all candidates must be given equal airtime.
Ajdari stressed that Arcom would only monitor major French video content creators, while audio-only podcasters would not be affected.
"This issue arises in very concrete terms for creators whose audiences exceed those of traditional television channels," Ajdari added.
France has been at the forefront of efforts to regulate online content, passing legislation in 2023 that introduced potential prison sentences and fines for influencers who fail to disclose paid promotions or advertise fraudulent products.

noticias.titulo: Macron backs reopening 'the question' of Ukraine's NATO accession
noticias.resumen: French President Emmanuel Macron said that Ukraine's NATO accession was brushed aside in early 2022 in a "completely different" context.
noticias.texto:
French President Emmanuel Macron said that Ukraine's NATO accession was brushed aside in early 2022 in a "completely different" context.
French President Emmanuel Macron backed "reopening the question" of Ukraine's NATO membership on Thursday, while urging Kyiv's allies to do the "maximum" to provide it with the necessary air defence systems.
"Faced with the maximalist nature of the Russian position, I believe we need to reopen the question of Ukraine's accession to NATO," said Macron, following a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in Berlin, co-chaired by France and the UK.
Macron stated that Ukraine’s NATO accession had been set aside in early 2022, albeit in a "completely different" context.
Following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Western allies ruled out Kyiv's NATO's membership for the short-term, fearing that admitting a country at war with Russia could trigger a direct NATO–Russia confrontation under Article 5.
Following two day US-mediated peace talks in Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy declared that US negotiators had floated the idea of Ukraine withdrawing from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for NATO membership.
He said that Kyiv was not prepared to concede territory, but said that "specific security guarantees" were being discussed with NATO and the EU.
"The question arises, including for us Europeans, of what happens the day after, because Ukraine will be a country with a very well-equipped and sizeable army. For our long-term security, Ukraine’s membership of NATO makes sense", stated Macron.
Macron's remarks came hours after Russian President Vladimir Putin, US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping held a historic trilateral in China.
Zelenskyy added that if Western countries laid out assurances, he would consult Ukrainian society on the proposition, saying he had “no right to make this decision alone”.

noticias.titulo: European leaders reject 'Yalta 2.0' for Ukraine after Trump meets Putin and Xi
noticias.resumen: "A Yalta format will not bring peace," German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said at the end of a Coalition of the Willing meeting in Berlin just hours after Trump, Putin and Xi held talks in China.
noticias.texto:
"A Yalta format will not bring peace," German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said at the end of a Coalition of the Willing meeting in Berlin just hours after Trump, Putin and Xi held talks in China.
European leaders have forcefully rejected any attempts to re-enact the 1945 Yalta Conference to end Russia's war on Ukraine and split the continent into spheres of influence.
The pushback went public on Thursday at a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing, comprising Kyiv's allies, hosted by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
The gathering in Berlin took place just hours after Russian President Vladimir Putin, US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping held a historic trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China, dubbed "Yalta 2.0" by media commentators.
Trump, Putin and Xi discussed Ukraine, but their joint statement, titled "Declaration Toward Peace", did not mention the country.
"A Yalta format will not bring peace," Merz said, flanked by other leaders.
"At Yalta, Europe was divided up. It was parcelled up. And we won't allow anything like that to happen again."
Merz gifted the over 40 delegations that took part in the talks a piece of the Berlin Wall, which, he said, is "what Yalta represented".
By his side, French President Emmanuel Macron said the four-point statement issued by Trump, Putin and Xi in Shenzhen did not replicate the outcome of the 1945 conference, which set the stage for the four-decade-long Cold War.
"I don't think that it amounts to a reorganisation of the world," he said.
"If there is one critical element for the reorganisation of Europe and its security, it is the meeting that took place (today) in Berlin."
Macron stressed that negotiations to end the war would need to involve Ukraine, Europe, the US and Russia seated at the same table.
"Europeans have taken decisions. They have decided to determine their own fate," the French president said. "Europe is not a subject on a menu of discussions, but a series of powers who want to build their own future".
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham echoed Macron's message, saying "there is no decision about Ukraine without Ukraine in the room (and) there's no decision about European security without Europe represented in the room".
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the meeting in Berlin bore "testament" to Russia's failure to sow division among European allies.
The four leaders agreed that the time has come for Europe to engage in face-to-face negotiations with Russia, marking a step that has yet to take place in the negotiation process.
Europe has appointed a joint team of seven representatives from France, the UK, Germany, Poland, Italy, the EU institutions and NATO for the next round of talks.
US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who flew to Berlin to attend the meeting, also called on Russia to allow European participation.
"We do believe that having Europe at the table will be essential to ending this war in a just and long-term, durable way," Kushner said at the closing press conference.
"And the Russians are willing to trust that instinct on our behalf."
Moscow, though, has not committed to a multilateral format.
Speaking in Shenzhen, Putin said he had suggested "via diplomatic channels that the Europeans come to Moscow to define their positions," and, after that, the Kremlin would "decide on continuing the dialogue with Ukraine".
Putin also said that it "would be strange to discuss Europe's security without Europe itself", referring to the demands that Moscow has tabled to restructure the continent's security architecture, which Macron slammed as "maximalist".
Merz said the debate on European security would happen only after peace has been established in Ukraine. The future security guarantees to the war-weary country will inherently have "repercussions" for the transatlantic alliance, he said.
Among the guarantees in the works is a clause emulating NATO's Article 5 of collective defence should Russia attack Ukraine again. Another guarantee would be a Europe-led peacekeeping force, which Putin says he would not allow in any scenario.
"From America's perspective, giving an Article 5-like security guarantee is a really, really big deal," Kushner said. "And I think that that's something that President Trump is open to, but obviously it has to be in America's interest to do that."
During the closed-door discussions in Berlin, Trump phoned in from his plane and addressed the room, Kushner confirmed. Media reports suggest that Trump expressed scepticism about Europe's military support for Ukraine.
Leaders seemed unmoved and agreed that assistance will continue unabatedto put Ukraine in a strong position at the negotiating table.
"I hope that message is heard very clearly in Moscow," Burnham said.
"For as long as it takes, we will be there at the side of Ukraine, and we will not falter. Our support will be unwavering. And that's the biggest weapon we have together."

noticias.texto:
The US, Chinese and Russian leaders pledged to hold talks on nuclear risk reduction, but made no mention of North Korea in their joint peace declaration.
US President Donald Trump left China on Thursday without meeting North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, a get-together he had sought during his visit to Shenzhen for a rare three-way meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.
Trump had repeatedly raised the possibility of meeting Kim during his Asia trip, although a White House official had said no such meeting was planned.
“We may meet with Kim Jong-un also, so that'll be good,” Trump told reporters at the White House on Monday.
Meanwhile, Kim inspected sites in North Korea’s South Hamgyong province on Tuesday and Wednesday, according to South Korean news agency Newsis.
The two leaders have not met face-to-face since June 2019.
Although the three leaders agreed to pursue dialogue on nuclear risk reduction and non-proliferation, the joint “peace declaration” made no explicit reference to the Korean Peninsula or Taiwan.
However, Chinese state news agency Xinhua later reported that the three leaders had exchanged views on the Korean Peninsula, Ukraine, nuclear non-proliferation and the situation in the Middle East.
The summit has fuelled concerns in South Korea, Japan and Taiwan that major powers could make decisions affecting regional security without consulting those directly affected.
South Korea fears being sidelined
Before the three-way meeting, South Korean media compared it to the Yalta Conference in 1945, where leaders of the US, the UK and the Soviet Union discussed the post-war international order.
Seoul has been keen to avoid major powers making decisions on the Korean peninsula without its involvement.
Although the omission of the Korean peninsula from the declaration has somewhat alleviated concerns over a second Yalta, it has raised concerns that denuclearisation is slipping down the major powers’ diplomatic agenda, according to South Korean news outlet Money Today.
Park Won-gon, a professor of North Korean studies at Ewha Womans University, told the outlet that China and Russia may have sided with Pyongyang.
Kim Jae-chun, a professor at Sogang University, said the three powers view North Korea’s nuclear programme very differently.
However, Newsis suggested that the absence of a Trump-Kim meeting for the second consecutive year may ease concerns over potential US recognition of North Korea as a nuclear-armed state.
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung reiterated, during Thursday’s APEC summit, the importance of achieving peace and stability on the Korean peninsula to bring prosperity to the region.
Japan seeks reassurances from Washington
The three-way meeting has raised concerns in Japan, where relations with Beijing are tense.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi exchanged greetings with Xi during APEC, but the two leaders did not meet formally.
A Japanese ruling-party lawmaker said Japan’s exclusion from the three-way meeting could be seen as a diplomatic setback, Fuji TV reported.
However, Takaichi said at a press briefing in Shenzhen that she did not believe Japan’s interests would be undermined by the summit, Japanese broadcaster TBS reported.
Takaichi is also arranging a phone call with Trump to discuss the outcome of his talks with Xi and Putin and reaffirm bilateral cooperation, TV Asahi reported, citing Japanese government sources.
Japanese media also highlighted the three powers’ position on the International Criminal Court (ICC), which is currently headed by Japanese judge Tomoko Akane.
The joint declaration called for respect for the immunity of state officials and said that the ICC and similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction.
In March 2023, the court issued an arrest warrant for Putin over the alleged unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children.
Taiwan wary of great-power diplomacy
As with South Korea, mentions of "Yalta 2.0" emerged in Taiwanese media in the lead-up to the meeting. Taiwanese broadcaster TVBS highlighted concerns that Taiwan could be used as a bargaining chip in the negotiations.
The question of Taiwan was raised in the bilateral meeting between Xi and Trump earlier on Thursday.
Tsai Jung-hsiang, a professor of political science at National Chung Cheng University in Taiwan, told the island’s Central News Agency that the US and China have very different views on strategic stability.
While Trump has aimed to avoid conflict over Taiwan during his time in office, Xi wanted the US to recognise Beijing’s position on sovereignty and territorial integrity, Tsai said.
However, he said he did not expect any changes to US policy regarding Taiwan as a result of the meeting.
State-run media in China said the three-way meeting allowed the three major powers to work together to promote international security and stability.
Xi said the meeting was “positive, constructive and fruitful”, as the three nations were committed to “world peace”, Xinhua reported.
Earlier, Xi said the three nations should hold regular high-level meetings and establish mechanisms to prevent and manage crises.
Neither proposal was explicitly included in the four-point peace declaration.

noticias.titulo: Euronews Verify: Is Hungary turning the page on its rule of law problems?
noticias.resumen: Hungary is under new leadership, and reforms are underway. But can Péter Magyar restore the rule of law and win back the EU's trust?
noticias.texto:
Hungary is under new leadership, and reforms are underway. But can Péter Magyar restore the rule of law and win back the EU's trust?
EU affairs ministers met on Thursday, 19 November, for the EU's annual rule of law dialogue, which examines judicial independence, corruption, media freedom, and institutional checks and balances.
This is a regular review, not a special hearing against Hungary or a vote on sanctions.
However, the timing is significant, as Brussels assesses whether the changes under Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar are delivering lasting results.
"I think we have seen clear efforts to break with the rule of law situation that has existed under Viktor Orbán and that the new government under Magyar has really put an effort into implementing reforms to restore judicial independence," Thu Nguyen, the Acting Co-Director at the Jacques Delors Centre, told Euronews Verify.
Why is the EU still keeping Hungary under scrutiny?
Since taking office in 2026, Magyar's government has moved quickly to reverse some of the policies that put Hungary on a collision course with the EU.
The emergency rule by decree has ended.
The controversial Sovereignty Protection Office, which investigated civil society organisations and media outlets, has been abolished.
Hungary has also joined the European Public Prosecutor's Office and introduced new anti-corruption and judicial reforms.
A European Parliament delegation visiting Hungary in October praised the pace of these changes, describing them as substantial progress.
Despite all that, Hungary is also still subject to a separate EU procedure known as Article 7.
Launched in 2018, it addresses concerns about a serious risk to the EU's founding values, including democracy, the rule of law and fundamental rights.
Could the UK rejoin the EU?
Today's episode also focuses on the long-awaited EU-UK summit that will take place this Friday, 20 November.
After a decade of Brexit, London now wants closer ties with Brussels, not a divorce.
And there is public support too: 56% of Britons would now vote to rejoin.
The reset began under Keir Starmer and picked up pace under Andy Burnham, who stirred the Brexit debate but stopped short of committing to rejoining.
Five European leaders have called for closer collaboration in areas, including on energy.
But will the UK be able to re-join under the same conditions as before, including its opt-outs?
"If the UK were to rejoin the EU, it would not be rejoining the EU that it left," said Sébastien Maillard, associate fellow at Chatham House.
"It's much more a geopolitical EU that would be joining, and it has to be ready [...] to accept the idea of European sovereignty. I think if the UK is ready to go fully on the idea that there is a need to side with the EU as a member state, to build sovereign capacities independently from the US or from China, then it can negotiate all kinds of opt-outs."
How long would it take for the UK to rejoin the bloc?
The UK's Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, has held off on the possibility that he could ask to rejoin at some stage, while ruling out major changes before the next election.
"This government has been clear that at least until the next election they are still committed to those red lines, so we wouldn't expect to see the UK's relationship change in this parliament with the European Union," said Oliver Nicholls, senior policy manager of Best for Britain
Yet, the first step to rejoin the bloc is getting the conversation started in the UK.

In just under 11 minutes, our new format goes beyond the headlines to make sense of what's happening, fact-checking and untangling the day's most pressing issues to explain why they matter to you.

noticias.titulo: US: Protesters warn of AI bubble as Anthropic makes stock market history
noticias.resumen: Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut with a record-breaking IPO valuing the AI company at $1.5 trillion. Outside the exchange in New York, police detained three protesters warning of financial risks.
noticias.texto:
Priced at $83 a share, the artificial intelligence company behind the Claude chatbot raised over $80 billion and achieved a $1.5 trillion valuation on its Wall Street debut. Inside Nasdaq, co-founders Dario and Daniela Amodei rang the opening bell to celebrate the start of trading; outside, protesters chanted against the flotation and the concentration of tech-sector wealth in a demonstration that saw three people detained by police.
The listing overtook SpaceX’s blockbuster June offering, highlighting relentless investor enthusiasm for AI despite growing talk of overheated technology valuations. Robust demand carried the share price clear of its earlier $70 to $78 guide range. Yet demonstrators warned that ordinary investors could pay the price if the AI surge ends in a financial bust. Jose Gonzalez, among those protesting outside, questioned who would bear the brunt of a market reversal, arguing that wealthy investors enjoy protections unavailable to the public.
The meteoric surge of artificial intelligence is sparking hope and alarm in equal measure. While global spending on AI approaches $850 billion in 2026 and enthusiasts hail a sweeping economic and technological revolution, economists and watchdogs warn of a looming financial bubble, swelling debt and growing inequality, alongside fears that automation will wipe out jobs and funnel vast wealth into the coffers of a few tech titans.

noticias.titulo: Anthropic shares open 34% above IPO price in Nasdaq debut after record listing
noticias.resumen: Anthropic shares opened at $111.50 in their Nasdaq debut on Thursday, 34% above their $83 IPO price, putting the Claude maker on track for a $2 trillion valuation (€1.8tn) after it raised $81.3 billion (€74bn) in the largest initial public offering in history.
noticias.texto:
Anthropic shares opened at $111.50 in their Nasdaq debut on Thursday, 34% above their $83 IPO price, putting the Claude maker on track for a $2 trillion valuation (€1.8tn) after it raised $81.3 billion (€74bn) in the largest initial public offering in history.
Shares in Anthropic, the AI firm behind the Claude models, opened 34% above their IPO price on the Nasdaq on Thursday, at $111.50 against $83, putting it on course for a $2 trillion (€1.8tn) valuation.
It raised $81.3 billion (€74bn) in the biggest stock market listing ever, beating SpaceX's record raise back in June.
That fully diluted value, up from $1.5 trillion (€1.36tn) at the IPO price, puts Anthropic roughly level with SpaceX, the world's sixth most valuable listed company.
In a speech at Nasdaq's opening bell, CEO Dario Amodei stated: "I believe sufficiently powerful AI, working in concert with humans, could compress a century of scientific and medical progress into a decade."
"We will not bend to either business nor political pressure," Amodei added, as the company remains locked in a dispute with the Trump administration over military uses of its technology.
President Daniela Amodei said Anthropic had been "a safety company since day one" and bore ultimate responsibility for training its AI models to be safe.
Anthropic priced its shares above its initial $70 to $78 range and enlarged the offering to 980 million shares from 825 million. More than half of the roughly 1,200 institutional investors that bid for shares reportedly got none, with allocations heavily favouring US-based investors.
About 15% of the public offering, or roughly $12 billion (€10.9bn) of shares, went to retail investors, according to Bloomberg citing people familiar with the deal.
That is below the 20% maximum set out in the prospectus and SpaceX's roughly 20% retail allocation, but far above the norm.
Investors including Nvidia, Google and AMD are also buying $26 billion (€23.6bn) of non-voting shares at the IPO price in a separate private placement, taking the total raised to $107.3 billion (€97.7bn).
The Wall Street banks that ran the deal made an estimated $550 million (€501mn) in fees.
What investors are buying
Anthropic was founded in 2021 by seven former OpenAI researchers and executives, including siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei, now its CEO and president respectively.
Its revenue jumped to about $17 billion (€15.4bn) in the third quarter from $1.4 billion (€1.27bn) a year earlier, and the company puts its annualised revenue at about $81 billion (€73.7bn) as of the end of October.
It booked a $104 billion (€94.7bn) net loss in the first nine months of the year, but almost all of it stems from accounting revaluations that disappear once the company lists.
Excluding stock-based pay and donations, its operations made a $2.5 billion (€2.27bn) profit in the third quarter.
It has also committed at least $518 billion (€471bn) to cloud computing and infrastructure suppliers over roughly a decade.
The founders keep 50.1% of the voting power, while a trust appoints four of the seven board members, a set-up a shareholder advocacy group says leaves investors with almost no voice.
Anthropic is also locked in a dispute with the Trump administration, which in February ordered federal agencies to stop using its technology after the company refused to let Claude be used for mass surveillance of Americans or fully autonomous weapons.
Retail investors in nine European countries, including France, Germany and Spain, were able to apply for shares through participating brokers.

noticias.titulo: Europe Tonight: Trump, Putin and Xi hold talks as Ukraine allies meet in Berlin
noticias.resumen: Trump, Putin and Xi sign a joint declaration in China with no breakthrough on Ukraine, European leaders meet US envoys in Berlin, Spain’s election rivals debate, and COP31 talks enter their final stretch in Turkey.
noticias.texto:
Trump, Putin and Xi sign a joint declaration in China with no breakthrough on Ukraine, European leaders meet US envoys in Berlin, Spain’s election rivals debate, and COP31 talks enter their final stretch in Turkey.
On today's show:
Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin, and Xi Jinping hail "making history" after signing a joint "Declaration on Peace" on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen.
Yet despite Trump referring to Putin as "my friend," the talks produced no breakthrough on Russia’s war in Ukraine, overshadowed by fresh Kremlin threats of retaliation over the Crimea Bridge. Is this a dangerous "Yalta 2.0" sphere-of-influence carve-up, or a superpower flop?
Meanwhile, Europe pushes back from Berlin, where the European-led Coalition of the Willing and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy convened today alongside US negotiators Jared Kushner and Special Envoy Steve Witkoff to hammer out future security guarantees and a peace mandate. Our Germany correspondent, Lena Roche, joins us live from Berlin with the latest.
With just ten days to go before Spaniards head to the polls on November 29, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez faces off tonight against his conservative rival, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, in a decisive televised debate.
With polls suggesting Spain could swing to the right, former MP and IE University professor Antonio Roldán joins us from Madrid to break down Sánchez’s high-stakes snap election gamble.
And finally, as the COP31 climate conference enters its final stretch in Turkey ahead of Friday's deadline, negotiators remain deeply divided over climate financing and the phase-out of fossil fuels.
After EU Climate Chief Wopke Hoekstra told Euronews that Europeans are focused on implementation rather than money, we ask whether governments have stopped caring about climate—joined by UN Secretary-General candidate and former UN General Assembly President María Fernanda Espinosa, alongside Club of Rome Honorary President and Earth4All Executive Chair Sandrine Dixson-Declève.
When and where to watch Europe Tonight?
You can join Euronews’ Mared Gwyn live on TV and Euronews' website as well as digital platforms (YouTube, Facebook, X, and Instagram), every weekday at 6 pm, 7 pm and 8 pm Brussels time.
In just 28 minutes, our new format brings the day's top stories through a European lens, with live analysis and debate with MEPs and leaders.
