noticias.titulo: Iraq orders armed factions to withdraw from strategic area amid alleged oil smuggling and US pressure
noticias.resumen: Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zaidi has given the Iran-backed group until Friday to leave Jurf al-Nasr, as Baghdad faces growing pressure from Washington to bring powerful militias under state control.
noticias.texto:
Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zaidi has given the Iran-backed group until Friday to leave Jurf al-Nasr, as Baghdad faces growing pressure from Washington to bring powerful militias under state control.
Joint Iraqi forces will begin implementing a plan to redeploy security units in the Jurf al-Nasr area (formerly Jurf al-Sakhr) in the north of Babil province on Friday, the day of the government deadline given to Kataib Hezbollah to leave its stronghold before the armed forces enter it expires.
That's according to an informed source, which spoke to the Iraqi News Agency (INA) on Thursday.
According to the source, the redeployment will take place under security arrangements which divide responsibilities between army units, the federal police and the Popular Mobilisation Forces, as well as securing oil transport routes and reopening roads.
The deployment plan, set out in a document issued by the director of the office of the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces, Lieutenant General Abdul Amir al-Shammari, defines the tasks of the security units in the area, based on official letters dated 15 and 16 November 2026.
Details of the deployment plan
Under the plan, the 38th Brigade of the Defence Ministry’s 10th Division will secure the area from the Ya Hussein berm to the Fadhiliya junction, extending to the boundary with Anbar Operations Command.
The Federal Police’s 17th Brigade will take responsibility for central Jurf al-Nasr, covering the area between the Euphrates River to the east and the Musayyib-Fadhiliya road to the west.
Two Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) units – the 72nd and 79th Brigades – will secure the area from the Musayyib-Fadhiliya road to the boundary with Karbala Operations Command.
The plan also assigns an Energy Police regiment to protect oil transport routes. Babil police will set up a checkpoint at the Fadhiliya junction towards Musayyib, while Anbar police will establish another towards Ameriyat al-Fallujah.
Authorities will also begin reopening the road linking Musayyib, Bahbahani, Fadhiliya junction and Ameriyat al-Fallujah.
A counter-terrorism regiment stationed at al-Hamiya camp will remain on standby as a reserve force, under the direct authority of the commander-in-chief of the armed forces, to respond to any emergencies.
On Wednesday, PMF chief Faleh al-Fayyad sent a proposal to the prime minister's office calling for PMF units to take responsibility for securing the area. The letter, seen by the Iraqi News Agency (INA), named the 72nd and 79th Brigades and the PMF Operations Command's Special Forces Regiment, with the Energy Police responsible for protecting the oil pipeline.
Al-Fayyad's letter referred to an earlier directive from the commander-in-chief's office, numbered 1954 and dated 16 November 2026.
The Iraqi government has since confirmed that a formal order has been issued to establish a command headquarters in Jurf, following instructions from the commander-in-chief. The headquarters will bring together one army brigade, one Federal Police brigade and two PMF brigades.
It will oversee all security units in the designated area, with the aim of bringing the different forces under a single chain of command.
Qaani holds talks as officials seek to contain crisis
Separately, Iraqi armed group Kataib Hezbollah said on Thursday that its secretary-general, Abu Hussein al-Hamidawi, had met Iran's Quds Force commander Esmail Qaani.
The meeting was also attended by Badr Organisation chief Hadi al-Amiri and PMF leader Faleh al-Fayyad. In a statement reported by Agence France-Presse (AFP), the group said the discussions focused on the crisis, describing their outcome as "good". It did not disclose when or where the meeting took place.
Two Iraqi political sources told AFP on Tuesday that Qaani had also met Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zaidi in Baghdad on Monday to discuss tensions surrounding Jurf al-Sakhr.
Qaani took over as head of the Quds Force after his predecessor, Qasem Soleimani, was killed in a US strike near Baghdad airport in January 2020. He has made several visits to Iraq since then, although his trips are rarely officially announced.
Oil smuggling allegations fuel dispute over withdrawal
Tensions between Prime Minister al-Zaidi's government and Kataib Hezbollah have escalated after he ordered the armed forces to enter Jurf al-Sakhr (al-Nasr) and gave the armed group until Friday to withdraw.
The deadline follows an investigation by a government committee which Baghdad says uncovered evidence of oil smuggling in the area.
Government spokesperson Haider al-Aboudi said authorities had drawn up a plan to clear the area of anyone exploiting Iraq's oil wealth, which belongs to the country's people under the constitution.
Kataib Hezbollah has rejected the allegations, accusing the prime minister's office of fabricating the case to force the group to surrender its weapons.
On Tuesday, the faction organised a media tour of Jurf al-Sakhr, attended by several outlets, including Agence France-Presse (AFP).
During the visit, senior figure Abu Taleb al-Saidi insisted the group would not leave the area "even over our dead bodies", while also saying it did not want "bloodshed".
US pressure mounts over armed factions
The standoff comes as Washington steps up pressure on Baghdad to bring armed groups with close ties to Tehran under government control and disarm them.
Al-Zaidi, who has led the government for more than six months with US backing, pledged to tackle the issue when he took office. While some factions have indicated they are willing to cooperate, Kataib Hezbollah has refused to give up its weapons.
The final deadline for armed groups to hand over their weapons is 30 June 2027.
Jurf al-Nasr, formerly known as Jurf al-Sakhr, lies around 100 kilometres south of Baghdad.
Iraqi forces and Popular Mobilisation units retook the area from the Islamic State group in 2014. It has remained under tight security ever since, with Kataib Hezbollah among the most influential armed factions operating there.
The return of many residents displaced during the fighting has also yet to take place.

noticias.titulo: From Carthage to Grenoble: 'Les Carthagi'Noix' opens a window on Arab culture in France
noticias.resumen: In a city renowned for its walnut trees, and at a cultural distance that surpasses geography, a group of culture and art lovers chose to begin a new story called the dialogue between the Arab world and France.
noticias.texto:
In a city renowned for its walnut trees, and at a cultural distance that surpasses geography, a group of culture and art lovers chose to begin a new story called the dialogue between the Arab world and France.
Attended by members of Arab communities, city council representatives and members of the Tunisian consul, the cultural association Les Carthagi'Noix came into being, during a celebratory evening last weekend in Grenoble in south-eastern France.
The choice of name was not a minor detail. Les Carthagi'Noix brings together Carthage, with all its historical and cultural symbolism in Tunisia and the eastern Mediterranean, and the French word "Noix", meaning walnut, one of Grenoble's best known specialities.
From its very first letters, the name embodies the association's core idea, bringing two cultures together and creating a shared space where Arab memory meets the city's local identity.
Speaking at the opening, the association's president, Aya Ben Azzouz, explained that the idea stems from a simple desire to build a cultural link between the Arab world and the Grenoble area by honouring the culture and arts of the Arab region and introducing them to the French public, while at the same time building bridges with the local cultural scene.
Ben Azzouz said that the association hopes this exchange will be present in many fields, from culture and art to music, dance and food, as well as workshops and activities that allow the public to discover different aspects of Arab culture and engage with it directly.
From music to memory: a culture presented through living experiences
Les Carthagi'Noix does not want to limit its work to presenting Arab heritage as something belonging to the past, but aims to show it as a living, evolving culture with its own artists, voices and contemporary experiences.
In this context, Middle Eastern music is one of the areas the association plans to work on, through the "Mouzaik" ensemble, along with art workshops and activities focused on cultural exchange, and on highlighting Arab history and heritage.
Among the association's other goals is to shine a light on Arab artists living in Grenoble and give them the opportunity to present their work and experiences, while also showcasing local artists and creating spaces for collaboration between them and their counterparts from the Arab world.
The association hopes its activities and events will go beyond the Arab communities in Grenoble and reach a wider audience beyond the city.
The association's executive board consists of Aya Ben Azzouz as president, Taieb El Faleh as vice-president, Jihan Al Jaridi as secretary-general, and Adam Abdelhadi as treasurer, while music teacher Abdelaziz Dhib serves as the association's honorary president.
The opening evening included speeches by some members of the executive board, along with artistic and musical segments, during which the "Mouzaik" ensemble performed a selection of Eastern pieces, while the "Mery Muse" band provided the evening's entertainment.
From the outset, Les Carthagi'Noix has set itself a clear target that goes beyond organising one-off events, aiming to build an ongoing presence for Arab culture in Grenoble, engage with local cultural institutions and actors, and create opportunities for meetings between artists and audiences from different backgrounds.
In a city that is used to being a meeting point for many cultures, the association is trying to add a new space to this landscape, one that does not stop at invoking Carthage or celebrating Arab heritage, but explores what can emerge from their encounter with Grenoble.

noticias.titulo: Beaujolais nouveau 2026: a fresh, light vintage hopes to revive a struggling sector
noticias.resumen: The party to celebrate the 2026 vintage of Beaujolais nouveau, said this year to be fruity, light and easy to drink: the ideal recipe for forgetting the sector’s crisis.
noticias.texto:
The party to celebrate the 2026 vintage of Beaujolais nouveau, said this year to be fruity, light and easy to drink: the ideal recipe for forgetting the sector’s crisis.
They were up early to taste the 2026 Beaujolais Nouveau in this Paris restaurant, which was offering a hearty breakfast with a glass of red wine.
It is a late November tradition, and winegrowers are banking on the freshness and lightness of this vintage to boost a sector that badly needs it.
"It is an exceptional vintage, both because of the weather conditions and because of its roundness and indulgent character" rejoices Gilles Gelin, a winegrower at Domaine des Nugues. "We are dealing with a very sunny year, which has produced wines that are very approachable, very smooth and particularly easy to drink" he continues.
"It is emblematic, you have to come early in the morning and share this moment with people who love food as much as you do" advises Joanna Piccio, head of communications at Le Pied de Cochon, a famous Paris restaurant. "It is incredible, there is a unique atmosphere. You really have to experience it to understand what it is all about" the young woman enthuses.
Beaujolais Nouveau: the French are attached to it, they drank 13.8 million bottles last year.
Abroad, Japan and the United States are the two biggest importers.
The sector is going through a difficult period, sales have been falling since Covid-19 and climate-related disruptions are weighing on the harvests.
In some plots, yields this year are 60% lower than last year.

noticias.titulo: Islam to become world's largest religion by 2035 as Christianity also grows, study says
noticias.resumen: Pew Research Center has projected that both Islam and Christianity will grow between 2020 and 2070, with Muslims rising by more than 80% to over 3.6 billion and Christians by 30% to close to 3 billion.
noticias.texto:
Pew Research Center has projected that both Islam and Christianity will grow between 2020 and 2070, with Muslims rising by more than 80% to over 3.6 billion and Christians by 30% to close to 3 billion.
Islam is projected to become the world's largest religion by 2035, when the number of Muslim faithful is expected to surpass Christians by around 50 million people, according to Pew Research Center latest projections.
The study, which covers demographic changes among the world's major religions between 2020 and 2070, projects that the percentage of Muslims will grow faster than the world's population overall.
Meanwhile, the number of Christians in Africa will increase despite declines in Europe and the US.
The number of Muslim faithful worldwide is projected to grow by more than 80% between 2020 and 2070, exceeding 3.6 billion and raising their share of the global population from 26% to 36%.
Asia will remain the region with the largest number of Muslims, but faster population growth in sub-Saharan Africa will raise the continent's share from 18% of the world's Muslims in 2020 to 27% by 2070.
Asia and the Pacific's share will fall from 59% to 50%, even as the absolute number there continues to rise.
Pakistan is projected to overtake Indonesia by 2070 as the country with the world's largest Muslim population, with around 461 million people, followed by India with approximately 334 million and then Nigeria.
In Europe, population growth will increase the Muslim share of the continent's population from 6% in 2020 to 13% by 2070, with Sweden and France expected to see notable increases.
In North America, the number of Muslims is projected to rise from about 6 million to 20 million over the same period.
Christianity to grow, Israel central to Jewish religion
Despite declining numbers in Europe and the United States, the global Christian population is expected to grow.
By 2070, Pew projects close to three billion Christians worldwide, an increase of 30%, while their share of the global population holds at around 29%.
Sub-Saharan Africa will drive most of that growth, with more than half of the world's Christians expected to live there by 2070.
The Democratic Republic of the Congo is projected to overtake the US as the country with the largest Christian population, at around 299 million.
In Europe, a shrinking population and rising rates of religious disaffiliation are expected to reduce the number of Christians from 505 million in 2020 to 324 million by 2070.
In the US, the figure is expected to fall from 217 million to 174 million, with Christians projected to drop below half the population by 2065. In Canada, that threshold could be crossed by 2030.
Meanwhile, Israel is projected to become home to most of the world's Jews by 2070, as numbers in the US and Europe decline.
Pew projects that Israel's share of the global Jewish population will rise from 46% in 2020 to 62%, with the country's Jewish population growing from 6.8 million to 11.1 million, driven mainly by higher fertility rates.
The US' share is projected to fall from 39% to 26%, a decline of about 1.2 million people. Europe's share will drop from 9% to 5%.
Globally, the Jewish population is expected to grow from 15 million to 18 million by 2070, although more slowly than the world's population overall. The global Jewish share will decline slightly, from 0.19% to 0.17%.
The study calculates these figures based on religious affiliation and generally excludes people who identify as Jewish for cultural or family reasons without practising the religion.
What drives the shifts?
The main factors behind differential growth rates are population age structure and fertility rates, as groups with more young people tend to grow faster.
In 2020, the median age of Muslims was 24, compared with 33 for non-Muslims, meaning a larger share are of childbearing age or approaching it.
Between 2020 and 2025, around 252 million children were born to Muslim mothers, compared with 208 million to Christian mothers.
Fertility differences within Judaism also affect geographic distribution. Jewish women in Israel have an average of three children, against 1.5 in the US, where the Jewish population is older overall.
In some Western countries, people raised as Christians are leaving religious affiliation entirely, adding to the decline in Christian numbers.
Among Muslim believers, the effect of changing religions is limited: Pew estimates that 99% of those raised Muslim continue to identify as Muslim in adulthood.
Pew has cautioned against treating the projections as evidence of a competition between religions, as a dip in any religion's share does not mean a decline in its numbers.
Most of the projected growth in both religions will occur in countries where each already forms a majority of the population, Pew said in its report.

noticias.titulo: AI being run in a 'medieval' way, says UN rights chief
noticias.resumen: UN high commissioner for human rights Volker Türk warned that while AI might sound something futuristic, underneath it is based on an age-old narrative of power.
noticias.texto:
UN high commissioner for human rights Volker Türk warned that while AI might sound something futuristic, underneath it is based on an age-old narrative of power.
Artificial intelligence is being governed in an almost mediaeval fashion, the UN rights chief warned Thursday, with power concentrated in the hands of a few tech barons.
Speaking at the RightsX summit in Geneva, UN high commissioner for human rights Volker Türk said that while the story of AI sounded futuristic, underneath it was an age-old narrative of power.
"A handful of men still control much of the world's AI computing power, data and infrastructure. And we still have no common rules to pace or steer AI development," he said.
Turk said there was a glaring democratic deficit when five technology companies owned more than 70% of global AI computing capacity.
"We have the technology of the future governed in an almost mediaeval way: by a select few, with virtually no checks, no balances, no participation, and no accountability," he said.
"History has taught us: with this kind of power, the rights and freedoms of ordinary people are the first to suffer."
Reiterating his call for rights-centred AI regulation, the UN high commissioner for human rights said the technology was increasingly controlling people's lives.
And this, he warned, was often happening without their knowledge, and could distort public debate in "subtle, insidious ways".
Meanwhile biased algorithms could reproduce injustice on an industrial scale, he cautioned.
'Civilisational collapse'
"Our transport, food and healthcare are increasingly digitised. We may not be far from the day when AI can cut off the critical infrastructure of entire communities or countries, either on its own or in the wrong hands," Turk warned.
"When people discuss the chances of civilisational collapse because of AI, we need to ask: who decides what chances we take?"
He voiced optimism that people would ultimately challenge unchecked power, with the democratic deficit turning into a deficit of trust.
He cited young people already stepping offline to regain greater control of their lives.
Turk said AI's benefits should be shared equitably, which would require goodwill from technology companies, but also regulation and accountability.
He said he had written to frontier AI companies urging them to introduce effective safeguards "before it is too late".
Turk noted that a bottle of milk could not make it to a shop without layers of testing, rules and regulations.
So for AI, "it's a no-brainer that you need some form of regulation", given its potential for harm, Turk said.
As for how models are trained, he suggested giving the Universal Declaration of Human Rights "as the task to AI".

noticias.titulo: EU moves towards 10-year probation period for new members - starting with Montenegro
noticias.resumen: EU ambassadors broadly backed a 10-year probation period for newcomers, with voting rights open to suspension for Orbán-style breaches, as a basis for Montenegro’s treaty.
noticias.texto:
EU ambassadors broadly backed a 10-year probation period for newcomers, with voting rights open to suspension for Orbán-style breaches, as a basis for Montenegro’s treaty.
EU countries have taken the first step towards establishing a 10-year probation period for new members, during which newcomers, starting with Montenegro, could have their voting rights suspended for serious rule-of-law breaches or obstructing EU decisions.
The European Commission unveiled the proposal last month to avoid a repeat of the experience with Hungary under Viktor Orbán, whose government violated the bloc’s basic values and repeatedly wielded its veto to block decisions requiring unanimity.
The Commission initially proposed a 15-year probation period. However, several countries, notably Italy and other members of the Friends of the Western Balkans group, which champions the region's accession, argued that such a long period could hardly be considered temporary.
Ireland, which chairs talks among member states as holder of the rotating EU Council presidency, proposed shortening the period to 10 years, with a possible five-year extension. The proposal received broad support from EU ambassadors on Wednesday.
According to an EU diplomat with direct knowledge of the discussions, ambassadors showed far greater willingness to compromise than the officials who had spent weeks negotiating the details.
The more contentious question is what would trigger a suspension of voting rights. Montenegro, the country closest to joining the bloc, has warned that any decision must be based on objective criteria and systematic breaches of EU values and rules.
Several member states sympathetic to the candidate countries object to including breaches of “sincere cooperation”, the EU treaty principle requiring members to work together in good faith and refrain from jeopardising the bloc’s objectives. They argue that such breaches are difficult to assess objectively.
These countries also oppose suspending new members’ voting rights altogether, fearing the mechanism could be used to force newcomers to abandon positions close to their national interest, creating a de facto second tier of EU members.
Ireland also proposed changing how the safeguard is triggered, with decisions taken by qualified majority, meaning a majority of countries representing at least 65% of the EU’s population. Here, too, member states did not object strongly.
Discussions will now shift from the general rules for future members to how they would apply to Montenegro. Ireland’s proposal will form the basis of the safeguards in Montenegro’s accession treaty, which the Commission aims to have signed by June 2027.
Officials are expected to hold their first technical discussions on a draft of the relevant section of the treaty, Chapter 35, early next week. Podgorica, which cannot negotiate this part of the treaty, has been lobbying member states in the meantime.
What remains unclear is whether the safeguards will be tailored to Montenegro or establish a precedent for all future EU members.

noticias.titulo: EU must move beyond piecemeal trade deals with China, MEPs warn
noticias.resumen: MEPs are calling on the European Commission to “ease” the regulatory burden on EU companies and deploy “horizontal” trade defence tools to tackle Chinese competition.
noticias.texto:
MEPs are calling on the European Commission to “ease” the regulatory burden on EU companies and deploy “horizontal” trade defence tools to tackle Chinese competition.
The EU needs a “systematic” approach to China that goes beyond its current sector-by-sector trade strategy, according to a cross-party coalition of MEPs.
In a letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič, the MEPs warn against pursuing more deals like the one the Commission struck with Beijing in October to curb imports of Chinese hybrid cars.
“Carving out single-sector export limits cannot substitute for both, faster regulatory simplification and comprehensive defence of Europe’s industrial baseline against systematic market disruption,” reads the letter, initiated by Slovak MEP Miriam Lexmann (EPP).
The EU faces a trade deficit with China of €1 billion a day, while a surge in low-cost Chinese imports is widely seen as a threat to thousands of jobs across European industries.
EU countries gave the Commission a mandate in June to negotiate with Beijing to rebalance trade relations while developing new trade defence tools. In October, France and Germany called for a new instrument that would restrict market access for foreign competitors causing serious market disruption.
In the letter sent to the Commission president, MEPs from the centre-right European People’s Party (EPP), the largest political group in Parliament, the liberal Renew group, the Socialists and Democrats (S&D), the Greens and the Eurosceptic European Conservatives and Reformists (ECR) call for “horizontal” quotas and tariffs to address Chinese overcapacities.
The MEPs also highlight “weak” customs enforcement, which enables tax evasion and breaches of safety rules, and warn that lengthy EU investigations risk leaving European companies facing closure before protective measures are introduced.
“The Commission must now implement a systematic approach,” the letter adds, including regulatory simplification to “ease regulatory burden” on EU companies and the deployment of “horizon-wide” trade defence instruments. The MEPs also call for “strict local supply chain content rules” and the “harmonisation” of EU customs controls.
The letter comes as Šefčovič prepares for talks with his Chinese counterpart, Commerce Minister Wang Wentao, in January and March next year.
The Commission is also expected to unveil the new trade defence instrument sought by Paris and Berlin before the end of the year.

noticias.titulo: Dutch embassy in Kyiv damaged by a projectile crash nearby
noticias.resumen: A projectile struck the area behind the Dutch embassy in Ukraine on Thursday, causing minor damage to the building; no casualties were reported.
noticias.texto:
A projectile struck the area behind the Dutch embassy in Ukraine on Thursday, causing minor damage to the building; no casualties were reported.
Dutch Minister of Foreign Affairs Tom Berendsen reported damage to the Netherlands' embassy in Kyiv this Thursday. A projectile struck the area behind the embassy, causing minor damage to the building.
"Our colleagues are unharmed, although there has been minor damage to the building," Berendsen said. "We are investigating exactly what happened. Our priority now is the well-being of our staff."
While there was no confirmation on the Dutch side, Ukraine’s Minister for Foreign Affairs, Andrii Sybiha, has said on Telegram that it was a Russian attack.
"Russian attacks on Kyiv have once again damaged a diplomatic mission. This time, the building housing the Dutch Embassy in Ukraine was hit," Sybiha said.
"We call on the international community to strongly condemn Russian attacks on foreign diplomats and express our firm support for our Dutch colleagues."
The Kyiv Independent says the embassy's windows were shattered and that cars and a security post were damaged.
About 40 people work at the Dutch embassy in Kyiv, including Dutch and local employees; none of them was injured during the attack.
'We must support Ukraine', Dutch Defence Secretary
"It's not the first time there have been impacts at an embassy," Dutch Defence Secretary Derk Boswijk told Dutch public broadcaster NOS.
"It is additional confirmation that we must support Ukraine. I see above all an encouragement to continue to do that," he told NOS.
The impact on the embassy comes two days after a Ukrainian attack on the Crimean Bridge was carried out, allegedly using Dutch missiles and drones.
Russian President Vladimir Putin, speaking at the APEC summit in China, called for retaliation after Ukraine's attack on the Crimean bridge.
The Dutch-based arms manufacturer Destinus, which allegedly provided the weapons for the bridge attack, was previously mentioned as a "legitimate" target by Former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev because it regularly supplies weapons to Ukraine.
Several attacks on Kyiv
Kyiv has suffered massive drone strikes on the same day, injuring four people, according to the city's mayor, Vitali Klitschko.
Several districts of the Ukrainian capital were hit by drone strikes and drone debris, including the district where the Dutch embassy is located.

noticias.titulo: Doing More with Less: Why Cost-Effective AI Agents Are European SMEs’ Hidden Asset in Global Trade
noticias.resumen: As European SMEs embrace AI, Alibaba.com's Accio shows how agentic tools can bridge the productivity gap, easing expansion and routine e-commerce tasks.
noticias.texto:
Most small business owners don’t have the luxury of delegating. In a survey of 501 French business leaders by OpinionWay for Alibaba.com, 78% said everything rested on their shoulders, while six in ten spent too much time on repetitive tasks.¹
Taking a business into a new country adds more work, whether it’s finding suppliers or understanding the differences in regulations. For an owner already doing most of the heavy lifting, expanding abroad can feel daunting.
“For SMEs, complexity is often one of the biggest challenges of doing business, particularly when it comes to sourcing, supplier assessment and operating internationally,” explains Patrick Sostmann, General Manager Europe at Alibaba.com.
Despite these challenges, the appetite for international trade is growing among European SMEs. Alibaba.com, the business-to-business marketplace connecting buyers and suppliers in more than 200 countries and regions, says the number of products listed by European sellers has surged by 78% to 1.28 million. European order numbers have grown by 70% over the past three years.
The challenge for smaller firms is making the most of that growth without taking on more work. Alibaba.com believes AI can help through Accio, its agentic AI platform built specifically for the needs and budgets of small businesses. Accio’s AI agents for e-commerce are specifically designed to help founders research markets, find products, assess suppliers and manage sourcing.
Growing confidence in AI
Research by the Small Business Institute and Alibaba.com found that 70% of UK small business owners feel confident using generative AI, yet fewer than half (48%) use it regularly. Of those who do, 74% use it for content and marketing, while just 5% apply it to supply chain management. Familiarity has grown faster than the hours saved, highlighting the AI productivity gap.
68% want to learn more about AI agents, while half believe the technology could give them more time to find new customers.
Priorities vary across Europe. In Italy, a Censuswide survey for Alibaba.com found that 23% of SME decision-makers saw the greatest potential for AI in customs procedures and import documentation, followed by comparing suppliers and prices (22%).² In Germany, 32% of respondents to a YouGov study for Alibaba.com and the e-commerce association bevh (Bundesverband E-Commerce und Versandhandel Deutschland) identified administrative overload as a challenge.³
AI: From Ask to Task
While a chatbot can answer a question, an agentic AI platform, such as Accio, can take on a multi-step task. It can gather market data, compare suppliers and pull quotes together before an owner signs off on a purchase.
An effective AI agent needs three things: a model to provide the intelligence, a harness, which is the set of tools it uses to carry out tasks, and context, which is the business knowledge behind its decisions. Alibaba refers to this as Model × Harness × Context.
Capable and affordable
Powerful technology is of little use to a small business if it costs too much. As Kuo Zhang, President of Alibaba.com, puts it, “for small businesses, unaffordable AI is useless.”
Accio breaks larger requests into smaller steps and identifies the most efficient way to handle each one, using lighter models for routine work and more powerful ones when a task needs deeper analysis. It can also reuse information and coordinate agents to avoid duplicating work. By matching resources to the complexity of each task, it can keep costs down.
In Alibaba.com’s benchmark of 107 e-commerce tasks, the company reports an estimated total cost of $3.69 for the full task set. This was more than 50% lower than general-purpose agents in the comparison, with comparable quality. The benchmark, Commerce Agent Bench, is publicly available for others to examine.
Alibaba.com expects the next step in business-to-business trade to be agent-to-agent (A2A) transactions, with digital agents handling more of the buying and selling.
Seeing it work
Alibaba.com’s flagship event CoCreate Europe, a two-day event opening in London on 19 November, demonstrates in practice how access to AI-powered tools and global sourcing opportunities can help businesses turn promising product ideas into commercially viable ventures. For the first time this year, Alibaba.com is introducing the ‘One Person Company (‘OPC’) Market which brings together 30 founder-led European brands to show what it takes to turn an idea into a business. Across beauty, fashion, homeware, food and outdoor products, visitors can meet the people behind the brands, experience their products and discover how they were developed.
Owners will still need to weigh up risks and make the big decisions. But if AI agents can take some research and routine work off their hands, growing internationally may become more manageable.
Perhaps the next survey will find fewer business owners feeling that everything rests on them.
_____________
References:
¹ Survey conducted by OpinionWay for Alibaba.com from August 24 to September 11, 2026, among a sample of 501 business leaders in the industry, construction, commerce, and services sectors, representative of French private sector companies with under 50 employees.
² The research was conducted by Censuswide between 18 and 24 August 2026 on 1,000 decision-makers, aged at least 25, belonging to Italian SMEs with less than 250 employees.
³ The data from this survey is based on online interviews with members of the YouGov panel who had agreed in advance to participate. For this survey, a total of 438 owners, business proprietors and decision-makers from the e-commerce/internet services and procurement/purchasing sectors in Germany were surveyed between 8 and 15 September 2026

noticias.titulo: How much does sick leave cost Europe, and which countries take the most?
noticias.resumen: Sickness absence costs the EU up to €810 billion every year, highlighting the need for better prevention and earlier treatment to reduce its economic impact, a new report has found.
noticias.texto:
Sickness absence costs the EU up to €810 billion every year, highlighting the need for better prevention and earlier treatment to reduce its economic impact, a new report has found.
The average European misses nearly three weeks of work each year due to ill health, a new report has found.
This accounts for around 6% of potential working time in the European Union, representing about €540 billion in lost labour costs each year, according to the report by the Environment and Public Health Institute. That is equivalent to 2.9% of the EU’s gross domestic product (GDP) in 2025.
However, this figure captures only part of the economic impact of ill health, which includes everything from viral infections to mental health issues or cancer. The calculation covers only sickness-related absence among people who are still classified as full-time employees and does not take into account the full economic cost of long-term ill health, the report noted.
A person who needs to reduce their working hours or leaves the labour market due to illness is no longer recorded as a sickness absence.
Beyond the direct loss of working time, illness also carries wider economic consequences.
When people are unable to work because of illness, economic output also declines, while employers and colleagues have to manage the consequences of their absence, such as hiring a replacement or asking other employees to work overtime.
Longer periods of sickness absence can also lead people to leave the labour market altogether, reducing tax revenues and increasing spending on social insurance, the report noted.
Taking these direct and indirect costs into account, the report calculated an additional cost of around €135 billion to €270 billion per year, bringing the total annual cost to €675 billion to €810 billion.
How much sick leave do people take across Europe?
While economic loss for sick absences is a Europe-wide issue, there is a “dramatic difference across Europe”, Adrian Mehic, author of the report, said while presenting the report at the European Parliament in Brussels.
According to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), Slovenia had the longest average sick leave in 2025, with just over five weeks per employee, followed by around five weeks in Finland and Spain.
France, Sweden and Germany are slightly above three weeks, while in Italy and Greece, full-time employees average less than one week of sickness absence.
However, these figures do not necessarily reflect differences in population health, the report warned.
A country recording fewer sickness absences may have a healthier population, but it can also reflect low compensation, weak employment protections or people going to work despite being ill.
How can the economic burden be reduced?
Reasons for sick absences range from poor mental health and musculoskeletal diseases to accidents and chronic illnesses.
But a significant proportion of these absences could potentially be prevented or shortened. Many are linked to conditions for which preventive measures, early treatment and rehabilitation can potentially reduce both the risk and duration of the absences, the report noted.
Preventive measures include better workplace ergonomics, earlier treatment for mental health concerns, faster access to primary care, physiotherapy, mental health and earlier detection of risks, Mehic said.
“Prevention itself is also costly, so not all of these things are free, but properly implemented, the benefits would be bigger than the costs,” he added.

noticias.titulo: Serbia's student movement takes another step towards power with parliament speaker election
noticias.resumen: Aleksandar Čupić's appointment marks a historic breakthrough for the grassroots movement, which ended 14 years of rule by Aleksandar Vučić's party after campaigning against corruption.
noticias.texto:
Aleksandar Čupić's appointment marks a historic breakthrough for the grassroots movement, which ended 14 years of rule by Aleksandar Vučić's party after campaigning against corruption.
Serbia's student-led opposition has taken a major step towards forming a government and ending the era of Aleksandar Vučić, appointing a university lecturer as parliament speaker after its election victory last month.
Aleksandar Čupić, a lecturer, doctor of science and assistant professor at the University of Belgrade, won 140 votes in the 250-member assembly, while the Serbian Progressive Party candidate won just 97.
The new generation of student-backed lawmakers are mostly teachers, professors and experts with established careers but little or no political experience.
It’s the first time in Serbia’s history that a grassroots protest movement has won the majority needed to form a government.
“I have been given a huge honour, obligation and responsibility,” Čupić said after his election. He promised to restore Parliament's dignity and “dialogue and tolerance” among the lawmakers.
“I pledge to be strict and just in this position, as I always have been in life,” he added.
Last month’s parliamentary election marked a significant shift for Serbia.
The students' election victory came after they led anti-corruption protests for two years following a canopy collapse at a train station in northern Serbia that killed 16 people in November 2024. Many involved in the demonstrations blamed the disaster on rampant corruption in construction projects.
Čupić's election as speaker came after more than two days of heated debate, which was dominated by Vučić's accusations that his opponents were attacking and pressuring him and his party. That’s despite the fact that they still control the government administration and other state institutions.
According to Serbia’s laws, a new government must be voted into office within 90 days after the new Parliament's first session. In his role as speaker, Čupić will also serve as Serbia's acting president. He’s expected to schedule an early presidential election in due course, which must be held by the end of the year.
Vučić has accused the students of “revolutionary terror”, following a surge in post-election arrests which included officials, police officers and a private bank owner who allegedly attempted to siphon off money.

noticias.titulo: Plenty of healthy people are low on iron. Here’s why it gets missed
noticias.resumen: Many people with iron deficiency aren’t diagnosed right away.
noticias.texto:
Many people with iron deficiency aren’t diagnosed right away.
Iron deficiency is the most common nutritional deficiency, affecting over a billion people worldwide — yet many people do not realise they aren’t getting enough iron.
Iron, which is found in red meat, beans, dried fruit and other foods, is an essential mineral that plays a major role in the body. It helps make haemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen, and myoglobin, which supplies oxygen to the muscles. Iron is also needed for energy production, immune function, growth and brain development.
When someone doesn’t get or retain enough iron, they may experience fatigue or difficulty concentrating — or no symptoms at all. As the body’s iron stores run out, iron deficiency can progress to iron deficiency anaemia, which makes it harder for blood to transport oxygen in the body and can lead to serious complications.
“People rarely die of iron deficiency, but it has a very big effect globally,” Hal Drakesmith, a professor of iron biology at the University of Oxford, told Euronews. “If you don't have enough iron, you don't have enough energy.”
Some people are at higher risk of iron deficiency, including teen girls and women with heavy periods. Pregnant women and their foetuses, infants and children all need extra iron for growth and development, which diet alone can’t always provide.
Older people can become iron deficient due to intestinal bleeding or chronic health problems. A 2022 study found that iron deficiency is fairly common among relatively healthy older adults in Europe. Those aged 80 or older and living in Austria and Portugal were at the highest risk.
Diets low in red meat or other iron-rich foods may also contribute to iron deficiency. Frequent blood donors can become iron deficient, though they are usually tested before they give blood, Drakesmith said.
“It is enormously common,” Drakesmith said.
Even so, many people with iron deficiency aren’t diagnosed right away. Common symptoms are vague and not specific to iron deficiency, and it takes time to develop because people don’t lose all of their iron at once, Drakesmith said.
Iron and ferritin, a protein that stores iron, have become hot topics in wellness circles. A viral claim that people with low iron have “ferritin face” — visible signs such as pale skin and thinning hair — is “not clinically useful,” Drakesmith said. But if the trend raises awareness about iron deficiency and prompts people with symptoms to seek testing, he’s all for it.
Routine screening for iron deficiency is rare, even among higher-risk groups, said Elaine McCarthy, a senior lecturer in nutrition at University College Cork in Ireland. For example, while blood checks are standard in pregnancy, they typically measure haemoglobin.
“This is a problem as haemoglobin is a very late-stage indicator of changes in iron status, meaning we miss those individuals in the earliest stage of the deficiency and miss the opportunity to prevent it worsening,” McCarthy told Euronews.
She advocates for testing both haemoglobin and ferritin, which serves as “a marker of the earliest changes in iron status.”
In September, the American Society of Hematology (ASH) issued new clinical guidance for diagnosing iron deficiency. It suggests that adults, pregnant women and those with periods be diagnosed if their serum ferritin is 30 micrograms per litre or lower, instead of 15 µg/L. That’s in line with recommendations from the European Crohn’s and Colitis Organisation.
However, identifying the right ferritin threshold has not been settled globally, Drakesmith said.
“Where you set that ferritin threshold basically will determine the prevalence” of iron deficiency, Drakesmith said. “I think they're erring on the side of making sure they don't miss the diagnosis, which is perfectly sensible. But at the same time, you might end up including people who probably aren't that iron deficient.”
Relying only on ferritin levels also won’t catch everyone with an iron deficiency. People with inflammatory conditions, such as chronic kidney disease, can have normal or even high ferritin levels but still be low in iron. Inflammation in the body can cause ferritin levels to rise even when iron stores are low.
People with inflammatory conditions may have a serum ferritin of up to 100 µg/L and still be iron deficient, according to the European recommendations.
Iron deficiency can often be fixed with supplements, as long as its underlying cause is identified and addressed. But iron supplements can cause side effects such as constipation and stomach pain, which can make people reluctant to stick with them, Drakesmith said.
Too much iron can also be a problem, McCarthy said. Very high doses can be fatal, especially for children.
“You shouldn’t take an iron supplement unless you have been diagnosed with iron deficiency or iron deficiency anaemia,” McCarthy said. “High-dose iron supplements can be dangerous if your body doesn’t actually need the iron.”

noticias.texto:
European champions Italy and four European debutants are among the 48 teams taking part, while last year’s finalists Portugal and Austria are absent. Qatar is hosting the second of five consecutive editions from 2025 to 2029. The final is on 13 December.
The FIFA Under-17 World Cup got under way in Qatar on Thursday, with 48 teams taking part, including 11 from Europe.
Eight matches were on the opening-day programme at Doha’s Aspire Zone, including France against Haiti, Greece against Egypt and hosts Qatar against Panama.
The 104-match tournament ends with the final at Ahmad bin Ali Stadium on 13 December.
Greece, Montenegro, Romania and Serbia are making their first appearances at the U-17 World Cup. For Montenegro, it also marks the country’s first appearance at any FIFA World Cup.
Italy enter as European champions after beating Belgium on penalties in June’s final, while France are seeking their first U-17 world title since 2001.
Belgium, Croatia, Denmark, Ireland and Spain complete Europe’s line-up.
Defending champions Portugal and last year’s runners-up Austria are both absent after failing to qualify.
The Dominican Republic replaced the US, which withdrew over security concerns. FIFA said the US decision was linked to an existing travel advisory for Qatar and that its own security assessment remained unchanged.
Qatar is hosting the second of five consecutive editions, from 2025 to 2029. The tournament expanded from 24 to 48 teams last year.
All matches except the final will be played across eight pitches at Aspire Zone.
The teams are divided into 12 groups of four. The top two in each group and the eight best third-placed sides will advance to the round of 32. The group stage ends on 27 November, with the knockout rounds beginning on 30 November.
Past participants include Neymar, Phil Foden and Victor Osimhen.

noticias.titulo: This country’s AI ambitions: From public services to global markets
noticias.resumen: Azerbaijan is pursuing regional AI ambitions through digital public services, stronger data infrastructure, skills development and businesses targeting international markets.
noticias.texto:
Azerbaijan is pursuing regional AI ambitions through digital public services, stronger data infrastructure, skills development and businesses targeting international markets.
From public services to financial technology, Azerbaijan is looking to turn its AI ambitions into practical applications. Speaking on Business Horizons, Rashad Hasanov, Deputy Minister of Digital Development and Transport of the Republic of Azerbaijan, outlined plans for AI agents to deliver government services, supported by a national data lakehouse and stronger digital skills.
The programme also visits Simbrella, where Ali Akbar Mammadov explains how the company uses AI and machine learning to assess financial risk. Operating in more than 20 countries, the business offers an example of locally developed technology reaching international customers, while highlighting the importance of talent in sustaining growth.

noticias.titulo: Data centre energy consumption could double by 2030 straining grids, IEA warns
noticias.resumen: Data centres could use roughly 1,000 terawatt-hours of power annually by 2030 under the International Energy Agency’s (IEA) Stated Policies Scenario.
noticias.texto:
Data centres could use roughly 1,000 terawatt-hours of power annually by 2030 under the International Energy Agency’s (IEA) Stated Policies Scenario.
The amount of electricity used by data centres could double by 2030, reaching up to 1,000 terawatt-hours of electricity a year, straining energy grids and driving carbon emissions up 70%, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA).
In the IEA’s Stated Policies Scenario report, the organisation warns that the rise in electricity demand could stretch power grids and even delay new projects.
The report cited data centre projects in Finland, the United Kingdom, and the United States in states such as Texas and Virginia.
It estimates that electricity would account for nearly 30% of global final energy consumption by 2035, up from 23% in the IEA’s main scenarios.
Peak electricity demand is projected to rise 40% to 50% by 2035, according to the IEA. In the report, grids should be expanded by 26 million kilometres of new lines by 2035, while about 16 million kilometres of existing lines need to be replaced or refurbished.
The IEA also warned that the supplies of copper, transformers and cables needed for data centres are already lacking and grid spending is projected to rise 75% over the next decade.
The report comes as backlash grows against data centres in the US and Europe due to their impact on local communities' public infrastructure, land, water and energy use.

noticias.titulo: French Comté crowned world's best at the 2026 World Cheese Awards
noticias.resumen: A 24-month-aged cheese from France's Jura mountains has won the top prize at the 2026 World Cheese Awards, beating more than 5,300 entries from 45 countries.
noticias.texto:
A 24-month-aged cheese from France's Jura mountains has won the top prize at the 2026 World Cheese Awards, beating more than 5,300 entries from 45 countries.
A French cheese has been named the world's best at the 2026 World Cheese Awards, bringing the prestigious, and much coveted honour to the country's eastern Jura region.
The winning cheese is a 24-month-aged Comté, produced by Fromageries Arnaud under the JuraFlore brand.
It narrowly beat another Alpine heavyweight - an 18-month Le Gruyère AOP from Gourmino in Switzerland – and another worthy contender from the Basque Country and Béarn regions in southwestern France, an Ossau Iraty AOP made by Agour.
The competition brought together 270 judges from 51 countries, including cheesemakers, retailers, buyers and food experts to assess each entry on its appearance, texture, aroma and taste.
“What I liked about this cheese was the complexity,” said judge Rafa Dominguez Gonzalez, who championed the winning Comté on the final panel. “It evolves in the mouth. Those beautiful, nutty savoury flavours really left a mark on me. Sometimes you just know. The moment I tried this one I said straight away ‘This is my choice’.”
Why did Comté win?
The world beating Comté was chosen from 5,330 entries representing 45 countries at the four-day competition, held in Córdoba in southern Spain.
Aged for two years in the cellars of Fort des Rousses, a former military fortress in the Jura mountains, the presiding panel also praised its complex, savoury notes and a long-lasting finish.
Comté has been produced in eastern France for centuries, with its origins tracing back to the Middle Ages.
From the 13th century, farmers in the Jura began joining forces to make large wheels of cheese. They pooled their daily milk production in shared facilities known as fruitières.
The system allowed them to produce larger quantities of cheese that could be stored and transported, particularly through the winter months.
Today, Comté is still made according to strict geographical and production rules in the Jura massif. It received France's Appellation d'Origine Contrôlée (AOC) designation in 1958 and European Protected Designation of Origin (PDO) status in 1996.
Which other cheeses made it into the top 14?
The final shortlist featured cheeses from five European countries, with France, Italy, Spain, Switzerland and Portugal all represented.
France secured two of the top three positions, with Ossau-Iraty, a sheep's milk cheese from the French Basque Country, finishing joint secondwith 81 points.
Switzerland's Le Gruyère AOP Réserve, aged at the Village Dairy Rossens, also scored 81 points, taking third place after the tie-break.
Italy and Portugal followed closely behind. Italy's Erborinato di Capra, a goat's milk blue cheese, and Portugal's Queijo de Ovelha Curado, a matured sheep's milk cheese, both scored 79 points.
Spain's Curado Fuente La Sierra came next with 78 points, followed by Switzerland's Kaltbach Appenzeller with 77.
The remaining finalists included Italian and Swiss specialities, as well as two Spanish cheeses made from goat's and sheep's milk. Italy's Blu Notte – La Fossa dell'Abbondanza completed the top 14 with 68 points.

noticias.titulo: 'COP31 has been muzzled': Latest draft deal scrubs all mention of fossil fuels
noticias.resumen: The transition away from fossil fuels (TAFF) has become a flashpoint discussion at the annual UN climate summit.
noticias.texto:
The transition away from fossil fuels (TAFF) has become a flashpoint discussion at the annual UN climate summit.
All mentions of fossil fuels have been scrubbed from the latest COP31 draft deal, despite growing momentum to establish an exit plan.
Co-host Australia unveiled a draft deal on Thursday (19 November) that removes earlier proposals that called on nations to accelerate the phaseout of coal, oil and gas – the leading driver of climate change.
Almost 200 nations involved in the annual UN climate summit have until tomorrow (20 November) to strike a final agreement but analysts expect the discussions may overrun.
COP31 agreements require consensus from all parties which means progress is often slow and incremental.
It’s a deja-vu moment from the COP30 summit in Belém last year, where the transition away from fossil fuels (TAFF) was erased from the final deal following resistance from fossil-fuel exporting countries.
COP31 shies away from fossil fuels
The draft "cover decision" is designed to capture the outcome of COP31 and set the course for future action as global temperatures rise and climate disasters multiply.
But after days of tense consultations, negotiations chair Australia published a slimmed-down text, half the original length, containing fresh language and new proposals on some of the most contentious issues.
This includes a call to increase the global share of final energy demand met by electricity to 35 percent by 2035 – a key initiative of COP31 host Türkiye.
The 35 x 35 pledge has gained criticism for not explicitly stating that the additional power should come solely from renewables.
No baseline or goal has been clarified for tripling adaptation finance so far, despite a UN Environment Programme (UNEP) report published days before the summit warning that even tripling current international public adaptation finance would only meet 23-29 per cent of developing countries’ needs.
Rich nations have resisted calls to increase support for countries struggling to adapt to climate change, citing budget constraints and insisting that big emerging economies also contribute.
The draft deal also contains a recognition of the "best-available science" and a reference to the work of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), a key battleground at COP31.
COP31 has been 'muzzled'
Nations agreed at COP28 in Dubai in 2023 to transition away from fossil fuels, but language around energy sources is highly contested at the yearly talks.
"If the latest version of the COP31 text remains, this will be a ghost COP," warns Mohamed Adow, founder and director of climate think tank Power Shift Africa.
He wrote on LinkedIn: "The summit will have nothing to show for what happened here. After the progress made in 2023 at COP28 in Dubai where fossil fuels were mentioned for the first time, there is now no mention of the f-word at all."
Despite the erasure of TAFF from the draft deal, several countries have published their own roadmaps to transition to clean energy.
On 11 November, Finland affirmed its commitment to TAFF by publishing a national roadmap, following in the footsteps of France, Germany and the Netherlands.
Almost a week later (17 November), Denmark, Portugal, Luxembourg and Spain announced their own national plans.
While “you can always wish and fight” for TAFF to be anchored in the cover decision, “this is not for us the ultimate benchmark for success,” German Environment Ministry State Secretary Heike Henn told reporters on Monday (16 November), ahead of the draft’s publication. “The success is in doing, in a growing coalition,” she said.

noticias.titulo: Myanmar guilty of genocide against Rohingya UN court rules
noticias.resumen: The International Court of Justice ruled by nine votes to six that Myanmar had "committed" genocide against the Rohingya community.
noticias.texto:
The International Court of Justice ruled by nine votes to six that Myanmar had "committed" genocide against the Rohingya community.
The International Court of Justice has found Myanmar guilty of genocide against its Rohingya minority. It is the first time in the court’s 80-year history that it has ruled a state committed the crime.
"The Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine State, in violation of its obligations under the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide," ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said on Thursday, reading the verdict in The Hague, Netherlands.
For almost three hours, Iwasawa set out the evidence from the military’s 2017 campaign against the mostly Muslim Rohingya, which drove hundreds of thousands of people across the border into Bangladesh.
He said Myanmar's security forces had killed thousands of Rohingya civilians and committed "widespread sexual violence" against women and "extreme violence" against children.
The judges found that Rohingya villages had been systematically destroyed and resettled with non-Rohingya people. They concluded that the "only reasonable inference" was that Myanmar intended to destroy the group, which is the legal test for genocide.
Compensation and return
The court ordered Myanmar to compensate the Rohingya for "the damage caused by the violations of its obligations... in so far as such damage is not made good by restitution". The amount will be decided at a later date.
Myanmar must also "allow and facilitate the safe, voluntary, and dignified return" of those who fled, and investigate and punish anyone suspected of taking part in the genocide.
ICJ rulings are binding and cannot be appealed. However, the court has no power to enforce them, and it is unclear whether Myanmar’s leaders will comply.
The verdict is likely to add to pressure on Min Aung Hlaing, who led the military during the 2017 crackdown. He seized power from Aung San Suu Kyi's elected government in a 2021 coup, and this year he was installed as civilian president after tightly restricted elections. The ruling could complicate his push for international recognition.
Agnes Callamard, Secretary General of Amnesty International, called the ruling "a historic and authoritative recognition of the atrocities committed against the Rohingya and a rare moment of justice for survivors, victims and their families".
Legal experts are watching the case for signs of how the ICJ might rule on South Africa's separate case accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza.
'I want justice'
More than a million Rohingya now live in the world’s largest refugee camp, across the border in Bangladesh. Refugees there have described gang rapes, mass executions and attacks on families and children.
"I want justice," said a 23-year-old survivor of rape, speaking to AFP before the verdict from the cramped shelter she shares with her family. She asked not to be named.
"There should be stringent punishment for those who raped women," she said.
Mohammed Osman, 20, said he hoped the ruling would let him go home to perform last rites for his parents and younger brother, who were killed by the military.
"They shot my father dead, forced my mother into a house with a few other women, raped them and burnt down our homestead," he told AFP.
Seven-year case
The Gambia brought the case in 2019 under the 1948 Genocide Convention, which allows any signatory state to take another to court over suspected breaches. It has the backing of the 57-member Organisation of Islamic Cooperation.
"It is not about esoteric issues of international law, it is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings," said Dawda Jallow, The Gambia’s justice minister.
Myanmar has always denied genocide. It says it was responding to an insurgency after militant attacks killed about a dozen members of its security forces.
"Myanmar was not obliged to remain idle and allow terrorists to have free rein," Ko Ko Hlaing, Myanmar’s representative, told the judges at hearings in January.

noticias.titulo: Corrado Augias dies aged 91, journalism world mourns, minute of silence in Senate
noticias.resumen: A leading figure in Italian journalism for decades, the journalist Corrado Augias has died at the age of 91.
noticias.texto:
A leading figure in Italian journalism for decades, the journalist Corrado Augias has died at the age of 91.
Corrado Augias, a historic voice of Italian journalism, an author and television presenter, has died at the age of 91. The news was announced by the Italian daily newspaper Repubblica, with which Augias had been collaborating since its foundation.
"With the death of Corrado Augias, Italian journalism loses an indispensable point of reference. Journalist, essayist, playwright, presenter, Augias was an intellectual capable of deciphering in every era the changes in Italian society, which he was able to recount with authority," the Usigrai executive said in a statement.
Corrado Augias's career, from newspapers to television
Born in Rome on 26 January 1935 to parents of French origin, Augias registered with the journalists' association on 1 April 1969, but had already been working with Rai since 1960, six years after the start of its broadcasts. In 60 years of intense activity, in addition to his long-standing collaboration with Repubblica as correspondent and columnist, from 2001 to 2021 he oversaw the newspaper's letters page, where readers' letters were published.
Augias was not only a print journalist, he also became well known as a television presenter, with a style marked by elegant and courteous yet incisive manners, and no shortage of irony, able to engage with the most diverse guests. His fame on the small screen came thanks to the programme he devised for Rai on famous unresolved crime cases, Telefono Giallo, which he presented from 1987 to 1993.
The best-known episode of Telefono Giallo is the one broadcast on 6 May 1988, in which an officer on duty at the time of the Ustica massacre called the programme, providing previously unknown details that prompted the then public prosecutor Paolo Borsellino to reopen the case.
In recent years, Augias mainly worked with the broadcaster La7, on the programme La Torre di Babele. Alongside his journalistic work, he successfully tried his hand at writing crime novels and essays.
Applause and a minute's silence in the Senate in memory of Corrado Augias
After the news of his death was learned, announced in the Senate during the debate on the school decree law by Italia Viva's group leader Raffaella Paita, senators from both the majority and the opposition joined in a long applause.
"We have just learned of the death of Corrado Augias and I would like this Chamber to pay him a round of applause," Paita said. The president of the Senate, Ignazio La Russa, also joined in the condolences, asking for a few minutes of silence.
The mayor of Rome, Roberto Gualtieri, also commemorated the intellectual before the city council meeting. "Corrado Augias was a major figure in culture and journalism, an engaged intellectual and a Roman citizen to whom we owe a great deal. I want to express all my personal sorrow, that of the administration and, I think I can say, of the entire city. I offer my most heartfelt condolences to his family, his friends and his relatives," Gualtieri said.
The director of La7, Andrea Salerno, also expressed his condolences for Augias's death and his closeness to the family.

noticias.titulo: How to watch the UK-EU summit like a pro
noticias.resumen: After more than two years of talks, can London and Brussels finally agree on a reset? Here’s what to look out for as their leaders meet.
noticias.texto: BRUSSELS — Andy Burnham has gone big on Britain’s relationship with the EU during the first months of his premiership. By the weekend, he may actually have something to show for it. The British prime minister is heading to Brussels on Friday for his first U.K.-EU summit. But on the eve of the meeting, what exactly he’ll be coming back with is still up in the air. POLITICO analyzed leaked draft communiqués and spoke to diplomats and officials on both sides of the talks to piece together how the agreements are shaping up — and what’s still to be decided. Here’s what you need to know. Why is this happening? The U.K. and EU have committed to holding annual summits to build on the relationship they were left with after Brexit. This is the second such meeting, and is primarily about concluding negotiations on agreements announced at the first gathering back in May 2025. That summit was attended by then-British Prime Minister Keir Starmer. This week’s meeting was originally due to be held in July, but it was postponed after Starmer stepped down — to give Burnham time to put his stamp on the process. What’s on the table? Three new international agreements are set to be announced at the meeting. The first is a sanitary and phytosanitary deal that would align British food and drink standards with the EU’s. The aim of the agreement is to remove bureaucracy and to eliminate the need for border checks on food exports, smoothing trade. The two sides have also negotiated a deal to link their emissions trading systems. The main benefit would be to exempt U.K. and EU businesses from having to pay new carbon border taxes levied by both sides. It would also provide more liquidity in carbon trading markets. It still wasn’t clear on Thursday night when the deal will take effect, though. The longer it takes to introduce, the longer firms would be caught between the two competing tax regimes. Brussels and London also want to establish a youth experience scheme, which would provide low-cost visas for young people to live and work abroad for a fixed period of time. The U.K. has insisted the system should be subject to a cap on numbers — expected to be around 100,000 after fraught negotiations. Complications implementing the scheme in some member countries means it isn’t set to take full effect until 2030. This would also mean its full impact on politically-sensitive U.K. migration data won’t register until after the next election, which must be held no later than 2029. In addition to these three agreements, the two sides will also publish a “joint statement” outlining their plans for other areas of cooperation. This isn’t a binding international agreement, but a statement of intent, covering areas ranging from migration and defense to cultural exchange, a digital partnership and a health security pact. On tech, British firms are concerned that they could be shut out of parts of the EU public administration market because of the proposed Cloud and AI Development Act (CADA) and its new sovereignty requirements. They’ve lobbied hard for reassuring language in talks, both with the negotiators working on the law and with those drafting the joint statement. On health, the U.K. and EU are looking to strike a deal to tackle medicine shortages by sharing intelligence on supply disruptions and stockpiles. As Brussels steps up efforts to manage medicine shortages across the bloc, Britain risks being left out of the increasingly joined up system. Closer cooperation could help both sides “avoid procurement battles” for limited stocks and “tit-for-tat export bans, as happened during the pandemic,” said Mark Dayan, Brexit lead at the Nuffield Trust. One area the statement will definitely cover is the question of tuition fees. EU countries want European students studying at British universities to qualify for lower domestic fees, as they did before Brexit. The U.K. is open to the idea but wants, in turn, assurances its businesses won’t be hit by new EU Made in Europe rules. Brussels says it can’t give those assurances yet, so the statement is likely to include a compromise to delay talks by up to six months. Only then will we find out how much lower tuition fees might get. Another key question is whether the implementation of the agri-food, emissions trading and youth mobility deals will be contingent on a successful outcome for tuition fee talks — which some member countries have been pushing for. This will be determined by the wording of the final statement, but the latest version does not make this link explicit. What does Burnham want to talk about? Since Labour Party conference in September, Burnham has talked up building a closer relationship with the EU — ditching some of the caution that characterized his predecessor’s approach to European relations. He may try to use the meeting as an opportunity to sound out EU leaders on where things could go next. But grumblings from Burnham’s own Cabinet about his policy shift on Europe could mean he keeps a lot of that under his hat. He’s expected to set out options for a new look-relationship in mid-December. In the meantime, the government wants a political win from the deals to be agreed on Friday. In the run-up to the meeting, European Relations Minister Hamish Falconer has been making the argument that the SPS deal will help bring down the cost of living by controlling food inflation. Expect more of that. There are also topics that Burnham won’t want Brussels to forget — chiefly shielding British industry from Made in Europe protectionism. The EU wants the joint statement to “bind” the U.K. to implementing EU tariffs against Chinese vehicles. But London hasn’t made up its mind and merely wants to commit to guarding against the risk of “circumvention.” What does the EU want to talk about? Equally, there are topics Brussels won’t want London to forget about. EU member countries are very keen on that tuition fees cut, for example. But for the EU, building a closer relationship with Britain is mostly about geostrategic aims. With an uncertain Atlantic alliance and war raging in Europe’s east, the EU wants to build new defense, industrial and security relationships — and the U.K. is the most obvious partner. How does the day unfold? The summit will kick off at 10 a.m. Brussels time, so 9 a.m. London time. How long it goes on for will depend on just how done those deals are by the time Burnham steps off the Eurostar. If things go smoothly, officials on both sides are estimating a joint press conference to announce the package and take questions around lunchtime. That’ll be attended by Burnham, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, and European Council President António Costa. But if there’s no sign of a white smoke by around 2 p.m., things may not be going entirely to plan.
