noticias.titulo: Trump presses European leaders about Ukraine aid in call after Putin summit
noticias.resumen: In a surprise call, the U.S. president followed up his meeting with Russian and Chinese leaders by quizzing Kyiv's European allies.
noticias.texto: BERLIN — U.S. President Donald Trump called in to a meeting of Ukraine’s European allies on Thursday, according to four European officials who were briefed on the discussion, where he sharply questioned their continued spending on military support for Kyiv. Hours after concluding a meeting with Kremlin chief Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China, Trump called Berlin from Air Force One and said the Russian leader was serious about peace negotiations about Ukraine. On the call, Trump vigorously expressed his skepticism about further billions in aid being provided to Ukraine by the so-called Coalition of the Willing, according to three of the European officials, who were granted anonymity to describe a private meeting. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. When asked at a press conference following the coalition meeting whether Trump held too rosy a view of Putin’s desire to end the war, U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said it was “quite the opposite” and that Trump had talked about the “horrific” loss of life in the nearly five-year war. Trump envoy Steve Witkoff, who attended along with Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, added: “He sent Jared and I here specifically to be a part of the Coalition of the Willing, and he’s given us instructions on doing everything possible to end this war and be supportive of that effort. And what I heard from him on the call today, was that he mentioned these very same principles to the other two leaders he was meeting with.” One person who was in the room for the Trump call said the president talked in a general way, and made the point to leaders that a lot of people were dying in this war and countries should stop wasting money on it. Trump also told leaders that Putin is ready to have a negotiation to reach a peace deal, the same person said. Germany’s chancellor Friedrich Merz said at the press conference, however, that Europe is providing funding for Ukrainian defense “to enable peace negotiations in the first place and to conduct them from a position of strength.” Merz added: “We are not providing this strong support to prolong the war. We want to end this war.” This is a developing story. Alex Gangitano contributed to this report from Washington. James Angelos contributed from Berlin.

noticias.titulo: Britain shouldn’t rush to a second Brexit referendum, say pro-EU Lib Dems
noticias.resumen: Al Pinkerton, the party's Europe spokesperson, says the public would have “an expectation” there would be a referendum on rejoining the bloc.
noticias.texto: LONDON — The U.K. must get on with domestic reforms and not hurry into another Brexit vote, the Liberal Democrats have warned. Al Pinkerton, the party’s Europe spokesperson, told POLITICO that there’s “deep trauma” associated with the 2016 vote to leave the bloc which sparked years of parliamentary gridlock and opened up gaping political divisions. “We rush that at our peril,” Pinkerton said Thursday when asked whether his party will accelerate its support for a referendum to rejoin the EU. Any steps to closer ties need to make sure “that the British population are brought forward on that journey as well,” he added. Pinkerton was speaking ahead of Friday’s U.K.-EU summit in Brussels, where the two sides are set to sign a deal on food trading, carbon emissions and youth mobility. It comes amid a heightened debate about the merits of Brexit after British Prime Minister Andy Burnham pledged to look at longer-term options for Britain’s relationship with the EU. Three Labour ex-Cabinet ministers — Rachel Reeves , David Lammy and Peter Kyle — have called for Britain to re-enter the EU in recent weeks. Burnham has said Labour will stick by its 2024 election manifesto — which promised no return to the EU single market (including freedom of movement) or the customs union — during this parliament. The Liberal Democrats — the third largest party in the House of Commons — advocate rejoining the single market, agreeing a bespoke customs union and a growth and defense partnership with Brussels. The party’s official position is that it ultimately wants to re-enter the bloc , but argues incremental steps are a “pathway of building trust, of showing the economic benefits” before getting something “more substantive down the line.” Bre-join? Pinkerton said there are active discussions in the party “all the time” about whether to bring forward its support for Britain to rejoin the bloc, but highlighted a “certain level of distrust in that relationship” between the the U.K. and EU. There would be “an expectation” from the public a referendum would be held if Britain was to seek to rejoin because it is the way Britain left, he said: “The public would rightly ask the very difficult questions of a political party that did seek to make that move without going back to them.” The debate around rejoining the bloc has fired up campaigners who backed Brexit a decade ago. They argue another referendum would again dominate time and attention in Westminster. Pinkerton conceded it is an “entirely fair criticism” and “one of the reasons that I wouldn’t necessarily want to trigger that process right now, because I think there are so many domestic reforms that we need to be getting on with too.” He is optimistic Britain could remain outside the euro and Schengen area, though warned there’s “no guarantee” the previous rebate negotiated under Margaret Thatcher in the 1980s could be achieved again. Tackling the populists Pinkerton said he is not concerned Burnham’s willingness to discuss Britain’s ties to the bloc will leave the Liberal Democrats outflanked by Labour on the issue. “I look at the whites of the eyes of so many of his own MPs and I can see that there’s not an appetite for him to go any further than the light flirtation that he’s been engaged in over the last few weeks,” he said. Pinkerton said he is “deeply uneasy” about the prospect of the far right National Rally leader Marine Le Pen winning next year’s French presidential election as well as the recent state election performance of the Alternative for Germany, but said that shouldn’t “change our ambition” to be far closer to Europe as a vehicle for improving economic growth, something he argues could help neutralize populism. “We’re not making our propositions through a blind adherence to the idea that Europe is entirely virtuous and has no flaws,” Pinkerton said.

noticias.titulo: Startups call on Commission to salvage or scrap EU Inc proposal
noticias.resumen: Lobby groups call on Brussels to withdraw and resubmit after proposal for new corporate form was watered down by EU member countries.
noticias.texto: HELSINKI — The European Commission should withdraw and resubmit its proposal for a new EU-wide corporate law framework, startup lobby groups said, denouncing the current text as a “Frankenstein” proposal. A position on the law adopted by EU capitals in October “weakened or removed some of the very provisions that would make EU Inc. a true European standard,” Startups for Europe and EU Inc. said in a joint press release. Both groups pitched the withdrawal to European Commissioners Henna Virkkunen and Ekaterina Zaharieva, who oversee tech policy and startups, during a policy roundtable at Finnish technology conference Slush on Thursday morning. They also sent a joint letter to European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen earlier this week. The European Commission published its proposal for a so-called 28th regime, also known as EU Inc., earlier this year, to harmonize how founders can incorporate a company and reward their personnel, so that startups can scale more easily across the bloc. The scheme was seen as a challenge to the U.S. state of Delaware , which is known for its flexible incorporation laws. Lobby groups now say that EU capitals have rolled back key provisions, such as the freedom to set up shop in any EU country and simplified insolvency rules. With their demand to withdraw and submit a new proposal, the groups hope that EU capitals will rethink their position. “This is an opportunity for Member States to reconsider their positions and make sure EU Inc. delivers on its original promise,” said Simon Schaefer, president of Startups for Europe. Jeannette zu Fürstenberg, managing director of General Catalyst, a fund that backed leading European companies such as Helsing and Legora, also criticized the EU Inc. proposal as it stands. “If it comes out like that, it’s going to be Frankenstein that the whole world will laugh at,” she said in an interview at Slush. She said the EU Inc. proposal should specifically address how stock options, often used to reward startup staff, are taxed. “If you need to pay dry income on something that’s essentially illiquid, you’re bankrupting the people building it,” zu Fürstenberg explained. A separate group of 38 tech executives, including Spotify founder Daniel Ek, Exor CEO John Elkann and Skype co-founder Niklas Zennström, took a softer line in a declaration published at Slush. They called EU Inc. “the most important first step” toward a true single market and did not ask for the proposal to be withdrawn. They also urged Brussels to enforce the Digital Markets Act, the EU’s rulebook for the largest online platforms. Europe must “simplify regulation that limits growth and at the same time enforce competition law and the Digital Markets Act,” the declaration said. Still to play for The EU Inc. legislation has also hit a roadblock in the European Parliament, where lead lawmaker René Repasi’s report on it has yet to clear the committee stage. Repasi, a German Social Democrat, told POLITICO he could understand the frustration of the supporters of the original legislation. “The political groups that in principle support EU Inc. should now quickly reach a common parliamentary position,” Repasi said, adding that this would enable the Parliament to negotiate in favor of key provisions for startups in the interinstitutional negotiations that are still to come on hammering out a legislative compromise. Asked for comment, EU Justice Commissioner Michael McGrath said the objective from the outset had been “to establish a genuinely European corporate framework that is simple, attractive and enables innovative companies to start, grow and scale across the Single Market.” While he did not directly address the criticism of the startups, McGrath said the Commission stood ready to work with the European Parliament and Council of the EU to “preserve the ambition” of the legislation. “The forthcoming trilogues will be an important opportunity to address outstanding concerns and work towards an agreement that delivers real benefits for companies across the Single Market,” McGrath said in a statement to POLITICO. This article has been updated.

noticias.titulo: Video: EU-Gesundheitskommissar wird aus Protest gegen Pestizidregeln mit „Asche“ beworfen
noticias.resumen: Olivér Várhelyi wollte gerade auf einem Krebsgipfel das Wort ergreifen, als eine graue Substanz auf ihn geworfen wurde.
noticias.texto: BRÜSSEL — Aktivisten einer Gruppe von Krebsüberlebenden haben eine ascheähnliche Substanz auf den EU-Gesundheitskommissar geworfen, um gegen die neuen europäischen Vorschriften zur Lockerung des Pestizideinsatzes zu protestieren. Gesundheitskommissar Olivér Várhelyi wollte gerade auf einem Europäischen Krebsgipfel eine Rede über die Maßnahmen der EU zur Bekämpfung der Krankheit halten, als zwei Demonstranten die Bühne stürmten und ein graues, staubiges Pulver auf ihn warfen. „Ich bin Krebspatientin. Ich protestiere gegen das Sammelgesetz“, sagte eine der Aktivistinnen der französischen Gruppe Cancer Colère. „Das ist die Asche der Menschen, die ihr mit den Pestiziden töten werdet“, sagte eine andere. Eine der Demonstrantinnen war Fleur Breteau, eine französische Schriftstellerin und Aktivistin. Die andere konnte nicht identifiziert werden. Die Kommission stellte das Omnibus-Gesetz als Möglichkeit vor, den Rückstau bei der Zulassung von Pestiziden abzubauen und den Landwirten das Leben zu erleichtern. Viele zivilgesellschaftliche Gruppen lehnen es jedoch entschieden ab. Mehr als 2.000 Wissenschaftler haben einen Brief unterzeichnet, in dem sie fordern, den Vorschlag so lange auszusetzen, bis eine unabhängige Folgenabschätzung durchgeführt wurde. Die Verbraucherorganisation Foodwatch hat die Angelegenheit vor den Europäischen Bürgerbeauftragten gebracht und der Kommission Verwaltungsmissstände vorgeworfen. Außerdem haben Nichtregierungsorganisationen zahlreiche Proteste organisiert. Mehr als 300 Nichtregierungsorganisationen – darunter Umweltverbände, Imkerverbände und Gruppen von Pestizidopfern sowie Ärzte und Wissenschaftler – aus 25 europäischen Ländern wollen sich am 24. November um 14 Uhr vor dem Europäischen Parlament in Straßburg versammeln , um ihre Unzufriedenheit mit dem Sammelgesetz zum Ausdruck zu bringen. Video, aufgenommen am 19. November 2026 im „The Hotel“ in Brüssel. | Emma Pirnay/POLITICO Várhelyi wischte sich sichtlich verärgert den Staub ab und fuhr wie geplant mit seiner Rede fort. „Was für Leute seid ihr denn?“, bemerkte er. „Wie ich schon sagte: Guten Morgen. Ich bin ein bisschen überrascht, dass sie es wagen, im Namen der Krebsopfer die Asche der Verstorbenen zu verstreuen.“ „Das übertrifft alles, was wir uns hätten vorstellen können. Es tut uns leid“, sagte Elisabetta Zanon, Leiterin der European Cancer Organisation, vor dem Publikum.

noticias.titulo: Nigel Farage is back in Brussels
noticias.resumen: The veteran Brexiteer is in town to attack Andy Burnham's efforts at building bridges with the EU.
noticias.texto: LONDON — Brussels beware. Nigel Farage is returning to the European Parliament for the first time since abolishing his role as an MEP with his successful Brexit crusade. The Reform UK leader is back in Brussels to launch his campaign against Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s push to bring Britain closer once again to the EU. Coinciding with Burnham’s visit to sign a new deal with Europe on Friday, Farage will give a speech to try to ward the PM off going even further. Farage will attack that deal but go further to attack Burnham’s ambition of getting closer to the EU as negative and backwards looking, according to his spokesperson. Instead, the veteran Brexiteer will try to paint a vision of an optimistic future of Britain outside the bloc — in stark contrast to how the U.K. public feels about the country’s current status. But before the speeches, Farage will be visiting the European Parliament on Thursday and Friday. It’ll be his first time back in the building since 2020, his spokesperson said. Back then, just two days before Brexit was implemented after protracted negotiations, Farage received a final reprimand, for waving Union Jacks against the flag-bearing rules. Farage used that final speech to say the looming formal departure from the EU, at 11 p.m. on Jan 31, 2020, was “the point of no return — once we’ve left we are never coming back.” Whether that is true or not appears more up in the air today than it has done in the decade since the Brexit referendum. Burnham chose to reignite the debate this summer by saying he wants a national conversation about the next steps in bringing the U.K. closer to Europe. He even went as far as not taking a full-blown rejoin off the table. The PM has since been learning just how challenging that ambition is to realise , with cabinet members in his center-left government expressing hesitancy and Eurosceptic campaigns firing back into life. Farage’s spokesperson said his speech in Brussels on Friday will be the start of his “personal” campaign but he’s also left open working with one or both of the rebranded Vote Leave and Leave.EU campaigns.

noticias.titulo: Présidentielle : pourquoi les youtubeurs ne veulent pas être régulés comme les télés
noticias.resumen: Dans un entretien à POLITICO, l’Umicc défend fermement ses positions face aux règles de pluralisme que veut soumettre l'Arcom aux créateurs de contenus.
noticias.texto: PARIS — Un million de vues pour son interview de Jean-Luc Mélenchon : le succès d’audience des “Dossiers”, le nouveau programme de Gaspard G diffusé en partenariat avec TF1, n’est plus à prouver. Le youtubeur politique le plus connu de France a pourtant du souci à se faire. L’Arcom, le régulateur de l’audiovisuel et du numérique, doit présenter ce jeudi les nouvelles règles applicables aux médias audiovisuels et numériques — créateurs de contenus compris — dans le cadre de l’élection présidentielle de 2027. Provoquant sans surprise et bien que Martin Ajdari, président du régulateur, ait tenté de rassurer sur ses intentions, quelques secousses dans un secteur peu disposé à s’aligner sur l’obligation de pluralisme imposée aux radios et télévisions. A la veille de cette présentation, POLITICO a échangé avec Gaspard G — Gaspard Guermonprez à la ville — et Bénédicte de Kersauson, respectivement vice-président et déléguée générale de l’Umicc (Union des métiers de l’influence et des créateurs de contenu), sur la place des influenceurs politiques dans la campagne. “On se demande comment une règle de pluralisme qui a été créée pour répondre à la rareté des fréquences télé et radio sur la TNT peut s’appliquer à des chaînes que vous pouvez créer en quinze secondes aujourd’hui, avec une adresse mail, sur YouTube ou TikTok”, pose d’entrée de jeu Gaspard G, qui a rejoint l’équipe de l’Umicc en 2024. Et l’influenceur de poursuivre : “On ne peut pas programmer, à une certaine heure [comme le font les chaînes de télévision], un bout de leurs interventions pour respecter les règles de temps de parole et de pluralisme. Moi, par exemple, je sors une ou deux vidéos par mois.” Les inquiétudes sont donc fortes du côté des créateurs à l’idée de devoir recevoir tout l’échiquier politique. “Tous les politiques ne voient pas l’intérêt de passer sur nos chaînes…”, souligne Gaspard G. Et pour cause : les candidats n’ont aucune certitude de faire des grosses audiences quand bien même l’influenceur qui reçoit est une star. “La vidéo sur Jean-Luc Mélenchon a fait 1 million, celle sur Gabriel Attal 250 000 vues. Mais je n’ai pas d’impact là-dessus, c’est l’algorithme qui décide et qui répond lui-même à une logique commerciale.” Pour limiter la casse, la déléguée générale de l’Umicc a pris les devants et fait quelques suggestions au régulateur. “Au lieu de cibler idiotement la masse des 200 000 créateurs de contenu en France, on pourrait peut-être s’intéresser à ceux qui ont une influence sociétale”, estime-t-elle. Comprendre : seraient concernés les influenceurs dont 30% des contenus, sur les douze derniers mois, traitent de sujets d’intérêt public et qui ont touché au moins 5% de la population. Deux critères cumulatifs qui pourraient bien trouver leur place dans la recommandation — non contraignante — du régulateur, qui s’appliquera en principe aux créateurs à partir du mois de mars. “Ils sont dans une logique de discussion. Ils se veulent hyper rassurants, concède Bénédicte de Kersauson. Mais on sait très bien que c’est glissant… Donc on reste vigilant”, conclut-elle. “La creator economy mérite mieux” L’autre gros chantier de l’Union des créateurs de contenu porte sur le financement du secteur, et notamment les aides publiques. Le lobby a ainsi œuvré ces derniers mois pour faire rétablir le fonds d’aide à la création sur les plateformes sociales, suspendu par le Centre national de l’image animée et du cinéma (CNC) en avril 2026. Son retour, annoncé le 5 novembre à la Paris Creators Week, a toutefois laissé l’Umicc sur sa faim. Son vice-président espère une vraie revalorisation du dispositif. “La creator economy mérite mieux et reste largement sous-dimensionnée en matière d’aides publiques par rapport à l’impact culturel qu’elle a au quotidien sur tous les Français”, regrette Gaspard G. Ce fonds n’ayant vocation à soutenir que les œuvres dites “patrimoniales” (fictions, documentaires et programmes d’animation), l’Umicc planche sur une autre piste pour aider les créateurs de contenu d’actualité. Son projet : obtenir un fonds ad hoc auprès de la direction générale des médias et des industries culturelles (DGMIC). Les aides publiques à l’information venant rarement sans contreparties — notamment en matière de transparence et de déontologie —, l’association a d’ailleurs décidé de montrer patte blanche et travaille, avec l’aide de journalistes indépendants comme Benoît Le Corre ou Charles Villa, sur une charte déontologique pour les créateurs de contenu d’actualité. “On ne peut pas imposer de la régulation sans accompagnement, et nous on fait ce premier pas d’accompagnement”, insiste Bénédicte de Kersauson. Un message qu’elle porte aussi à Bruxelles, avec l’ European Influencer Marketing Alliance (EIMA), son pendant européen, dans le cadre de la révision de la directive européenne sur les services des médias audiovisuels (SMA). Cette réforme-là fait aussi trembler le secteur, car elle pourrait faire basculer les créateurs de contenu sous un nouveau statut : celui de “service de médias audiovisuels à la demande” (Smad), qui inclut actuellement les télévisions de rattrapage comme TF1+ ou france.tv, les plateformes payantes de vidéos à la demande (Netflix, Amazon Prime…) et la vidéo classique, avec paiement à l’acte. “On craint que Bruxelles ne joue la facilité et qu’ils ne s’embarrassent pas d’essayer de comprendre nos acteurs pour créer des règles propres au secteur”, regrette-t-elle. Le lobby européen défend plutôt la création d’un statut à part, qui prenne en compte le critère d’impact sociétal des créateurs, comme proposé à l’Arcom. Ce combat “sera au cœur de nos activités de 2027”, conclut la déléguée générale.

noticias.titulo: Beaujolais Nouveau: A French tradition uncorked
noticias.resumen: Every year on the third Thursday of November, France raises a glass to one of its most joyful traditions: Le Beaujolais Nouveau! That means that this Thursday, millions of bottles of the 2026 young red wine will be uncorked around the world, from Lyon to New York. Olivier Badoureaux, wine expert and director of the French trade organisation Inter Beaujolais, tells us what we should expect from this year's vintage.

noticias.titulo: France: Retirees march against 2027 budget cuts
noticias.resumen: More than a thousand people marched in Paris on Thursday, called by a union alliance joined by student and high-school groups, to protest social and tax measures targeting retirees in the 2027 budgets. The government wants retirees to contribute about €5.4 billion, by freezing the indexation of pensions above €1,260 and reforming their 10% income tax allowance. Union leaders say the money should not come from retirees’ pockets, as FRANCE 24's Luke Shrago explains.

noticias.titulo: Italy’s hard definition of antisemitism will shield Israeli crimes and harm free speech
noticias.resumen: Italy's Meloni has doubled down on her populist and performative claims to care about Jewish minorities, by imposing a hardline definition of antisemitism that risks gagging debate.
noticias.texto: Anti-Jewish discrimination and legitimate criticism of Israeli state actions became conflated into one offence by Italy’s parliament on Tuesday (17 November). Adopting the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance’s ( IHRA ) official definition of anti-semitism, Rome’s bill will apply across schools, universities, social-media platforms, and beyond. The move has raised serious concerns about what this will do to freedom of expression and protest. Despite not imposing financial penalties or criminal sanctions for offenders, it shows which side of history far-right prime minister Georgia Meloni’s Italy has chosen. “Branding criticism of Israel’s brutal occupation, its system of apartheid, and its ongoing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza as antisemitic – which could happen under the new law – also risks shielding state policies and practices from legitimate public scrutiny and debate,” said Erika Guevara Rosas, Amnesty International’s senior director for policy and research. Read more Fastest EU citizens’ initiative ever pushes Brussels to end EU‑Israel trade agreement “By blurring the distinction between antisemitism and criticism of a state’s actions, the law also risks undermining efforts to identify and effectively address genuine antisemitisms,” she said. Not only does Tuesday mark a bleak beginning for press and self-censorship on issues of public interest in Italy, following the path of the UK’s persecution of the Palestine Action group, who has now arrested over 4,000 activists involved in peaceful protests against Israel’s offences in the occupied territories. Not only does this also indicate the start of an authoritarian slippery slope, which could end in silencing political criticism that is not favoured by the ruling powers, or debate concerning those in office. But it is largely a display of the narrow priorities subscribed to by Meloni’s stagnant government. Read more [Interview] Italy’s Meloni is EU’s best hope of charming Putin at Ukraine peace talks, former Russian spy says Although she has held power for longer than any of her predecessors in the history of the Republic, there is little to show for it, with headline measures that included tightened citizenship rules, anti-rave actions, cuts to welfare benefits, and limited offshoring of migrant processing to an exorbitantly expensive centre in Albania. And stalled economic growth matches the trend. Meanwhile, in a 147-93 vote in Rome’s Palazzo Chigi, supporters of the pro-IHRA definition bill cited soaring anti-Jewish violence and aggression as their main motivation, while forgetting about the abundant relics of fascism that still scar whole cities and regions across Italy, influencing every generation with hatred of minorities. Even the granddaughter of Italy’s late fascist dictator, Rachele Mussolini, has quit Meloni’s Brothers of Italy party for being too rightwing in its treatment of minorities, which should speak volumes on the government’s lack of integrity in its claims to care about Jewish people in Italy. As repression increasingly hits press and NGO freedoms in Europe and beyond , laws that seek to police the vocabulary of crucial democratic debates risk pushing our societies back into dark times, which our grandparents fought to end. In 2024, the German parliament passed a non-binding resolution backing the IHRA definition. Two years later, Germany is considering a law that would make denying Israel’s right to exist a crime, with up to five years in prison. Read more Germany’s historical struggle and the legal debate on Israel’s right to exist

noticias.titulo: UK-EU summit to see mutual love-bombing, but British must decide what to do next
noticias.resumen: There will be agreements aplenty in Brussels on Friday, but the UK needs to decide how ambitious its plans for closer integration with the EU will be.
noticias.texto: As a public relations exercise, Friday’s (20 November) EU-UK summit in Brussels will be a collective love-in, with new agreements galore. UK prime minister Andy Burnham wants to prove that he is delivering the EU ‘reset’ that his predecessor Keir Starmer had promised. But there are limits to the number of sectoral agreements – or cherry picking – on offer. Ahead of the summit, EU officials have warned that there’s not much more fruit left to pick. A draft joint summit statement points to further discussions on the UK linking up with the EU’s energy single market, as well as on co-operation on migration control, and a closer defence and security relationship. Read more ‘Emperor’s New Clothes’: Burnham breaks 10-year taboo on Brexit The UK needs to decide whether it wants to join the single market, rejoin the EU, or accept the status quo, say EU diplomats. In a fact sheet published earlier this week, the UK government said that the ‘food & drink’ trade deal “could add up to £5.1bn [€6.1bn] a year to our economy, cutting back on paperwork for businesses and easing pressure on prices.” The agreement to align agrifood standards will scrap border controls and certification requirements for “the vast majority” of animal and plant products traded between the UK and the EU from 1 March 2028. The factsheet adds that an emissions linking agreement could add up to £3.8bn a year, and protect critical industries, such as steel and aluminium, from the EU’s carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM), on approximately £6.5bn in exports. The EU and UK are also to launch a digital partnership in early 2027 covering secure connectivity, artificial intelligence, and digital identities. A Youth Experience Scheme (TES), meanwhile, will let young people live in each other’s territories for up to three years to work or study. The aim is to seal the agreement by 2028 and have the scheme running by January 2030. The total number of participants has not been decided yet, although sources say it is likely to be around 100,000. But the UK will probably have to wait for an agreement on its main priorities: inclusion in the EU’s ‘Made in Europe’ industrial support scheme, and participation in the EU’s €150bn ‘Security Action for Europe’ (SAFE) instrument for common defence borrowing. The talks on ‘Made in Europe’ are more complicated than simply aligning regulation. The EU’s Industrial Accelerator Act, which sets out the rules on supply chain inputs, is still being negotiated by EU governments and MEPs and is unlikely to be finalised before early 2027. Any deal between London and Brussels would need to be based on the EU law that is eventually adopted. It would also need to be in line with the demands of a Franco-German paper from October, which proposed Britain be granted special status for automobiles, subject to “dynamic alignment with EU conditions for investment from third countries and with EU trade protection measures”. That will likely require the UK to impose tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles and curbing imports of Chinese hybrid cars, in line with the EU. Read more EU‑UK carbon market deal close, with UK courting access to ‘Made in Europe’ before Dublin summit So what does Burnham want? noticias.titulo: Hungary’s new government claws back motorways and tobacco monopoly after years of taxpayer‑funded Orbán luxury travel (Day 191 of the Tisza government)
noticias.resumen: Hungary’s new leaders rip up motorway and tobacco deals that once enriched Orbán’s allies, raising the prospect of a massive financial and political reckoning.
noticias.texto: The series continues as we report on developments following April’s historic election and on the steps taken since then by the Tisza government. This week, we cover the following topics: Viktor Orbán travelled in luxury on trips abroad Treasure hunting, Hungarian style The state is taking back motorway operations from Mészáros and Szíjj The government moves to dismantle part of Hungary’s controversial tobacco concession system It has been an eventful week in Hungary. As investigators seized billions of forints in cash buried in forests and hidden in safes, the government began dismantling some of the most controversial concessions awarded under its predecessor. The state is taking back motorway operations from the consortium linked to Lőrinc Mészáros and László Szíjj, and the government has moved to end the monopoly on supplying tobacco shops. Meanwhile, foreign ministry records obtained through a court case have revealed how much Viktor Orbán’s luxury travel cost taxpayers. Orbán luxury travels The news outlet 444.hu obtained records from the ministry of foreign affairs and trade through a freedom-of-information lawsuit. The records detail the cost and circumstances of former prime minister Orbán’s official trips by air between 2015 and 2025. Who paid for his foreign travel had been a recurring question since 2010. Reports suggested he travelled on private jets belonging to OTP Bank or to various oligarchs, while others suggested he paid his own way. The records show that the ministry alone spent HUF 4.8bn (€13.03m) in public funds over 10 years, covering all or part of the cost of 327 trips by air. The figures exclude trips on military aircraft. The ministry covered an average of 32 trips a year, with both the number of trips and spending peaking in 2024, when it paid nearly HUF 800m (€2.17m) towards 44 trips. The ministry’s flight costs fell sharply after the Hungarian Defence Forces acquired two Airbus troop transports and two luxury Dassault Falcon jets in 2018. The cost of using military aircraft was charged elsewhere. The foreign ministry’s overall travel spending rose sharply again from 2022 as hotel bills and “other” expenses, including meals, official hospitality and car hire, increased. In 2025 alone, the ministry spent HUF 450m (€1.22m) on hotels, almost as much as it had spent from 2016 to 2021 combined. Brussels was Orbán’s most frequent destination, with 74 trips costing a total of HUF 550m. Warsaw followed with 18 trips and Belgrade with 16. Orbán visited the United States only five times during the period covered by the records, but the size of his delegations made it the second-costliest destination overall, at HUF 380m. The five most expensive trips : Vietnam and Singapore, 2017 — HUF 180.4m (€490,000). The 23-member delegation stayed four nights. Flights accounted for most of the cost. Buenos Aires, Argentina, 2023 — HUF 159m (€431,000). A delegation of 27 stayed three nights for Javier Milei’s inauguration. Expenses included luxury hotels, HUF 12 million in catering and a meal at a Michelin-starred restaurant. Doha, Qatar, 2022 — HUF 131.8m (€358,000). The four-person trip included stops in Europe between the FIFA World Cup semi-final and final. The foreign ministry paid HUF 126 million of the total in hotel bills. Washington and Palm Beach, United States, 2024 — HUF 127m (€345,000). The 73-member delegation stayed two nights. The trip included a meeting with Donald Trump and had no official government programme. Beijing and Shenzhen, China, 2023 — HUF 106.5m (€289,000). The 26-member delegation stayed five nights. The trip included the Belt and Road Forum and meetings with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping. Travel requests from the prime minister’s cabinet office often left out the name of the event, the mode of transport or the point of departure. In some cases, it is still impossible to establish exactly why the trip took place. In others, the circumstances point to private engagements or sporting events for which the foreign ministry covered the cost of a private, high-security airport lounge reserved for government use or a stay at a luxury hotel. The line between official and private travel often blurred. Read more Hungary digs up €17m in buried cash during probe into Orbán-era minister Seszták The 444.hu report also recalls that government ministers, Orbán himself and Sándor Csányi, who chairs both the Hungarian Football Federation (MLSZ) and OTP Bank, gave conflicting accounts over the years of who paid for private flights to football matches or holiday destinations. In 2019, Csányi said Orbán had always paid for his own trips. In an interview in autumn 2025, Orbán acknowledged that the Hungarian state paid for his private flights to national team matches abroad, citing invitations from the federation. The newly released ministry records corroborate that account. Treasure hunting, Hungarian style Investigators from the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH) found nearly HUF 6.5 billion (around €17m) in cash in the course of criminal proceedings involving Miklós Seszták. The money had been buried in forests and concealed in warehouses and a hidden safe. Read more Hungary digs up €17m in buried cash during probe into Orbán-era minister Seszták The office says it is still unclear who owns it. Hungarians were confronted with the sight of a sum that someone earning an honest living could hardly make in a lifetime, hidden underground, in buildings and in safes. noticias.titulo: Ukrainians hit Crimea’s railway bridge with Neptune missiles, but it is harder to destroy than the road bridge (Ukraine Battlefield update, Day 1,729)
noticias.resumen: Ukraine’s strikes on the Crimean railway bridge and Russia’s refineries are no longer just symbolic blows, but a coordinated effort to choke off fuel, supplies, and troop movements deep inside Russian-held territory.
noticias.texto: Ukraine attacked the railway bridge to Crimea, hitting it with Neptune missiles, according to the General Staff. It was unclear how badly the bridge was damaged, but traffic was suspended. Why it is harder to put the railway bridge to Crimea out of action than the road bridge, part of which collapsed on Tuesday. Ukrainians continue their attacks on the overland route to Crimea. Russian refinery output has fallen by 45 percent compared with the end of October, Reuters reported. Chart of the day: Russians have advanced in recent weeks, but only slightly. Videos of the day: Russian air “defence” of refineries; a Russian drone evacuates a destroyed motorcycle. The General Staff of the Ukrainian Armed Forces trolled the Russian army effectively on Thursday morning. It published a post in which it congratulated Lisbon’s Vasco da Gama Bridge on gaining the title of Europe’s longest bridge. The congratulations were premature, however. Europe’s longest bridge remains the railway section of the Crimean Bridge, which connects the occupied peninsula to Russia. While Ukrainians destroyed almost 300 metres of the road bridge, including its arch, on Tuesday (17 November), the railway section remains standing. Although the term Crimean Bridge is often used, it is in fact two bridges running parallel to one another. They are connected only at certain points, for example on the deck near the arches. As early as Tuesday afternoon, the Russians allowed passenger trains to cross the undamaged railway bridge. “Only a complete fool could allow trains to run without a thorough inspection of the bridge after it had been hit. So I would not be surprised if the order came from Moscow,” soldier and engineer Oleh Doerfler told the Ukrainian website Glavcom . It was to be expected that Ukrainians would also attempt to destroy the railway bridge. And that is what happened. At 1.30AM local time on Thursday, Sergei Aksyonov, the Moscow-installed governor of occupied Crimea, wrote that the Crimean Bridge was again under attack and traffic — railway traffic, what else — had been suspended. noticias.titulo: EU gives oil and gas importers until 2029 on methane checks, rules out more delay
noticias.resumen: After all-night talks, EU governments and MEPs agreed to delay methane regulations until 2029, but scrapped the legal possibility for further fob-offs, in a win for centre-left politics.
noticias.texto: EU governments and the European Parliament agreed, in the early hours of Thursday (19 November), to delay the EU’s methane rules for oil, gas, and coal importers by two years, which is double the lag that the European Commission had proposed. Methane is a powerful greenhouse gas that traps around 80 times more heat than carbon dioxide over 20 years. A lot of it leaks into the atmosphere from wells, pipelines, and coal mines, which the EU rules aim to address. Originally, they were to kick in on 1 January 2027, but under the new provisional deal, the rules for importers will now apply from 1 January 2029. Importers and EU producers will also get two more years to report the methane intensity of the fossil fuels they sell in the EU, now from 5 August 2030. The agreement settled halfway between an earlier compromise by member states, which wanted a one-year delay earlier this month, and parliament, which voted for a three-year delay in October. But gone was the option, pushed by member states, to extend the delay again. Centre-left MEPs had warned it could be used to postpone the rules indefinitely, after centre-left MEPs pushed back against it, warning that it could be used to delay the rules one more time after 2029, or keep postponing them for ever. Instead, the commission will only look at how the law is being implemented at the start of 2028 and whether there is any risk to security of supply. And any further delay would need a whole new methane law, which came as some relief to campaigners. “Despite the delay, the integrity of the regulation is preserved in the final deal,” said Léa Pilsner of Environmental Defense Fund Europe in Brussels, adding that governments had “bought themselves two years the regulation never needed”. But Pilsner also said 24 billion cubic metres of methane will leak into the atmosphere during the extra two-year delay, which equals two-thirds of what France uses in gas in a year. Governments said the delay was needed due to supply risks and worries over high fuel prices after the US-Israeli war on Iran disrupted Gulf oil and gas supplies. “We are not suspending the Methane Regulation; we are ensuring that it can be effectively implemented,” said Greek centre-right MEP Dimitris Tsiodras, who led the talks for parliament’s environment committee. His Polish centre-right colleague, Borys Budka, the lead MEP for the industry committee, said that “security of supply comes first”. Meanwhile, the cost of adapting fuel infrastructure to align with EU rules is relatively low. Modelling by Rystad Energy in Oslo puts the cost of the rules at a few euro cents per million British thermal units, or about 0.3 percent of the current gas price. And the International Energy Agency in Paris, in its most recent projections, sees overseas gas markets remaining tight next year, it still expects a gas glut to arrive relatively soon, due to a very large increase in gas export capacity, primarily in the United States. A separate analysis by Data Desk, commissioned by the European Climate Foundation in The Hague, found in September that some central and eastern European countries reliant on Russian gas could face supply challenges, but also argued that “in no case are these sufficient to disrupt the implementation of the regulation in its current form”. Thursday’s decision to delay follows an intense and years-long campaign led by US president Donald Trump administration and the oil and gas industry. Internal commission documents, reported by EUobserver earlier this month, showed how the commission tried to placate Washington with technical fixes, while US officials and industry lobbied national capitals directly. Seven of the eight central and eastern European member states courted by Trump’s energy officials at a Washington summit in February later backed a three-year delay. Parliament is due to vote on the deal next week, and member states still need to formally sign off before the end of the year, when the original rules are due to otherwise kick in.

noticias.titulo: MEPs gut EU Commission plan for regulating space industries
noticias.resumen: Brussels is racing to keep up in the global space race, after MEPs slashed green demands from the EU’s first Space Act, in a bid to win over capitals and industry.
noticias.texto: Substantially watered down EU rules on safer and more competitive space activities came a step closer to life on Thursday (19 November), when the European Parliament’s industry, research, and energy committee (ITRE) voted on its position on the proposed EU Space Act . The vote allows the full parliament to move towards establishing its negotiating mandate, paving the way for ‘trilogue’ talks with the EU Council of member states and the European Commission. The draft report was adopted with 72 votes to 1, with 2 abstentions. With the same majority, MEPs also voted to start negotiations with Council. “If everything goes fine next year with the proposal, we have another three years and a half to be implemented,” said German MEP Angelika Niebler, of the centre-right European People’s Party (EPP) and shadow rapporteur on the file. The new EU space rules are to replace a patchwork of national regulatory measures, but the text approved by ITRE differs significantly from the commission’s original proposal. It is around 22 percent shorter, with the number of articles reduced from 119 to 97, according to Italian MEP Elena Donazzan, the lead rapporteur for the rightwing European Conservatives and Reformists (ECR) group. The proposed Union-level legal framework – a harmonised set of rules governing safety, resilience, and environmental sustainability for space activities – has been removed, Donazzan said, arguing that it would have added costs for companies and member states. This means the commission’s vision of a common legal baseline failed, leaving regulatory flexibility for member states. The mandatory environmental certificate has also been dropped, while a standalone cybersecurity regime has been removed, as space-related cybersecurity requirements are now addressed through amendments to the NIS2 directive . The changes come amid growing pressure for Europe to strengthen its position in an increasingly contested space sector. Read more [Interview] Europe’s labs are chronically underfunded and sovereignty is at stake, says French Academy chief Françoise Combes “The EU Space Act means greater clarity, predictability, and less fragmentation,” Maria Fernández Molinero, head of unit for Space Policy at the commission’s directorate-general for defence industry and space , told the Space Tech Expo Europe in Germany on Wednesday. “Across Europe, countries face different regulatory arrangements. A common framework can address those challenges,” she said. “Maintaining the status quo as we see it now, while impressive, is not enough for the decade we see ahead of us,” Molinero added. “Europe’s response to changing geopolitics must match a new reality,” she also said, while warning that greater dependence on space also created new vulnerabilities. Europe, she added, must not only innovate in space, but also protect what it builds. For the shadow rapporteur, Niebler, the incoming legislation still marked a “historic moment” in the EU’s approach to space policy. The commission’s original proposal envisages the rules applying from 1 January 2030, a timeline which Donazzan, the lead MEP, described as “realistic”. The Council position on the Space Act will not be finalised during the Irish presidency, which ends on 31 December, but a progress report will be submitted at a “ Space Council ” in early December, and the file will be handed over to the Lithuanian presidency next year, said Peadar Ó hÚbáin, an Irish spokesperson.

noticias.titulo: Erdoğan is strangling Turkey’s last free media, as EU turns a blind eye
noticias.resumen: Turkey's state takeover of independent broadcaster Sözcü TV was met by loud EU silence, in a broader pattern of appeasement, as Erdoğan strangles what is left of free speech.
noticias.texto: “Free media in Türkiye is dead,” Europe’s Socialist and Democrats (S&D) party declared on Tuesday (17 November), after a Turkish pro-opposition media, Sözcü TV, was raided by police in Istanbul. One of the last critical news channels standing in Turkey has faced repeated sanctions from Turkey’s broadcasting regulator, as president Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s government keeps up pressure on its opponents ahead of the next general elections, expected in 2028. Sözcü TV had earlier gone dark for 10 days, in July 2025, after getting a ban from Turkey’s broadcasting regulator following its coverage of protests sparked by Istanbul mayor Ekrem İmamoğlu’s arrest. After police searched Sözcü TV’s building under a court order on Tuesday, authorities replaced the broadcaster’s direction with a government trustee. And for many European observers, the raid was a further step in a vicious crackdown, which has seen independent media toppling into the hands of state control. Ankara also placed Erdoğan-sceptic news channel Halk TV under state trusteeship in October, while the opposition-leaning TELE1 broadcaster was given a state trustee a year before, due to espionage allegations lodged against its editor and chief. Read more EU and Turkey explore closer trade ties to reduce dependence on China With state sanctions affecting most major broadcasters across the country, what remains of independent journalism is some print news, niche online outlets, and independent digital publications. “As writers and journalists in Turkey we often feel things can’t be any worse for us, that we have reached the bottom, but the government continues to prove us wrong, and freedom of expression manages to shrink even more,” said Kaya Genç, author of The Lion and the Nightingale, chronicling Turkey’s crackdown on the country’s creative communities. The European press prize laureate found the Sözcü takeover particularly unsettling, as it broadened expectations among his colleagues that Ankara may be prepared to remove all critical media. “I watched Sözcü TV this morning. The caretakers of the network had managed to surgically remove the political coverage, leaving space only for news about crime and traffic,” Genç told EUobserver from Istanbul. The writer fears that the crackdown will push more Turks to get their news from WhatsApp groups and YouTube streams of opposition journalists, such as the formerly imprisoned Fatih Altaylı, who “has a social media following and views larger than all pro-government media combined,” instead of reading professional and independent journalism. Read more Could Islamophobia one day become EU law? Meanwhile, the increased silencing of media, NGOs, and associations, is enshrined in Turkish law. Article 299 of the penal code foresees one to four years’ imprisonment for insulting the president, while article 301 criminalises “denigrating the Turkish nation”. The result has been a “chilling effect” on all forms of civil society, according to Amnesty International, and the law has meant that 17 journalists and media workers are currently in prison. noticias.titulo: Coalition of the Willing meets in Berlin as counterweight to Putin-Trump diplomacy
noticias.resumen: Leaders and representatives from roughly 37 countries gathered in Berlin Thursday for a high-level meeting ...
noticias.texto: Leaders and representatives from roughly 37 countries gathered in Berlin Thursday for a high-level meeting of the Coalition of the Willing, an informal grouping of mostly European states supporting Ukraine. Co-hosted by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, French President Emmanuel Macron and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, the summit took place on the same day as the first-ever trilateral meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the APEC summit. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul described the Berlin gathering as the largest meeting of Ukraine’s supporters to date and a strong signal to Moscow that it is time to take negotiations to end the war seriously. He stressed that allies remain firmly behind Kyiv and are prepared to ensure Ukraine can negotiate from a position of strength, while warning that peace talks could still fail. Discussions focused on implementing the European Commission’s proposal for €45 billion in support for Ukraine’s budgetary and military needs in 2027, strengthening air defences (including through the PURL mechanism for U.S.-made systems such as Patriot interceptors), a winter package of anti-ballistic interceptors, new joint European defence capabilities, and preparations for robust, legally binding security guarantees that could include a multinational force after any ceasefire. U.S. special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner attended, as did Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte and EU leaders including European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. According to some reports, Trump briefly joined the meeting online, from Air Force One upon his return from Schenzhen. Participation was substantial but not universal among EU members. Official German listings of the broader Coalition include countries such as Bulgaria and Hungary, yet several Central and Eastern European states have been skeptical. Slovakia is not a member: Prime Minister Robert Fico has repeatedly stated that Slovakia “wasn’t, isn’t and won’t be” part of the Coalition of the Willing and will not participate in further loans for Ukraine. Bulgaria has similarly said it has never officially joined the informal grouping; Rumen Radev’s government has ruled out supplying weapons from national stockpiles and limited further lethal aid. EUalive has also noted opposition from Slovakia, Hungary, Czechia and Bulgaria to additional EU financing mechanisms. EU tables €45bn Ukraine loan as Slovakia, Hungary, Czechia and Bulgaria opt out The timing was widely viewed as deliberate. While the three major powers conferred in China on issues including the Ukraine war and nuclear arms control, European allies used the Berlin meeting to reaffirm support and push for a European role in any peace process. Zelenskyy said the talks covered further support and diplomacy aimed at a dignified peace. After the Shenzhen trilateral, Putin told reporters that Russia had invited European representatives to Moscow through diplomatic channels to clarify what Europe would bring to the negotiations. He said the United States was “quite insistently” urging Moscow to accept European participation in talks that had so far mainly involved Russia, the U.S., and Ukraine, and that discussing European security without Europeans was “pointless.” Once European representatives stated their position in Moscow, he added, Russia would decide the format for continuing the dialogue with Ukraine.⁠ At the same time, he restated longstanding maximalist positions. He indicated that Russia would not withdraw from territory it controls in Ukraine, saying both sides must “face up to reality” on the ground; that any deployment of foreign (including European) troops in Ukraine would be unacceptable; that Ukraine’s security should be addressed only within a broader European security framework that also guarantees Russia’s security; and that Kyiv and Europe were not yet ready for the compromises Moscow said it had accepted from earlier U.S. proposals. He also warned that Russian forces would continue operations to create buffer or “security zones” along the border. The Berlin meeting underscored that, even as Putin and Trump disregard Europe when discussing Ukraine, a significant group of countries continues to coordinate military, financial and diplomatic support for Ukraine and to prepare for post-ceasefire security arrangements.
