noticias.titulo: UN could soon be leaderless as race to succeed Guterres stalls
noticias.resumen: With under two months left in António Guterres’ term as UN secretary-general and no agreement ...
noticias.texto: With under two months left in António Guterres’ term as UN secretary-general and no agreement on a successor, the world body faces a once-unthinkable possibility: it could soon have no ​leader. The United Nations Security Council is expected to hold another secret ballot this week to pick the next UN chief, but after eight rounds of voting, the council’s five veto-wielding ‌members have not agreed on a successor. Officials are scrambling to draft contingency plans in case no one is at the helm when Guterres steps down on 31 December. The failure to pick a successor, analysts say, is partly the result of a long, opaque selection process built on secret ballots that exemplifies the slowness and gridlock the next secretary-general will be expected to cure. The council required six rounds to select Guterres in 2016. More fundamentally, observers say, the stalemate exposes a decline in the veto-wielding ​powers’ willingness to compromise, exacerbated by a U.S. administration that increasingly sidelines the UN and is distracted by its own foreign entanglements. “What is worrying is how late in the year this is and ​what it means for pulling together a team,” said Shamala Kandiah Thompson, executive director of Security Council Report, a think tank that monitors the council. “Given how early ⁠all this started, we shouldn’t be here.” Grynspan Nusseibeh among contenders The contender field includes mostly longtime UN insiders and figures who either have limited global name recognition, like frontrunner Rebeca Grynspan from Costa Rica, or, like senior United Arab Emirates diplomat ​Lana Nusseibeh, face pushback over accusations her country has backed the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces in Sudan’s civil war. The UAE denies this. Whoever wins will inherit a body facing daunting problems: wars it has struggled to influence, cuts in ​U.S. contributions, declining political relevance as Washington has pulled out of dozens of UN agencies, and mounting pressure to make the organization leaner, faster and more accountable. Richard Gowan, a UN expert at the conflict-prevention think tank International Crisis Group, said reaching the end of the year without a secretary-general selected for 2027 “would be excruciatingly embarrassing for the veto powers, and it would give a lot of ammunition to the many UN member states who say that the P5 no longer have the credentials to ​run this organization.” The five permanent members, or P5, received their seats as World War Two victors in 1945. The council’s 10 other members are elected for two-year terms by region. The permanent members – Britain, China, France, ​Russia and the United States – have long been united in resisting changes to a structure many UN members say no longer reflects geopolitical reality. The UN Charter is silent on how to handle a leadership vacancy. A secretary-general has never ended ‌their term without ⁠a replacement. A September briefing by 1 for 8 Billion , a campaign for a more open selection process, mapped the possible routes, from the council naming an acting chief to the General Assembly extending a term on its own. Each faces hurdles, the briefing said, though leaving the UN leaderless would be “highly irresponsible.” The UN spokesperson declined to comment. Secret ballots In an era of AI and social media, the selection process is a vestige of an earlier age. Candidates lobby council members, often for months, to win their governments’ backing. They then face a series of secret straw polls in which members vote “encourage,” “discourage” or “no opinion.” The results are not published but leak quickly. Members can hold color-coded polls in ​which the permanent members vote with red ballots, ​revealing the leanings of the real power on the ⁠council. Once a frontrunner emerges, the council votes on a resolution recommending that candidate to the 193-member General Assembly. The resolution needs at least nine of the 15 votes and no veto from a permanent member. The assembly then formally appoints the secretary-general, and it has never rejected the council’s choice. The council does not disclose the ​reasons behind the timing and format of the polls, or how individual states voted, to the public that ultimately funds the UN. “Is this a rational way ​to select the world’s chief ⁠diplomat? Absolutely not,” Gowan said. Yet Gowan said a messy process may be the price of a leader the big powers will listen to. Critics say Guterres lacks that influence, having fallen out with both Washington and Moscow. No one in charge Russia is one of the few members to address the deadline publicly. “It is also unclear what will happen after 31 December,” Kirill Logvinov, a senior Russian Foreign Ministry official, told TASS last week. The options under consideration include temporarily extending Guterres’ ⁠term or ​naming another official, he said. “As far as I can tell, on 1 January, if there’s no secretary-general, no one is in charge,” ​said Daniel Safran-Hon, a former UN official. The lights would stay on, he said, and the Security Council and General Assembly could keep meeting, at least for a while. “But it’s a bit like a supertanker where the captain dies: the first officer can do lots of ​things, but there are certain things you can’t do. You can’t do senior appointments. You can’t do the budget,” he said. With Reuters Caption: (L-R) Vietnamese Prime Minister Le Minh Hung, U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong prepare to pose for a group photo during the 16th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)-United Nations Summit in Manila, Philippines, 16 November 2026. EPA/Firdia Linsawati / POOL

noticias.titulo: EPP issues ultimatum to Vučić: ditch Putin, Milošević and media crackdown
noticias.resumen: The European People’s Party (EPP) has set seven conditions for Serbia’s ruling Serbian Progressive Party ...
noticias.texto: The European People’s Party (EPP) has set seven conditions for Serbia’s ruling Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), led by former president Aleksandar Vučić, including support for Ukraine, alignment with EU sanctions against Russia and a definitive break with the legacy of Slobodan Milošević. The demands come as the centre-right political family prepares to suspend the SNS’s membership, following an internal review launched in September 2025 at the initiative of EPP president Manfred Weber. The proposal will be submitted to the EPP’s Political Assembly, which is expected to approve it at its meeting in Brussels on 7- 8 December. If adopted, the suspension would give the SNS one year to meet the conditions before its membership is reviewed again. The seven sets of requirements are outlined in an internal document seen by several European and Serbian media outlets. The EPP says the Sерbian party, which is moving into opposition after losing October’s parliamentary elections, must reform and redefine its political identity. “We need an unambiguous commitment to the values of the EU,” the document states, quoted by FAZ. This means aligning with the EU’s common foreign and security policy, supporting reconciliation and good-neighbourly relations, and taking concrete steps towards normalising relations with Kosovo. The EPP also wants the SNS leadership to end its political cooperation with Russian President Vladimir Putin and the Russian government.According to Vučić himself (stated in a October 2026 interview), he has met Putin in person 23 times. Other conditions include tackling corruption, cooperating with investigative authorities, and ensuring a peaceful and orderly transfer of power. The Serbian party is also expected to stop verbal attacks on EU member states, particularly Croatia, and to support reforms strengthening independent media and parliamentary oversight. The EPP plans to monitor the SNS’s progress for 12 months, from December 2026 to December 2027. The Serbian party will be required to submit written monthly reports to the EPP presidency detailing the steps it has taken to meet the conditions. A monitoring mission is also expected to visit Belgrade in spring 2027 to assess progress following talks with the SNS and other relevant stakeholders. A further assessment could be conducted around June. At the end of the year, the EPP will decide whether to restore the party’s membership rights, extend the suspension or move towards full expulsion. The SNS has been an associate member of the EPP since 2016. Its suspension would mean losing its membership rights within the political family, including the right to vote, while retaining its associate-member status during the review period. Brnabić plays down threat of suspension The announcement has triggered an immediate response from the SNS leadership, with senior party official and former Serbian PM Ana Brnabić seeking to present the move as an opportunity for political adjustment rather than a break with the European centre-right. Brnabić confirmed on 19 November that the party had received official notification of the proposed suspension. However, she stressed that the party would remain an EPP member and would have time to clarify or change certain policies. “I will be in Brussels for the EPP Political Assembly on 7 and 8 December, and we will discuss this,” she said. Brnabić, who serves as the SNS’s international secretary, said she would present the EPP’s demands to the party leadership and members at its own congress on 13 December, after which the party would decide how to proceed. She also insisted that the SNS maintained good relations with the EPP’s institutions and enjoyed considerable support from other member parties. “We have seen enormous pressure, particularly following Ratko Mladić’s funeral, which changed a lot,” she said, thanking EPP partners for what she described as their understanding and support. Brnabić also sought to turn the issue against the party’s domestic opponents and critics in the region, saying that those who welcomed the prospect of suspension should not mistake it for expulsion. Mladić’s funeral: a political show directed by Vučić Her remarks suggest that the SNS may try to negotiate the conditions rather than accept them wholesale. Several of the demands, however, concern the party’s long-standing political alliances and its approach to Serbia’s relations with Russia, making substantial concessions potentially difficult. Mladić’s funeral proved a turning point The EPP’s decision follows more than a year of growing frustration with the SNS over Serbia’s democratic record, its close relations with Moscow and the government’s handling of anti-government protests. The internal review, coordinated by EPP secretary-general Dolors Montserrat and vice-president Kostis Hatzidakis, concluded that Serbia had experienced years of democratic backsliding under SNS rule. The document identifies problems involving the rule of law, electoral integrity, judicial independence, media freedom and links between state structures and organised crime. One particularly important turning point was the Serbian authorities’ involvement in the state-supported funeral of former Bosnian Serb military commander Ratko Mladić, who died in a UN detention facility in The Hague while serving a life sentence for genocide and other war crimes. The presence of senior Serbian officials at the funeral and the public glorification of Mladić provoked particular anger within the EPP. The European party now wants the SNS to distance itself from the convicted war criminal, stop glorifying those responsible for atrocities during the Yugoslav wars and abandon the denial of the Srebrenica genocide. The document also calls for a definitive break with the political legacy of Milošević and the ideology of the so-called “Serbian world”, which has been associated with attempts to extend Belgrade’s political influence over Serb communities in neighbouring countries. The EPP also wants the SNS to end its political and electoral cooperation with the Serbian Radical Party of Vojislav Šešelj. Radical Party MPs elected on the SNS list should form a separate parliamentary group, with cooperation between the two parties reduced to a minimum. Novi Sad disaster, Banjska and media freedom The EPP’s demands also address several unresolved issues that have become central to Serbia’s political crisis. The SNS leadership is expected to cooperate fully with a transparent investigation into the November 2024 collapse of the railway station canopy in Novi Sad, which killed 16 people. The EPP also wants the party to support the prosecution of those responsible for the September 2023 armed attack in the northern Kosovo village of Banjska. The attack was led by Milan Radoičić, a former senior Kosovo Serb politician with close links to Belgrade, who is under investigation in Serbia. The EPP expects the SNS to support efforts to bring the main participants to justice and to make progress towards normalising relations between Belgrade and Pristina. On media freedom, the document explicitly names pro-government broadcaster Informer and Informer TV. The SNS is expected to cooperate with any investigations by Serbia’s media regulator, REM, into the outlets and to respect any lawful regulatory measures resulting from them. The EPP also wants the party to stop using Russian state-backed media RT and Sputnik as platforms and to support the withdrawal of their broadcasting licences in Serbia. The demands extend to strengthening the independence of the media regulator, improving transparency in media ownership and political financing, and introducing effective anti-corruption and lobbying rules. Foreign policy is another major area of disagreement between the SNS and its European political partners. The EPP wants the Serbian party to end its political alignment with Putin and senior Russian officials, including cooperation with the ruling United Russia party, participation in its events and invitations to Russian representatives to attend SNS gatherings. The party is expected to support the implementation of EU sanctions against Moscow, prevent their circumvention and maintain and strengthen support for Ukraine. The document also calls for the SNS to distance itself from political events promoting alternatives to Serbia’s EU accession, including the “BRICS – Serbia Among Friends” conference. The EPP is also critical of the SNS’s growing cooperation with China, particularly in military, security and surveillance matters. It specifically points to a memorandum of cooperation between the Serbian Progressive Party and the Chinese Communist Party, calling for a change in this approach. On regional policy, the party is expected to abandon the concept of the “Serbian world”, support Bosnia and Herzegovina’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, oppose separatism and back Montenegro’s European integration. Vučić accuses neighbors of anti-Serbian campaign and military alliance in Republika Srpska speech Sources: FAZ, N1, Beta, BGNES Caption: SNS deputy Aleksandar Vucic attends the inaugural session of the National Assembly following the 25 October parliamentary elections in Belgrade, Serbia, 17 November 2026. Serbia’s new parliament convened for its constitutive session after the opposition ‘Student List’ movement won a landslide majority, securing 140 of the 250 seats and ending more than a decade of dominance by the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS). EPA/MARKO DJOKOVIC

noticias.titulo: The Shenzhen “Peace Declaration” has nothing to say about Ukraine
noticias.resumen: The first-ever trilateral meeting of U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian ...
noticias.texto: The first-ever trilateral meeting of U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin produced a short, largely symbolic “Declaration toward Peace” focused on avoiding nuclear war, UN reform, energy supplies, and official immunities. It contained no concrete steps to end Russia’s war in Ukraine, and Putin’s post-meeting remarks underscored continuity of Russian maximalism. The leaders met for roughly 80 minutes on 19 November at Kylin Villa (also referred to as Qilin Shanzhuang) in Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the APEC summit. Xi chaired the round-table session after separate bilaterals. Trump called the gathering historic and flagged Ukraine, nuclear reductions, Iran’s nuclear program, and sovereignty issues including the International Criminal Court. Putin noted shared interests in settling regional conflicts “including, of course, the conflict in Ukraine.” Xi emphasized that harmony among great powers brings peace while clashes bring turmoil, and later described the meeting as constructive. Trump left without further public comment. No joint press conference was held by the three. The four-point declaration Chinese state media and the Kremlin released the “China-Russia-US Heads of State Declaration toward Peace.” The full text affirms that the leaders exchanged views on the international situation and committed to strategic stability and international security. The points are: As permanent UN Security Council members, the three are committed to reforming the UN so it can respond more effectively to global challenges and fulfill its core mission of international peace and security. They plan to increase production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations and reaffirm the importance of stable energy flows. They recognize that the principle of state consent and respect for the immunities of state officials are of paramount importance, and agree that the International Criminal Court and similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction. They reaffirm that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought” and will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing nuclear proliferation. The nuclear language is the long-standing Reagan-Gorbachev formulation (reaffirmed by the five nuclear powers in 2022). Xi went further in his remarks, describing nuclear weapons as a “Sword of Damocles” hanging over humanity that should be comprehensively prohibited and completely eliminated, aiming at a nuclear-weapon-free world. The declaration itself stops short of specific reductions, timelines, or new mechanisms. This nuclear emphasis is notable given the record. Putin and Russian officials have repeatedly issued nuclear threats and adjusted doctrine in connection with the Ukraine war – moves that have drawn private and public discomfort from Beijing. Xi has previously warned against nuclear use, Chinese officials have responded sharply to Russian eclear rhetoric (including, according to European leaders relayed by Ukraine’s Zelenskyy, an ultimatum-like rejection of any discussion of nuclear escalation), and U.S. officials have indicated Beijing told Moscow “Don’t go there.” China maintains a no-first-use policy while expanding its own arsenal and has sought to limit the risk of nuclear escalation that could damage its interests or the broader strategic environment. The Shenzhen text restates the “must never be fought” principle without endorsing threats or use. The ICC/immunity language is particularly relevant to Putin, who faces an ICC arrest warrant related to the Ukraine war (including the deportation of children). The declaration omits any direct reference to Ukraine, Iran, specific arms control measures, Taiwan, or North Korea. Putin’s post-meeting statements In a press briefing afterward, Putin offered no indication that Russia intends to end its aggression in Ukraine. He praised Trump as someone who “sincerely strives” for resolution of the Ukrainian conflict and improved bilateral relations, while criticizing Kyiv and European capitals for stalling and lacking readiness for compromise. He framed the conflict’s continuation as the fault of Ukraine and the West rather than Russian policy, reiterated Moscow’s willingness to discuss a new European security architecture on its terms, and rejected European military cooperation with Ukraine or any troop deployments as part of a settlement. Russia would not accept energy-sector or Black Sea ceasefires after recent Ukrainian strikes. On the Kerch (Crimean) Bridge – the symbolic link to occupied Crimea that Putin inaugurated in 2018 – he was explicit. Ukrainian strikes on 16–17 November (and reportedly a third) damaged the road section, collapsing part of the central arch into the water. The timing, just ahead of the summit, was widely viewed as deliberate humiliation. Fact check: What is confirmed about the Crimean Bridge as Putin faces Trump and Xi Putin claimed the bridge is exclusively civilian infrastructure (not used for military equipment or petroleum products, contrary to Ukrainian assertions) and stated: “We will not negotiate after the strikes on the Crimean Bridge – we will respond to these strikes. Our actions will be much more painful.” He said the rail section had already been restored and that the bridge would be rebuilt. This matches the pattern of previous responses to bridge attacks, which Putin has previously cited as justification for escalatory strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure. Broader assessment Expectations were low going in, and the outcome matched them. The main result is the creation of a trilateral format itself – an optics and prestige win for Xi as host and arbiter, a platform for Putin to reappear on equal footing with the U.S. and China without a Ukrainian precondition, and a photo opportunity for Trump. Concrete deliverables were minimal: vague pledges on UN reform, energy supplies, official immunities, and nuclear-risk dialogue. There was no progress toward ending the Ukraine war, no specific nuclear reductions, and no new mechanisms. The Kerch strikes and Putin’s retaliatory vows highlighted that battlefield dynamics and Russian maximalism continued in parallel with the diplomacy. The declaration’s nuclear language is a restatement of existing consensus rather than a new constraint. Given Beijing’s long-standing aversion to the kind of nuclear brinkmanship associated with Russia’s Ukraine policy, the joint text can be read as a lowest-common-denominator affirmation of restraint. Whether it leads to actual dialogue that constrains arsenals or threats remains to be seen; China has historically preferred to keep the U.S. and Russia focused on their own bilateral nuclear relationship while expanding its own capabilities. For Ukraine and its partners, the summit produced neither leverage nor relief: Putin left reiterating blame on the West, maintaining maximalist demands, and promising more painful responses to Ukraine’s strikes. Caption: (L-R) Russian President Vladimir Putin, US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping attend a trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit at the Qilin Shanzhuang State Residence in Shenzhen, China, 19 November 2026. EPA/VYACHESLAV PROKOFYEV/SPUTNIK/KREMLIN POOL

noticias.titulo: Fact check: What is confirmed about the Crimean Bridge as Putin faces Trump and Xi
noticias.resumen: Ukrainian accounts and the General Staff publicly congratulated Portugal’s Vasco da Gama Bridge on becoming ...
noticias.texto: Ukrainian accounts and the General Staff publicly congratulated Portugal’s Vasco da Gama Bridge on becoming “the longest in Europe” after repeated strikes on the Crimean (Kerch) Bridge. The post also claimed the structure could “no longer fully serve” as a Russian logistics artery, with road traffic suspended and debris blocking the navigable channel. The Armed Forces of Ukraine congratulate the Vasco da Gama Bridge (Lisbon) on holding the title of the longest bridge in Europe! This means the Crimean Bridge has been destroyed. 🔥🔥🔥 pic.twitter.com/5s723ulG9E — Jürgen Nauditt 🇩🇪🇺🇦 (@jurgen_nauditt) November 19, 2026 Here is what is confirmed as of the time of publishing this article. The Crimean Bridge is not completely severed or destroyed, but it has suffered serious damage, that has substantially degraded its function. – On the night of 16–17 November, Ukrainian forces struck the road section. The main road arch and a span collapsed into the Kerch Strait. Verified imagery and Russian and Ukrainian reports confirm a large gap in the roadway. Road traffic has been suspended since then. – Debris from the collapsed road structures has blocked the main navigable channel (Kerch-Yenikale Canal, roughly 120 m wide and up to ~8–9 m deep). This has halted merchant shipping between the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov, affecting grain, oil products and other cargo from ports including Mariupol, Berdiansk and Russian Azov ports. – The railway section remained standing after the 17 November strike; trains were reported running on 18 November. An overnight drone attack on 18–19 November temporarily suspended train services. Russian-installed Crimea head Sergei Aksyonov said rail traffic was planned to resume around 16:00 local time on 19 November. Some local reports indicated the railway arch itself was not visibly destroyed. The image is genuine satellite imagery of the Crimean (Kerch) Bridge. It originates from Dnipro Osint (also known as Harbuz / @GarbuzYe ), a Ukrainian open-source geospatial intelligence analyst who specializes in satellite imagery analysis of the war https://t.co/9HoDVisNmj — Georgi Gotev & EUalive (@GeorgiGotev) November 19, 2026 Ukrainian officials and the General Staff have described the road link as out of action and highlighted the blocked channel as a logistics problem for Russian forces in occupied Crimea and the southern fronts. Russian officials have acknowledged the attacks, temporary traffic suspensions and ongoing damage assessments, while stating there were no casualties and that the bridge will be repaired. Complete physical destruction of the entire complex has not been confirmed; the structure remains partially usable once temporary measures are applied. The “Lisbon” line is a communication stunt, not a technical claim. The Vasco da Gama Bridge in Lisbon is about 17.2 km long. The Crimean Bridge was previously the longer structure at roughly 19 km (including approaches). Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha made a similar remark on 18 November while meeting his Portuguese counterpart. It is rhetorical commentary on the damage, not a statement that the Kerch Bridge no longer exists. Timing and the Shenzhen talks The latest (19 November) strike occurred hours before Russian President Vladimir Putin met U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on the sidelines of the APEC summit. Putin first held a bilateral with Trump (reported as roughly 35–40 minutes). Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said Ukraine was the main topic and that Putin left in an “excellent mood.” Trump publicly called Putin a “friend.” The subsequent trilateral was described by participants as historic; discussions touched on Ukraine among other issues (trade, nuclear arms, Iran). No major public agreements on Ukraine were announced immediately afterward. European and Ukrainian officials have expressed concern that talks involving the three leaders could produce understandings without Ukraine or European participation at the table – echoing historical precedents such as Yalta. Parallel U.S. envoy activity with European and Ukrainian officials on security guarantees has continued separately. Whether the bridge strikes were timed to influence the talks is not confirmed by public statements from either side, but the sequence is clear from the timeline of attacks and the summit schedule. Logistics impact In a 19 November piece, EUalive’s partner Suspilne examined the consequences of the blocked Kerch-Yenikale Canal. Experts noted that the collapsed arch (reported around 5.5 thousand tonnes) and road span have interrupted the primary shipping route for grain, agricultural products and oil products from both Russian ports and occupied Ukrainian ports. One specialist estimated that 40–60% of certain regional cargo flows used this route. Clearing the channel is expected to be technically complex and time-consuming; alternative river routes (such as the Volga-Don system) have lower capacity. The piece also highlighted risks to military sustainment of Russian forces in Crimea and southern Ukraine if land and sea alternatives remain constrained. Bottom line The cheeky Lisbon congratulations accurately reflect substantial, confirmed damage that has taken the road bridge offline and blocked key maritime traffic. They do not mean the entire bridge has been permanently severed or reduced to rubble. Rail service was interrupted again on 19 November but was expected to restart the same day. The strikes coincide with high-level diplomacy in which Ukraine and Europe are not direct participants, amplifying the strategic and symbolic weight of the damage. Claims of total destruction or permanent isolation of Crimea go beyond what is currently verified, yet the confirmed damage still influences the climate of the Shenzhen talks. Second attack on the Crimean Bridge in two days: what is known This fact-check draws on reporting by EUalive’s partner Suspilne . Caption: Russia’s President Vladimir Putin attends a trilateral meeting with China’s President Xi Jinping (not pictured) and US President Donald Trump (not pictured) during a trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) China Summit in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, China, 19 November 2026. EPA/ANDRES MARTINEZ CASARES / POOL

noticias.titulo: Switzerland to propose Austria-Norway-Kazakhstan trio to break OSCE chairmanship deadlock
noticias.resumen: Switzerland plans to propose a three-country package involving Austria, Norway, and Kazakhstan to chair the ...
noticias.texto: Switzerland plans to propose a three-country package involving Austria, Norway, and Kazakhstan to chair the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) from 2027 to 2029, in a bid to resolve a long-running leadership impasse that risks leaving the organization without a chair for the first time in its history, according to a scoop first reported by Austrian journalist Stephanie Liechtenstein. The package has been described by diplomats as having a realistic chance of attracting the necessary consensus, though significant political hurdles remainл Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis, whose country currently holds the 2026 OSCE Chairmanship, is expected to float the idea at a special meeting of the Permanent Council in Vienna on Thursday. The unusual proposal aims to secure the consensus required among the OSCE’s 57 participating states and preserve the organisation’s ability to function amid Europe’s ongoing security crisis. The order of the three countries has not been finalized. Diplomats note that Austria, which holds a non-permanent seat on the UN Security Council in 2027–2028, would likely take the chair later in the sequence, possibly in 2029. Officials familiar with the discussions say the package was designed with an eye toward potential acceptability to Russia, which has generally opposed NATO members chairing the organization. Deadlock over Cyprus and Georgia The OSCE requires consensus for all major decisions, including the annual chairmanship. Cyprus put forward its candidacy for 2027 as early as late 2024 and has received strong support from EU member states. Turkey, however, has blocked the bid because of the long-standing Cyprus dispute. Georgia has also expressed interest in the role, but multiple European states have declined to consider alternatives while Cyprus remains in the race. Analysts have warned that failure to agree on a chair before the end of Switzerland’s term on 31 December could leave the OSCE in uncharted territory. Without a Chairperson-in-Office, the organization would struggle to set priorities, manage field operations, or advance its role as one of the few remaining inclusive security forums that still includes Russia, the United States, and Ukraine. Budgetary difficulties have compounded the problem, with the OSCE operating on a non-valorized budget for several years. Swiss push for continuity Switzerland, which is chairing the OSCE for the third time, convened Thursday’s special Permanent Council meeting specifically to mobilize the 57 participating states. Cassis is also scheduled to hold bilateral talks with Austrian Foreign Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger in Vienna. Swiss officials have stressed that ensuring continuity of the chairmanship is essential to maintaining the OSCE’s capacity to act, particularly given the “severe security crisis in Europe.” No formal decision is expected at Thursday’s meeting. The next major deadline is the OSCE Ministerial Council in Lugano on 3–4 December, where Switzerland hopes to secure agreement on a successor. The OSCE’s chairmanship has rotated among its members since the organization emerged from the 1975 Helsinki process. Past chairs include Kazakhstan (2010) and Austria (2017). Whether the proposed trio can overcome the current deadlock will depend on the willingness of key players – including Turkey, Russia, and EU states – to prioritize institutional continuity over bilateral disputes. Caption: Swiss Federal Councillor and Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis, OSCE Chairman-in-Office (C); Feridun H. Sinirlioglu, OSCE Secretary General (L) and Pierre-Andre Page, President of the Swiss National Council (R), drink water prior to the start of the international conference ‘From Geneva to Helsinki and Beyond’ at the University of Bern in Bern, Switzerland, 03 September 2026. Hosted jointly by the Swiss 2026 OSCE Chairpersonship and the Dodis Research Centre (Swiss Diplomatic Documents), the conference brought together diplomats, historians, and policy experts to examine the founding principles of the 1975 Helsinki Final Act and discuss the future of European security. EPA/PETER KLAUNZER

noticias.titulo: EU tables €45bn Ukraine loan as Slovakia, Hungary, Czechia and Bulgaria opt out
noticias.resumen: The European Commission has proposed an additional loan of up to €45 billion for Ukraine ...
noticias.texto: The European Commission has proposed an additional loan of up to €45 billion for Ukraine in 2027 to cover roughly two-thirds of a projected €70 billion financing shortfall, but the plan has immediately exposed deep divisions inside the European Union. Slovakia, Hungary, the Czech Republic and Bulgaria have already indicated they will not participate in the new package, setting up a collision course with Germany and other northern member states that insist the burden must be shared by all 27 countries. Merz issues ultimatum on EU budget: Ukraine financing must be guaranteed by all members The proposal comes on top of a €90 billion loan agreed only months earlier and is due to be discussed at an extraordinary EU leaders’ summit on 26–27 November. Ukraine’s government has warned that without extra external support it will struggle to maintain both military operations and basic state functions next year. Russian attacks on energy infrastructure, ports and civilian targets have intensified, reducing Kyiv’s ability to collect tax revenue and forcing higher spending on air defence, drones and reconstruction. The Commission’s plan would allocate €25 billion to military needs – weaponry, air-defence systems, anti-drone technology, missiles and ammunition – and €20 billion to budget support that keeps schools, hospitals and public administration running. The money would be conditional on continued reforms, particularly in the rule of law and the fight against corruption. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen framed the package as both practical and strategic: “Europe will continue to provide maximum support to Ukraine and exert maximum pressure on Russia.” Defence Commissioner Andrius Kubilius stressed the operational urgency, noting that Ukraine expects Russia to field tens of millions of drones by 2027 and that European funding is essential if Kyiv is to match that scale. The financing design relies on future profits generated by immobilised Russian central-bank assets held in Europe. Those profits are already earmarked first to service a G7 loan package of approximately $50 billion agreed in 2024. Only after that obligation is met could the same stream of income be used to repay the new €45 billion facility and the earlier €90 billion EU loan. Interest and servicing costs of the previous package are currently covered by the EU budget, with the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia explicitly exempted from any additional financial liability. No equivalent exemption has yet been agreed for the new loan, and that is precisely where the political resistance has crystallised. Four EU countries draw a line against further military financing Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico has been the most vocal opponent. He has repeatedly declared that Slovakia will help with civilian needs – generators for the winter or schools for Ukrainian children on Slovak territory, but will not fund weapons or “war loans.” Fico has accused German Chancellor Friedrich Merz of blackmail for linking progress on the EU’s next seven-year budget (2028–2034) to unanimous agreement on Ukraine financing. Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar has avoided the word “blackmail” but publicly questioned the wisdom of tying the two issues together, saying it sends a poor signal outside the Union. Bulgarian President Rumen Radev has confirmed that Sofia likewise does not intend to join the new financial package, while emphasising continued bilateral support through electricity exports, infrastructure projects and assistance to Ukrainian families. The Czech government has already secured an opt-out from debt-servicing costs on the previous €90 billion loan and shows no appetite to reverse course. These four countries are all net beneficiaries of the EU budget. Their stance therefore carries particular weight: any arrangement that requires formal changes to the multiannual financial framework still needs unanimity, even if the underlying loan is organised through enhanced cooperation among a smaller group of states. The precedent of the 2024–2025 package, which allowed three of the four to stay outside the liability structure, has made further exemptions politically difficult to refuse yet fiscally and symbolically unacceptable to the largest net contributors. Germany insists on shared responsibility Chancellor Merz has taken the opposite position. In a letter to European Council President António Costa he made clear that Germany will not approve the next multiannual budget unless every member state commits to financing Ukraine’s needs in 2027 and beyond. “Supporting Ukraine is a matter of our indivisible European security. Therefore, the burden of this support must also be shared,” Merz argued. Northern European governments, long among the most generous bilateral donors, back the German line. Poland supports continued military and financial assistance and has called for greater use of frozen Russian assets, but it is wary of linking the issue to budget negotiations. Polish officials note that Ukraine’s financial collapse would sharply raise security risks for Poland itself and that the two dossiers – Ukraine funding and the 2028–2034 budget, should be kept separate to avoid compounding already difficult talks over cohesion and agricultural spending. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has welcomed the Commission proposal and urged rapid adoption, writing that strong European support remains the clearest signal to Moscow that the war must end. The Commission has also invited non-EU partners – the United Kingdom, Canada, Norway, Japan and others, to cover the remaining €25 billion of Ukraine’s estimated shortfall, either through direct contributions or by extending G7-style guarantees backed by the same Russian asset profits. Officials privately acknowledge that significant new American financing is unlikely in the near term. The legislative path still requires approval by the European Parliament and the Council. Even if a technical fix lets some member states stay outside the funding liability structure, the political signal would still be Ukraine fatigue after five years of war. Sources: European Commission announcements, FocusEurope.pl, Kyiv Post, The Guardian, Reuters Merz holds firm after Fico calls EU budget–Ukraine link “classic blackmail” Caption: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen (C), European Commissioner for Economy and Productivity Valdis Dombrovskis (R) and European Commissioner for Defence and Space Andrius Kubilius (L) attend a press conference on EU financial and military support for Ukraine at the European Commission in Brussels, Belgium, 18 November 2026. The European Commission adopted legislative proposals to provide up to 45 billion euros in additional financial support to Ukraine in 2027, aimed at addressing the country’s estimated 70-billion-euro financing gap amid Russia’s ongoing war of aggression. EPA/OLIVIER HOSLET

noticias.titulo: Student List foreign policy program: largely a continuation of Vučić’s course
noticias.resumen: The student movement has recently published its foreign policy program. Until now, assessments of its ...
noticias.texto: The student movement has recently published its foreign policy program. Until now, assessments of its positions had been based only on partial conclusions drawn from statements by prominent Student List representatives. The program is largely a continuation of the policy pursued by Aleksandar Vučić, with two notable exceptions: a distinctly more critical attitude toward Israel and a harder line on the Kosovo issue. Equally significant is the complete absence of any reference to Serbia’s membership in the European Union – an objective that Vučić himself had effectively abandoned in the later years of his rule. The program has been posted on the website of the Student List – Students Win Citizen Group, the ticket formed to contest the 25 October general election. It is known that the document was drafted by Student List candidates, but it remains unclear whether, and to what extent, university students participated in the process through plenums. The published program should therefore be treated with caution—as a general guideline rather than a definitive blueprint. Changes remain possible as circumstances evolve, especially since foreign-policy issues are unlikely to dominate the new government’s agenda in its early months. Much will also depend on the eventual composition of the cabinet: both the prime minister and the foreign minister will shape policy, as will domestic and external pressures. The document opens with general principles. It states that the Student List will conduct foreign policy in accordance with the Constitution of Serbia. This formal commitment was expected, yet it contrasts with Vučić’s more pragmatic approach. The program further affirms that the new government will maintain military neutrality as Serbia’s strategic choice – again, a position that had been widely anticipated. The Student List pledges a thorough reform of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and an end to the long-standing practices of nepotism, politicization, and appointments made without relevant expertise, professional experience, or clear criteria. It also announces a review of the discretionary granting of citizenship and issuance of passports, particularly in cases where corruption is suspected. Kosovo The program declares that the Student List will “fight for the preservation of Kosovo and Metohija as part of Serbia,” in line with the Constitution of Serbia and UN Security Council Resolution 1244. “We will consistently oppose the unilaterally declared independence of the so-called Republic of Kosovo and will not allow its admission to international organizations,” it states. While this language echoes Vučić’s public rhetoric, his actual policy was different. The stated position directly contradicts the 2023 Agreement on the Path to Normalization between Kosovo and Serbia (the Brussels Agreement), which Vučić accepted. That agreement, now incorporated into Chapter 35 of Serbia’s EU accession negotiations, provides that Serbia and Kosovo will develop good-neighborly relations on the basis of equal rights and that Serbia will not oppose Kosovo’s membership in any international organization. The program’s approach to Kosovo – and, by implication, to the EU – is further clarified by its pledge to prosecute all responsible officials of the Vučić regime for any criminal offenses connected with the conclusion and implementation of agreements deemed unconstitutional and harmful to Serbia. “All agreements shall be subjected to assessment of constitutionality, and the implementation of any unconstitutional provisions of any concluded agreement is unacceptable,” the text reads. This is a clear reference to the agreements reached in the Belgrade–Pristina dialogue under EU auspices, which has been stalled since September 2023, when the two leaders last met in Brussels. Consistent application of this provision would almost certainly render progress on European integration impossible, as the 2023 Brussels Agreement would in all likelihood be ruled unconstitutional. The program also states that the Student List will devote particular effort to improving the position of Serbs in Kosovo, both north and south of the Ibar River – in the six Serb-majority municipalities and in localities with a substantial Serb population outside them. “We will aim for such places to be administratively connected and included in local self-government units with a Serb majority, and for those units to achieve the greatest possible autonomy relative to the provisional institutions of self-government in Pristina,” it says. The text does not specify whether this will be pursued through the Brussels dialogue or by other means. Notably, there is no mention whatsoever of the Association/Community of Serb-majority Municipalities provided for in the 2013 Brussels Agreement – presumably because that agreement is also regarded as unconstitutional. European Union The European Union is treated primarily as an economic rather than a political partner. The program identifies the EU as Serbia’s most important economic partner and announces deeper cooperation with the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development and the European Investment Bank in order to secure financing for development projects. On European integration itself, only Chapters 23 (Judiciary and fundamental rights) and 24 (Justice, freedom and security) are mentioned. The document states that the new cabinet will seek to obtain IBAR status through visible progress in these chapters, long recognized as areas of overlapping interest between the Student List and the EU. No other chapters are referenced, nor is there any mention of EU membership or the broader European integration process. When this is read alongside other elements of the program – the determination to defend Kosovo, protect the rights of Republika Srpska, and refrain from imposing sanctions on Russia – it becomes clear that a Student List government would not steer Serbia toward the EU. It would most likely, as Vučić did in his final four years, seek merely to “remain on the European path,” as Student List lead candidate Ilija Srđanović put it after the elections. Also noteworthy is the speech delivered by Student List representative Aleksandar Baucal at the EU Enlargement Forum in Brussels on 16 November. His address, which ended with applause and a standing ovation, spoke moderately of Serbia’s European path, framing it as a set of internal reforms without any reference to European integration or EU membership. At the same time, Baucal argued that a democratic Serbia should contribute to a stronger and more resilient Europe – an outcome he described as unimaginable without alignment with EU foreign policy, including sanctions on Russia. He also drew a clear distinction between those who supported Serbian citizens’ struggle for democracy and those who did not, a remark that can be read as implicit criticism of the United States, Russia, and China. After the elections, Student List representatives met twice in Brussels with European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos. According to both Kos and Student List representative Ana Dimitrijević, the talks focused on Serbia’s domestic situation and on the possibility of accessing European funds previously earmarked for Serbia but withheld because the previous authorities failed to meet conditions on the European path. This is consistent with the stated intention to remain on the European road. The open question is how long Brussels will remain accommodating of the new authorities’ hardline positions on Kosovo and Russia. When that tolerance ends, a split within the Student List between its pro-European and nationalist wings will be difficult to avoid. The region and the great powers The program states that the new government will cultivate good-neighborly relations and develop regional cooperation with all neighboring states. This marks a departure from Vučić’s approach, which featured strained relations with Zagreb, Sarajevo, and Podgorica. Whether relations with Sarajevo will actually improve is uncertain, however, given the Student List’s noticeably tougher stance than Vučić’s regarding the position and powers of Republika Srpska. The Student List says it will re-examine the practice of implementing the Bonn Powers of the High Representative in Bosnia and Herzegovina, insist on the legal appointment of that official, and employ all necessary diplomatic and legal mechanisms against any overstepping of the mandate defined in Annex 10 of the Dayton Peace Agreement, particularly when such actions infringe upon the rights of the entities as guaranteed by the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the section titled “Serbia and the World,” the longest and first paragraph is devoted to Russia, followed by the United States and then China. The penultimate paragraph addresses relations with Latin American countries, India, and Africa, while the final paragraph deals with Israel and Palestine. The program states that the Student List will preserve the traditional partnership with Russia and maintain “the principled position” of not imposing sanctions on Moscow. It also affirms that the new government will continue to respect the territorial integrity of all sovereign states, including Ukraine. This policy would be identical to Vučić’s. The program further envisages the development of relations with the United States and continuation of the strategic dialogue launched the previous summer, as well as the building of a “comprehensive strategic partnership” with China. Student List representatives have not yet met with Chinese officials, and there is public speculation that the new government may ask Chinese companies to align their projects with environmental and labour standards. The Student List has also announced the renewal of Serbia’s diplomatic presence in Latin America, India, and Africa, building on the traditional friendships established during the era of the Non-Aligned Movement. The most significant departure from Vučić concerns Israel, with which the previous government cooperated very closely. By contrast, the Student List program states that the new government will not be complicit in what it describes as Israel’s systematic attempt to destroy the Palestinian people in Gaza. The original article by EUalive’s partner BETA can be found here Caption: Student List deputies wave to supporters ahead of the inaugural session of the National Assembly following the 25 October parliamentary elections in Belgrade, Serbia, 17 November 2026. Serbia’s new parliament convened for its constitutive session after the opposition ‘Student List’ movement won a landslide majority, securing 140 of the 250 seats and ending more than a decade of dominance by the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS). EPA/MARKO DJOKOVIC

noticias.titulo: Who publishes the Kremlin in Bulgaria
noticias.resumen: The Kremlin’s version of the war in Ukraine is now available in hardcover in Bulgaria. ...
noticias.texto: The Kremlin’s version of the war in Ukraine is now available in hardcover in Bulgaria. After television studios, websites, and YouTube channels, it has reached Bulgarian bookstores. It is enough to read the cover to see who, according to the author, started the war. In the subtitle of Provoked, Scott Horton identifies Washington as responsible for the “catastrophe in Ukraine.” In the blurb for The Battle of the Giants by Daniele Ganser, NATO is described as waging war against Russia. These books are part of the catalogue of the publishing house “Knizhen Pluh” (“Book Rat”). The ideologue of “neo-Eurasianism” and the concept of the “Russian World,” Alexander Dugin, already has two Bulgarian publishers – not only “Knizhen Pluh” but also “Iztok-Zapad” (“East-West”). Recently, Scott Ritter also presented his book in Bulgaria. The former UN weapons inspector in Iraq now explains the war in Ukraine the way the Kremlin does. His book is called Highway to Hell and is published by “Scorpio.” Behind “Knizhen Pluh” “Knizhen Pluh” is a family publishing house run by the historian Alexander Sivilov and his wife, the archaeologist Sirma Alexandrova. Sivilov is a professor of the history of Russia and the USSR and heads the Department of Modern and Contemporary History at Sofia University. From 2020 to 2024 he had his own column, “After the End of History,” in Politically Incorrect, the radio programme of journalist Petar Volgin on Bulgarian National Radio (BNR). In 2024 Volgin was elected a Member of the European Parliament from the pro-Russian party “Vazrazhdane” (“Revival”); he had also been the party’s candidate for vice-president alongside its leader Kostadinov. The same title – “After the End of History” – is used for Sivilov’s book with which “Knizhen Pluh” made its debut in 2024. By then the couple already had their own YouTube channel on history and politics, “Dimna Zavesa” (“Smoke Screen”). The Centre for the Study of Democracy (CSD) lists “Dimna Zavesa” among the media partners of the petition “Referendum for Peace and Sovereignty” in its report “Operation Disinformation.” The channel publishes misleading and controversial claims about Ukraine and Russia’s war there. “Ukraine cancelled the human rights charter” is the title of a “Dimna Zavesa” episode from 30 April 2024. In the description the channel claims that Kyiv notified the Council of Europe that it was cancelling a large part of its articles. The documents show the opposite. On 4 April Ukraine notified the Council of Europe that it was narrowing the scope of the temporary derogations from the European Convention on Human Rights introduced under martial law. The Council of Europe published a rebuttal on exactly 30 April, the day of the episode. The video nevertheless accumulated more than 45,000 views, and the website “Glasove” (“Voices”) spread the same headline. In 2026 “Knizhen Pluh” is also publishing Dugin. In the catalogue his book is presented as The Arrangement of the Great Powers. Donald Trump’s Conservative Revolution. In Trump’s return to the White House the Russian ideologue sees an opportunity to dismantle the liberal world order and replace it with an order determined by the “great powers.” Dugin before Trump Five years earlier “Iztok-Zapad” published The Fourth Way. An Introduction to the Fourth Political Theory by Dugin. There he proposes his political theory beyond liberalism, communism, and fascism. The book appears in the “Katehon” series, the one that prompted publisher and owner of “Zhanet 45” Manol Peykov to write an open letter to the owner of “Iztok-Zapad,” Lyuben Kozarev. “How comfortable do you feel sitting on two chairs, fully aware that one of them is electric?” Peykov asks. He recalls how Kozarev had spoken with admiration about Anne Applebaum before a packed auditorium at Sofia University. The American journalist, a Pulitzer Prize winner for her book on the Gulag, presented in Bulgaria her book Autocracy, Inc., published by “Iztok-Zapad.” Applebaum defends Ukraine’s right to decide its own future and is among the most prominent advocates for Kyiv. At the same time its Bulgarian publisher gives a platform to Dugin and to authors whose ideas, according to Peykov, serve to justify the war with which Russia is trying to take away precisely that right. If Kozarev leaves his questions unanswered, Peykov threatens to stop buying books from “Iztok-Zapad” and to send his open letter to its authors and collaborators in Bulgaria and abroad. Kozarev replies with a parable about a fight in the mud. Both will get dirty, it says, but only one of them will enjoy it. He then calls on his colleagues to fight the battles that are worth fighting. The name “Katehon” does not appear at all in his reply. Scott Ritter gives lecture On 13 November, hours before the premiere of Highway to Hell at the literary club “Peroto,” Scott Ritter gave a public lecture at the University of Library Studies and Information Technologies (UniBIT). He was introduced by Prof. Stoyan Denchev, former rector and chairman of the university’s Board of Trustees. Among the audience were former Defence Minister Krasimir Karakachanov and the MP from “Progressive Bulgaria” Rumen Milanov, a member of the parliamentary committee overseeing the security services. What Ritter said there he recounts himself. In a post from 16 November he writes that on the first day of his visit he dined with Denchev, his editor Svetoslav Iliev, and the former head of the Military Academy, Gen. Grudi Angelov. At the dinner Denchev outlined his idea that Prime Minister Rumen Radev should represent the EU in negotiations with Russia to end the war. Ritter repeated the proposal at both of his public appearances in Sofia. In his post he presents Radev as the only European leader ready to negotiate on terms that take into account what Ritter calls “Russia’s legitimate interests.” In the “Scorpio” blurb Ritter is presented as an analyst of “legendary fame.” There is one fact from his biography that the publisher omits. In 2011 in Pennsylvania Ritter was sentenced to between 18 and 66 months in prison. Among the offences of which he was found guilty were indecent exposure and three counts of unlawful contact with a minor. The case concerned online communication of a sexual nature with a police detective who posed as a 15-year-old girl. Kremlin propaganda is advancing in Bulgaria. The publisher gives it a place in the catalogue, the university provides a lecture hall, the host provides a microphone. While those in power in Sofia talk of peace, Ritter sees in the Bulgarian prime minister a man who would negotiate on behalf of Europe while taking into account “Russia’s legitimate interests.” Moscow knows what to expect from Rumen Radev; does Brussels?

noticias.titulo: Trump says historic summit with Xi, Putin already a ‘win’ before event
noticias.resumen: U.S. President Donald Trump said his meeting on Thursday with Chinese and Russian counterparts Xi ...
noticias.texto: U.S. President Donald Trump said his meeting on Thursday with Chinese and Russian counterparts Xi Jinping and ​Vladimir Putin was already a “win” before it took place, as China gave him a lavish welcome filled with fanfare and pageantry. The unprecedented diplomatic gathering of the leaders of the world’s ‌largest nuclear powers is unlikely to produce major agreements, analysts say, while it unnerves smaller countries that fear their interests might be disregarded. In an interview with Fox News, Trump highlighted the pomp surrounding his arrival, which contrasted with the more muted greeting of other leaders, including Putin. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi landed without any welcoming ceremony. Xi’s protocol choreography at APEC: a message in the greetings Xi greeted Trump at the airport, the first time he has done so with any visiting leader since becoming president, reciprocating his counterpart’s gesture at Joint Base Andrews ​in September when they last met. The leaders also briefly hugged. “This is a great president, one of the great presidents of China, and he’s never gone to the airport to meet somebody,” Trump ​said, when asked what he wanted to get out of the trilateral. “And not only that, the fanfare, the beauty, the pageantry, the thousands of people, the ⁠young children, the soldiers, the whole thing. It was great respect, and I appreciate that. That’s a big win for us. It’s a big win for China too.” Trump arrived after Xi and Putin delivered pointed speeches ​at an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen, denouncing Western trade “protectionism” and sanctions. During Thursday’s APEC proceedings, Xi reiterated his advocacy for what he called “free and open” trade. Western leaders say China’s ​growth model favouring industrial strength over consumers is unfair and creates destabilising global trade imbalances. Putin, fresh from a setback in his war against Ukraine after the crippling of a key bridge linking Crimea to Russia, said Russia was an integral part of the Asia-Pacific region’s food and energy security. Trump told the audience the US has been a Pacific power for hundreds of years and touted the strength of its economy. On AI, he said: “It’s almost completely good, but it’s got some bad elements, and we have ​to be very careful,” adding he opposed regulation that would “stifle” the industry. Tough nuclear arms discussion Trump has insisted nuclear arms control be a central topic of the summit, despite China’s repeated objections to joining talks with ​Washington and Moscow, which have far larger nuclear arsenals. “They’re going hot and heavy on building nuclear weapons. I’d love them not to do it,” Trump said of China. “But when they look at me and they say, ‘OK, we’ll do it, but ‌will you ⁠reduce your nuclear weapons by 2,000 weapons?’ It’s a hard thing to do for me,” he said, adding “It’s probably hard for them to do also.” The president has also expressed interest in meeting North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, but there was no confirmation of an imminent encounter. South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said on Thursday he hoped a reopening of dialogue with North Korea would build a lasting peace. Ahead of the three-way talks, Trump will meet Xi and have a working lunch, while U.S. and Russian officials said he would also meet Putin one-on-one. Moscow officials said no full-scale talks were planned for that meeting. Trump’s Asia trip has offered a ​chance to showcase U.S. influence, strengthen ties with regional ​allies and pursue a high-profile diplomatic opening with ⁠Xi and Putin. But the U.S. president will return home facing political and policy challenges, including the fallout from bruising midterm elections, the Nvidia spy scandal and a spate of tech and air travel outages that have rattled Americans. The leaders have plenty of reasons to appear together but far fewer to agree on substance, given ​differences over Ukraine, Iran, nuclear weapons, trade and China’s military buildup, said Craig Singleton of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies. “A photograph could serve all three ​men well,” Singleton said, adding ⁠that he thought the “agenda is much harder to agree on.” ‘Beijing’s worst nightmare’ White House officials have said Trump is not expected to raise the issue of the Ukraine war during the meeting, though Trump has suggested he could bring it up. He last met Putin in Alaska in 2025 for talks that failed to end the war. In the Fox interview, Trump said he would not seek help from Russia and China to bring the Iran conflict to a close. Trump’s ⁠talks with Xi ​will offer a chance to assess the durability of this month’s trade truce. It comes amid growing tension over reports of Nvidia ​chips being diverted to China through Southeast Asia, raising questions about the effectiveness of U.S. export curbs and the future of Chinese access to advanced technology. “This is Beijing’s worst nightmare. China wants chip access that it can negotiate with the president. It may get ​chip restrictions written into law by both parties,” Singleton said. With Reuters Caption: US President Donald Trump meets with Chinese President Xi Jinping ahead of the Leaders Meeting group photo during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, China, 19 November 2026. EPA/LUKAS COCH

noticias.titulo: Hackers spent 5 years inside Bulgarian state networks, stealing 62 million pages of documents
noticias.resumen: Hackers had covert access to Bulgarian government networks for five years, stealing at least 130 ...
noticias.texto: Hackers had covert access to Bulgarian government networks for five years, stealing at least 130 gigabytes of information which is equivalent to more than 62 million pages of documents, Innovation and Digital Transformation Minister Ivan Vassilev announced on Wednesday . The stolen data covers virtually every area of government activity, including the work of the Council of Ministers, reports prepared by state institutions and correspondence between ministers and government bodies. Vassilev said he had no information suggesting that the stolen documents had been published on the so-called dark web. The unauthorised access had been ongoing since 2021, with attackers gaining entry to the infrastructure used by government institutions to exchange documents and information. They moved between different components of the systems, collecting sensitive data relating to the functioning of the state. The targets were government document-sharing systems. So far, investigators have found no evidence that personal data of Bulgarian citizens was compromised. The breach was discovered in August following the deployment of a new national cybersecurity system. At the time, the ministry announced that unauthorised access to administrative networks had been detected and that a large-scale technical investigation was under way. Vassilev said several international hacking groups were behind the cyber-espionage operation, with their activity traced to different locations around the world. He declined to identify specific countries, stressing that there was no established evidence showing whether the attackers had acted independently, as an organised operation or on behalf of foreign intelligence services. “Whether they were serving the interests of these countries has not been established. We do not know what the hacking groups did with the information they extracted from the Bulgarian state,” the minister said. Whether the five-year breach was the result of deliberate negligence or possible assistance to the hackers is now for the Prosecutor’s Office to establish. “That is for the Prosecutor’s Office to determine when it examines the report I have submitted,” Vassilev said. The latest revelations revive memories of Bulgaria’s massive National Revenue Agency (NRA) data breach in 2019, when hackers stole and leaked millions of files containing personal and financial information. The incident raised serious questions about the state’s ability to protect sensitive information. It was arguably the country’s most significant cybersecurity scandal, highlighting vulnerabilities in public institutions long before the latest five-year intrusion came to light. A risk for national security The minister added that some of the findings concerned national security and could not be disclosed publicly. He said cooperation between Bulgarian security services and international partners from the EU and NATO had made it possible to identify the attacks, terminate the hackers’ access and remove the malicious software discovered in the systems. T he hackers operation went undetected under successive governments because the security tools previously in place did not function as a single, integrated system. The investigation is now involv ing state-owned Information Services, private-sector experts and international partners, including the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA). The affected environment was then isolated, access controls for critical systems were tightened and the connection between the attackers and the infrastructure they were using was severed. “We have successfully completed the third phase – the complete removal of the attackers from government systems,” Vassilev announced. Authorities are also addressing the vulnerabilities identified, introducing stricter controls over administrator accounts and extending the national cybersecurity system to 28 municipal and regional administrations. State-sponsored espionage likely The duration and scale of the operation suggest that it may have been backed by a foreign state, former e-Government Minister and co-chair of the liberal opposition party We Continue the Change – Democratic Bulgaria (PP-DB) Bozhidar Bozhanov said. He named China, Russia, Iran and North Korea as the countries most commonly associated with state-sponsored cyber-espionage operations. “What they (the government) are both telling us and not telling us is that this was a cyber-espionage operation. Cyber-espionage is not an activity carried out by criminal online groups. An operation lasting five years suggests hacking groups funded by governments, with China, Russia, Iran and North Korea among the most likely,” Bozhanov said. He explained that states collect information through cyber-espionage operations against other countries, initially seeking access to as much information as possible before assessing how it could be used. Bozhanov suggested that the Bulgarian authorities would be unlikely to publicly name either country. “Based on all the indirect evidence, everything that has been made public and information I have, these are the more likely origins of the cyber-espionage operation. China is the most likely, followed by Russia,” he said. Bozhanov said that when he became e-Government Minister at the end of 2021, he found that Bulgaria’s state infrastructure was extremely vulnerable. “Hacker attacks could be carried out not by nation states, but by 16-year-old children,” he said. He added that his team had closed some of the easier entry points and adopted an emergency action plan following a meeting of the Cybersecurity Council. A contract was subsequently prepared to address the remaining vulnerabilities. However, the measures could not be fully implemented before the government led by PM Kiril Petkov fell too soon. He ruled out the possibility of attackers moving from the civilian government network into the system used for classified information. Classified material is exchanged on paper, while information classified as “Confidential” is handled through a separate electronic system, isolated from other networks in line with security standards, he explained. Bozhanov also said that liberal parliamentary oposition h ad proposed legislation over the past 18 months to establish a dedicated Cybersecurity Agency, arguing that a single specialised authority was needed to ensure professional oversight and clear accountability. “We will most likely re- introduce this bill in parliament very soon,” he said. The infrastructure targeted in the attack belongs to the State Agency for Electronic Governance, established in 2016, Bozhanov added. Caption: Bulgarian Minister of Innovation and Digital Transformation Ivan Vasilev presents the sector’s budget to the media in Sofia, November 17, BGNES

noticias.titulo: El perro andaluz by Manu Sánchez
noticias.texto:
Àngels Barceló rompe su silencio sobre su salida de la SER: "No quisieron que siguiera, nunca me ofrecieron la renovación"
- La periodista habla de los motivos de su despedida, su nueva vida y sus planes de futuro
- Todos los programas de El perro andaluz están en RTVE Play
Durante más de 40 años, su voz nos ha acompañado en algunos de los momentos más importantes de nuestra historia reciente. Acostumbrada a hacer las preguntas, esta vez le ha tocado responderlas. Àngels Barceló ha elegido El perro andaluz, el programa de Manu Sánchez en La 1, para conceder su primera entrevista en televisión tras su salida de la Cadena SER.
Los motivos de su adiós a la SER
En uno de los mejores momentos de su carrera profesional y batiendo récords de audiencia al frente de Hoy por hoy, Àngels Barceló decidió cerrar una etapa. Una decisión sobre la que la periodista se ha sincerado con Manu Sánchez.
"Yo tenía que pasar mi duelo. Después de 21 años no es fácil dejar la casa donde he dejado toda mi vida, los mejores años de mi vida y a mis amigos. El duelo ha sido favorecido por el verano, pero ahora ya estoy en la fase de poder hablar de todo lo que supuso aquello". Y cuando Manu pregunta sobre si se fue ella o la echaron, ella cuenta que "no quisieron que siguiera. La SER nunca me ofreció la renovación, algo que yo hacía año a año, a final de cada temporada. Nadie se preocupó por mi renovación ni me la ofrecieron y cuando llegó la conversación querían que le diera una sacudida al programa justo cuando mejor audiencia estaba dando. Se me pedía pluralidad, cosa que yo no entendí." Al final, sentencia: "Yo soy una persona incómoda para la derecha y hay una evidencia: Feijóo solo vino una vez al Hoy por hoy estando yo y no volvió nunca más a pesar de ser invitado y reinvitado. En cuanto yo me he ido, ya ha estado en el programa. Soy una persona incómoda para la derecha y a mucha honra."
Una nueva vida y mucho futuro por delante
Después de años levantándose a las cuatro de la madrugada para dar los buenos días a millones de oyentes, Barceló afronta una nueva etapa vital. La periodista ha compartido cómo es ahora su día a día, qué supone este cambio de vida y cuáles son sus planes de futuro.
"Ahora estoy en otros proyectos, estoy haciendo uno de gastronomía, pero solo hago cosas que me divierten y que no había podido hacer hasta ahora y siempre he tenido que decir que no. Antes siempre decía no puedo no puedo y ahora sí puedo". Además, ha contado cómo vivió el primer arranque de temporada sin estar ella: "La noche anterior a que empezara la temporada, el 31 de agosto, pensé en cómo lo iba a llevar, pero me levanté ese día con la Cadena SER, como lo he hecho siempre y lo llevé bien."
Sus primeras elecciones lejos de los micrófonos
Si hay una noche que Àngels Barceló ha disfrutado especialmente a lo largo de su trayectoria profesional, esa es la noche electoral. El próximo 29 de noviembre vivirá sus primeras elecciones en muchos años sin estar al frente de un especial informativo.
En pleno arranque de la campaña electoral, la periodista ha reflexionado con Manu Sánchez sobre el momento que atraviesa el periodismo, la relación entre los medios de comunicación y la política, la crispación y los desafíos de la desinformación.
"Los medios tradicionales que han cogido la bandera del partido que sea o del líder político que sea y que utilizan sus programas para demostrarle al político que te cae mal, hacer malas entrevistas y lo que tú haces está mal… No me gusta. El periodismo no está mucho mejor que la política y el fango parece que va de la mano. La tertulia está muy bien si aporta, si hay análisis político, si hay tranquilidad, sosiego… Pero todo lo contrario es lo que está ocurriendo y es lo que se ha trasladado al Congreso de los Diputados".
Las preguntas cambian de protagonista. Acostumbrada a entrevistar a algunas de las figuras más relevantes de nuestro país, Àngels Barceló ha cambiado de papel por una noche. Manu Sánchez ha recuperado preguntas de grandes referentes del periodismo, como Jesús Quintero, Iñaki Gabilondo y Carlos Herrera, para conocer cómo respondería ella y reflexionar sobre la profesión.
"Si no he hecho algunas preguntas ha sido porque he tenido un mal día, pero no me he dejado preguntas nunca en el tintero. Y eso que he tenido enfrente a personas que me han mentido y yo sabía que me estaban mintiendo. Lo intentaba por la izquierda, por la derecha y por el centro y he tenido jefes que me han mandado un WhatsApp diciendo ‘suelta el hueso’".
La Àngels Barceló más desconocida
La periodista también ha compartido escenario con Petite Lorena, que ha aportado su particular sentido del humor a una conversación sobre el paso del tiempo y la madurez.
Entre el humor y la complicidad con Manu Sánchez, hemos descubierto también la faceta más personal y desconocida de la periodista, que no ha escapado al particular Confesionario de El perro andaluz ni a su singular Consejo de Ministros.
Ante la pregunta de Manu sobre lo que podría estar escrito en la página de la izquierda que dejó con su salida de la SER y lo que cree que podría poner en la derecha, ella contesta contundente: “en mi pagina de la izquierda, pondría "nos volveremos a encontrar”" y supongo que en la de la derecha pondría ‘¿qué haremos sin ella, no?’”.
Manu Sánchez le ha preguntado por Zapatero y ella ha contestado muy sincera: "Me he sentido muy decepcionada por Zapatero y me costó creerlo, sobre todo ahora en esta etapa en la que te cuelan la desinformación mucho más fácil, es complicado saber lo que es verdad o no y me sentí muy decepcionada".
Admite que "no hay dinero para pagar para que ella presente horizonte", que "tiene muchas cucharillas diferentes en su casa" y que es mejor que la UCO no encuentre en su casa para que no descubran el desorden. Así se ha convertido en una ministra de la información y el buen periodismo.
Horario y dónde ver El perro andaluz
No te pierdas un nuevo programa del Presidente de este late night cada miércoles en La 1 y RTVE Play a las 23:00 h. ¿Quiénes serán sus próximos ministros?

noticias.titulo: Debate entre Sánchez y Feijóo: los candidatos llegan al plató donde se celebrará el encuentro
noticias.texto:
Debate entre Pedro Sánchez y Feijóo, en directo hoy el cara a cara: los candidatos llegan al plató donde se celebrará el encuentro
- RTVE analizará las claves del encuentro antes y después del debate en un especial informativo conducido por Pepa Bueno con verificación en directo
Los candidatos a la Presidencia del Gobierno del PSOE y el PP, Pedro Sánchez y Alberto Núñez Feijóo, respectivamente, se enfrentan este jueves a un esperado cara a cara organizado por la Academia de la Televisión y presidido por su presidenta, María Casado.
Lo harán en un debate que durará aproximadamente dos horas y que contará con cinco bloques temáticos de 16 minutos. En concreto, hablarán sobre Vivienda, Economía y Fiscalidad, Política Social y Servicios Públicos, Lucha contra la corrupción y Regeneración Democrática, y Migración y Política Exterior.
